The Business Council on National Issues says profits as a percentage of Canada's economic action "are now almost certainly at a post-war low."
Of course, this reflects upon the revenues which the government obtains from private activity in Canada and upon the amount of money the government must borrow when industrial activity and economic activity in the country decline drastically. Mr. McArthur continued:
If profits had dropped more moderately ... there'd be less executive gloom .. . The lay-offs ... would have been less severe and the delays in spending for new construction and equipment not as ruinous for jobs and incomes.

Blamed in varying degree are the general effects of recession in Canada and abroad; high interest rates that devour the profits of companies unfortunate enough to be debt-heavy; "excessive" taxes and government intervention in corporate decision-making; wage and salary increases averaging around 13 per cent annually.
Government intervention is the chief cause of our economic woes. This government, which is the root cause of the problems faced by large and small businesses across the nation, now comes to the House to ask through Bill C-93 for the authority to borrow as much as $6.6 billion so that, as Liberals, they can maintain at full pace the damaging policy they have pursued for 14 years under the leadership of the present Prime Minister. Such inattention to basic facts of economic life! It is such a waste of our Canadian substance. It is nothing but waste. Waste is the mark of excellence of this Liberal government.
We have to look no further than the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to see this waste. It is a pit of fiscal unaccountability to this House and to the country. Worst of all, in my experience no one in the system seems to care. All they are interested in is protecting their backsides and their futures. Saddest of all is that ministers absolutely
refuse to get involved in rectifying situations which are damaging Canadians.
We need leadership. I have an article from the Montreal Gazette dated Thursday, April 29, headed, "Liberals losing control of government, study says." The article says:
The government can no longer control the political conflicts and divisions created by its policies, says a study of federal spending by Carleton University School of Public Administration.
Further, energy spending is out of control and plans to reduce the federal deficit are doomed to failure, says the highly critical report made public this week.
The article goes on to say:
-"they face potentially unmanageable problems" as they try to carry out the rest of their political strategy, writes the studies editor. Professor Bruce Doern, in the opening chapter of "How Ottawa Spends Your Tax Dollars".
It states further:
-Ottawa's battle to restrain its spending to fight inflation "is flawed", says the study.
I think it could be stated in much more dramatic and emphatic terms than "flawed".
The article goes on:
The report also says that energy spending is out of control because the National Energy Program made numerous public commitments that energy decision-makers know cannot be met.
In the face of this, what do we have happening out west? Well, it is sad to see the Liberal token efforts to give recognition to the legitimate needs to western Canada. On May 1, Charles Lynch wrote in his article:
The Government of Canada has just announced the upgrading of its embassy in that far-off land of which it knows so little, Alberta.
He writes further:
The "ambassador" in this case, Bruce Rawson, ceases to be known as Senior Advisor-Western Affairs to the Privy Council Office. He becomes Federal Economic Development Co-ordinator in Edmonton.

"The right people in Ottawa will get his message", says Senator Olson, "up to the top deputy ministerial level. This ensures the clarity and rapid delivery of the signals and their appropriate targeting.
What a barrel of tripe! The west does not want recognition by the top bureaucrats. It wants some recognition in the political system of this country. This will take major reforms and it is to this that the House should be addressing its creative abilities in the next few weeks and months.
There is much more that one could say and I have much more material prepared, but I hope the tone of my comments have left little doubt about where I stand in reaction to this government's delivery of programs and policies of benefit to Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, it was just a little over a year ago that I stood and talked about a similar bill. It was similar to the extent that they are both borrowing authority bills. A year ago I said that I was impressed with the simplicity of the bill and that it was smaller than most which we get a chance to debate. There was only one clause other than the title. That one clause of the bill was seeking to borrow $14 billion.
May 4, 1982

Today we have a bill with a different number-C-93- which has 34 pages, and perhaps 34 clauses as well. I think the House should first ask itself why the government could borrow $14 billion on the strength of a one-clause bill when it needs a 34-page bill this year to borrow $6.6 billion.
The answer is that the Liberals are at it again. This bill combines the more conventional borrowing authority bill with a number of amendments to the Excise Tax Act as well which arise out of the November 12 budget, and amendments to the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act which implements the ways and means motion to amend the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act which was tabled by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) on January 27, 1982.
I know that we had some discussions about omnibus bills and we had a couple of noisy weeks when the bells rang over this question, but we clearly have one again with this bill. That is why it takes up 34 pages. It is not just a bill to authorize the borrowing of $6.6 billion. This is the aspect of the bill to which I want to address most of my remarks, however. That, along with the fact that this has become an annual event. Why must the government come back to the House year after year to borrow billions of dollars? I suppose there is a simple one-word answer and that is "deficits".
If we had a government which paid some attention to balancing its revenues with its expenditures, we would not have the kind of problems which this bill is presenting us with in this debate. While saying that, however, we are relieved that the government is forced to come back to the House with this bill. If it were not, with this government we would be in a position as members of the opposition and as individual Canadians of never knowing where we stood or how detrimental our position was.
What about deficits? I suggest that this bill results from the deficits caused by the budgetary problems brought upon us by the government. We can discuss the revenue side first. Obviously, it is easy for a government to spend money, but first it should figure out where it will obtain the money from. Of course, the major source of revenue has always been the individual Canadian taxpayer, worker and businessman. At this moment the government has done everything in its power to discourage individual initiative, enterprise and work.
I have often said they probably destroyed the work ethic of a whole generation of Canadians with their policies over the last 15 years. It should be clear to anyone, and it is certainly clear to an accountant, that you cannot hope to increase revenues through taxation by putting people out of work or out of business. It is a very simple axiom. If you have no business, you have no tax revenue. If you have no profits, there are no tax revenues. If there are no jobs, there will be no tax revenues. Later this week we will be debating the problem of hundreds of thousands of jobs not being created in the west. I realize that is another debate. However, we have hundreds and probably thousands of examples of jobs which have disappeared. They have dried up and gone away or were never created because of
Taxation
the policies contained in budgets such as the one tabled in this House last November by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen).
People still do not know where they stand with the famous or infamous budget of last November. Just this week I received a copy of a letter sent to the Minister of Finance by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of British Columbia, signed by the president of that body, Mr. T. A. Cook. He makes references to the fact that he has already written to the minister once expressing the members' concern about the uncertainty and frustration that the federal budget process is causing Canadian taxpayers. He said he had been requested to write the minister on specific problems that chartered accountants, their clients and British Columbia businesses are facing during this period of uncertainty about the new legislation.
It is now six months since that budget was introduced and the government has not yet seen fit to take the uncertainty out of the provisions in that budget. We have not yet had the legislation before the House, six months later, and the date for filing personal income tax returns has come and gone. Individuals engaged in certain kinds of transactions during the last taxation year do not know what to do. They do not know how to file their income tax returns. Everyone is in a terrible state of confusion.
The minister referred to a special committee he would be setting up to consider five special areas, such as life insurance, which were dealt with in the budget. He does not know when that committee will be set up. He hopes that some of the problem areas will be settled before he has to send that topic to committee. That is the problem on the revenue side. The government has not done anything to encourage Canadians to invest, earn or produce more goods, housing, or whatever.
One of the reasons more housing is not being produced is that policies have been introduced by this government which have discouraged the construction of housing. Dozens of large corporations which have been expert in the field of providing housing for Canadians-I hope the minister responsible for housing is listening-have said, "No more, thank you very much". They have withdrawn from the creation of housing in this country.
The old tax policies of the Liberal government had driven individual investors out of the rental housing market a decade or more ago and they are no longer producing rental housing. That is one problem. Now we have the withdrawal of housing contractors from providing single family and other kinds of individually-owned housing from the market.
We might ask why. It is obvious. It is more attractive for these investors and mortgage investors to invest their money in other types of investment where they can get a secure return that is higher than they would get in mortgages for housing.
Would you believe that the very government which wants to encourage activity in the housing and economic fields has taken the wind out of the sails of the housing mortgage market by issuing billions of dollars worth of Canada Savings Bonds

May 4, 1982
Taxation
last November at an initial rate of 19'/2 per cent? Naturally when deposits with trust companies and banks are paying in the range of 14 per cent to 16 per cent and people are lending money at 16 to 18 per cent or perhaps 17 to 20 per cent in house mortgages, investors would rather put their money somewhere for a medium term. They invest in Canada Savings Bonds which have the liquidity and the security of the country behind them and which bring as well 19*/i per cent on the money.
All of the borrowing which the government does creates a tremendous pressure, and in some cases a shortage, in the borrowing activity in the normal money markets. It should be no surprise that when the government dips into the market and takes all of the money that is sitting around waiting to be invested there will not be anything left for the entrepreneurs who want to provide housing or create a project or business, or whatever they want to do in our economy.
It is difficult to look at the government's record on the economic side of things and judge whether or not it is doing things in a proper fashion without looking at an area which is not always as open to examination by members of the House as it would be if it were not hidden behind the cloak of Crown corporations. I want to say a few words about some of our more well-known Crown corporations.
A good one to start with would be Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. That corporation is run by people appointed by this government. There have been quite a few of them in and out of the front door of Atomic Energy over the past decade. Chairmen and presidents have come and gone like members in the House from certain constituencies.
The first prominence that Atomic Energy had was when that corporation paid a $20 million fee to a foreign national for arranging the sale of a Candu reactor to South Korea. We had hours and hours and days and days of debate about that, particularly in the Public Accounts Committee, where I spent a lot of time.
I think that corporation has sold six Candu reactors altogether, unless a couple of sales have fallen through. With the possible exception of two, it has lost hundreds of millions of dollars on these activities. The current order book of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited shows sales to Roumania. Although the contracts are signed with Roumania, there is some question as to whether the financing will be completed so that the sales will actually go through.
We have not had the total story yet, but it appears that the money for the sales to Roumania will be provided by none other than those generous taxpayers of Canada. Isn't that strange? Here we are selling Candu reactors for the generation of electrical power to Roumania, but there is an agency between Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and the Government of Roumania, The Export Development Corporation of Canada. It will use Canadian taxpayers' dollars to finance the sale to Roumania. Of course, the terms are such that Roumania will probably never pay back the money. In fact, EDC and its bankers are now putting a freeze on the payment of
moneys to Roumania because they are worried about the financial situation of that country.
Since that Crown corporation has had so much trouble selling Candu reactors, the Public Accounts Committee was moved, in one of its recent reports, to recommend to the government that the government should either expand its effort and decide that it is going to sell Candu reactors, or decide that it cannot sell Candu reactors and close down. It hardly seems fair to the taxpayers of Canada to be subsidizing, to be funding, to be covering the massive debts and deficits of a Crown corporation that shows no signs of ever breaking even, let alone making a profit on its investment. I do not know what Atomic Energy's initial investment was because that corporation in its present form grew out of certain amalgamations and it is hard to trace it back.
The government has had to bail out Atomic Energy of Canada Limited more than once. It was a recommendation of the Public Accounts Committee last year that Atomic Energy of Canada Limited should not be allowed to get itself into a position where its debts were so overpowering that it would once again have to come to the government and say: "We are insolvent, we cannot carry on, we need a further injection of funds." I guess that they listened to the Public Accounts Committee a little bit, because when Atomic Energy came before us in recent weeks we found that the build-up of inventory of heavy water-and that, of course, is the ingredient which makes the Candu reactor work-was so great that there were hundreds of millions of dollars worth of heavy water in stock in Canada. There was no prospect as to when these millions of barrels of heavy water would ever be used. The total production of the two heavy water plants that now operate in Canada will fill one Candu reactor. We have two years' inventory on hand now, that is enough for two reactors. In October of this year we will have three years' inventory in stock and that is enough for three reactors.
If none of these reactors come through, Mr. Speaker, we will have all this heavy water on hand with no takers, because there are no other customers for heavy water except for the Candu reactors that Canada sells. Roumania has let us know that unless we get the reactors operating before they get their own heavy water plants up, they will provide their own heavy water.
Why does that affect the deficit, you might ask? Here is the reason. The company and the government agreed sufficiently that Atomic Energy should not be allowed to go into debt so deeply that it could not dig itself out. What happened? A sum of $133 million was voted through the estimates of this House and it went straight into the pockets of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited to finance the current inventory of heavy water and also to wipe out the deficit, because it does not look good to have $147 million deficit on the books of a Crown corporation. Then, because there was another adjustment, for whatever reason, they also reduced the invested capital of the government as shown on the books of Atomic Energy of
May 4, 1982

Canada Limited. Any group of politicians who can foul up the operation of a fairly tidy Crown corporation, as they have with that one, Mr. Speaker, probably should have reason to go and borrow the $6.6 billion that we are being asked to authorize in this bill.
Atomic Energy is not the only fiasco in the Crown corporations. Another one that has been in the news a lot recently is Eldorado Nuclear. They were on a fixed plan of expansion which spread over the period of more than a year; they were expanding their capacities in Uranium City for the Beaver Lodge mine. They were bringing workers into the mine site from all over the country. Right up to the day they announced they were going to close the Beaver Lodge mine, effective June 30, 1982, right up to that, they were on an expansion program. Here was a situation where one arm of the company obviously did not know what the other arm of the company was doing. It is curious, Mr. Speaker, that this is the same company that objected so strenuously to a comprehensive audit by the Auditor General, who was then the auditor of Eldorado Nuclear Limited. The company objected so strenuously to a comprehensive audit of their records that they actually fired the Auditor General. They persuaded the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) who, as a shareholder, was the sole representative of the taxpayers-I think he was embarrassed about it, and he should have been-to dismiss the Auditor General of Canada and substitute for him a private firm of auditors.
I am not suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that there is anything wrong with a private firm of auditors. I am sure they do a good job and I am sure they are competent. But I suspect, Mr. Speaker, that that Crown corporation was very worried that the Auditor General, if he got himself in there with his troops and did a comprehensive audit, would come out later with his troops and would tell the House, probably in a special report, that the company was on a collision course, with an expansion plan on the one hand and a shut-down plan on the other hand.
That shut-down of the Beaver Lodge mine would have made Eldorado Nuclear insolvent, if not in fact bankrupt. Well, Mr. Speaker, even the Liberal government does not like to go around with insolvent or bankrupt Crown corporations. So what did they do? This was done before the closure was announced, so there was no apparent relationship. We will see, when we study the history of it. The Government of Canada had a stockpile of uranium. The value of that uranium was something like $300 million. What did the Government of Canada do? It decided to recapitalize Eldorado Nuclear Limited. It transferred to that Crown corporation its total stockpile of uranium and took back in payment therefor $300 million worth of capital stock in Eldorado Nuclear Limited. All of a sudden, we find a very strong Crown corporation that can easily withstand the loss of $130 million because, when you take $130 million away from $300 million you still have $170 million left, and that is pretty good capitalization in anyone's books.
Eldorado Nuclear was then left with the question, "What are we going to do? We have all this money now, we have a mine that is shut down, what shall we do?" Lo and behold,
Taxation
Mr. Speaker, they traded recently-we have not got all the details yet-their uranium stockpile for all the shares in Gulf Minerals Limited which they bought from Gulf Oil of Pittsburgh. I do not know if that is Canadianization of the mining industry in Saskatchewan or what their reasoning was, Mr. Speaker. It cannot be to consolidate the operations, because the new property of Gulf Minerals Limited is 100 miles away from Beaver Lodge. It is not going to help the people in Beaver Lodge who have been put out of jobs. It is not going to help the people in Uranium City who did not work in Beaver Lodge but who nevertheless have seen the value of their businesses and of their homes plunge.
That can only be described, Mr. Speaker, as another example of pretty awful management. Again, what can you expect from a government which took our fairly well functioning petroleum industry and injected into it a Crown corporation called Petro-Canada to finance which the government used $1 billion of the taxpayers' money? The taxpayers did not need to invest that much to get their oil. They were getting their petroleum products as cheaply as they are now, and they did not have to invest $1 billion in straight capital to get them. What the intervention of Petro-Canada into the petroleum industry in Canada has done is anyone's guess and would probably be the subject of another debate. But then it was not sufficient to have Petro-Canada standing there with $1 billion in taxpayers' money in the till. The government had to go out and borrow another $1.46 billion to expand and buy the share of Aquitaine. Canadianization is fine, but where does the government get the money, the $1.46 billion? We suspect that much of it came from foreign lenders. That just meant that the Canadian government had to come back to Parliament with a bill, just as it is today, to borrow another $1.46 billion, which it would not have been necessary to borrow had the government just kept the status quo, which was not so bad after all, was it?
I have touched upon Petro-Canada and those matters. I do not want to get into a debate on that now, but I think it is worth mentioning the National Energy Program because we are discussing borrowing. In the past several years the National Energy Program has required payment under the oil import compensation program amounting to approximately $4 billion every year in subsidies to Canadians for imported oil. In 1980, during its campaign, the Liberal party told Canadians that 18 cents a gallon was far too much to pay in increased taxes on petroleum products and that all they had to do was to elect a Liberal government and, by golly, there would be cheaper gasoline. I am sure that Canadians have had their dreams shattered concerning that promise. However, the fact is that $4 billion a year has been going toward that subsidy program. Where has the money been going? It has not been going to other Canadians, as it does through many government subsidy programs. It has been going straight out of the country and into the hands of the foreign oil producers. It is interesting, and I made this comparison in the House a few weeks ago, that the amount paid out by this subsidy program which goes

May 4, 1982
Taxation
right out of the country is the same amount that 11 million individual taxpayers in Canada paid to the federal government in income taxes in 1978, the last year in which the figures were available from Revenue Canada. In other words the total amount of taxes paid by every taxpayer who earned $17,000 or less, which, by the way, amounted to 78 per cent of all individuals who filed income tax returns that year, or 11 million taxpayers, went straight out of this country to support the National Energy Program. As well, there were complications within the world market and the government opposite is now learning that it cannot really control world markets. As a result, along with the confusion and falling prices in the world market, we experienced the situation where Canadians were subsidizing imports of foreign oil while 300,000 barrels of oil a day produced by Canadian companies were shut in the ground. Your Honour can be sure that none of those oil companies which had their oil shut in are paying any income tax to help the government balance its budget. Furthermore, they are not creating any jobs for Canadians in further exploration of petroleum resources in Canada or in the production or transportation of petroleum products from Canadian wells.
I suspect we will hear more about national energy in another debate. Let me touch on another Crown corporation which might give an example of the managerial abilities of the government. I am referring to the Canada Post Corporation. When we had the Post Office Act before us, we on this side pleaded with the government to allow the Auditor General to report to Parliament. After all, he is Parliament's servant. He is not a hired gun who reports to someone else. He is employed by the government for the service of Parliament. He reports only to Parliament. He does not report to the shareholders. He does not report to the Public Accounts Committee or to anyone else. The Auditor General of Canada reports to Parliament and, in that way, he is unique. Other corporations may have other auditors who report to the minister, and then it is up to the minister to decide when Parliament should be allowed to look at that auditor's report. That is a change that we could see if we could ever get the government to agree to introduce a bill concerning Crown corporations and amendments to the Auditor General Act. We could obtain special reports from the Auditor General. The House might even have direct reports from other auditors. However, at the moment, in the way it stands, and we cannot get this government to move on this matter, the Auditor General is the only one who can report to Parliament directly.
The office of the Auditor General has had 113 years of experience in auditing the Canada Post Corporation. However, what does the government do? It says it will not name the Auditor General in the legislation as the auditor of the Canada Post Corporation. We do not know why. The government would not tell us why. However, two joint auditors were to be appointed. I do not know whether it was pressure or luck but, in any event, the Auditor General was named as one of those
auditors, and he will be one of the joint auditors for the first two years of the existence of the Canada Post Corporation. It has since been revealed by the Auditor General, before the Public Accounts Committee, that he has recevied a personal letter from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) indicating that at the end of his two year appointment, his services as auditor of the Canada Post Corporation will no longer be required. It is totally unnecessary to throw out that kind of expertise or even to have joint auditors for something like the Canada Post Corporation. This duplicate effort is a waste of the taxpayers' money. Anyone in the auditing profession will say that joint audits are not efficient. It costs more to have joint auditors than it does to have a single auditor. However, we could clarify that situation if the government would only show some good management and bring in legislation dealing with Crown corporations so that we would know who was in charge. One cannot get an answer from anyone around here concerning Crown corporations. No one knows who is in charge of any particular Crown corporation. Of course, the audits are spread all over the map. We need this kind of legislation and we also need some changes to the Auditor General Act.
All of this simply adds up to the fact that this government is out of touch with what is going on in the country. It is out of touch with the people. I think that is exemplified by a couple of events which I have recently observed in committee. Last week the Minister of Finance indicated that exemptions for individual taxpayers who registered pension plans or retirement savings plans, which exemptions have remained unchanged for five years, had not received his consideration. Deducations for child care expenses, which have been set at $1,000 per child to a maximum of $4,000 per working mother, have not changed for five years. However, the Minister of Finance knows very well, as he has been told by working parents and by all members on this side, that costs of child care have dramatically increased during this period, while the exemption remains at $1,000 per child. One cannot possibly care for a child for $1,000. It is an unjust situation when working parents are unable to deduct normal business expenses, and child care expenses are normal business expenses.
I see that it is six o'clock and perhaps I will continue my speech on another day.

That this House do now adjourn.
He said: Madam Speaker, we are meeting tonight to discuss not simply a crisis in the life of the country but a crisis of a kind and of a cause that this country has not seen before. It is a crisis which, in a time of economic recession around the world and acute economic hardship at home, is caused by the fact that instead of taking action which could create jobs and create growth, the Government of Canada has taken consecutive actions which are destroying jobs, which are destroying growth and which are destroying opportunity for the country to become secure in the one area, energy, where our security is most possible and where our security is most important.
What we have seen with the Liberal government's energy policy, starting in March, 1980, has been the step by step destruction of the energy jobs, of the energy growth, of the energy industry and the energy potential of this country.
Tonight in this debate-and we will be here late into tomorrow morning and perhaps we will be here longer than that-we are here not simply to lament or to condemn what the government has been doing but to try to call upon the care for Canada that I hope exists in Liberal backbench ranks, to try to call upon them to urge their government to stop this terrible damage, this terrible and unnecessary damage which it is doing to our country.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
I think it is important that we review what has happened and why it has happened.
First of all we have to put in perspective what the Liberal policy has been doing. We have recently seen the loss of the Alsands project. It was not just Alsands that was lost; we have also seen Cold Lake lost, we saw the Judy Creek tertiary recovery project lost, we saw the Syncrude expansion lost, we saw the heavy oil upgrading project in Saskatchewan lost, we have seen 270 drilling rigs and service rigs driven out of this country. These were drilling rigs and service rigs that were, by and large, owned, directed and controlled by Canadians and were turning the energy industry into a Canadian-controlled industry. Now they have picked up and moved, at great cost- not just cost in dollars but cost to our future. They are investing Canadian money, they are investing Canadian incentive
and intelligence not to create growth and jobs in this country but to create growth and jobs elsewhere.
It is not just energy that is at stake here; it is the very economic recovery of this country. Every expert you consult will agree that the energy potential of Canada is not simply a guarantee of our future but that it is the best way to lift this nation out of recession and the best way to guarantee the kind of economic strength and economic future that we all owe to our children.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
While I regret having to say this, I want to say it and I want to put it in the context of the national problem that exists: this is not just a problem for the west or for the north, although the Alsands project and the Alaska highway project touch those regions most directly-this is a problem for all of Canada. If you need proof of that you need only look at the government's own estimates of the jobs that would be involved.
All across Canada there would have been 255,050 potential jobs. These are not my figures, Mr. Speaker; they are the figures of the Government of Canada issued in 1978. There would have been 71,000 direct jobs in energy projects that the government boasted would be built. These energy projects have now been abandoned because of the step by step disintegration of the energy industry in this country by the Liberal government opposite.
We are, finally, not just speaking about the impact that will be felt today, but we are speaking also very dramatically about the impact that will be felt tomorrow in this country. Energy is one of the major keys to the future of this country. We have in Canada a potential that other nations do not have. We have in Canada the capacity to become self-sufficient in energy.
Let me review for a moment what this goal of self-sufficiency in energy can mean to this nation. It is, first of all, an achievable goal for Canada.
Let me say in passing that this is a nation which has always needed goals to lead it forward-not a list of failures but a list of challenges. The challenge of energy self-sufficiency was clearly an achievable goal for this country. Indeed, the government which my colleagues and I had the honour to serve had established the year of 1990 as the year of energy self-sufficiency in this country. That meant that by that year, with the policies we had firmly in place, the maritime provinces could have expected to be supplied with Canadian oil by 1990. What has happened is the reverse. As things now stand with this Liberal wrecking policy, there is a very good chance that by 1990 Toronto will be dependent on foreign imported oil.

The Alsands project, Mr. Speaker, which was cancelled last week, was ready to start in 1980. The construction teams were on the site, an energy agreement had been negotiated which would have let the project proceed. But then there was a new government. speechtext:
The minister pretends that the blame lies with the companies because they refused to accept a last minute offer-an offer which might have been accepted had it been made even four months earlier. In fact, what happened last week was just the final step in a process which began in March, 1980, barely weeks after the Liberal party had been elected to office by promising to keep the increase in the price of gasoline below 14 cents a gallon.
Their first step was to declare that the world price would no longer be paid for oil sands production. Their second step was the National Energy Program. Their third step was the energy agreement of September, 1981. Together those steps destroyed the climate which would have made Alsands possible.
Back in 1978 the then energy minister, Mr. Gillespie, boasted about energy projects which the federal government would encourage as the basis of Canada's future. The hon. member for Restigouche was asking for the list, and it is worth reading that list today. That list included the Dempster pipeline, which is on indefinite hold. It would have created
6.000	jobs directly, and 26,000 jobs indirectly. That is now on hold and probably gone. The Alaska highway gas pipeline which would have created 13,000 jobs directly and 55,000 jobs indirectly, has been postponed for at least two years. The Polar Gas project, which would have created 15,000 jobs directly, and 45,000 jobs indirectly, is gone. The Tenneco LNG projects is cancelled. The Kitimat pipeline to the Alaska highway oil pipeline-they proposed one or the other-is cancelled. The Alsands project is cancelled. The Syncrude project expansion is cancelled. The heavy oil upgrading in Saskatchewan is postponed. The Cold Lake project is cancelled. The oil storage project at Wabanex is cancelled. Cancelled! Cancelled!
What is the total? The projects which have been cancelled, according to the government's own figures, would have created
71.000	jobs directly in the oil and gas industry, and 255,050 indirectly. That means jobs in Quebec, Ontario, Atlantic Canada. That means jobs across the country lost because the Liberal government has followed the direction of a bunch of theorists who know nothing about the energy business except how to drive it out of Canada and how to drive people out of jobs!

At a federal-provincial conference, the government announced a series of energy projects that were supposed to create nearly 100,000 jobs in the oil and gas industry and 320,000 jobs in related industries. And now, four years later, most of these projects have been abandoned. Why? Because of the Liberal government's policy. Most of these jobs in Canada will never materialize. The Liberal government has lost the Alsands project. It lost Cold Lake, the Syncrude
May 4, 1982

expansion, the Alaska pipeline project, and it lost the Arctic gas project. According to their own figures, the Liberals have lost 71,000 jobs in the oil and gas industry and 225,000 Canadian jobs in related industries. A large number of the latter would have been created in Quebec and Ontario.
Moreover, if the Alsands, Cold Lake and other projects were in operation, Quebecers could go and work on site and bring their families or send money back home which would help the economy in Quebec. All these projects have been lost as a result of Liberal policies. Instead of creating jobs, the Liberal government is creating unemployment.
Of course, the government will try to put the blame elsewhere. It will blame the provincial governments. It will blame the Americans. It will blame the oil companies. It will blame the world economy. I am sure they will also blame Rene Levesque. But who is governing Canada? The Liberal government. The Liberal government has taken Canada's potential and destroyed it.
The majority of Canadian families have been affected by the failures of the Liberals. Most communities in Canada are going to lose jobs and opportunities for growth, because Liberal policies have stifled energy projects. This evening, we demand that the government change its policy and stop destroying Canada.
I would invite the Liberal members to take part in this debate. They remained silent during the debate on the Constitution and during the debate on the budget. Are they going to remain silent while Liberal policies keep destroying projects and eliminating jobs?

They will try to blame everyone they can find: the provinces, the oil companies, the United States, the opposition, the international economy.

What is at issue here is not simply a wrong-headed policy. What is at issue here is the fundamental question of trust.

I heard another member from New Brunswick, who had something to add. I hope he will find the courage this evening to speak in defence of his own constituents and not abandon them as he did with the financing program.

What is at issue here tonight is whether or not we will allow the Government of Canada to squander the future of Canada, whether or not we will allow the Government of Canada to continue a policy called Canadianization that has the consequence of driving active Canadians in Canada either out of the country or causing people who want to work, find jobs and build a future here, instead only to find hopelessness.
The question is whether or not this government is so bound to an ideology that already has a casualty list of unbelievable proportions, that it will not put the country ahead of the advice it is getting from "fonctionnaires", from public servants in the senior levels of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources; that it will not jettison the Minister of Energy in the interests of saving the country.
What we need to do in this country is to establish a climate of trust. We have operated without that climate. The consequences are all before us; project after project has been lost and job after job has been lost. Canadians are losing a sense of hope and they are losing a sense of the future. That is a betrayal of this country.
This debate offers the opportunity to this government to say, "All right, we accepted advice that was wrong. We see the evidence. We will change it." Just a few minutes ago the Tories were virtuous. Because of the attitude they took on the pipeline, which was the same position as that taken by the government, we will not have access to our Arctic gas. The Americans have access to Canadian gas from southern Alberta, but the northern pipeline has not been built because of the Liberal-Tory vote. We want access to our northern gas in the Arctic; that is the reality.
Even some Tories at the time, and certainly some Liberals in addition to members of the New Democratic Party, said that it was a disgrace in terms of our long-range energy interests to sell off low cost gas from southern Alberta to the Americans, unless there was the possibility of negotiating swaps later on when gas came down from Alaska. Many of us in the country, not only those of us in the House of Commons, were saying
that it was a fundamental obligation on the part of the Government of Canada to be in a position to engage in trade, if the northern pipeline were built and American gas started to come down. We said that the only conditions under which they should get that low cost gas from Alberta now would be if we could get gas at equivalent or comparative prices from the United States when that pipeline was built. If it is not built, where are the tradeoffs? The reality is that they will not take place. The Americans have the gas and we will get the empty holes in the ground. That is the reality.
In short, with this project which was initiated by the federal government, for which they have to assume primary responsibility,-but aided and abbetted by the Tory party-Canadians were defrauded of cheap gas and in the process we have been defrauded of low-cost gas in the future. Canadians will not get it now under this kind of agreement, an agreement which was supported by the two old-line parties.
I was asked about the Alsands project. I believe that any dispassionate analysis would lead one to conclude at this point, frankly, that what happened is that the Alsands project collapsed under its own weight. When the government realized that Shell and Gulf were no longer interested in the project- these great multinationals which were defended so vigorously but in unstated terms by the Tory party now, because I would remind all Canadians that they wanted the project to go ahead by giving more concessions to the oil companies-and when it saw last week that the Alsands project was failing because Shell, in its financial analysis of world price in oil and long range interest expectations and so on, saw that it was not financially viable, what did the Liberals do? Did they indicate that it was all right because those resources will not disappear? Did they indicate that the resources will remain for future Canadians and those resources can be brought under the public auspices with Petro-Canada? After all, Petro-Canada was created initially so that we would not be held for blackmail by the multinationals. However, the Liberals did not say that. Instead, they raised the ante for the multinationals by presenting a new package which would have given billions of dollars to Shell and Gulf. Of course, this was done with the support of the Tory Party.
However, for business reasons which were substantially related to prices in oil, the business community, the multinationals even, turned down that offer.
As I have indicated, we say that those resources will not go away. As long as these two old-line parties do not have anything to do with it, these resources will remain part of our country. In the future, when those resources become economically viable we hope we will be able to develop those resources jointly with the government of Alberta, totally under public Canadian control.
I also want to say to my Tory friends, both figuratively and literally on my right, that every Gallup poll done of Canadians
May 4, 1982

indicates that not only are they interested in Canadian ownership of those oil resources, they support public ownership. The Tories should learn that.
While discussing the collapse of these two projects, it would in some manner be comforting to think that the only failure involved was these two resource projects themselves, which is very significant. I regret to say that what is really involved, of course, is that the whole economic thrust of the Liberal government as announced in its budget last fall has been completely undermined by the collapse of these two projects. In this context I would like to say that the thrust of that budget was not an accident. The House knows, as does the whole country, that many of the particular details of that budget were economically foolish and unjust, or both.
One of the important aspects of the budget which has not received national debates was the industrial strategy, which had its general framework outlined in the budget. That strategy was not an accident. There has been a debate raging in the Liberal party-and had been over the summer months leading up to the production of the budget-which had on one side that very earnest but totally ineffective Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) in terms of what he has produced in the country. He wanted a serious industrial strategy. He talked as if he were a Japanese finance spokesperson, trade spokesperson or someone from any industrial country in western Europe. At least he did talk about the need for a manufacturing strategy. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce was on one side of the debate which related to what the Liberals had promised in the 1980 election-a serious manufacturing strategy. On the other side of the debate was Senator Olson whose arguments were very different. His arguments were what emerged in the budget. Senator Olson said that what the country really needed was another traditional Liberal quick-fix. What Senator Olson argued for, which is what ultimately triumphed in the cabinet, was that we should be spending hundreds of billions of dollars in the decades ahead for megaprojects, which is simply a new and updated term for resource sellout. That was the side of the argument which won out in cabinet.
Now these projects are dying. With them go the manufacturing jobs which were supposed to be the spin-off benefits of these megaprojects. That was the manufacturing strategy, to have megaprojects for the resource sellout on the one hand which would produce manufacturing spin-offs. The government decided on that strategy rather than following the strategies of other industrial nations which concentrated on developing a first-rate manufacturing nation. The Liberals had intended this to occur simply as a byproduct of resource production.
With the collapse of these two megaprojects we have seen the end of the hopes of getting the manufacturing spin-offs which might have occurred. What is particularly infuriating for anyone who has seriously looked at the performance of the Canadian economy in the past year but, more important, beyond our borders to see what is happening in the world economy, is to find that this occurrence could have been envisaged. The weakening of OPEC and the decline of the
world price of petroleum has made marginal and high cost energy projects uneconomical all over the world, not just in Canada. The Government of Canada, in signing its agreement with Alberta, was projecting its income from oil prices that were based on what was already-I want to stress-an unrealistic projection of future world oil prices.
Since last spring, not just in the past few weeks or months, before the budget, economic analysts have been noting that the decline of OPEC was well under way. 1 say, not only for the benefit of the Liberals but for the benefit of the official opposition as well, that analysts were discussing the effects on all megaprojects in energy in any country in the world, including Canada. Instead of noting that OPEC was in fact on the skids, the Liberal government gambled. That is the only way to describe it. They gambled on a steady increase in world oil prices as being the virtual cornerstone of their manufacturing policy.
Three months ago, on behalf of my colleagues, 1 warned the government about the folly of the course on which it embarked. I quote very briefly what I said at that time:
Pierre Trudeau's economic strategy, besides all the tortuous twists and turns it has taken, has always been based on resource exports. Over the years he has continually assured Canadians that Canada's strength lies in its oil and gas and its metal minerals. Exports of resources have always been Pierre Trudeau's idea of how to provide the good life for Canadians.
I said then, and I repeat now, that this Liberal approach, continuing as it does, to see Canada as some sort of resource hinterland for the rest of the world, is perilous. This Liberal approach to the economic development of Canada must be challenged, and must be fundamentally changed, if this country is to grow in any secure way in the future.
For years the Liberals had a strategy which was, on the one hand, the selling off of resources as a permanent source of wealth and on the other, the manufacturing strategy which saw the establishment of rather inefficient branch plants here. It created the economic mess in which we have found ourselves in the last year or so in terms of the budget-making process of the government. That is what they had to consider.
What did they do to get us out of the mess? Once you get beyond all the hype and rhetoric of the budget and what has taken place since the budget, you find that all they presented was simply a rehash of their old strategy. Having used the resource hinterland model of the past and having created the mess, they have been trying to persuade Canadians, ever since the budget, to continue with this old model as a means of getting us out of the difficulty.
I want to say that this vision is faulty. In particular I want to say tonight for western Canada that these resource projects-

I want to make two points and two points only. First we have to start developing in a serious way a manufacturing strategy in this country. The place to begin is by recognizing that we have a $21 billion deficit in manufacturing trade each year, which represents a net loss to this country of 200,000 jobs if only we replace those imports by goods produced in this country.
We in this party have said that we should learn from what has been done in western Europe, what is being applied now down in Australia and what is being done by the Mexicans.

And Sweden. If you watch the upcoming election in Sweden you will see Olof Palme back in office. Watch that one. The place to begin is by learning from the experience of these other industrialized countries. Canada, with 52 per cent of our manufacturing sector foreign-owned should insist that any foreign-owned company in this country has to start working just a little bit on behalf of Canadians.
We would say that if a company is making $20 million of sales in this country, they must, as they have learned to do in
May 4, 1982

other countries, adapt themselves and start producing in Canada by Canadians $20 million worth of products. That is the kind of approach we would take.
Second, in order to overcome the deficit that is so crucial and fundamental to a serious job and employment strategy, we must go after export markets. We must adapt our financial institutions in the way that western European countries and the Japanese have done so that when we send exporters around the world they are not undermined by inadequate financing.
We have to change our banking system to ensure that when we have a product, as I learned in the past seven months in no fewer than three countries, we can capture the markets elsewhere in the world. Now when we have such an export product, we find it is inadequately financed at home. This party would take steps to ensure that the pursuit of export markets is done as vigorously as is capturing our own market.
In conclusion, we in this party at this point in the twentieth century no longer believe that Canada should remain a nation of hewers of wood and drawers of water. My generation of Canadians believes that we can produce in an imaginative and vigorous way like other modern nations. The NDP says, let us put the old Liberal-Conservative resource sellout behind us and become a first-rate manufacturing nation in a modern world.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde)-who, despite what you have heard from the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), was about the business of Canada tonight and unfortunately could not get here in time, but he will return in time to participate in a good deal of this debate-it is my pleasure to rise not only to defend but to take the responsibility for the success of the national energy policy.
The Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) with his usual style pretended to debate the Alsands issue this evening but brought in all of the old chestnuts, including the hewers of wood and the drawers of water. He brought in election predictions from foreign lands, banking and foreign ownership but did not deal with the issue at hand, which 1 intend to do.
The Leader of the Opposition would have you believe that the failure of the Alsands project is the total collapse of the national energy policy. Nothing could be further from the truth. Yes, the companies said no to the Alsands offer. But I would like to point out, and I want to make it very clear, that
1,200,000	Canadians have said yes to the national energy policy and have said it in a very positive manner. They have said yes to the CHIP program; over one million homes have been insulated. Over 200,000 oil conversions have taken place. What is the net result of that? It is a 7 per cent reduction in the consumption of crude oil this year.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Hear, hear! Bravo!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: For your interest, leaders of the opposition, members of the House and Canadians, that 7 per cent reduction represents roughly the equivalent of the production from one oil sands project a year.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Bravo!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
I repeat that. In terms of self-sufficiency, this is definitely a set-back, we agree that the termination of the Alsands project is a set-back, but it does not affect our determination to be self-sufficient by the year 1990. I want to make that absolutely clear. I think any other indication is not fair and is misleading Canadians to believe that the government has been drastically affected in our goal to achieve selfsufficiency.
I want to point out that that 7 per cent reduction in consumption, which was a very firm thrust of the national energy policy, has resulted in a 17 per cent reduction in the consumption of heating oil alone this year. That is significant.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: They could not afford any more.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: This is part of the national energy policy. Selfsufficiency in oil has increased from 79.5 per cent to 80.9 per cent. Do not forget that we made three promises when we delivered the national energy policy-self-sufficiency, opportunity, and fairness. I might suggest to you that those goals are being met and that they are receiving the overwhelming support of Canadians across the country.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
Let us look at our goals and let us look at them fairly. It is important that we put all of this in perspective and in balance. Let us look at oil self-sufficiency. We have decreased consumption. That is proved. We have new projects coming on. The fact of the matter is-and we will get into the Alsands offer-that I would like to put that offer out on the table so that all can understand what that offer was, just how fair it was and why it was turned down. I will get into that in just a moment.
We have agreed to energy revenue sharing in this country. We agree that it was a very arduous process. None of this happened during that brief tenure of office enjoyed by the other party. I would like to add that the opportunity of ownership, which was a very real thrust of the national energy policy, has resulted in a 6 per cent increase in Canadian ownership.
We have a number of projects as well that indicate to you what is happening on the Canadian scene in terms of energy self-sufficiency and the kind of projects that this government is committed to and will continue to see through.
Let us look at the TQM Pipeline; $2.4 billion; Norman Wells development, $600 million; Quintette coal development, $700 million; Ridley Island coal and grain terminals in British Columbia, an investment of $600 million. As well, there are upgrading projects under way in Montreal and Saskatchewan.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
What about oil self-suffiency?

May 4, 1982

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: I am talking about self-sufficiency. If the hon. member would return to his seat, I could remember where he came from. I would like to remind him of this. Let us look at Hibernia. Cheaper oil is coming on stream and Hibernia is a perfect example. We have proven that there is one and a half billion barrels of oil in Hibernia. That is one of the reasons why we can look forward to oil self-sufficiency.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that members of the opposition are not interested in the facts. What are the facts? We are speaking to Canadians. Fortunately, Canadians are providing us with the kind of proof that the national energy policy is indeed a policy that they support. We have just given you the figures.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
The consumption is down. I can say to those opposite that they will have time to participate in this debate. I would like to say here and now that it is Canadians across the country who know that we must cut back on consumption, Canadians who agreed with the thrust of the national energy policy. It is they who have made this work, and they will continue to make it work.
Let us get back to Alsands offer. On April 26 the Governments of Canada and Alberta made a joint offer to the Alsands consortium. I would like to make something perfectly clear here. The Leader of the Opposition said that we would stand here and try to lay the blame on the provinces and on people across the country. We have no intention of doing so. I would like to pay tribute to the province of Alberta for the kind of co-operation that existed in the entire work of the Alsands project.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
The Governments of Canada and Alberta did make a joint offer which included a major new financial arrangement designed to make the project substantially more attractive to the participants. Here are the major elements.
It was agreed that the two governments would provide a 50 per cent equity share in the total project. The two governments would provide loan guarantees of 68 per cent of private expenditures in lieu of normal tax write-offs. That is only part of it. The loan repayments would be limited to 58 per cent of net revenue from the project. Except for a minimum gross royalty, the project would pay no taxes federal or provincial until the loan was repaid. The normal taxes and royalties would apply after the guaranteed loan was repaid, but only after that. Output from the project would receive a new oil reference price or its equivalent.
The private sponsors of this project considered the offer through the course of the previous week, and on Friday last, October 30, they announced that the project was being suspended indefinitely. Why? I will get to the main reasons for
the suspension in a moment, and this is absolutely true and it was responsible for the failure of a number of other oil projects worldwide. These main reasons were falling international oil prices and increasing project costs. All of these factors combined to generate too much risk and uncertainty for the private sector. There was an apparent difficulty in attracting new private sponsors.
Significantly, however, and I think this is worth repeating, the Alsands consortium did not find any fault with the government's latest offer.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
Indeed, it would have been very difficult for them to have done so. This last offer represents one of the most generous packages of commercial terms that has been made available to any private energy project in Canada.
Let us look at what they would have received. The offer would have provided a rate of return on the project in excess of 20 per cent, even based on an oil price forecast lower than that which was assumed last fall. There would have been an ROR in excess of 20 per cent, considering the reality of current costs of production. The offer would have provided more security from future price fluctuations by stretching out that period of non-taxability which gave them a real cushion, would have financed 68 per cent of the private sector expenditures under extremely attractive commercial terms, and would have provided up to 84 per cent of the total project financing requirements.
I think every hon. member of the House and all Canadians would agree that this offer represented the realistic limit to which any government could go in providing the right commercial terms.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Two years too late.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Beyond this point, both governments felt that all of the potential benefits from Alsands, financial, economic and psychological, would be exceeded by the costs and risks to society. I heard a comment, "Two years too late".

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: It was two years too late.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
It is a fact that that agreement which was so elusive to the opposition should have taken place at that time and perhaps it also would have come to that much earlier. But the fact is, the opposition did not.
Canada and Alberta went more than half way on this offer. Both the federal government and the government of Alberta went as close to a balancing point as possible. However, the fact is that governments cannot and should not create a set of conditions which eliminate all risks to a private sector project. But we came mighty close to that in this particular one.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: How far away?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
We all know, despite the government's offer to assume the vast majority of the up front capital risks through
May 4, 1982

direct equity participation and loan guarantee, and despite the rhetoric from the oil industry about the virtues of risk taking and free enterprise, who was taking the real risk. Who was taking the real risk? In the final analysis, the private sector was not willing to accept even a vastly more reduced level of risk than they said they were prepared to accept as little as six months ago.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Because they didn't trust you.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: So let us dispel this business of too little, too late.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: No confidence!

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: The Alsands companies were concerned about their projected rates of return, despite the guarantees, and about their cash flow position as the project went ahead. The governments responded. I say "governments" because I want to accentuate the fact once again that the government of Alberta was a very real, active and co-operative player. The governments proposed an offer which provided a good rate of return and maintained that rate even with lower expected rates of growth in world oil prices. That offer was out there on the table. It substantially reduced the risk by taking a direct share in half the project. We, and by "we" I mean the Governments of Canada and of Alberta, addressed cash flow concerns by guaranteeing loans and taking the companies out of the tax system until those loans were repaid. Was it not a generous offer?

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Absolutely.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Your socialists think so.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
Well, the hon. members cannot have it both ways. At one point they say we are not generous enough, and then they call us socialists. "Hypocrisy" was a word very freely expressed on the other side of the House just a moment ago, but I see it practised with monotonous regularity from both ends of the House.
The rationale for the extremely generous degree of support offered was to ensure that the project would receive benefits equivalent to those implicit in Alberta's earlier promise of a 20 per cent loan guarantee and the ability of a fully taxable firm to use conventional tax write-offs on a current basis. These were the problems. With our guaranteed loan offer and the special features for repayment which were incorporated in it, we directly addressed the concerns which the project sponsors had earlier expressed to us. One such concern, and it was a real one, was their inability to use tax write-offs on a current basis. Our offer guaranteed them an equivalent basis. The second was their cash flow problem and risk, and our offer addressed this with a guaranteed loan and 50 per cent joint participation. Finally, the companies were concerned about the risk of low rates of the oil price increase, and this we addressed
by designing loan repayment terms which, in the case of the lower than anticipated oil price growth, would have delayed the time when the project would become taxable. Of course, if oil prices rapidly escalated, the loan would be repaid more quickly and would advance the date on which the project would be subject to full taxation. Therefore, the governments jointly created a package which did not provide excessive rates of return but which was extremely generous in terms of reducing the risk for the participants.
It should be clear from the scope of these terms that the two governments not only addressed the specific concerns of the companies, but also put forward an attractive total proposal under which the Alsands project could have gone forward. Unfortunately, it did not. However, I would like to assure Canadians that the door is still open and that that oil is still in the sand. It has not disappeared off into the night. It is there.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Too late.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: For Canadians it is still oil in the bank.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: You are still buying it from Mexico.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: The fact is that we had cheaper oil, and those companies which turned this down have asked, "Should we look at this project somewhere down the road when the national oil prices escalate, or should we look at some of the projects which will bring us the oil that we need at a far lower cost?"

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Now.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Hibernia?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Hibernia.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Beaufort Sea?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: I mentioned just a moment ago that Hibernia is a very real possibility, with proven reserves. We have proven a flow of 1.5 billion barrels a day. There is a number of other ways in which we will achieve our self-sufficiency goal by 1990. We have enhanced oil recovery projects, upgrading projects-

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Cold Lake?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: -and the offshore exploration and development to which this government has devoted millions and millions of dollars and which we will continue to do. I want to emphasize that developments in these sources of oil will make us selfsufficient by 1990.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Want to bet?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
It is absolutely true that over the last year we have become increasingly optimistic about the prospects of oil, as we mentioned, from Hibernia, from the east coast, from the Beaufort, and we expect, with a good degree of certainty, that these supplies will more than offset the output that we might have obtained from the Alsands project.

May 4, 1982

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Poppycock.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT

No, it is not poppycock. It is absolute truth. If the hon. member were not hung up on the Alsands project alone, he would not continue to delude Canadians that the collapse of the Alsands project is the collapse of the NEP. We admit that it is a setback. I repeat, and I want to make sure that all Canadians know, that the failure of the Alsands project to go ahead at this moment does not mean the collapse of the NEP. I want to again assure hon. members that we in Canada and this government will continue to pursue those objectives set out so clearly in the National Energy Program, those objectives which are supported by Canadians. We will be self-sufficient by the year 1990.
I should like to bring to the attention of the House some of the projects which we are continuing to support. As a matter of fact, the Leader of the Opposition had quite a lengthy list of those projects which he said were not going forward. I would like to add my list of those projects which are going forward, and it is quite a lengthy one. Perhaps it would be better to table the document.
