We have Sable Island offshore gas, Norman Wells, as I mentioned, La Grande Phase II at James Bay, and Hibernia Oil development. All of these projects are now under active consideration and a good deal of money has already been put into them.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, the loss of Alsands is regrettable, but in the face of similar decisions being made in other countries at this time-

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: That is a cop-out.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of State (Mines)
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
It is not a cop-out, it is reality and it is time hon. members on that side faced up to reality. I am sure hon. members read the report in The Globe and Mail this morning of Exxon's decision to shut down its oil shale project in the United States after investing some $400 million, due to the decline of international oil prices.
I want to state unequivocally at this time that although the Alsands project failure is a setback, it will not-and I say it again-it will not undermine the basic objectives of the National Energy Program nor our ability to achieve them.

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a couple of comments on the remarks of the Minister of
State for Mines (Mrs. Erola). It is obvious that the minister lives within the confines of Ottawa and is briefed daily by the upper echelon of the civil service. She sure as hell does not live in northeastern Alberta where those plants are supposed to be developed or she would not talk the rot she talked tonight.
She holds out the CHIP program as the bastion of the National Energy Program and as evidence of its success. It was the very first thing she mentioned. Mr. Speaker, it was a money giveaway to the people of Canada so that they could insulate their homes and conserve energy. I should like to suggest another program-the BAPP program-buy a parka program. That could be implemented and it would be a wonderful success. The people who now cannot afford fuel oil for their homes because of the price and people who cannot afford to live in this country in the wintertime, will buy parkas.
The goals of the energy program are oil sufficiency, opportunity and fairness. I should like to deal with the matter of self-sufficiency. Clearly the Hibernia fields are not to be developed. Clearly the technology is not there. Is this government so unilateral in decision-making that it is going to steamroll over Newfoundland and not discuss the ownership of the off-shore with that province? That matter has yet to be settled. Taking into account the Newfoundland election, it does not appear to me that the government is going to be able to pull any strings in Newfoundland. That province is going to hold the line, and the federal government will have to deal with it properly, in fairness and in co-operation. Co-operative federalism is not dead.
Now 1 should like to deal with the matter of opportunities, Mr. Speaker. I would ask the Minister of State for Mines what kind of opportunity there is for the people who went up to northeastern Alberta. The minister is now leaving. She is afraid to listen to what can be said about some of her statements.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM CANCELLATION OF PROPOSED ALSANDS MEGAPROJECT
speechtext: Bye, bye!

speechtext: Bye, bye!

The next item is fairness. Where is the fairness for the farmer who is now paying double for his fertilizer because of the National Energy Program which was brought in by this government? Where is the fairness to the trucker who is now paying $2 per gallon for gasoline when he can go across the border and buy it for $1.10? That is the result of the National Energy Program. That is how fair the government is.
We do not even have the technology for Hibernia. What is going to happen about the Beaufort Sea? Is the government going to steamroll over the Indian claims, the native claims, the Dene claims? All those land claims have yet to be settled



May 4, 1982
and they are not being addressed. A pipeline is needed, but how will it be built if the land claims are not settled first?
We saw what happened when the government would not face the political problems and develop a program with Alberta that was fair and equitable for all.
I am not going to say any more about that, Mr. Speaker, because the minister has gone. She is not about to listen anyway. Her statements are all rot and we hear it all the time.

speechtext:
The situation in many parts of the world with regard to the petroleum industry is substantially the same. It is affected by high interest rates, the decline in demand for petroleum products, the impact of inflation, which have all had a part in the state of the petroleum industry today. Against that background, it is clearly absurd to assume Canada is somehow immune from the adverse factors which are affecting all other industrialized nations.
Currently a number of major oil-related projects throughout the world are either being delayed or cancelled. The reasons given relate to the current world oil surplus, rising costs, the high cost of money and the general uncertainties about financing feasibility.
Some members in the House may be aware from comments made earlier this evening that in the United States projects have been shelved, projects on the leading edge of technology in a comparable way to that of the Alsands technology. But in addition to those that have been cited in the United States, in Venezuela a major upgrading oil project has been shelved. In the North Sea, the Netherlands is withdrawing from some of the major projects which have been contemplated. That

May 4, 1982
country is looking instead at smaller projects requiring minimum financial commitment. British Petroleum in the North Sea is backing off various costly projects to concentrate on alternatives of a less costly character. All these are also indications of the general situation facing a petroleum industry in a world where oil surpluses have developed, where world price has been dropping and where inflation and interest costs have been increasing.
Against that background, the Alsands project has been temporarily set aside, despite a very generous offer from both the federal and Alberta governments in terms of the tax regime and other financial incentives. Despite those very attractive offers, the two remaining private sector members of the Alsands consortium decided that to proceed with the project at this time was not in their best interests. There is a limit to which any government can go on making conditions right for any project. There is a point at which the expected benefits of the project are exceeded by the costs and the risks involved. The Alsands companies were concerned about their projected rates of return and their cash flow positions as the project developed. The government of Alberta and the Government of Canada proposed an offer which, in my view, provided a good rate of return and maintained that rate even with lower expected rates of growth in world oil prices. The two governments together substantially reduced the risks facing private sector partners by taking a direct share in half the project. The two governments addressed cash flow concerns by guaranteeing loans and taking the companies completely out of the tax system until both loans were repaid. In other words, the participants in the project were being offered world price and no taxes until they had recovered their total investment.
I would not want to try to emulate the colourful language of The Edmonton Sun in connection with the offer made by the government of Alberta and the Government of Canada, but I should like to quote for the record the comment of The Edmonton Sun on the offer. It indicated that "not for 100 years ... has there been anything to match the hauteur and disdain with which Shell and Gulf spurn the offer of public largesse ... If anything could turn a dedicated capitalist into a socialist, a believer in Petro-Canada and a fan of Marc Lalonde, this must be it . . . Since when is a guaranteed return on an investment of at least 20 per cent not enough?" The Edmonton Sun was certainly clear in its opinion that the offer made was a most generous one which, in other global circumstances, would have meant that the project would have gone forward.
As the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) noted, it is important to consider the Alsands project in the perspective of the wide range of petroleum possibilities in the country. There is a variety of encouraging projects in which to invest in our search for oil during the current decade. Oil sands projects must compete with other investment opportunities for available capital. Unquestionably the promising exploration results in the Beaufort and Hibernia areas offer
tremendous investment opportunities, as the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) indicated in her earlier statement. But generally in Canada there are strong incentives to invest in oil exploration. For example, the netbacks to the petroleum industry have grown dramatically in recent years. Under the agreements with Alberta and the other producing provinces flowing out of the National Energy Program, the netbacks for oil discovered prior to 1974 have risen from S4.95 per barrel in 1979 to $5.82 in 1982, an increase of some 18 per cent, and for new oil the value has increased from $6.56 per barrel to $16.58 per barrel in 1982, an increase of some 107 per cent.
Against the background of these numbers, it is not surprising that there are investors who recognize the great opportunities which await those who want to participate in the petroleum industry, especially Canadians who for the first time have a major opportunity to join in the petroleum play. Solomon Brothers, a respected New York investment house, as early as October last year noted that first year netbacks on new oil in Canada will be up to 80 per cent higher than in the United States. Greenshields, a major Canadian investment house, indicated a few months ago that exploration for new conventional oil will surge ahead because the price of new oil has almost doubled since December, 1981. Also Greenshields added that with higher netbacks, small or poor quality reserves which were previously passed by will merit development. The relative netback to new oil discoveries is 2.5 times higher than it was in 1979, even after adjustment for interest rates.
With world price for new oil and with the petroleum incentives program available, it is obvious that Canada offers investors great new opportunities. Those opportunities are being recognized not only by Canadian but by American investors. Recently the United States department of commerce issued a report on the basis of a survey of United States petroleum companies with subsidiaries in Canada. The report dealt with projected capital expenditures abroad by foreign affiliates of United States companies. A notable feature of the forecast was the estimate of the United States department of commerce, drawing on material provided by United States petroleum companies, that Canadian affiliates of United States petroleum companies plan a 28 per cent increase in expenditures in Canada in 1982 compared with the 1981 level.
Also the report of the United States department of commerce noted that the Canadian National Energy Program, designed to promote Canadianization of the domestic oil and gas industry, does not seem to have dampened the capital spending plans of affiliates operating in Canada. Indeed, the United States department of commerce forecasted that there will be a 28 per cent increase in Canadian investment compared with a worldwide increase of United States affiliates of only 18 per cent.
I suggest that the Canadian petroleum industry has a wealth of opportunities ahead of it which will contribute substantially to the realization of self-sufficiency in oil, self-sufficiency which we already enjoy in all other energy sectors. Of course, conservation is also playing a key role in achieving self-
May 4, 1982

sufficiency. In line with the goal of the National Energy Program of reducing demand for oil in Canada throughout this decade, we now estimate a total demand of approximately 1.4 million barrels per day by 1990, down from 1.7 million barrels per day last year. Part of the decline in demand is the direct result of government incentive programs to encourage Canadians to move away from costly oil to less expensive and more plentiful forms of energy and, of course, to encourage Canadian industry to develop alternative fuels.
In 1981, the demand for all petroleum products in Canada dropped by some 8.7 per cent. The expectation for 1982 is that there will be a further decrease of 5.6 per cent. The combination of the Hibernia sources, the Beaufort sources, oil from conventional lands and upgrading projects which are now under way, coupled with a sharp reduction in oil consumption in Canada, will certainly place Canada in a situation where we can be certain that our supply and demand will once more be in balance. That balance of oil supply and demand which we seek by 1990 will also be paralleled by greater Canadianiza-tion of our petroleum industry. I have no doubt that during the years ahead we shall undertake a major overhaul of our manufacturing industry to make it more competitive in world markets. Our best prospects to achieve that sort of competitive stance will be as a result of greater Canadianization of our own enterprises. Canadian research and development will benefit and grow, and worldwide marketing as well as entrepreneurial challenge will flow from a greater Canadianization of our industry, including the petroleum industry.
Recently, a report by Touche-Ross and partners, a major Canadian consulting group, noted that people may disagree on details or methods in the National Energy Program, but the report stresses that there can be little quarrel with the intent of the program from any reasonable person, Canadian or American, who believes in the existence of an independent selfgoverning nation on the northern part of the North American continent.
Now that we have our own Constitution at home, we should be redoubling our efforts to own and control more of our economy for good economic, social and political reasons.

In fact, the nature of this debate would not be as serious if all were well in other areas. Especially during the past two years, since February, 1980, this government has betrayed and deceived the Canadian people on almost all counts. Considering what the government has said and what it has done during those two years, it could be charged with misleading advertising. This evening's subject is extremely important, because the decision to abandon a project so earnestly desired by all Canadians has added a substantial note of discouragement and has raised general consternation with respect to recent events. I think it is important, Mr. Speaker, to show Canadians how the government's sorry performance in the economic sector today contrasts with its forecasts, promises and commitments in the energy field where, as in other economic sectors, government forecasts have been patently false. Members on this side of the House have called for a debate this evening, in order to try to raise the conscience of this government and to force it to listen to reason. At the very least, we might expect some hon. members to act according to their consciences and force their own government to prepare forecasts that provide a more realistic and honest view of what Canadians can expect.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, we are not going to congratulate this government. The opportunity afforded by this debate will be used to make the Canadian people aware of this disastrous performance, the government's lack of initiative and the monumental failure for which the members of this government are largely responsible. The Canadian people are concerned, the country is concerned and millions of Canadians are suffering at a time when, once more we are trying to persuade the government to make proposals that are more acceptable and effective than they have been able to produce up to now. The Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) was a pitiful sight just now when she had to read a speech prepared by a couple of senior officials and had to try to justify the government's action, just as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and so many ministers on the opposite side of this House have done, by blaming the provinces and the oil companies for turning down the government's generous offer. Perhaps we should ask ourselves, Mr. Speaker, why the government had to show such generosity to companies that did not even bother to accept this generous offer, because of their previous experience with the same government. Should this not be seen as evidence of a loss of confidence in government on the part of the private sector? For two years, Mr. Speaker, this government has tried in every possible way to encroach on areas that were formerly the domain of the private sector. The time will come when this government will have to deal honestly with the private sector. Perhaps we should remind Canadians-because some may have forgotten-that the Prime Minister of this country was in bed with the New Democratic Party not so long ago. Should

May 4, 1982
we be surprised at the government's desire to socialize just about everything, and why not the energy sector? This government, this political party, is led by a Prime Minister who believes in socialization, and we can see the results today. People are concerned and are asking why the private sector is reacting negatively to the government's policies and objectives. 1 do not think there is any reason to be surprised.
I was also listening to the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent), who went so far as to accuse the Progressive Conservative Party of having hurt this project, when it is common knowledge, Mr. Speaker, and Canadians will surely remember, that it is the New Democratic Party which has kept the people opposite in power since 1974, and that Canadians have the New Democratic Party to thank for being subject to the inadequate legislation under which Canadians are now suffering.
1 wish to congratulate the leader of my party on the comments he made in the House this evening, because thousands of Canadians would love to have a chance to say what he said this evening to the face of the minister responsible for the economic catastrophe and failure perpetrated by this government today. I believe it is important that Canadians should be reminded of the disastrous performance of this government. Certainly, Mr. Speaker, we were dreaming, as all Canadians dreamt, about this particular project. When $13 billion are involved in a project such as the one at Cold Lake-in fact it was $12 billion-it is clear, Mr. Speaker, that if instead of being obstinate and insisting on challenging the provincial governments two years ago, the government had taken action to settle these issues with a view to self-sufficiency in energy supplies, the projects would have come on stream two years ago, Mr. Speaker. My own province, which also has a substantial unemployment rate, would have benefited from these major investments as well. Why did the government fail? Procrastination, obstinacy, and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources himself, who orchestrated the daily confrontation with the provinces, that is where we should lay the blame for the loss of billions of dollars of investment in this country. We all know it would have been nice to see this money invested in Canada. And I repeat, my province and the other provinces would have benefited from these very desirable and necessary investments. However, after trying to blame the provinces and the opposition leaders for its disastrous failure with respect to this particular project, the government, and I think it is important
that Canadians should realize this, the government is going to try to put the blame on the oil companies.
Mr. Speaker, at this moment, Canada is losing an opportunity to create 100,000 jobs as a result of the disastrous performance of this government. At this very moment, when
1,500,000	unemployed workers are looking for jobs, and because of the government's failure to meet its objectives and the commitment made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, we are going to lose 320,000 jobs in related industries, an opportunity that was open to all the provinces of this country because, as we all know, all the provinces would have benefited from these major investments and these immensely lucrative projects.
There is no doubt that this government will go down in history and that the Right Hon. Prime Minister himself will go down in history on the basis of this pitiful performance, Mr. Speaker.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, as the leader of my party said yesterday, that there is an element of confidence in such things. Now that the government has lost the confidence of businessmen, it will be more difficult for the government to carry out necessary projects. However, Mr. Speaker, I cannot condone the government's attitude in trying to blame just about everyone and in trying to justify its actions on the basis of the performance of other countries when it is criticized for its lack of competence, or rather when its incompetence is demonstrated as it is today. Mr. Speaker, you cannot lie to the public all the time. You can lie to the public some of the time but you cannot lie all the time. This is the moment of truth. The government is realizing daily that it is no longer able to govern this country and can no longer rely on the confidence of the majority of the people of this country. I think that in the circumstances, Mr. Speaker, if, as members of this House, we have a sense of responsibility and an earnest desire to serve the majority that elected us, I think that our sense of responsibility would oblige us all to force the government to change its course of action or to resign if it is unable to demonstrate that it can lead the country down a road that will not take us straight into bankruptcy. I think this is a question we can ask the members opposite, these government members who endorse every day the incredible failure of the government, who support blindly and unconditionnally the attitude of this government which causes unacceptable hardships to thousands of Canadians. We cannot repeat this too often.
It is obvious that this country is on the edge of disaster. It is also obvious that this government is mostly responsible for the economic situation, even though it tries to justify itself by saying that since the situation is not too good in the United States or in Europe, it is quite normal for Canada to experience the same problems. Mr. Speaker, this government has
May 4, 1982

shown its inability to make wise decisions, and it is very important to make the right decisions in politics. The government has not done so. Its attitude is such that the energy industry no longer trusts it. Businessmen in general no longer have any confidence in the government either and the programs which are announced every day are simply disguised welfare and unemployment insurance programs. Is this the way to build a prosperous country? This government is no longer able to take new initiatives, and this has been obvious for a long time. One only has to hear the Prime Minister contradict himself nearly every day.
Faced with all these problems, and naturally disappointed because of the all-around terrible performance of his ministers every day, the Prime Minister said yesterday, "I believe the time has come to co-operate with the provinces." Yet, he has ignored them and treated them as strangers since he has been prime minister. He is now making amends. He needs the provinces to solve the problems and correct the mistakes of his own government. Is it possible to have any confidence in a prime minister who behaves in this way? Is it possible to have confidence in ministers and a cabinet who have failed so completely? It is too late, Mr. Speaker.
The Minister of State for Mines, who spoke earlier, tried to indicate that there is still some hope. For thousands of Canadians it is too late to have any confidence in this government. It refuses to listen to its own members when they dare from time to time, not too often and never the same ones, because it would be dangerous for them, to make a constructive recommendation to the government, whether on housing or on other issues, and most recently on interest rates. If a member opposite does so, he can do it only once because he is warned solemnly by the prime minister that he will have to resign if it happens again. We then have the whole flock of Liberal sheep who follow their shepherd, if I may use such terms. This is a pitiful sight, for a Canadian, for a Quebecer coming from a province with an unemployment problem. Seventy-four Quebec members out of 75 endorse and support the dictatorship of this man who will go down in history as having caused such harm to a nation that had put its confidence in him. This is the type of Canada in which we now live. And they spend millions on advertising to make the Canadian people believe that things are not really that bad.
After the patriation of our Constitution I was very upset, Mr. Speaker, because there were references to one Constitution, one country and one future, which is pure hypocrisy. The Constitution is incomplete, as we all know, Mr. Speaker, the country is torn and on the brink of bankruptcy, and the aged and over one and a half million unemployed are facing an uncertain, dangerous and difficult future-that is the kind of country the government is building for us today. There are hon. members who go along with that and who applaud such actions, Mr. Speaker, and I deplore this. These things must be said this evening and must be repeated tomorrow, and I hope there will be people with a moral sense who will be able to
meet the aspirations of all Canadians, and I hope that this debate will force the government to listen to reason or at least to resign, if it is sincere in its desire to serve the Canadian people.

Mexico has postponed its nuclear energy program, a $30 billion project. The liquefied natural gas programs in Nigeria amounting to $14 billion have been postponed. Why? I think all of us who are mature know that we are in a world of recession and that at this very moment in history the pool of capital available to government and private enterprise is not all that large that competition will not drive up interest rates and frighten people.
I do not try to minimize the Alsands project, but I think it is fair to point out that similar programs around the world are being cancelled or postponed for exactly the same reason that private industry backs out of this particular project at this particular moment. As one who believes in the free enterprise system, in all probability the right decision was made, if made from the boardrooms of Shell or other companies. It will help that wonderful part of the country lower its fuel bill and lower its dependency on coal. It

I get very little satisfaction out of knowing that the same problem or dilemma faces the Governments of France or Mexico or of other countries which have had to postpone their projects. However, I ask hon. members opposite, and people who may be listening, whether the postponement, for instance, of the Aquitaine purchase of heavy oil from Venezuela and the building of the plants needed for processing can be blamed on the Canadian Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources or the Prime Minister of Canada or the national energy policy. Tonight one would think that the world had come to an end because the Alsands project had been dropped. If one listens to the hon. member for Joliette, one would think that Canada has come apart.
It is amazing how important Alberta is to certain people in Quebec at particular times in history while it is relatively independent and unimportant at other times. I do not pretend to speak for Quebec, but I am a Quebecer. I am a Canadian. I am not a hyphenated Canadian. I do not even use the term "Quebecois". I use the term "Canadian" rather than "Quebecer", if you like. I know what goes on, but I get a certain amount of satisfaction when I hear the hon. member for Joliette speak with such passion about products in Alberta and the spin-off effect they would have in Quebec because that is precisely the message the Prime Minister and my Canadian friends have given for the last 20 years in this House. These are federalists who have said to Quebecers, "Remain within Canada, and these types of programs benefit all of us, all of Canada, including Quebec."
Just how important is Alsands? To the hon. member for Athabasca it is all important. What has been the impact out west? I like to read what people out west think of these great tragedies. The president of the Alberta Chamber of Commerce, and I do not want to be selective, a former provincial cabinet minister, predicted that the demise of Alsands would be a disaster for the provincial economy. He is entitled to his view. If he is entitled to his view, then so is Melville McMillan, a well-known professor of economics at the University of Alberta, who said that in his view Alsands was a bad investment because its oil production techniques were too costly. He was honest enough to say, "My views are not typical, I realize, but I think that this requires the governments to look at more
responsible energy alternatives", such as providing further incentives to the conventional oil industry for recovery of heavy oil and oil from older wells. This is perhaps the answer in the meantime. That may have to be the way we must go.
In fact, even Mr. Lougheed-not the Prime Minister of Canada, not the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources- said while speaking with reporters that there was far too much pessimism amongst Albertans after the Friday announcement and that Alsands did not play a part in provincial economic strategy for this year or next. I agree with Mr. Lougheed, because we have an energy surplus in this country, even if we are short of oil. However, when we add up all of our other sources of energy, it becomes not only a question of conservation but also one of conversion. The more people we convert to natural gas, the better it will be for the economy of Alberta, for the economy of central Canada and the maritimes because, as a rule, natural gas is cheaper than conventional oil.
I have read the Edmonton Journal, and I will not pay too much attention to the view of Jim Russell, a New Democratic Party candidate, who said, "If Alsands cannot stand by itself, it should be allowed to die." I think that is a rather rough statement. However, I must look at the views of the member of another party out there who said, "The trouble with Alsands is that it keeps the province off the main issue-looking after the junior oil companies in Alberta. Alsands has become an albatross." Independent Tom Sindlinger said Alberta does not need Alsands even if Canada does. Liberal leader Nick Taylor said Alsands is only useful as insurance, in case other projects do not proceed.
I am not for one moment minimizing the impact of Alsands. 1 know the spin-offs which Alsands would have for my riding which has a badly depressed steel industry, and for Secondary manufacturing in Ontario and in Quebec. I am not unaware of the spin-offs and I am not trying to minimize them. However, I just do not think the world has come to an end. Mr. Speaker, I was rather pleased to hear the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey) close with the remark about a little knowledge being a dangerous thing. I would challenge him to drink much deeper of the Pierian cup. On the basis of his remarks tonight there is much left to be said and much more knowledge to be accumulated.
He referred to the collapse of the shale program in the western United States. If we have drunk of the Pierian cup we know that the cost of oil from the shales of Colorado runs at roughly three times world price and that it is not the policy of the United States government, and has not been its policy in the past, to subsidize that production or blend it into any blended cost. Therefore, there was no way that that particular program could get off the ground.
He mentioned that Exxon was withdrawing from its coal gasification program. Let us compare the program of the United States over the last ten years with that of Canada today. We find that the exploration incentives provided to the oil and gas industry are such that it will be some time before the United States requirement will bear the cost of coal gasification. That is quite a contrast to the policy under which we operate today. When we compare the two policies, ours does not come up equal.
The hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) and the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) issued an invitation to the government backbenchers to look at what the executive branch of that party is doing to the nation. It is high time that they took careful notice of public opinion and its reaction to what is going on.
It is not long since it was virtually impossible for a member of the opposition to pick up a newspaper and find something that indicated that perhaps the government was going the wrong way and that perhaps the opposition had some ideas which should be accepted by the government.
I should like to quote from "Canadian Business" of May, 1982, an article entitled "The Economy" by Charles Davies. He had this to say:
In one sense, Alsands presents a real conundrum. It's important to Ottawa's commitment to national energy self-sufficiency (depending on what happens in the Beaufort Sea and offshore Newfoundland), as well as being a linchpin project in the government's industrial strategy for the 1980s. But with the outlook for international oil prices now as foggy as that for interest rates, Alsands' economics are becoming more dubious with each passing day.
The article continues as follows:
What's also striking about Alsands though, is the degree to which it demonstrates that Canada has become an investment ghetto. When Lalonde talks about using the public purse to support projects that have lost their sex appeal for the private sector, he may just be making a virtue of necessity. Given the rate at which we've managed to discourage foreign investors in recent years-not to mention a goodly number of large domestic ones-this could be the first of many incidents where we have to bail ourselves out.
That is certainly not complimentary to the results of the oil sands negotiations and the National Energy Program.
The article later discusses the balance of investment in Canada. There was a point when that balance created a cash flow which Canada needed. In the 1980s the cash flow became negative by $2 billion. In 1981 it escalated, but I have not seen the final figure.
Although we may talk about the dissatisfaction of Canadian investors in foreign jurisdictions, I have not seen any mention in the press of a single Canadian investment being returned to Canada because of a less favourable climate elsewhere. That speaks ill of the policies of the government.
We heard a few remarks from the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola). It is rather interesting that she referred to the Hibernia field and other offshore resources, and stated that the resource in Hibernia has proven to be 1.1 billion barrels. I presume that must be recoverable, and since the figure comes from a cabinet minister we must accept it as accurate. But what does it mean to Canada's requirements? If it were all drawn out in a three-year period it would not satisfy the national requirements of this nation under the present policy.
The oil that would come from Hibernia is a decade away, Mr. Speaker, and that did not have to be the case. Our policies have discouraged offshore investigation to such a degree that Newfoundland and all of Atlantic Canada are suffering from the stagnation of exploration prior to any possible development. The 1.1 billion barrels represents less than a three-year national requirement if it were drawn off in that time. If it were drawn off in a 12-year period it would represent approximately our import requirements. But that is in the future, Mr. Speaker. Alsands could have done much better had it come into production-and it would have come into production much more quickly than is apt to be the case with Hibernia. That reflects on the policy of the government and emphasises the need for Alsands.
We have found it virtually impossible to establish an economic environment in which anybody can be sure of anything if they are investing in the oil industry. We have gone so far in
May 4, 1982

that much hailed agreement with Nova Scotia that the government insisted that it retain a veto on the board which was to be established for the control of the offshore resources as it applied to Nova Scotia. I am sure the premier of Nova Scotia obtained the very best deal he possibly could.
The minister also referred to falling crude oil prices. I do not believe she has done any reading or has listened to the electronic media, because in the last 72 hours the emphasis has been, first, that the petroleum cartel of the world plans and can achieve a two million barrel per day cutback in production and, second, that those who hold supplies of oil, the international corporations, are now drawing down on the surplus that exists by two million barrels per day. If this is extended for a six-month period it becomes very obvious that there will no longer be a free market in which we are going to get bargain prices for oil, that is if the cartel can put its act together, and it is trying its best. We cannot go on drawing from our purchased reserves at the rate of two million barrels a day for very much longer either. So everything indicates that world prices, as of the last 72 hours, are very apt to turn around.
Among those reports one should pay very strict attention to the one which says that the United States anticipates a 3-cent to 4-cent per gallon increase in the price of gasoline at the pump in the very near future, and it could happen next week. I realize, Mr. Speaker, that it is the obligation of the Minister of State for Mines to protect her government. But I submit that her argument was frail and not what one would want to present on the hustings to an informed audience.
One of the items mentioned was the TQ & M pipeline. I may be all alone in what I am going to say, but I am concerned about the construction of that pipeline, for two reasons. First, because the energy policy of the government has retarded exploration on the east coast offshore as it has everywhere else. We do not know how much gas has been found, but using a figure which apparently emanates from cabinet, we are talking about three trillion cubic feet of proven reserves. We are also advised by the press that further exploration may increase that reserve immensely. If that be the case, a proper energy policy would be directed toward every possible incentive to explore and develop the gas fields off Sable Island, the property of Nova Scotia. That should be policy. Should we in fact be bragging about the construction of a pipeline with a reduced diameter as it goes eastward, and is it in fact going to be something like eight inches to a foot when it reaches Canso?
Then we talk lightly of reversing that pipeline. Mr. Speaker, if that is done we then have to do two things. We replace it from Canso to Montreal with a larger bore, or we parallel the line we have already built and reverse the pumping stations at a massive cost to the taxpayers.
Why don't we visualize the importance of development of the resource assets of these provinces? Why are we a stumbling block? What kind of pure greed and narrow mentality stands in the way of resource development in provinces which have been so disfavoured in the economic structure of Canada that surely they should have priority? Like the hon. member
5.0. 26
for Athabasca and the hon. member for Joliette, I appeal to the government backbenchers to please inject an element of intelligence into the policies of the executive structure of the government.
This Liberal government has been deteriorating for all those years it has been my privilege to be in this House. I watched the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) knuckle under to the NDP and the socialist tendencies of his own party. I saw him plead and argue, I am sure against his conscience, to put through the first budget which indicated the socialist trend the government is now following. We have seen the total and complete erosion of the principles of social responsibility, coupled with private investment and the free enterprise system, which used to be the trademark of the Liberal party. That has gone by the boards, but only because backbenchers do not care how much the fuel costs to run the pulp mill in Campbellton. They do not care how much it costs to run a fishing boat off Newfoundland, or a farm tractor anywhere in Canada. They have swallowed their pride and taken this gobbledegook of economic nonsense which has been passed to them by the executive structure of the Liberal party. And they have supported it.
Like the hon. member for Athabasca, I claim several generations of ancestry in this nation and I do not look at it as New Brunswick alone, or Quebec alone, or the prairie provinces alone, or British Columbia alone. I look at Canada as being a co-operative effort by people to govern themselves to the benefit of all Canadians and all regions of Canada. Perhaps there are some in Atlantic Canada who would criticize me because I support a party which opposes a negative energy policy which has defeated the Alsands project. But, Mr. Speaker, I cannot serve Canada and my region by supporting any policy which has a negative effect on economic development anywhere in Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the narrow and contracted minds of backbenchers in the Liberal party from Atlantic Canada have contributed to the plight of that area for too, too long. They have contributed to the consternation of western Canada over a policy which is going to turn it from an affluent society into a dependent society if something is not done to replace the greed and ideological philosophy we have seen with reality and practicality. It may be the west which suffers today, but it will be Ontario tomorrow and Quebec the day after. If ever there was a time in this nation when backbenchers should rise to the cause of the Canadian economy, it is now. Failing that, it is high time that the government put its policy, of which it is so proud, on the line in the hustings.
It may be early for an opposition to suggest an election should take place, Mr. Speaker, but when we find the CBC, that loyal proselytizer of the Liberal party, in some of its programs criticizing the policies of the Liberal party and depicting Grande Prairie as going from prosperity to a dependent society with 30 per cent or 40 per cent unemployed, it is

speechtext:
May 4. 1982
high time that the backbenchers on your right take note of the developing catastrophe.
Alsands would have been a fait accompli by 1979 had there been a rational energy policy. Cold Lake would have been with us and, as I said earlier this afternoon, that presented a problem for Canada. Our resources, both financial and manpower, might well have been strained. That was the problem which existed when the Liberal party found it wise to call an election in 1979. They have found one roadblock after another to place in the way of development across Canada. 1 am pleased to be taking part in this debate because, like the members opposite, I believe this is an extremely serious matter. First I would like to quote from an editorial in Le Droit which appeared on May 1, 1982, and reads as follows:
Shell's decision to pick up its marbles was based on a series of factors, and could not possibly have been changed by a last-ditch attempt by Ottawa and Edmonton to save the project. There was, of course, the whole issue of private sector participation, which was intended to make up 50 per cent or more of the project. Furthermore, there is a certain risk involved in this kind of technology, and although Syncrude has been operating for nearly three years, all has not been smooth sailing, and incidents have been many and costly.
That is a fairly accurate analysis of the situation, and this morning, there was an article in the Globe and Mail which I would also like to quote. It shows that there is a fairly basic understanding of the problems we are facing.

The article is written by Peter Cook. In part it reads:
However, despite the general dismay that greeted news of the demise of one megaproject and the postponement of another, economists point out the decisions were not unexpected, and that the loss in growth need not necessarily occur.
Expansion in the economy will almost certainly be set back in the short term. And the cancellations represents a blow for the federal government's economic strategy. But growth could still take place at a similar rate through 1985, and may not be diminished at all.
Indeed, some economists look to a revived international economy-spurred by the lower oil prices that torpedoed Alsands-and contend this could provide fresh momentum for Canadian exports, and the economy, in the next few years.
The opposition members have failed to recognize this, and I do not blame them, because they do have a function in this House, and that is to oppose systematically. They must advance the most negative arguments they can muster. They do that quite liberally, 1 might say, and sometimes it tends to distort the public's perception of the truth. I might point out that I was very pleased with the attitude of the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent). speechtext: On the other hand, the Tories feel that by ranting and raving somehow the decision will be changed, as though it were in the hands of the government to change the decision on the Alsands.

speakerposition: Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
If you look at the press release issued by Shell Oil Company at the time of its decision, you will see quite readily that the decision was Shell's decision. Shell Oil recognized there was an effort on the part of both the Alberta government and the Canadian government, hand in hand co-operatively, to attempt to maintain the Alsands project.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, during the month of March the federal government paid for the operating expenses of Alsands because we wanted to have that extra month to permit some additional negotiations to take place. Shell stated as follows:
We respect the efforts governments put into developing the most recent proposal. In some respects it is an improvement over the previous offer. Shell has given careful consideration to the proposal but has decided that in the current and foreseeable economic and industry environments we cannot proceed.
A high level of debt is envisaged in the government's proposal. During the six-year-long construction period, major uncertainties over inflation, interest rates, capital availability and oil prices will prevail. In these circumstances, we believe it would be unwise to burden a project of this magnitude and operational risk with an extremely heavy debt load, even with government loan guarantees. Were Alsands to proceed on this basis, a very high proportion of the project's revenue would be required simply to cover operating and debt servicing costs.
Those are the reasons for the cancellation of the Alsands plant. The only solution there could have been would have been for the federal government to have undertaken the Alsands project and financed the whole thing itself. Could you imagine the opposition's opinion of that particular initiative? There is absolutely no way that they could recognize any right on this side of the House. Their basic philosophy is that
May 4, 1982

government ought not to interfere in the marketplace. The marketplace has made a decision. Shell Oil said the risk is too high, and those babes on the other side, in complete innocence and completely blinded by their own partisan interests, advanced certain principles that are completely contrary to the basic tenets of their particular philosophy. I could understand the position of the NDP.
It is like yours.

speakerposition: Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
The Leader of the NDP said in Vancouver, referring to the Alsands project:
Given that the Shell people made the decision-
Because he recognizes that it was the Shell people who made the decision.
-based on the current price of oil and the supply and their predictions about what the future holds, it doesn't make me question the decision not to proceed.
That is the hon. member for Oshawa speaking. He continued with the following:
The resources are going to stay where they are;-
That is evidently so. He continued:
-they aren't going away. So when it becomes economically viable to develop the oil sands then PetroCan or some combination of the federal and Alberta governments should go ahead.
That is a very commendable attitude to take, and it is the proper attitude to take. I can see quite well why the hon. member for Oshawa did that. On Friday, while the Tories thought that we were not doing enough, the NDP were thinking that we were doing too much. In fact, in the question posed by the Leader of the NDP to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, he said that we were bribing the private sector participants. Evidently we are in a difficult position being on the one side buffeted by the reactionaries and on the other by the radicals. I believe the decision that we made was the proper decision to make.
Another matter I should like to bring to the attention of the House is that oil sands programs and projects have had a hard time. The tar sands were discovered more than 100 years ago. Everyone attempted over that period of time to try to extract very valuable oil from the sands. They did not have to explore for it because it was there. There was a recognition that there were more than 600 billion barrels of potential oil resource.
We recognize that the first attempt was made by the GCOS group. They did not make any money until such time as international prices were somewhere in the vicinity of $8 to $10. Before that time they could not make money because the entire operation was a very expensive one. When Syncrude came forward Atlantic Richfield pulled out because in effect the proposition was too risky. At that time the federal government put in $300 million and talked the Ontario government into becoming involved as well, and we rescued the Syncrude plant. Although that plant was aimed at 125,000 barrels per day, it is now producing at the level of roughly 80,000 barrels per day because of difficulties in technology.
As the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources admitted quite candidly, it is not possible to get all wrinkles out of the tar sands technology as yet. We are doing immensely well, but we do not have all the wrinkles out. With high interest rates, high inflation, and difficulties in terms of international prices-up one day and down the next-a very risky environment is created. In that context we cannot blame Shell for pulling out, even though the federal government and its agent, Petro-Canada, were ready to stay in. I do not think it would have been a wise decision for the government to have gone ahead by itself, or in conjunction with the province of Alberta, with that particular project.
The Tories are so inconsistent that they are looking avidly for diversion or for some distraction in order to draw the attention of the public away from their own internal squabbling. The hon. member from Calgary, who is allegedly the Tory critic for the environment, is a loyalist of the first order. In effect he is attempting in any way he knows how to try to keep his leader in place.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. Is the relevancy rule to be applied, or will this jackass be allowed to continue?

walk around with a blindfold over his eyes. Ele is so partisan in his attitude that he cannot see the truth when it stares him in the face.

speakerposition: Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am right on point because in effect what I am saying motivated this debate. It was surely not the argument advanced by the opposition; its arguments were full of holes. Members of the opposition completely skirted the issue. I have indicated the reasons for the Alsands project being cancelled. They know the reasons full well. They know that Alberta co-operated with the federal government and recognized that it was impossible to go further than we went co-operatively. Hon. members opposite should recognize those facts. There must be another reason which caused them to disrupt the House and its proceedings since we resumed this session. Of course I am referring to the leadership difficulties within their own party and their inability to maintain SolidarityReturning to the question of the oil industry, there was an argument that the industry cancelled this project because of a difficulty- with cash flow. There has been a reduction in its profits this year over last year, but the profit in the industry in 1981 was $8.5 billion. "That ain't hay!" There are other figures which are of interest. Between 1970 and 1979, the last year for which I have figures, the industry spent $20 billion on exploration and development of resources. Of that, Canadian taxpayers paid $10 billion, or over 50 per cent of the expenditures for exploration and development.
Let us take the latest year, 1979. The profits in that year for the industry were $4.7 billion. Its expenditures for exploration and development were $5.4 billion. The cost to Canadian taxpayers for that exploration and development was close to $3 billion. When we consider the cost to taxpayers, we must remember that 61.7 per cent of the profits of that industry in 1979 were represented by tax expenditures generated as a result of its exploration activities. In effect, as Canadian taxpayers we put up 61.7 cents of every dollar which went into
oil companies in the form of profits in 1979. As the hon. members from the NDP admit, it is a result of government policy. We wanted to generate the kind of activity which has been generated in the oil and gas patch.
In 1981 their before tax profits were $8.5 million. Although there was a reduction, and there was a reduction in their percentage of profits, they managed to export from Canada over $956 million in dividends and interest payments. Nine hundred and fifty-six million dollars left the country from the profits of those companies.
At the same time, when you calculate that the number of proven reserves in the sedimentary basins of Saskatchewan and Alberta is close to 5 billion barrels, and that is multiplied by the value of today's barrel of oil at $25.75, you figure that the value of the oil in the ground is over $123 billion. That is a lot of money, and when I hear members opposite talking about financial difficulties 1 do not see where they are coming from when I consider that particular analysis. Also, that amount does not include Hibernia and the Beaufort Sea, nor does it include the heavy oil. It only includes conventional crude.
I merely say that the decision was made by the private sector. It was the proper decision under the circumstances. The hon. members opposite who support the private sector's wisdom shoud recognize that there was nothing that the government could have done besides what it did, which was to try to offer some way of keeping that project alive.
