speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think that anyone can be jubilant about the collapse of the Alsands project or the Alaska highway gas pipeline. It is an extremely serious situation for our country and no one can make light of it. I do not know how much partisan gain there is in it for anyone.
While I agree that these matters are serious, what is even more serious to me is that these projects, and a number of others which have collapsed or will collapse in the near future, due to the world economic condition, are based on the view that by launching enough megaprojects-approximately $400 billion worth by the year 2,000-the spin-offs will somehow solve all our problems. This is a band-aid approach to a very serious problem.
I am not saying that megaprojects are not necessary but that it is absolute lunacy to base one's country's whole industrial strategy on that approach. What disturbs me to a greater extent is that, while I criticize the policies of the Liberal government on these matters, I do not see any alternatives being proposed by those members to my right.
On the one hand we are told that the marketplace should determine what has happened, and in the case of Shell that is what occurred.
May 4, 1982

The hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte (Mr. McCain) says that, after all, the world oil prices will come down.
Up.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext:
The hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte has said during the past two days that there are indications that there may be an increase in the world oil price and an invigoration of the OPEC oil cartel. I am sure that I did not betray what he said. I would like to know how that hon. member knew that, while Shell Oil does not. That company is an internationally huge giant which has pulled out of Alsands at the same time that the hon. member for Carleton-Charlotte somehow knows that oil prices will rise and everyone will be happy again.
If you heard the speech of the Leader of the Opposition, it proves that both the Liberals and Tories have based their whole economic strategy on megaproject developments and their economic spin-offs as the key to industrial and manufacturing recovery.
It is our view that that confidence is misplaced for a number of reasons. 1 will try to outline a number of themes which have been heard before. It seems to me that this approach continues the export of resources at the expense of job creation in our manufacturing sector, something which has existed in Canada for around 50 years. What happens is that we export all the resources possible while exporting the jobs as well. The government adopts the band-aid approach philosophy which is to start the magaprojects as soon as possible in order to create many construction jobs. Many construction jobs are created, perhaps up to 40,000 on some jobs.
Is that bad?

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext: Not a bit. What I am saying, though, is that there is not a proper balance. Once those jobs are finished, what is left?
Seven thousand five hundred permanent jobs.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext:
There is nothing wrong with that either, but at what cost per job?
The other alternative is that if the same money is put into manufacturing-$4 million per job on a megaproject compared to $100,000 a job in manufacturing-it would be more beneficial. It would seem to me that the money used to create jobs in megaprojects is misplaced. I do not say that there is no need for magaprojects, or oil security, or protecting ourselves from vulnerability to supply cutoffs in international situation. What I am saying is that we are headed in the wrong direction when we go full bore for one project, the huge, centralized, capital intensive energy project.
We opposed the pre-build on the pipeline, and I will tell you why. There was no guarantee that the United States would ever fulfil its obligation. We saw what happened in the last number of days with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and his ironclad agreements. The Tories supported it, but Canadians got nothing out of it.
We had no guarantees in the Alsands project whatsoever, or for the Alaska highway pipeline that there would be Canadian
jobs or that the Americans would build their part of it or that we would even have Canadian content exclusive of import content. This same situation is happening in the Beaufort Sea and in the construction of drilling rigs and tankers. It is the same inane strategy which does not protect Canadian jobs. All it does is continue the complete dependency we have on exporting our raw resources.
We have called for an alternative stragtegy which at least should be considered. The government should not blindly and stubbornly carry on a policy which has resulted in the problems we now have. We know that the economic viability of many of the major projects is doubtful. The price of energy did not rise as was anticipated in the Alberta oil agreement. Within that agreement there was the anticipation of certain price structures rising in certain stages in world oil prices. We now have extreme interest rates, and difficult financing problems, combined with lower demand. Lower demand may be a result of high prices which would result in conservation. Obviously, if prices are high enough people will use less energy. That is one factor.
Megaprojects are collapsing around the heads of the Liberal government. The large coal plants in northern British Columbia are on the verge of collapse, but probably will not collapse because the current provincial government cannot afford to let them fail. They will not continue because of economic viability. No one is happy about this situation, but it is the reality.
The Conservatives ask us to look at the economic realities, but when we do address the realities we are called doomsayers or pessimists. If your whole strategy is based on megaprojects for the development of jobs and an industrial strategy for Canada, and that collapses, what do you have left? You do not have an alternative. We should be developing the alternatives far more. We should be putting far more effort into developing conservation and renewables. We are not doing that. We have a single-minded megaproject purpose that is capital intensive and, up until now, has been a flop.
The third point is that the Liberal government, and I do not think the Conservatives would be any different, has gone to extraordinary lengths to give incentives to private industry. Even those have failed. I do not have to remind hon. members of the speech by the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) about 65 per cent of the profits of the oil industry, almost a billion dollars last year, which was provided by the public.
Look at the PIP program, 93-cent dollars for poking holes in the Beaufort Sea and off Hibernia. I hope they find something there. It is a tremendous risk. We do not know what will happen to Dome Petroleum either. It sold a subsidiary the other day. That was to help the old cash flow.
We should be looking at the old cash flow all right. We have all kinds of money to give to the oil companies to provide jobs

May 4, 1982
and for them to find oil and that sort of thing. However, there is no money to lower interest rates on mortgages.
We do not intend to gloat about this business of the collapse of Alsands or the Alaska pipeline, all that fiasco. It is nice for us to stand here and say, "we told you so; you did not have the ironclad guarantees; you got what was bound to come." If North Slope gas is too expensive to ship to the Californias or the Californias do not want the stuff, why would any private consortium that is market-wise-they are not stupid or like socialists but are bright people-build a pipeline to carry that North Slope gas down the Mackenzie Valley if it is not economically viable? One cannot argue with that. They will not do that as long as they can get our gas nice and cheap.
We know the song about Canadian Hunter. What we do is say that we have all these gas rigs running around so we need some incentives for drilling. They say that if they are given a few incentives, they will get the industry going, but they have a cash flow problem. They go to government to get the incentive. They drill, and they poke a lot of holes, and find some gas. Then they find they have a little problem. They have all that gas and they have it capped.
The only way they can get anything out of the gas with their cash flow problem is to export it. After they export it, they need a little more incentive for drilling. They have exported all they had and again have a cash flow problem. What was done with oil will de done with gas. What was done with oil at a million barrels a day in the early seventies will be done with gas.
It is time that the government reordered some of its priorities. We are not opposed to Alsands per se, Syncrude per se, or Cold Lake per se. We are opposed to the lack of guarantees in megaprojects for Canadian workers, sourcing and content, when Canadians are putting up the bucks. That is all we ask.
The government should not be Santa Claus. It should get value for its money. We should have an equity return on our investment if we are going to poke the money in and not give it away. That is only sensible. Even those sitting to my right should agree with that, but they do not believe us. Maybe the shelving of these things is a blessing in disguise. Maybe the government will abandon this single-minded approach and look for other ways. Maybe it will seek other ways to create jobs for Canadians and not depend on the big ticket item.
Maybe the government will have learned something. I doubt it, but maybe it will have. Maybe we will give it equal opportunity now to lowering the demand side instead of always worrying about increasing the supply. Maybe we will put some money into the renewable fuels. We hear all the time, including from the minister's own department, how important it is that we have conservation. The cheapest barrel of oil is a barrel of oil conserved. That is what the government says, but it does not follow that. It does not put any money into that compared to what it puts into PIP. I will tell you what the government is going to put in. It may put in $5 million, SI25 million, $400 million a year or something like that, compared to $6 billion in the PIP program over four years. Give some of our energy-efficient manufacturers, the insulating people or
double window people, that kind of incentive, the 93-cent dollar in the PIP program, and watch them go.
We have the most energy-efficient housing industry in the world. Give that kind of incentive to those people and they will provide jobs that are environmentally benign. There will be jobs in Windsor, Vancouver, Ottawa and other such places. We would not then have to send welders and other workers up into the God forsaken north, off those islands or onto the extremely dangerous oil rigs. Think about that for a change. Let us have a little more balance in this.
Earlier this evening the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) tried to convince the House that the government has an admirable record of supporting conservation renewables. I cannot accept that. Let us look at the figures.
Here is the government's dedication to total conservation, $460 million per year. That is pretty good compared to what it was. The PIP program will spend at least ten times that much a year. We know where the priority is. Alsands is estimated to cost $13 billion. The Alaska pipeline, and maybe it should be called the Alaska pipedream, will cost $50 billion, the PIP program $6.5 billion, and the nuclear industry has already spent $4 billion developing the Candu which nobody wants. They cannot even sell it to Roumania. The Mexicans do not want it even though we will give them $6 billion along with each reactor.
What does the government offer? The free enterprise government of Alberta has offered 25 per cent ownership in Alsands, a bit socialistic I would say. A government like that buys Pacific Western Airlines. They would start things similar to the CNR and the CBC. Imagine that, 25 per cent ownership, and the feds put up 25 per cent. That is 50 per cent ownership for Shell and Gulf and PetroCan, and it was not enough. 1 can go into the details of the long-term financing and the other part of the offer, but it is obviously not enough. It is economically not viable in spite of that kind of generosity.
I do not blame the companies if they want to go on strike, but I do object to this. They went on strike in the case of Syncrude. They would not go ahead with it. I could give the details on that. I know they would fascinate you, Mr. Speaker. However, I will spare you of that. However, when it was all over in Syncrude, that 80,000-barrel-a-day wonder, the people of Canada put up 70 per cent of the money. In return they got 30 per cent of the equity. We want no more of that stuff. We have had enough of that. The government put up 70 per cent of the money and in return got 30 per cent of the equity. That is not enough. That is poor business.
I have heard a lot of catcalls from the romper room in the corner asking whether we are in favour of Alsands-is it necessary or not? I am not an energy expert, but we are committed to lay government. We have a lot of energy experts from Alberta. Virtually every member from Alberta is an energy expert. I do not know why that is. I suppose they are going to fight for their industry. I do not blame them for that. However, they are all experts. Everyone is an energy expert and a job expert. I am old enough to recall the Diefenbaker
May 4, 1982

depression. My father tells me about the R. B. Bennett depression.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Ask Les Benjamin about the Blakeney depression.

speakerposition: N.D.P. Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) is a little depressed; I do not know.
We do not have many experts in the House of Commons on many topics. We are not supposed to be experts. We have even fewer visionaries. There are certainly no visionaries on the government side. There certainly were no visionaries in the Economic Council when it advised the alternate energy committee last winter that by 1990 the low price scenario for oil would be $85 per barrel and the high price scenario would be $155 per barrel. If the government bases its decisions on that kind of vision, it is bound to get into trouble with respect to Alsands. Shell Oil Company will not get into trouble, but the government and the minister have been dead wrong on their estimates.
With respect to whether the Alsands project should or should not go ahead, if private entrepreneurs will not take the risk-even the minimal risk, in view of the latest offer by the Government of Alberta and the Government of Canada-then perhaps it should be shelved. 1 am not in a position to make that decision, but perhaps we should scrap it. Perhaps we should spend the money on enhanced recovery from existing wells. Perhaps we would be better to spend the money on the development of heavy oil, alternatives, renewables, or a thousand other things. However, let us not try to have it both ways. Let us decide whether the thing is worth it. If it is worth it, let us go ahead and, if Shell will not do it, we can operate it as a public utility. If it is not worth it, let us scrap it.

Mr. Speaker, I feel very sad indeed to be taking part in this emergency debate this evening on the demise of Alsands. I have been familiar with the Cold Lake project and the Alsands project for some time.
The Alsands project consortium applied to the Alberta Energy Resources Conservation Board for approval back on December 14, 1978, and the final approval for the project was given by the Alberta Energy Resources Conservation Board on December 21, 1979. 1 also remember that the application for the Cold Lake project was made in the fall of 1977. Why was the Alsands project not proceeded with within days after the approval by the Alberta Energy Resources Conservation Board on December 21, 1979? Why did the project not go ahead then? It was a very economic project at the estimated cost at that time. It did not go ahead because there was no agreement on oil pricing, and I will touch on that point a little later.
With respect to the Alaska gas pipeline, back in 1974 and 1975 I visited along the Arctic gas route to examine all the environmental installations which were being tested. It was the Berger commission which killed or sank the Alaska gas pipeline, and I will touch on that also a little later.
In the last 35 years the oil and gas industry in Alberta has grown by leaps and bounds, and both the provincial government and the federal government allowed the industry to grow and prosper. Indeed, both governments were very protective of the industry. The federal government was an ally of the industry back in those years. I was on the energy committee of the Alberta cabinet from 1971 to 1978, when I resigned. I was the only member continuously on the energy committee of the cabinet in Alberta, and I remember well how hard we fought to save Syncrude. We did save it because all governments cooperated.
However, we all know that the OPEC cartel started to set the price of oil and gas in the world in the middle 1970s. The establishment of the price structure in the world was transferred from the marketplace to political price setting. Indeed, the same thing happened in Canada. Our arguments as to how high the price of oil could be raised politically were many. I remember well the early arguments in the middle 1950s. Don Getty in particular said very clearly that the oil price would rise, then stabilize, and then drop. Most of us did not believe him, but I want to confirm today that he was right. Some thought that the price structure would just keep going on forever, and agreements were made based on price structures which were unrealistic.
As the price was going up, the Canadian government decided on two policies. I was a supporter of the government in 1979. The first policy was that the Canadian people would be protected from the world price. We all had different schemes and ideas as to how the price should rise and at what rate. I released a report. The Progressive Conservative government at that time had a remarkably good energy committee of caucus under the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) which put out a remarkably good report. As far as I know, that report was not even examined.
The second policy back in 1979 was that the federal government would get its share of price increases. The government simply said that the provinces and the industry could not handle all the extra money and that the federal government had to get its share. The government of those days decided that we would tax in the normal way, 18 cents a gallon at the pump, and we paid dearly for that. However, we said something else. As a government we said we would take 50 per cent of all the price increases above $2 a barrel.
What did that do to provincial thinking? The provinces felt that the federal government was coming in with a front-end royalty on oil and gas. The provinces got their dander up. Their hair was standing on its end, and they were prepared to fight tooth and nail. I remember sitting with the premier of Alberta, his cabinet, and some of the Alberta caucus. The tension was quite heavy because, for the first time, a federal government was introducing a royalty on a provincial resource. It was introducing taxation on crude oil at the wellhead. That happened in 1979. Many things have happened since.
If we had come to an agreement with the Government of Alberta back in 1979-and we could have-and if there had been some decent analysis on the part of ministers of the

May 4, 1982
federal government of the day and some of the members of that caucus, Alsands would be moving full steam ahead today, and so would Cold Lake.
But what happened? We were defeated on an energy policy of 18 cents a gallon tax at the pump. Some of us wrote to the people in charge saying that the tax should at least be split at nine cents a gallon per year for two years. Some of us said that the tax should be increased six cents a gallon per year for three years. However, we went forward with an 18 cents per gallon tax.
What really caused the difficulty was that 50 per cent tax on all increases above $2 per barrel because, as far as we in Alberta were concerned, that was a royalty. The PGRT is a royalty today, and that is the tax which has caused all the federal-provincial difficulty over the last several years. Certainly my provincial colleagues got their dander up, as I indicated earlier. They were adamant that they would get rid of such a tax.
Then when the new government came in and introduced its National Energy Program, what was its objective? Massively, it was to take money at the wellhead from the industry and recycle it in accordance with its policies, primarily to shift the activity from provincial lands to federal lands. Massive sums of money were to be shifted.
It was interesting that today in committee we spoke to Norcen. I asked Norcen how much of the PIP grants they would receive in the next 30 months, and they said some $130 million. How much were they to pay through the PGRT? They said that they would pay $20 million to $25 million over 15 months. However, they thought that their profits would be at least $40 million in 30 months. This is a massive transfer of money from some companies to other companies. That is the nature of the policy we have under the National Energy Program which we call Canadianization. When I look back to some of the letters I have written to prime ministers and to premiers concerning the energy matter since I came to this Parliament, I particularly like to refer to a letter I wrote to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the premier of Alberta on August 14, 1980, in connection with the Cold Lake plant. I wrote:
Your failure to evolve an acceptable long term energy pricing package and energy strategy for Canada prompts me to write this letter. The primary emphasis of your current negotiations has been on evolving a continuing oil and gas pricing formula as well as an appropriate split between governments and industry of the revenues so generated. Many Canadians are concerned that the negotiations have reached an impasse. The possible effects of the present impasse on the assurance of future energy supply for Canadians is of concern to every Canadian elected to office.
What particularly concerns me is the possible effect of the negotiating impasse on the approval and timing of the Cold Lake Heavy Oil project. It is critical that this project receive governmental approval, coupled with acceptable royalty and commercial terms, so that it may proceed. In my opinion, this project is, at this period of time, perhaps pivotal in assuring energy self-sufficiency for Canada beyond the year 2000. As you know, surface mining oil sands technology has been commercially established by virtue of the success of the Suncor and Syncrude projects. Subsequent surface mining plants are primarily based upon these two commercial successes. However, in situ extraction processes have not been proven commercially. Some 19 piloting proposals are in various stages of progress under the direction of the Alberta Oil Sands Technology and Research
Authority but the Imperial Oil Cold Lake project is the first attempt at commercialization.
The time frame on any commercial project is about 20 years-
How many people know that is from inception to its final production? My letter continues:
-from inception to completion and the second in situ commercial heavy oil plant is not expected until the mid or late 1990s. Therefore, the Cold Lake Heavy Oil project is the first of a kind. It is a critical technology that must be commercialized now. Recovery efficiencies, production costs, environmental implications are critical factors that must be commercially established before this vast resource can be adequately tapped.
That heavy oil resource amounts to approximately 50 billion barrels of oil.
The National Energy Program is a child which was eventually christened through the Alberta-Ottawa agreement. However, it was hatched and weaned, and in my estimation, by political ideology, by political greed, by political arrogance, by political ignorance and even stupidity. Let me just go through each of these briefly, if I have the time.
Political ideology; nationalization and Canadianization over such a short time frame are just unworkable. Certainly we can nationalize on Canadian lands and even Canadianize on Canadian lands because we are beginning and moving forward. However, when we stop to Canadianize the industry on provincial lands, that creates nothing but chaos.
I was in the oil fields in 1947 at Leduc when it started. I saw Atlantic No. 3 gush and then go up in flames. It is a very complex industry, and one does not turn it around overnight. There is no reason, like Norway or Australia, to require Canadianization requirements on Canada Lands. However, it is utter foolishness to try to convert an industry which has grown over 35 years and reorganize it structurally to Canadianize it in a very short time. Political greed, taxation and royalty levels are simply confiscatory and rob the industry of most of its cash flow. The industry in Canada simply decided to mark time, to hold its own, until some stabilization came to the energy policy in Canada.
Without self-generation of capital, and having to borrow capital to the extent of $13.5 billion for Alsands, the requirements for cash under today's economic policies are such that one needs $40 to $50 a barrel just to pay the interest on the money. How could a project of this nature go ahead in this economic and fiscal climate? It is no wonder it collapsed. However, it was extremely viable when indeed it was dreamed up, and when it came before the cabinet and the energy resources conservation board in Alberta. It was viable in its time, but politics killed it. It was the politics, not of one government but, rather, of several governments, which killed it.
I do not have much time left in which to speak, so I will not go into some of the others, such as political arrogance, political stupidity and so forth, because I want to say something about the Alaska gas pipeline.
The Arctic gas proposal was a very fine proposal to take both American and Canadian gas across Prudhoe Bay and
May 5, 1982

down into the Mackenzie River Valley. That project was studied over several years. Environmental requirements were gauged and tested every step of the way. Then the government-appointed Berger commission looked at this project. A selfmade messiah who was unsuccessful in politics decided that he would create a name for himself in history and he would kill the Arctic gas project. That was a project that was totally studied and 1 know because 1 visited most of the environmental study projects.
However, this Judge Berger, with the assistance of some self-professed technological experts, like the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell), decided to hold hearings up and down the Valley and killed it. Bob Blair, the opportunist that he is, and 1 know him so well, knew exactly when it was dying. This smart fellow, an engineer, said, "Oh, 1 will toss in a proposal at the very last minute", and he did, a proposal which was at least three times as expensive as the Arctic gas line. He tossed it in at the right time. Do hon. members know what happened? Without a single environmental or technological study, the federal government accepted that proposal. Down the Alaska highway, a complicated route of unbelievable proportion, with a Canadian spur line called the Dempster lateral, crossing three mountain ranges.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

How is it that you are talking to each other now?

Without a single environmental study the federal government approved a project of three times the cost, and yet people wonder why the United States hesitates. It is because the project never was economical. There is a much better route and I believe it is time, regardless of what the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) says, that the government took a look at the original route again. If the government simply took 10 per cent of the difference in the cost of the two lines, it could settle every land claim in the Northwest Territories; it would really be in the order of billions of dollars. It could set up a fund so that all the native people whould be particularly pleased-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, the hon. member has asked for unanimous consent to proceed. We are, of course, very willing to give it to the only independent member in the House. However, 1 wonder if he would explain whether he realizes that the route of the Dempster in traversing the Richardson Mountains goes through Rat Pass?
Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member is wrong.
That is not the first time.
No, it is not the first time.

1 understood it went through gopher tunnel! My difficulty is that if 1 get warmed up again 1 could go on for a long time on this issue.
I should like to say that this House has to make some changes to the National Energy Program and they have to be made in accordance with the motion I proposed under Standing Order 43 on April 29. When 1 put that motion I said;
I feel certain that, on reflection, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) will be pleased to second this motion.
I looked at the minister and he made no motion that he did not agree. Then I looked at Madam Speaker and she looked at the minister and the minister gave absolutely no indication that he was not seconding the motion. So Madam Speaker put the motion as if it was seconded, and if anyone reads Hansard they will see that Madam Speaker asked for consent and that some hon. members agreed and some said no. 1 wonder who said no, whether it was the Conservatives or the Liberals. 1 thought I had snuck on to the minister a terrific coup! My motion reads as follows:
That the government immediately (1) cut significantly the petroleum and gas revenue tax; (2) provide exactly the same incentives for exploration and development on provincial lands as is provided for Canada Lands under the petroleum incentive program; (3) drop immediately the retroactive 25 per cent ownership requirement on all Canada Lands:
1 honestly thought that the minister had seconded the motion because he did not jump up and say no; he did not shake his head and the Speaker put the motion. 1 hope he takes the matter seriously and moves to make some changes.
Today in committee I asked a representative of Norcen if they had a figure on the true cost of bringing oil from the Beaufort Sea f.o.b. Montreal. I am an engineer and we always make studies before we start to invest. The witness hummed and hawed and said it would be about $100 in 1990 costs.
How do they think they are going to bring that oil to Montreal on a profitable basis unless through massive federal subsidies-subsidies for transportation and boats, subsidies for loading and unloading stations, subsidies for exploration,

May 5, 1982
subsidies for development to a much greater degree than the government would ever have subsidized Alsands. The government is prepared to do it because it is a massive shift of activity from the provincial area to the federal government area. 1 think that is not fair, Mr. Speaker.
I want to speak briefly on megaprojects, Mr. Speaker, and then 1 will sit down. Megaprojects cost lots of money. When the Governor of the Bank of Canada appeared before the committee I told him that he was killing all the megaprojects and that the reason was that he was constantly juggling the three very important fiscal and monetary variables. One of these was the value of the dollar. He was varying it weekly, so why not yearly or every six months or every month? Thus the interest rate structure, the money supply and the inflation rate was bouncing. I said that under these circumstances there is no way a megaproject could be financed because they cost as much as $13.5 billion. You need stability for that, Mr. Speaker, so you must know what conditions will be five years or even ten years from now.
There is no stability in Canadian fiscal and monetary policy today at all. Megaprojects are dead. The only things that will be financed are projects that do not require much capital outlay and have a short period between beginning and production so that some of the money can come back. You must be able to get your money back in the shortest possible time in an era of economic instability. This means that we are going to have small projects in Alberta. There will be a small project at Cold Lake. In fact, if the federal government was really intelligent it would go to Imperial Oil and say that it wanted to fund that project totally as an experimental commercial project under that company's ownership and management. Someone has to commercialize that resource, Mr. Speaker. It is a fine resource-it has 50 billion barrels of heavy oil. It will be produced in little projects of 10,000, 20,000 or 30,000 barrels per day. The government would be acting intelligently to go along with Imperial Oil and the Alberta government on an experimental basis in order to commercialize that project.
I started out by saying that I was saddened, Mr. Speaker. I really am because I know how hard we worked on Alsands. I was responsible for choosing the town site and making the plans for the housing and infrastructure. We built a highway and we built a bridge and all that is down the drain now. It is indeed sad, Mr. Speaker, because it did not have to be that way.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to have the opportunity to join in this debate. This is the latest hour at which I have ever spoken in the House. It is late for us, but it is too late for the Alsands project.
As I sat and listened to the debate it is clear that the government has developed its strategy and taken its position. In the arguments made by the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola), the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) and the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey), there is the common theme that Alsands is not a great catastrophe and
really does not have much effect on the NEP. They said the industry would not take it up and it is the industry's fault that it would not go. When they make that argument, Mr. Speaker, they are denying arguments they have been making over the past number of years. They deny government documents and statements that are made; they deny what every Canadian knows the Trudeau government has stood for and has been saying for several years now, that the kind of economic activity these megaprojects represent will regenerate all of the things we have been gradually losing over the years in Canada-the economic progress, energy resource development, the things we have to have if we are to have economic recovery and renewal.
They are denying that now, Mr. Speaker, and in a way which I do not think can stand up to logic. It might stand up in the political argument they can and will be making in the days to come, but different writers-and we can quote as many as they have been quoting-are talking about the disarray of the NEP and the need for the government to look at its whole economic strategy and devise a new approach because of the failure of Alsands.
It is interesting to listen to the NDP right now because they are walking on both sides of the street, as usual, and we have not had a clear statement from them on whether they support this project or whether they think it is something we do not need. The hon. member for Mission-Port Moody (Mr. Rose) made several interesting comments. I know he has a lot of background on this and has spent a lot of time looking at renewable energy opportunities, but his comments would have to leave the listener wondering what he was really saying about this specific project.
The reality is, Mr. Speaker, that Canada's energy requirements demand that very important projects like Alsands and Cold Lake, indeed the piepline, whether it goes through "rat's pass" or "gopher's hole", be completed. Those kinds of projects can account for economic investment in Canada amounting to some $65 billion in the next few years. We have lost them because of the wrongheadedness of this government.
What is this resource we are missing? The hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) mentioned 50 billion barrels of heavy oil in Cold Lake. I know he was confining his remarks to that area, but really what we are looking at is a resource of possibly 900 billion barrels of oil in the oil sands, 250 billion of which are economically recoverable at today's prices. The development of that resource gave Canada the lead in technology which is being used by other countries, and we were developing these resources to meet our energy needs.
We are here tonight with a requiem for a tarsands plant. But beyond the economic investment what have we really lost in the last few days? We are holding an emergency debate and I wonder what Canadians will think of that. In fact, we have been at a constant crisis level with this government. We started out badly several years ago and it has just been getting worse. We go from crisis to crisis in such a way that I think people are becoming almost conditioned to serious problems. Whether
May 5, 1982

it is agriculture, home owners or the unemployed, we are in a constant state of disarray and crisis. That is unfortunate, but this example might be a good way of judging what the Canadian people think. Certainly we are seeing the political reaction from the Liberals, and it will be interesting to watch how that develops in the coming days because by itself it is enough to cause Canadians to defeat this government if they had the opportunity.
So what have we lost, Mr. Speaker? We have lost the technology which I mentioned. Beyond that, we have lost something in the national economy. A previous speaker talked about the effect of the loss of investment. We have seen the dollar drop in the last 24 or 48 hours by nearly one cent. People are looking for it to go lower. That has happened because of the understanding that people in the money markets around the world have of the importance of that specific project to our economy.
We lost not just at the national level, but also at the provincial level. Right across the country we have companies which would have thrived on the economic activity, and the economies of individual provinces would have benefited greatly had this project gone forward.
We have lost the opportunity in the reasonably near future to achieve energy self-sufficiency by 1980, which was important to the previous government and which has been taken up by this government as an objective. What did this specific failure really do to that objective? What it really means is that by 1990 we are going to be responsible for importing an additional 300,000 or so barrels of oil a day. We have had some grand projections, but all the government's projections show the oil from the tar sands and heavy oil deposits comprise a significant component of the energy self-sufficiency curve we are supposed to be on. That will be lost. No matter what our achievements are in conservation-a 7 per cent reduction this year, which is fine and dandy-in the long term, even though our total demand in 1990 may be somewhat less than it is now, self-sufficiency is going to have to include the tar sands and heavy oil components and they will not be there.
My crystal ball is no better than anyone else's; I do not know exactly what is going to happen in international markets, or whether we are going to have more difficulty than we have had in the past in obtaining supplies from other areas, but it is clear that an increasing proportion of our requirements is going to have to come from outside the country. That means increased balance of payments; it means increased insecurity in times of emergency. It means the line that was the Ottawa Valley is gradually moving west in spite of the fact that we have the reserves-if we could develop them-in the tar sands and in heavy oils.
Points have been made about the opportunities as far as Beaufort and Hibernia are concerned. I am sure the government will continue to make these points. However it is a
question of technology, whether it be the building of icebreakers, or the reason for the tragic sinking of the drilling rig off the east coast. Technology has yet to be developed in a way that will give us energy supply with a sense of certainty. Selfsufficiency in energy in Canada is in serious jeopardy now.
We have been talking about the megaprojects, megavisions, and perhaps the "microminds". All of these grand scale ideas have a common denominator that is important to Canadians. While they might be large projects, they impact on people and jobs. There are 100,000 people who are affected because of the job opportunities lost on these megaprojects. Those people are not just nameless blobs: they include students in school looking toward an engineering future or a future as control technicians trained specifically for these energy projects. We are looking at construction workers and all of the support systems required for projects like this. We are looking at employees in plants all across Ontario whether they are producing valves or steel, as in the riding of the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey). We are looking at jobs for countless numbers of Canadians. The projections are as high as 250,000. I do not know how many in total it would be, but if we do not start those projects and have a program that is able to continue, we have lost not just the investment, not just the energy security, but we have lost the opportunity for Canadians to be productive in their own country. That loss is a loss that even the New Democratic Party should understand, appreciate and for which they should be sorry.
The kind of planning the government has put forward has produced another loss with the tar sands plant. One member spoke about different situations around the world. He spoke about shales in the United States and projects in France. He mentioned that the Mexicans are not now going to develop a nuclear industry. But it is not that we might not be able to sell another Candu reactor to Mexico, on which we were counting; it is a question within this country of what kind of confidence business has. We must be cognizant of what kind of mood and climate there is for business, the way it looks at government, whether business is prepared to invest in Canada and Canada is considered a good risk.
The most powerful signal that anyone could get is the reaction of the consortium involved in the Alsands project. It has shown that there is no confidence among the business community. Business simply has no confidence in the kind of planning on programs which the government has envisaged. Procrastination has occurred in the government's planning program. Potentially that will affect the nuclear industry even at home because 40,000 jobs are at stake.
How many other industries or activities that have not yet been conceived are jeopardized now because of the lack of business confidence? How can Liberal Members of Parliament supporting government and government policy explain that while at the same time they talk about the rip-off perpetrated by the oil companies on consumers? How can Liberal Members explain why private investment in the billions of dollars has been flowing out of Canada at an extraordinary rate? Well over $5 billion in private investment in 1981 flowed out, quite

May 5, 1982
separate from the energy projects and the oil industry. That money flowed out of the country because there was no confidence here. This is just another example reinforcing what is already in the minds of people around the world-that Canada is not a good place in which to invest right now because of the government's attitude.
While we are looking at the losses we have had, I think we have come to the point in time when we have a requiem for a tar sands plant.
We cannot leave this subject without talking about the need to redefine what we have to do and what is necessary if we are going to avoid not just the loss of another megaproject but the continual erosion of confidence and the continual loss of the economic activity we need for Canada.
I do not want to leave things on a negative note. There can be specific examples in the energy area of things we could do. A small project in Cold Lake was not a bad idea. I believe that was put forward by the hon. member for Edmonton East. But I do not feel that it is adequate. It will not solve our problem. A small project like that, while serving as a reasonable example, will not restore the confidence of the business community or of Canadians in their country.
We have witnessed the introduction of the National Energy Program. That was followed by a budget and tax reform all on the same day. These measures have confirmed in the minds of Canadians that the government does not want to encourage investment. The government does not want Canadians to prepare for their own future. This government has taken away many of the options and opportunities that Canadians have as they work and try to build their own future. We need to restore those things. First, what we need is a new budget; there is no question about that. This is of paramount importance at this time. We need to do several other important things at this time. We need new and fresh ideas. There can be many specific examples within monetary and fiscal policy, but a new budget is the first part of a new process that we must have.
Second, we must have a new minister of energy. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) is in the United States now. If he stays in the United States too long he may start destroying their energy scene like he has destroyed ours. However, I have a lot of confidence that the Americans will not let that happen. However, I would not mind if the Americans kept him there for a while longer to give us a chance to recover.
He should go farther south.

He may feel more at home farther south. The next thing we need is a new Minister of Finance. The new finance minister will have to be accompanied by a couple of new top civil servants as well. Any new minister of finance will have to get off the track that is being followed now. The track we are on now is clearly not working. The present Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) has tried it for long enough now but so much of the restorative capacity has been placed in
jeopardy that we may not even have an opportunity to get back on track if we do not get rid of him quickly. Therefore, the Minister of Finance has got to go.
The final person who has to go is the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Shakespeare wrote in one of his plays that the fish starts to rot at its head!

Despite the specific actions of the Prime Minister which have caused confrontation and disunity, he is gradually uniting the country in its dislike of him. I am sure that if the Prime Minister were the final person to go it would be supported right across the country. It is important for this to come about quickly if we are to get on the track of economic recovery on behalf of Canadians.
I humbly request that Mr. Speaker use his good offices in some way to help us call an election.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take part in the debate this evening, or rather this morning, to say that I am sorry to learn that construction of the Alsands synthetic oil plant has been suspended. However, before speaking to the motion introduced by the hon. leader of the opposition, I would be remiss in my duty if 1 did not congratulate the hon. Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) for his gigantic and perhaps first class work during the last two years. While the minister has often been criticized, and severely criticized in the last few days by the opposition, the fact remains that the Canadian people are grateful for the energy policy he has formulated for Canada, especially as far as oil pricing is concerned. The suspension of construction at the Alsands plant does not jeopardize the energy policy of this government, and the Canadian public still has an advantage since the average price of crude oil amounts to 75 per cent of the world price and Canadian consumers still pay only 54 per cent of the world price for conventional oil.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians ask themselves one question at the present time: Will there be a shortage because of the suspension of work at the Alsands synthetic oil plant? The answer is no because Canada fortunately has other potential supply sources. The Alsands situation is regrettable, but we must now concentrate on these other sources, which will become more and more economically advantageous for Canadian taxpayers.
On April 30, the hon. Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources stated and I quote:
The new potential in the Arctic and the offshore areas is most encouraging, and we are still confident of reaching the target of self-sufficiency before 1990. We support exploration and development in these regions with our incentives and pricing policy. The large-scale exploration operations in these regions mean new contracts for the maritimes, oil equipment and related industries in Canada. As the traditional centre of the oil industry, Alberta, will receive considerable benefits from this activity, just as it will benefit from exploration for new oil in Western Canada, which is now as attractive as anywhere else in the world.
May 5, 1982

The minister went on to say:
Co-operation with the Alberta government will continue to be a priority and action will be taken to promote industrial activity in this province to compensate for the work planned by Alsands.
And the minister also stated:
Since the energy pricing agreement of September 1, there has been close cooperation between both governments and the final offer to the Alsands group was extremely generous.
The hon. Minister of State for Mines and Minister responsible for the Status of Women, who spoke earlier in this debate, gave the background of the joint offer which the governments of Canada and Alberta made to the companies of the Alsands group.
1 cannot go back to those details, however 1 must stress that despite the very reasonable and significant government offer, the companies did not find the project feasible in the current economic context, and the same situation prevails south of the border. All hon. members are aware that a few days ago Exxon suspended a gigantic oil deposit project in which it had already invested $400 million.
As mentionned by the minister, the financial challenge was too great at this point in time for the Alsands project to proceed, because the companies were reluctant to commit themselves, partly because they realized there were excellent alternatives, especially in the Canadian offshore areas. When the global economic situation improves, there will be an opprotunity to reconsider the Alsands and similar projects, perhaps within a year, as the minister stated. They could even be implemented at a lesser cost to the Canadian taxpayers.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I share the disappointment felt by hon. members and all Canadians who saw in that gigantic project a number of economic benefits, especially a great number of jobs. However, we all know there are limits to the sacrifices Canadians can make toward the implementation of such a project. The risks are too high, and the Canadian and Alberta governments did all they could for the Alsands project to proceed. Private corporations could assume no more risks, neither could the governments. And this by reason of the uncertainty on future global oil prices and interest rates. Private sector participants did not feel they could go ahead, even under the less risky conditions deriving from the Canadian and Alberta government offers. Canadians should not lose confidence in exploration and the revival of the Alsands project. In these days of special difficulties for the world economy, large energy projects are postponed throughout the world, even south of the border.
I referred earlier to the famous Exxon project. We have learned from experience that rapid changes in economic conditions are the rule rather than the exception. Economic circumstances might very well favour the Alsands project sooner than we think. Mr. Speaker, it should be noted that oil consumption declined significantly over these last few years in Canada. 1 learned this afternoon there was a 17 per cent
decline in the consumption of heating oil in Canada and a 7 per cent decline in crude oil during 1980. Moreover, 200,000 home owners used the heating oil substitution program. It is important that Canadians be made aware of these facts in this debate. Despite what the opposition may say about the government energy policy, Canadians can boast of paying less than the world price for their gas. In a few provinces of Canada, the price of gas per litre is much higher than, for instance, in Quebec. If a Quebecer pays more for gas, it is not on account of the Canada-Alberta agreement on prices paid to producers but as a result of the provincial tax recently decreed by the Minister of Finance. I see that the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) is looking at me when I say this, but he could have explained earlier why the price of gas is higher in Quebec than in the other provinces.
Also, under the Canada-Alberta agreement, natural gas will be made available in Eastern Canada, including Quebec, especially in the Gaspe Peninsula at very reasonable price. It is important to recall those steps taken by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Once again, the hon. member for Joliette could have mentioned it in his speech instead of asking for the resignation of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau).
Mr. Speaker, the expansion of the present networks of gas pipelines as well as their extension in new areas such as the Gaspe Peninsula will stimulate industrial development. It is a long-term development and we feel that new jobs will be created in depressed areas thanks to the gas pipeline. I see that the hon. member for Joliette is nodding, it will be built but it will take a few years. I said that it was a long-term project.
I would therefore say, Mr. Speaker, that the energy policy designed by the minister and the government deserves more praise than criticism.

Because I know that the hon. member who will rise after me and even the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) are not likely to say anything new, Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to remind the House that today is still May 4. Although an effort was made to advance the date on the calendar, 1 want to say to those who are responsible for that that we are still at the same time we were yesterday when the Progressive Conservative Party started this debate and that it has made no progress since, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I realize that it is getting late when I see that the ideas of my hon. friend have fallen asleep. It is now 12.45 a.m. and today is May 5, and we have merely adjourned the ordinary business of the House to deal with a very important issue. If the hon. member cares to have a look at Standing Order 26, he will see that we may even sit this afternoon to debate this motion and that the time will not be eight o'clock yesterday.

May 5, 1982
Would the hon. member allow me a question?

Not at all. In this respect, the hon. member might rise after me and make his own remarks.
This Alsands question is merely a symptom of the times. It is only the culmination of a situation which has been brewing over the last several years.
There are many things which I and my colleagues from the province of Alberta could demonstrate have happened over the past 18 months since the declaration of the National Energy Program, that ill conceived, dastardly raid by a greedy federal government on the petroleum resources of the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia. Ever since the commencement of that program we have seen a decline in cash flows; we have seen the government go back on its word to Suncor, for instance, with regard to the price of its synthetic crude; we have seen taxes at the wellhead imposed by the Government of Canada through the petroleum and natural gas resource tax. As well, we have seen the leaders in the petroleum industry have their profits drastically cut back.
Of course, that fact does not worry members of the New Democratic Party because according to them the leaders of the petroleum industry should not make any profits whatsoever. Those NDP members do not realize the expenditures which must be flowed into research and development projects for each subsequent year in order to develop new resources. Where will that cash flow come from?
What are they doing in the United States right now?

The hon. member who just intervened has displayed his obvious ignorance of, and the attitude of members from central Canada toward, the oil industry. What are they doing in the United States? It is Canadian drilling firms who are in the United States. There are 260 drilling rigs, both seismic and original, which went south. I can show the figures from the Canadian Oilwell Drillers Association as to the number of rigs which are operating in western Canada. There are only approximately 440, with some 70 which are sitting idle, far more than any previous year.
We have had nine out of 35 heavy oil equipment trucking firms going bankrupt in the past few months. In my constituency I have seen three long-established heavy equipment firms go bankrupt since November. One of the largest firms in western Canada is reputed to be on very shaky ground. I hope that is not true and the denial is correct but I have heard the story.
However, this is symptomatic of the problems which exist today. My colleagues from Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour), Edmonton North (Mr. Paproski) and the member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) will all attest to the fact that in our city, wherever there is an industrial patch in which there are oil industry supply and service firms, it is shameful to see
the number of "out of business" and "closed" notices. They are a shameful reminder of our economy today.
We have seen these small Canadian business firms go bankrupt. Did the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) have any concern for the damage the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) was wreaking throughout western Canada among the oil supply firms? No, not one bit. It is where the government's concern should be. It is not the Exxons, the Gulfs, the Texacos or Shells who are taking the worst beating. They are taking a beating but they are big enough to survive. You see that when you cut off, super-tax or pillage an industry. You cut off the cash flow. Then there is trouble. Even a company controlled by the Government of Canada, Panarctic, cancelled plans for two offshore drill rigs. That put 750 men and women out on the street in Edmonton, that one stroke of the pen.
The hon. member does not know that Alberta, Edmonton in particular, leads Canada in the construction of drill rigs that are sold all the way to Australia. They are put into operation in the North Sea. They are built for export. This is the scale that has been developed by Canadian workmen and women since the start of the oil play in 1947. At that time we did not have a welder who knew how to do anything with an oil pipe. With a lot of hard work and a lot of movement by Canadians into Alberta under Americans with know-how and money, the industry was built up in Canada. In just two years the Government of Canada has knocked it to its knees. Why? Because it was so money-hungry.
Ralph Hedlin wrote a very interesting article in the May 3 edition of the Alberta Report, page 16. I will read a couple of paragraphs:
A year ago, more or less, an Ottawa newspaper reported an interview with Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau. Self-sufficiency in crude oil, said Mr. Trudeau, could be achieved through any of several routes. Alberta could cooperate or not. Canada's oil supply world, on that euphoric day, was seen to be simple and manageable.
"Trudeau said he would work around Alberta and Premier Peter Lougheed if necessary to make Canada energy self-sufficient. The Prime Minister said he needn't use the federal government's declaratory power or give in to the western province to move the country closer to supplying all its own energy needs.
'I don't have to choose either,' said Trudeau. 'If that were the only choice it would be very, very difficult. Fortunately there is another possibility. We look toward Hibernia, we look toward the Beaufort, we look toward the high Arctic.' "
In this scenario incremental Alberta production wasn't necessary. There were many strings to the oil supply bow. Given the Beaufort, the Arctic Islands, given Hibernia, Alberta could peddle its papers; oil supply was seen to be easy. A year later the options had defined themselves more precisely in this prime ministerial scenario. The Arctic Islands are still promising for those able to wait a couple of decades. The Beaufort is probably commercial but a maze of regulatory processes have to be threaded before oil deliveries begin. The game, clearly and inevitably, must include Alberta and it must include the east coast offshore.
Then we get a description of the Prime Minister's fight with Premier Peckford and the people of Newfoundland. That is not going to go the Prime Minister's way. Therefore, it comes back to Alberta, but only belatedly. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources along with the province of Alberta made a one
May 5, 1982

minute to midnight offer to Alsands. It was done at the very last minute, but it should have been done much earlier.
Because of whom?

Because of the intransigence of the federal government. May I say that in this offer there are considerable concessions from the last budget under the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax Act. Those are the things that caused the problems all along. It started back in the days of John Turner and when Donald Macdonald was minister of energy. They laid down what the Government of Canada would take out of the petroleum industry when the OPEC countries started. They laid down the punishing gas export tax. They are the ones who put on this damm fool subsidy which costs Canada billions of dollars every year, paid for by the export tax which was taken out of the oil industry and the pockets of people in Alberta and Saskatchewan. It was also a tax on the rest of the people in Canada.
Progressively we saw taxes added to the price of fuel. Canadians paid a tax to encourage people in central Canada to consume more oil and gas. It culminated in the performance of the Liberal party in the 1980 election over the excise tax.
There is one Liberal in the House.

That is how much they care. However, I see my good friend from Valleyfield here. Outside of him, the Liberal party is not interested in what has happened to western Canada, and western Canada is not interested in the Liberal party. It has shown that in federal elections and provincial elections, and I can guarantee that the Prime Minister and several of his ministers almost require a visa in their Canadian passport to visit those western provinces. That is how welcome they would be.
About 18 months ago members on the government side were very proud to be twinned with western Canada constituencies. They would not dare go out there now. However, they were supposed to find out what the people thought. They have not listened. They do not want to listen to western Canada.
I could read miles and miles of statistics about towns like Brooks, Lloydminster, Drayton, Fort McMurray or Grande Prairie. When we go into these towns we see vast unemployment. The trucks have to be sold at auctions at a quarter their value because the operators cannot afford the heavy licence fees and heavy finance payments. A big truck costs perhaps $150,000 or $180,000. Try financing that when there is no work or very little work. In the cities, service firms, restaurants, catering companies and others are in difficulty. The hon. member from Valleyfield and other hon. members can say, "Well, come and see some of our shoe towns and some of our furniture towns". We have never refused to go and see them. We know they are in trouble. However, what they refuse to understand is that the policy of this government has deliberately put those towns in the same position. And hon. members opposite wonder why there is alienation, why people are
concerned and why today my leader insisted that there be a motion to adjourn the House for this debate. I wish hon. members opposite would come in and listen.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: They are all gone.
But no, we see a dumb insolence across the way. There is total neglect.
It is your day.

That is why there is frustration among my colleagues. If hon. members would just come in here, we could have a very worth-while dialogue. I would be interested in listening to them talk about their problems in the furniture industry, in the shoe industry and in the textile industry. We do listen to them. They do not realize it, but we hear them.
You support textile and shoe imports.

The hon. member is reading my mind. He has never spoken to me about this. He would not know what I think about these things. He has never talked to me about them. What he is talking about right now is just a lot of nonsense, with all due respect to our friendship.
You import Ladas.
I have a Canadian car.
I hope I go to Dieppe.
I will show the hon. member some good ways to get into Dieppe, right over the beach. It is a terrible reflection that in this debate-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. gentleman but his allotted time has expired.
Mr. Speaker, with all due respect, I think the hon. member should be allowed five minutes more.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
