I speak for my party.
Mr. Speaker, I will not abuse this beyond two minutes; otherwise I might place too much emphasis and too much value on those interruptions.
It is good to be friends.

What has to be done? The conventional oil industry is more than satisfied with the proposals put forward by Premier Lougheed whereby there will be a remission of royalties and an increase in certain incentives.
Speaking of incentives, 1 want to put the lie into the mouth of the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) when he says that incentives paid to oil companies as a result of activity are moneys paid out by the Government of Canada. That is nonsense. That is an utter fallacy. If there were not any

May 5, 1982
activity, there would not be any allowances. There would never be any income earned, so therefore incentives do not cost the Government of Canada one blessed penny because there would not have been any work done in the first place. The program put forward some two or three weeks ago by the Premier of the province of Alberta offers some help. It restores a degree of confidence. After all, this government does not know what confidence in the oil industry means. The government upset the industry once before with a white paper on taxation. It took three years to get things back on an even keel after that Benson white paper on taxation in 1968. It will take time to turn the industry around. Unfortunately, some more firms will have to go under. Time is against them, and people cannot live just on time.
Alsands would have been great, but what we have is a culmination of a tremendous effort by a government which knew not what it was doing. It was wrecking an industry because of an insatiable desire and greed for funds and power as it attempted to socialize the oil industry. Canadianization was nothing but another word for socialization.
1 hope our friends across the way will read some publications. I will supply them with factual, intelligent descriptions of what is happening in the petroleum industry in Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia. Let those who have some goodwill and intelligence read and understand. Then we in Parliament will have accomplished our task. We will have convinced the government that it has been in error and that this is a hairshirt Canada has fashioned for itself.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Supply and Services have resorted to an old barristers trick of confession and avoidance. The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey) has done that too. They say, "Yes, but look what happened elsewhere. We are no different from the others". That is a poor way out of this situation. Let us see what we can do to turn it around. Let us have faith with what Premier Lougheed was trying to propose, and let the Government of Canada participate in a similar type of program. Then we will believe the government; but until then it is out to lunch and cannot convince anyone of its bona fides and its interest in governing us in western Canada.
Mr. Speaker-
I will stay for my good friend!

I am delighted to see the hon. member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme) here.
It is a privilege to be able to participate in the debate this evening and also to get on so early. A while back we had a similar debate which went through the night and into the morning. I believe I rose in my place to speak at about ten minutes to seven in the morning, so I thank my colleagues for allowing me to speak a little earlier.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: You are more important now.
It is because of the high esteem in which we hold you.
My colleague says it is because of the high esteem in which my colleagues hold me. I do not know if there was gentle sarcasm in that!
No way!

Back in 1980, just over a year ago, the government unveiled its National Energy Program. At the beginning of the book outlining the government's strategy were introductory remarks by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) entitled "An Energy Program for the People of Canada". In light of the recent collapse of a major segment of the program, I feel it would be more than appropriate to recall some of the emphatic, self-assured statements by the minister concerning this grandiose scheme. I quote:
This is a set of national decisions by the Government of Canada. The decisions relate to energy.
They will impinge, however, on almost every sphere of Canadian activity, on the fortunes of every Canadian, and on the economic and social structure of the nation for years to come.
They have major, positive implications for the federation itself.
How prophetic, in a way not anticipated by the government, these words have become.
Because of these "national decisions by the Government of Canada", the fortunes of Canadians have indeed suffered. The economic and social structure of the nation has been dealt a devastating blow, now and for years to come. With the failure of Alsands, the very serious problem of western alienation will only increase and result in major, negative implications for our federation.
Also included in the self-congratulatory opening comments were the following remarks by the hon. minister:
We are second to none-and in many respects we lead the world-in the techniques and the organization required for the exploration and development of primary energy sources.
The government described itself as second-to-none. With its record in matters of energy being lowered to match that of its record in matters pertaining to the economy, 1 would agree that this government is unique; unique in a uncomplimentary form; unique in that, according to the dictionary, the government has no equal; unique in that no other government in the world today, given the resources and potential of this nation, has made such a mess of governing. In this it is unequalled.
Canadian expertise, the government said, was internationally acclaimed and such expertise would enable Canada to contribute in aid of others less fortunate. With the massive problems connected with the government's energy pricing policies and now with the collapse of Alsands, we will be making a contribution of our expertise, but not in the way intended. Most Canadians who are expert in the energy field have already moved out of the country and more are following week by week.
Referring again to the minister's opening remarks in the introduction to the National Energy Program, I quote now the
May 5, 1982

first of the three precepts which dictated the federal government's action:
It must establish the basis for Canadians to seize control of their own energy future through security of supply and ultimate independence from the world oil market.
It is very well known that whenever this government starts to seize control it has a habit of repeatedly choking its victim to death.
To put into perspective what has happened, I turn for a moment from the remarks of the minister back in 1980 and quote from today's issue of The Toronto Sun. Laura Sabia, an outstanding columnist-
Oh, oh!
Yes, that is quite right. But for a little ill luck, she might have been sitting in this very chamber today participating in this debate. We hope to see her here following the next federal election.
Hear, hear!

Laura Sabia states:
Friday, April 30th, will long be remembered as "black Friday". On this date was scuttled the $13.5 billion Alsands megaprojet. Into the scrap heap went the possibility of over 50,000 jobs, plus spin-offs for the steel, construction and manufacturing industries and an infusion of $450 billion into the economy. Gone, our hope for self-sufficiency in oil by 1990.
Not only did the Alsands go down the drain but the Alaska gas pipeline was delayed for two years by the oil companies and may never be built at all. Two hefty blows in one day, courtesy of Pierre Trudeau's disastrous leadership, Marc Lalonde's arrogant National Energy Program and Allan MacEachen's calamitous-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. 1 would remind the hon. member to refer to other hon. members by their constituencies, not by name. Order, please.

Your Honour must appreciate that I was reading the editorial from the The Toronto Sun, and those are the words in the article.
Mr. Speaker, I think these three could go down in history as the "demolition trio". There is no question about that. I heard the story going around Parliament today that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) has been discussing with the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Lamontagne), believe it or not, some assistance for Argentina. Therefore, they will send our three most devastating destroyers to Argentina-Trudeau, MacEachen and Lalonde. If they do not put Argentina on the rocks, nothing will.
Oh, oh!

The column went on to say that the federal government has lost all credibility and is incapable of governing. A passage worth repeating states:
It is incapable of governing. It has lied and deceived the electorate. It promised cheap gasoline and gave us the most expensive on the North American continent. It promised us the Alsands and the Alaska pipeline and scuttled both by stupid policies and arrogance beyond measure.
This reference to arrogance, a well-known trait of this government, leads me back to the second of the federal precepts for a National Energy Program. This one stated such a
program must offer to Canadians, all Canadians, the real opportunity to participate in the energy industry in general and the petroleum industry in particular, and to share in the benefits of industry expansion.
The government, promising that, under its National Energy Program, Canadians would share in the wealth, has created a situation in which Canadians give up what little wealth they have left. For Canadians, participating in the energy industry has meant higher prices for gasoline and home heating oil. It has meant that over two thirds of the cost they pay for these energy products goes toward taxes.
Again, let me remind the House that in December, 1979, when the Clark government was defeated on the proposed 18cent gasoline tax, the then leader of the opposition, the Prime Minister of today, went around the country saying that an 18cent a gallon tax was astronomical and terrible and that if he and his government were returned to office, there would be a ceiling of 14 cents a gallon for gasoline tax. We know what the story is today. We are now paying upwards of $2 a gallon. I am quite sure that the electorate of Canada would love to have second thoughts and the opportunity to vote again.
Participating, as I mentioned earlier, means buying Petro-Canada, with tax dollars, at four to five times the market value and paying additional tax dollars to complete the deal.
We now come to the third great theme behind the government's now crumbling energy program. The minister said in 1980:
It must establish a petroleum pricing and revenue-sharing regime that recognizes the requirement of fairness to all Canadians no matter where they live.
Just over a year later, this magnificent vision has become transformed into an opposite and depressing reality. The reality of the government's concept of fairness has been to impose a series of special taxes and levies, price increases which do affect all Canadians, no matter where or how they live. And how you live is often more important than where you live. Those least able to afford this peculiar brand of "fairness" are the ones who pay a greater percentage of their income in taxes to support it.
Speaking of fairness reminds me of a story which I believe I have mentioned before. A little boy had just entered school for the first time. He came home looking very glum so his father asked what was wrong. He said, "I don't like my teacher, she's mean." The father said "What do you mean, she's mean?" The boy brightened up and smiled at that and said, "She's mean but she's fair-she's mean to everybody!" I could say that the government is mean but it is fair-because it is mean to everybody.
In 1980 the government described its National Energy Program as a means of making more efficient use of energy for Canadians by Canadians. It was to be a means for bold, decisive steps, not generalities, for practical programs, not just

May 5, 1982
ideas, for rapid and concrete measures to resolve problems, not just pious hopes.
In 1980 the government said that the program meant security, opportunity and fairness. Those were fine-sounding words and I presume everybody was elated by them. In 1982 the government's National Energy Program means insecurity, lost opportunities and unfairness. In just a few short months the government has dropped the torch of energy self-sufficiency that it began carrying so high and so proudly and Canadians have third degree burns as a result.
When the government said that through its national energy policy it was going to set the country on fire, that was not just an analogy. Unlike the legendary Phoenix, the Canadian economy may not rise easily from the ashes of this latest government fiasco.
In its panic and haste to divert attention from the Alsands disaster the government, in addition to down-playing the consequences of the loss of the megaproject, has suggested it would get other projects going using money and concessions offered in the eleventh hour salvage attempt on the Alsands. The reaction of industry has been cool, to say the least. A spokesman for the Esso project at Cold Lake, Alberta has been quoted as saying that the generally unfavourable economic climate, coupled with the severe drop in the oil industry revenues resulting from the National Energy Program, makes it difficult, if not impossible, for that firm to contemplate resurrecting the Cold Lake project. The reaction from industry should come as no surprise-once burned, twice shy!
Having laid waste the economic base of one province, the government has been focusing its attention and its evil eye on the potential base of others, this time in the east. This is what the government means when it says that it wants to practise fairness to all Canadians regardless of where they live.
Our philosopher king, who obviously lives in the clouds, has spent most of his energy on the patriation of our Constitution and his Charter of Rights. We are now masters in our own house, he proclaims, as he pirouettes in glee. He does not care that the house is heavily mortgaged, that there is little food on the table, that most of the occupants are out of work, that the neighbours are angry, that the security devices are obsolete and that the foundation is crumbling. The response to another thunderstorm, another catastrophe, is another shrug from him. The contempt this government has for the people who pay its way seems boundless. The leader of the government, of this arrogant band of purse-snatchers and pickpockets, should not be allowed to continue his coy musings about retirement. He should be forced to retire, and naturally his cabinet should join him in exile. "Throw the rascals out" is an appropriate cry.
Hear, hear!

I will admit that there are some pretty good members on the other side, but it is those who got us into this mess that I am talking about. The unfortunate part is that some of the good guys have to go with the bad guys. That is the way it has to be.
Thank you!

The loss of the Alsands project is only one of the many disasters to hit the country under the rule of this government. I do not think this country can bear much more.
The Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) who spoke first in this debate for the government said that the demand for oil is not as great today because of the 7 per cent reduction in its use at the present time due to conservation, insulation and other things. I believe she is partly right, but another reason for the reduction in the use of fuel oil is the atrocious price that we pay for it. We are all aware that there is a glut of oil in world markets and that the price is going down as a result. The price has gone down drastically for our neighbours to the south. I believe that in some western states gasoline is selling for under $1 per gallon, but here it costs over $2 and is going up.
What can we look forward to? A bill was given second reading just a week ago which would give the government the power to add 58 cents per gallon to the price of gasoline and fuel oil, at its discretion.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: And without parliamentary approval.

I guess they will get that at third reading. This is another thing that Canadians can look forward to. I can assure you that will be a step in the right direction toward conserving oil even further.
It is a well known fact that people on low incomes have turned down their thermostats because they cannot afford the cost of heating. I suppose they wear sweaters and socks in the house in order to conserve fuel and still remain reasonably healthy.
We know that we might as well be talking to the wall as talk to the government. It does not have the guts to let the Canadian people decide. It has another two years in its mandate and we can be sure that it is not going to do much in that time.
Three ridings in this country have no representation at the present time, Mr. Speaker. If the government does not want to call a general election and defend its policies, the least it could do is call three by-elections within a reasonable time and test its popularity that way. We hear the minister say all the time that the people are behind them. They are a long way behind, Mr. Speaker, and they are not going to get any closer! Those three ridings, Leeds-Grenville, Timiskaming and Broadview-Greenwood are now vacant-

May 5, 1982
Why doesn't the hon. member talk about the tar sands? He didn't say a word about the tar sands.
The hon. member should read my comments. I certainly spoke about the tar sands or the lack of them.
Tell him again, Stan. Don't let him get away with that.

We are well aware of the tar sands. I am not an expert on the tar sands but 1 know the damage that has been done. Many of my expert colleagues from Alberta have put on record the figures which show what the government has done with respect to the tar sands.
You visited them, Stan.

Yes, I visited them on two or three occasions and 1 was absolutely amazed and thrilled to see the operation. To know that the expansion is now going to be phased out is certainly a tragedy. And this government has the responsibility for it. It is the old story of put off and put off. If this deal had been made two years ago the oil companies would have grabbed it, but no. This is the greatest government for putting things off; the former minister of national defence can certainly attest to that. 1 sat on the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence for a number of years. I spoke on this subject in the debate last Thursday and pointed out that through procrastination this government has left the Canadian Armed Forces in the worst shape they have ever been as far as equipment is concerned. We were promised six frigates about eight years ago, and where the hell are they now? Still on the drawing board. I am quite sure the former minister will say that the earliest they will be in the water is 1988, and probably 1989. The estimated price, talk about squandering money, was about $1.4 billion. It is now $4 billion, and what will it be by 1988? Probably $7 billion. This is just another example of a government that is squandering money and not doing what it should when it should.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise and speak on this motion. 1 commend the Chair for allowing this debate. It is important because of the simple fact that the government's economic strategy is based on these energy megaprojects, and the government expected them to stimulate the economy. That stimulus is essential at a time when we have close to two million unemployed, if you consider those Canadians who have given up looking for work out of despair and in recognition of the fact that the jobs are just not there. But now that has all gone by the boards and we have a situation of the highest unemployment rate since the depression, and inflation continues to rise.
That, Mr. Speaker, is really something which is new to industrialized economies. Traditionally, when unemployment rose, influence would fall. But now we have both evils together. High interest rates hurt the average Canadian, the small businessman, and in fact they have been a contributing factor to the destruction of these energy megaprojects. What we have today is a bankrupt economic policy which has led to high
unemployment with no let-up in sight. Not only was the economic strategy of this government based on energy megaprojects, but so was the economic policy of the last government. In fact, the famous, or shall we say infamous, remark of the former minister of finance, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) about short-term pain for long-term gain was simply a statement about energy resource development and the attempt to ride the wave of increasing world energy prices to prosperity.
Ever since it came back into office this government has attempted to build an economic strategy based on increasing world energy prices. It has just not worked, Mr. Speaker, because it is based on false assumptions. Somehow they got the notion that energy prices were going to continue straight up and the government could thereby increase its revenues and solve the deficit problem. They could create big energy projects and stimulate the economy to provide employment. However, world energy prices simply have not followed those straightline predictions, and it is rather ironic that the two free-enterprise parties made the same error in judgment. They did not take into account that world energy markets are not static and that rising prices would themselves bring on new sources and change the whole price picture.
The government also underestimated the impact of conservation. It did not realize that individual Canadians would take action by insulating their homes, driving smaller cars and driving less. They did not take into account the full impact of individual conservation efforts, and that threw off their whole strategy with respect to these energy megaprojects. The government has, in fact, misread the entire economic situation and built its vision of the future on false assumptions, on a misreading of world energy markets and an underestimation of the capacity of Canadians to conserve energy. They even misread the industry's capacity to finance these large projects because they did not take into account the impact of their own policy of very high interest rates. This policy is, of course, one that was followed by the previous government as well.
Rather than have governments which rely on the exports of natural resources to create employment, rather than a policy which relies upon a few very large projects to stimulate the economy, what we need is an alternative plan of investment, and we need it now because the economy needs stimulus now and the people need jobs.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I want to take some time to outline an economic strategy which the NDP has already unveiled to the Canadian public, and which we call a new employment option for Canada. I want to outline it in detail because I want people to be aware of the fact that there is another approach to economic matters, and that it is possible to stimulate the economy to create jobs in a very real, sensible and sane manner. The proposal which my party has outlined really consists of five basic steps. The first step is really a matter of economic planning, of planning for job creation in Canada. The notion here is that the government will negotiate seriously with multinational corporations to have them sign production

May 5, 1982
agreements with Canada in which they would ensure that goods were produced in Canada to service the Canadian market. In other words, if a multinational corporation wanted to have access to the Canadian domestic market, it would have to manufacture in Canada and produce goods in Canada. The corporation would have to take our natural resources and process them into finished goods for the Canadian market. We would make sure that companies understood we were serious about their manufacturing in Canada if they wanted to have access to our markets in order to make a profit. Companies would gain access to our markets based upon their willingness to manufacture in Canada, in other words, to create jobs in Canada. The first part of the new employment option for Canada would be to negotiate seriously with multinational corporations in order to create employment in Canada and not just take advantage of our market without doing any manufacturing here at all.
The second plank of this new employment option for Canada would be aimed at the export market. What we would be seeking to do would be to underwrite the risks that entrepreneurs take when they enter into the export trade. Other governments, such as West Germany and Japan, make available to companies and entrepreneurs capital to underwrite certain risks. We should be doing that in Canada. Canadians are some of the greatest savers in the world. We put aside much of our income in banks and in other financial institutions. We should use this capital which Canadians create by saving in order to underwrite the risks faced by our exporters. Comprehensive coverage of production, credit, accident, commercial, exchange rate, inflation and market development risks should be provided. This is already provided by countries such as West Germany and France. It is time that Canada took the export market seriously. We should have a comprehensive plan to underwrite the risks of exporters so that we could capture a greater share of the international market in order to provide jobs for Canadians.
The third plank of our new employment option for Canada involves tax cuts. We propose a tax cut for low and middle-income Canadians. The purpose of this tax cut would be to stimulate demande in the Canadian economy so that the presently underused capacity of Canadian manufacturers could be used now when there is a need for jobs. Therefore, by providing a tax cut for low and middle-income Canadians, we would put more dollars in the pockets of ordinary Canadians who would spend that money and thereby create demand for goods and a possibility for Canadian manufacturers to provide jobs for Canadians.
The fourth plank in our new employment option for Canada is an excess profits tax on banks. The reason for this is that banks have been benefiting from the very high interest rates presently prevailing in Canada. They have the capacity at the present time to pay excess profits tax. By imposing this tax we could take the revenue raised by the tax and invest it in a housing program in Canada to meet the much needed housing needs. In the process, we could create further employment. We could take part of the excess profits tax and put it into some
system of mortgage relief, as has been done by the new Manitoba government. The new Manitoba government has provided direct mortgage relief for ordinary Manitobans. An excess profits tax on banks could provide the revenue necessary to provide this necessary mortgage relief for ordinary Canadians right across Canada.
The fifth plank of our employment option for Canada relates to interest rates. Quite simply, it is time that we had a made-in-Canada interest rate to remove the threat of very high interest rates for small-business men, farmers and ordinary home owner. Any person who reads the financial pages of Canadian newspapers knows that there are many economists in this country who indicate that the present interest rate policy is far too high, that there is room to move the interest rates in this country downward, and that the present policy of this government of keeping very high interest rates is not justified on the basis of economic factors alone.
Those are the five points of the new employment option for Canada as proposed by the New Democratic Party. This employment option really comes back to the fact that we need to take our natural resources and process them here in Canada. We need to create manufacturing jobs here in Canada. It is not enough simply to take our rich natural resources and sell them off to other countries, whether south of the border, to Japan, or wherever. It is necessary for us to take hold of the wealth we have here and to process it here in order to create the kind of employment we need in the country. At a time when we have close to two million unemployed, if we take into account those who have stopped looking for work as well as those who are on the active unemployed lists, it is a time to adopt a new, different and aggressive approach to economic development in Canada, an approach that is based on the fact that Canadians have the education, the capital resources and the intelligence to manufacture goods in Canada. It is simply not necessary to give away our natural resources and our manufacturing jobs to other countries. It is time that we saw the possibility of manufacturing in Canada. We should also remember that manufacturing is not only done in Ontario, but that it is also done throughout Canada. If we took an intelligent approach to the creation of wealth and employment in this country we could have very strong centres of manufacturing in all regions of Canada. It is not necessary to leave all the manufacturing to one region of the country. We could make some rational and some intelligent choices so that every region of the country had a fair share of the manufacturing potential that is Canada's.
It is fortunate, indeed, that the Chair has allowed this emergency debate with regard to the energy megaprojects. It is important because this debate gives us an opportunity to point out the bankruptcy of the government's economic policy which has been based upon resource giveaways and based upon one or two very large energy projects. Fundamentally these energy projects were based upon false assumptions about the energy markets of the world and about the continued behaviour of individual Canadians. This debate really shows that the
May 5, 1982

economic strategy of the government is completely bankrupt and that it is time to find new ways in which to stimulate the economy. The energy megaprojects will not be here to stimulate the economy. We must have a rational plan of investment to stimulate the Canadian economy and to create employment. There is no greater need in the country today than the need for jobs for ordinary Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, it is approaching 2 a.m. on May 5 and we are almost in the same position we were in two years ago when we were debating the National Energy Program. It is sad that it has taken this long to discover that the policies of the present government are leading us fast down the road to high inflation and high unemployment. Also it is sad to think that the present government campaigned in the 1980 election by promising to create policies which would wrestle inflation to the ground, create maximum employment for Canadian people or less unemployment, and stimulate the economy so that it would recover from what it perceived to be a problem when we were in government.
Liberal mismanagement, namely in the National Energy Program, is creating major problems in my area of Peterborough with Canadian General Electric and in Oshawa with the General Motors Corporation. We must remember that there is no greater user of trucks and truck bodies than Alsands and similar projects. The government has created a policy which has driven the private sector out of the country to find areas in which it can develop in a free enterprise system, free of government intervention.
A leading editorial which appeared in a Toronto newspaper yesterday really summed up the situation. It reads:
We all know some of the villains in the megaprojects fiasco. Alsands is dead largely because Prime Minister Trudeau and Energy Minister Marc Lalonde wanted to play at being bigtime businessmen. That's what the National Energy Policy is about. Getting private oil companies out of the field and government oil companies in their place.
It's fun being a businessman based in the PMO's office. You get all the advantages-big limos, private planes, big big deals-and none of the disadvantages. Like using any of your own money or facing shareholders' meetings.
Eventually the taxpayers run out of money and the government runs out of rhetoric. Then the deal that should have been offered private oil companies in the Alsands project is finally offered them, except it's several years and God knows how many broken promises too late.
The companies don't trust the government and the megaprojects go belly up. All we can say is that if the Alsands deal offered was fair last week-it was fair two years ago.
1 know all these matters disturb members of the government because they have to return to their constituencies and justify why there are 1.25 million people out of work and why the inflation rate approaches 13 per cent when last month the Americans were in a minus position. They must explain why all these people are unemployed when they promised in the last federal election campaign that their programs would create jobs and lessen unemployment. This is simply not the case, and they have no logical explanation whatsoever for the disastrous situation in which the country finds itself. They can use all the
verbiage they want. They can spew out $70 million in advertising, using the money of taxpayers, in an effort to convince Canadians that their policies are working, but the bottom line is there and it will always be there-if people are unemployed, if they cannot put food on the table, if they are losing their homes, if they cannot adjust to economic policies which are creating high inflation and high unemployment, and if the agricultural community is facing the highest rate of bankruptcies it has ever faced, the government will not survive. The people will eventually realize that they have been literally hoodwinked.
Even the briefest review of energy and industrial opportunities awaiting the country, not only in the west but in the north as well, would impress and persuade anyone of the government's present folly and inexcusable mismanagement in letting these opportunities slip through its fingers. Month after month, year after year, Canadians have awaited an energy policy and an industrial development policy which truly match and do justice to the potential of the country. The size of the immense projects, highly touted by the government a mere six months ago, is truly awesome and together they are worth more than $400 billion. This size is only matched by the immensity of the blunder of the government in failing to get the ball rolling in the industrial energy sector.
Apart from this inexcusable lapse on the part of the government, a lapse which should demand the resignation of every minister involved, Canadians have faced record rates of gas price increases since the Liberals came into power only two years ago. The significance of rising gas prices and the loss of these megaprojects have not been lost on Canadians. We actually have a government in office today which told Canadians just two years and a few months ago that they should not re-elect the Conservative government because it was about to raise the price of gas by 18 cents. The assurance of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the campaign at the time was that he would not raise the price of gas in excess of 14 cents. Those were his words. What has he produced? What are the results of the campaign promises of Liberal members in 1980?
These Liberal sheep on the other side of the House-and I notice that they are all fast dispersing-have presided over one of the most divisive political and economic rifts between the provinces and the federal government the country has ever witnessed. Now they have pretty well scuppered the most important industrial project in Canada this side of 1990. The chances of Canada ever becoming energy self-sufficient by 1990 are fast disappearing. Hostilities between different parts of the country, between business and labour, and between government and corporate concerns have been fostered, encouraged and even initiated by this guilty government.
What makes this most hurtful to Canadians who care about the country is that these animosities need not exist. 1 am sure my colleagues from the west will support me when I say that there exists an interdependence of feeling or a mutual atmosphere of co-operation among all working people and their families right across the land. There is nothing which unites these people more right now than their frustration with the

May 5, 1982
absolute lack of pragmatic and practical initiative in the field of industrial energy development on the part of the Liberal government.
In October, 1980, when we were debating government mismanagement of the energy sector in Canada, I said in the House that the people of my riding of Peterborough and all those who live in the industrial heartland of Canada could see very clearly that what is good for the oil producing provinces is very good for the so-called consuming provinces. The government might also wish to ask an Ontario worker whether he would care to choose between losing his job because of lost orders to his firm, because it has gone under or because it has given up on a misguided and ill-thought-out energy program. It is a national energy program that has been pursued for political reasons and which has resulted in a great opportunity being lost.
I know that the workers of one Ontario company, which made the bucket wheel reclaimers for the Syncrude plant are a few of many who will be thrown out of work because the government has not been able to get Alsands and Cold Lake on the track to maintain their business. In my own riding of Peterborough, that city's major industry, Canadian General Electric, depends very heavily on our energy sector. Recently, I spoke to a representative of Canadian General Electric which employs over 4,000 people and he told me that any expansion in any area where electricity development is involved will benefit Canadian General Electric. He said, "Our whole market is based on the expansion of industry, and the more developments and capital investments there are, the better it is from our point of view." The better it is for virtually every company in Canada from our point of view. Obviously there is a tremendous ripple effect which would have occurred had Alsands gone ahead.
Why do you rejoice about it?

There is no rejoicing on this side of the House, Mr. Speaker. We are not here at 2 a.m. on May 5 to debate the National Energy Program because we are rejoicing about it, as the Liberals are. We are here now because the Liberals do not care.
It is not just Canadian General Electric or the bucket reclaimer manufacturers who are affected. It is also those factories which produce motors, industrial controls, wire and cable and many other products for the resource exploration market. I am sure that the hon. member on the other side has some industry in his riding-at least I hope he does-which is not suffering from the loss of Alsands through the ripple effect. If he does not have an industry, let him stand up when it is his turn to speak, and if he has enough nerve to speak to his constituents, let him tell them that the loss of Alsands and the Alaska pipeline means absolutely nothing to Canada because then he will be saying what he is saying in the House.
That is the problem. The Liberals do not repeat what they say in the House when they return to their ridings to explain the loss of Alsands. Surely I should not have to impress upon the hon. member-now there are two out of 145 Liberal members sitting on the other side representing Canadians from coast to coast-
No, no.

I very seldom take exception to anything one of my colleagues says, but I will tell you that I am a member of Parliament for Peterborough and I represent constituents from coast to coast. The problem is that very few of the Liberal members on the other side of the House are here. They know there is an emergency debate. Sixty per cent of them were present during question period at two o'clock this afternoon and less than 3 per cent are in the House tonight at 2 a.m. to take part in this debate. This debate is the result of action taken by the Liberal government, not by the Conservatives. The hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry (Mr. Laniel) has sat in his place all night and said nothing. I hope he will rise to speak.
I will be here all night.

If he wants to ask me questions in his 20 minutes, I will be very pleased to answer them.
It should not be necessary to impress upon this government the fact that losing the chance to develop the tar sands industry and the pipeline industry in the west, or indeed any other project in any part of Canada, is holding up industrial development and causing economic insecurity in the whole nation. That is very clear to everyone on this side of the House. I fail to see why it is not clear to every member on the government side and in the other opposition party. 1 am sure, however, that NDP members are more receptive to the loss of jobs than hon. members opposite. It is time that members in the government began to speak for the people they represent in their ridings.
I believe that Alsands alone was going to be responsible for approximately 129,000 barrels of oil per day-barrels which are still imperial. If those 129,000 barrels a day are converted into gallons, and if we converted that loss to see the money which is flowing out of Canada because of the cancellation of Alsands, we would find that we have lost $13 billion worth of capital to create industry and feed companies such as General Motors, Canadian General Electric and many other companies across Canada. If the hon. member does not care to admit it and just continues to sit back smugly, he will be held accountable at the time of the next federal election.
Eighteen months ago we told this government: "The Cold Lake project alone accounts for $10 million a month in running, development and support costs. Imperial reckons that this can continue for only four months at the outside under present Liberal government policy." That was 18 months ago.
During the debate earlier this evening I heard purportedly responsible people on the government side, as well as some from the NDP, trying to rationalize the removal of the oil
May 5, 1982

companies from the Alsands project by saying that the companies could not justify the investment. Why then are they investing that money in exploration and development in the United States of America? Why have they pulled money out of Canada and invested it in other places? If you listened to the press conference given by the principals of Alsands, you would have heard them state the reason. They said that one of the principal reasons they were pulling out of Alsands was the political climate. That climate was not conducive to investment and the injection of private capital.
If the hon. member has any experience in the business sector, which I hope he has, he will know full well that one would not invest one nickel in the business sector today if a return was not foreseen and there was fear of government expropriation. Business people are not prepared to invest money while there is fear of expropriation by a socialist government.

I would like to thank the lone government member in the House for agreeing to extend my time.
Let us discuss the Ontario economy. We are not only trying to develop the west. I wish this government would get it out of its head that anything that happens in the west benefits only the west. The loss of Alsands has cost millions of dollars to the province of Ontario alone; $6.2 million of that would have accrued directly to Ontario. The impact of Alsands alone on the Ontario economy would have been enormously helpful. For example, $800 million would have gone to the iron and steel industry in Hamilton, $730 million would have gone to the metal fabrication and machinery industries in Toronto, $740 million would have gone to the manufacturing and processing plants of central Ontario, $325 million would have gone to transportation equipment, $370 million would have gone to finance industries and $750 million would have gone to trade and services, and this is only a partial list.
I am sure that any member opposite could stand up today and talk about the spin-off effect of the loss of the pipeline. Ask the minister from Hamilton how many jobs that will cost Stelco and the city of Hamilton. I am sure he would inform you it is a terrific loss of jobs. It will create much unemployment in the peninsula and in the automotive industry in Oshawa in the riding of the Leader of the New Democratic Party. It will create acute problems in my riding of Peterborough with Canadian General Electric. This is a fact that is known by every political leader. If he is honest, he will report, first, that these two losses are a major contributing factor to unemployment and, second, that the major problem we have today is dissatisfaction with the present Liberal government. I know it pains the other side to hear about the only truly practical, sensible and workable budget that has been introduced.
In conclusion, it has been my personal misfortune to view over the last couple of years a series of legislative measures all of which come under the general heading of the National Energy Program and all of which have resulted, to one degree or another, in the situation we have today. What in fact this present government has imposed on Canada to the country's cost is a plan which will convert this nation into an impoverished, socialist state. It is doing this through its national energy policy in concert with various acts of Parliament. These acts have transferred exploration recovery incentives to Canada lands, for example. It has reduced the share of revenues to the oil companies by some 12 per cent, companies that have now quite properly put a halt to all further development and have shifted their teams to other parts of the world. They have decreased incentives and subsidies to those companies that have minority Canadian ownership interests. This will lower these companies' market values and thus make a takeover bid by the federal government easier in the future through the Canadian ownership account.
At the same time, the Liberal government sought to increase the proportion of oil and gas revenue it receives from the provinces. As nationalization of the oil companies increase, provincial revenues decrease because federal oil companies do not have to pay provincial royalties no matter where they are located. Consequently, the federal Liberal government is determined, along with its partners to the left in this House, to nationalize the Canadian oil industry by 1990 and put it into public ownership and not, as they maintain, forge ahead in industrial development and obtain self-sufficiency. Let us admit and let this government admit clearly that it alone is singularly and totally responsible for losing Alsands and the pipeline.

Mr. Speaker, in the summer of 1980 I was in Ottawa looking after some matters in my office. I happened to bump into a member of Parliament from Quebec at the entrance to the Parliament Buildings. We stopped in front of the door and chatted. He had just returned from Washington where, along with some other members of Parliament, he had met some American Congressmen. They have discussed the energy problem facing the United States and Canada. He said the Americans told them that if we did not move to the world price for oil, we would be the only country in the western world which had not moved in that direction. They forecast that if we did not move that way and did so rapidly, we would have a very serious problem with our energy pricing two or three years down the road. How prophetic those words were!
I asked him at the time what he was going to do about it. I will not identify the member. He is a good friend of mine, a Liberal from across the way. He named the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), something I cannot do under the rules of the House. He said that until we rid ourselves of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Energy, Mines and

Resources, we are not going to get anywhere with oil pricing or energy self-sufficiency in this country and we are going to be in trouble with our energy program.
I am not surprised he said that about the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. I am sure everyone remembers the oil pricing formula that he gave when he was energy critic. I will quote him in case anyone forgets. He said:
If the price of conventional is X, you will have a price of X plus Y for the nonconventional oil, and then the international price-you know what it is-but we have indicated we will continue to subsidize the price ... So what you would end up with would be a mix of these prices.
What does that mean? That is what he said. It was quoted in The Globe and Mail. Therefore, it is not surprising that we have to rid ourselves of that minister.
In question period on Friday, April 23, I told the Prime Minister that I would donate $1,000 to assist him in his adjustment to retirement if he would go. He replied that it sounded something like a bribe. I was serious. I said I did not even want a tax receipt for it.
A strange thing happened today. First I should say that when I was home on the weekend dozens of people approached me and asked me whether I was serious. When I replied yes, they wanted to donate money to this fund. Today I received a letter in the mail. Believe it or not, it came by courier from Kelowna, British Columbia. It reads:
We read recently that you had offered $1,000 to Prime Minister Trudeau to help him adjust to retirement, but that that was rejected.
Perhaps the amount was too small. With this in mind we decided to help out in our little way. We accordingly enclose cheques in your favour totalling $15- sorry it is not more but you will probably receive further contributions from other enthusiastic citizens across Canada.
This money is to be held by you to be given to Mr. Trudeau if he resigns as Prime Minister by November 1st, 1982-repeat 1982-and publicly says he will not run to replace himself. If this has not happened by that date then the money and any income accrued on it is to be given to the federal Progressive Conservative Party to assist in its expenses.
Hear, hear!

"This combination of a severe reduction in internally generated funds-which in turn affects a company's ability to borrow-and weakened investor confidence makes the accumulation of large-scale funding, through equity or debt, extremely difficult.
"For instance, any fiscal terms that could be struck for the Cold Lake project today would be purely academic, no matter what rate of return these terms created. Imperial simply doesn't have the money to invest on the scale required. For the same reason, and also because of a general lack of investor confidence, it would be very unlikely that we could find other participants."
