Another financial analyst, Mr. F. B. Lamont, managing partner of Richardson Securities of Canada, Winnipeg, said the federal government's National Energy Program must be changed because it is a major contributor to Canada's present economic and financial malaise. He said that besides heavy taxation, the NEP is based on suppression of prices to Canadian producers and a subsidization program that favours imported oil at the expense of Alberta production. He stated, as reported in The Globe and Mail, dated April 28, 1982:
We have been subsidizing the import of foreign oil out of the public purse to the extent of $17 billion annually. This is more than 20 per cent of our national debt. Indeed, the interest on the money we have borrowed to subsidize oil prices at 15 per cent is $2.5 billion annually, more than the entire 1981 budget of the Province of Manitoba.
This gives some indication of the dimension of this tax. He went on to state:
It is impossible to understand how Draconian tax levels, suppressed prices and subsidized consumption of foreign oil are consistent with the strategic importance of Canada's oil industry, conservation or self-sufficiency.
The tragedy is that the challenge of self-sufficiency is slipping away from us altogether. A survey on the recession in Canada as the result of the turn-back of many of these megaprojects and other disastrous effects in Canada has recently appeared in The Globe and Mail under the byline of Peter Cook. I will just read a couple of excerpts wherein he stated:
A comparison of leading indicators shows Canada's economy to be in a more pronounced recession than the rest of the industrial world, and suggests any improvement in business conditions will be delayed and could lag behind other major economies.
The findings run counter to assertions by federal Liberals-made after last weekend's Cabinet meeting at Meach Lake-that the economy's troubles spring from international difficulties and that little restorative action is possible.
He wrote that a study of several economies conducted by Geoffrey Moore, of the Centre for International Business Cycle Research at Rutgers University:
-rated Canada as the only economy where the decline was continuing to register in the leading economic indicators series in the first months of this year.
Mr. Moore stated:
"What we saw in Canada was an index which has reached a new low, whereas in the case of the United States, our leading indicator series had levelled off'-

May 5, 1982
The Rutgers study reported that the European economies, led by France and Britain, were in a recovery stage in January and had been pulling back from a recession that hit bottom last year. Japan's economy was even more buoyant, with its leading index rising 10 per cent annually, while Canada's position had worsened. In the first half of the year, the Canadian economy had fallen as fast, if not faster, than the U.S. The article continues to show that the information must cross the aisle to hon. members of this House who argue that we are part of the world economic problems, and there is nothing much we can do about it. It shows that other countries have done something about it. They have turned their economies around and are on their way up.
I do not know how many hon. members deal on statistical comparisons but, in 1968, Canada's gross debt was $32.5 million. Government spending has gone up from $12 billion in 1968 to an estimated $75 billion in 1982, according to the projected budget. If we look at a series of statistics taken from Statistics Canada and from the government papers which come to our office, we notice that there has been a decline of 16.5 per cent in industrial production averaged over the past three months. There has been a decline of 33.8 per cent in the production of trucks from a year ago. There has been a decline of 15,000 jobs in the level of employment in Ontario. There has been a decline of 127,000 jobs in the manufacturing sector in Canada since August of 1981. There was a decline in the corporate profits by 44 per cent in 1981 in the fourth quarter. There has been a decline in new motor vehicle sales of 24 per cent compared to February of 1981. There has been a decline in car production to the lowest level since 1967. There has been a decline in real housing investment, predicted to be 7.7 per cent in 1982, and there has been a decline in the number of housing starts of 15,000 units as the direct result of the recent budget.
To show that everything is not on the decline, I will give hon. members some examples of increases. Perhaps that will make them feel good. There has been an increase in the rate of unemployment. It is 9 per cent as of March, 1982. There has been an increase in the rate of unemployment in Alberta from one half of one per cent to 5 per cent in one month.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his allotted time has expired.
Carry on.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: I just have a few more items to add to balance up the declines.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I see two hon. members rising, and the allotted time of one of them has expired. Therefore, I must remind the hon. member that as long as two hon. members are standing, I must recognize the one who has the floor. The hon. member's time has expired, so I therefore recognize the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Masters).

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. However, in deference to my colleague opposite I would be pleased to give him
an appropriately short amount of time in which to give his summation.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
As I was saying, if there is an increase to balance up these declines, I must tell Your Honour that there has been an increase in the rate of unemployment in Alberta from one half of one per cent to 5 per cent in one month. There has been an increase in farm bankruptcies by 157 per cent in the first three months of 1982 over the first three months of 1981. There has been an increase by 86 cents a gallon for gasoline since the Liberals took over with promises of keeping gasoline prices down. There has been an increase in mortgage rates to 18 per cent or 19.5 per cent from 15 per cent to 15.5 per cent a year ago. There has been an increase in the current account deficit of $8 billion to $9 billion as compared to $1.9 billion. There has been an increase in bankruptcies of 33 per cent in the first three months of 1982 compared to the first three months of 1981 and there has been an increase in inflation from 12.5 per cent on an annual basis in 1981, which has been the largest annual average rate of increase, I might say, in the last 33 years.
The various presidents and chief executive officers of the oil companies have said that as well as onerous taxes imposed upon them by the National Energy Program, they have lost investor confidence. I suggest that the reason that confidence is lacking is the terrible economic performance of the government.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Masters (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Communications):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before I comment on the subject at hand I must say that I have a feeling of deja vu, being here at 19 minutes to three in the morning. It seems only a short time ago that there were very few of us in the House and we seemed to be all on this side with our few faithful servants of the House of Commons. At that time hon. members opposite were doing whatever they were doing for 14 days while the bells were ringing. Perhaps they were catching up on suntans and things of that nature.
Mr. Speaker, I have a point of order. The hon. member implies that members on this side were not working. Mr. Speaker, we were attending committees.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know I do not have to reply to that point of order. I did not imply anything. I simply said that we were here and we were all alone, for 14 days. But that is a red herring and this is a very serious debate. It is an opportunity for members on all sides to air their views and perhaps come up with new ideas and new initiatives. I hope it will help set the record straight.
On the weekend I had some very interesting discussions in my riding. People in the Thunder Bay-Nipigon area, like other Canadians, are disappointed that the Alsands project is not

Hear, hear!
May 5, 1982

proceeding at this time. Northwestern Ontario has many resources, one of which is gold. There was a time when gold mining in the small town of Beardmore where I was brought up, was a great thing. There were three gold mines. Then they closed-not because of government policy but because the price was not right. All of a sudden the price of gold is rising dramatically and the mines are re-opening after being closed for 30 or 40 years.
My point is that the marketplace is at work in the instance of the Alsands proposal. This is borne out by people such as a senior official of Exxon who commented on major projects of this kind in an interview shown on an American television station. This gentleman was part of the free enterprise system-and 1 happen to believe in that-and he was asked why Exxon and other oil companies are backing away from projects. His response was to the effect that the projects take an immense amount of capital and they cannot wait too long for that capital to come in. He pointed out-and this is true in the Alsands case and the pipeline that has been delayed for two years-that they had to put too much in for too long without the certainty that it would come back within a prescribed period. He said, as most Canadians with logical minds know, that things have suddenly changed. Two years ago we knew that we were running out of oil very quickly. That has not changed but the time-frame has changed.
A number of things have happened, Mr. Speaker. We do not consume the product as quickly as we once did due to a downturn in the world economy. That has helped to bring the price of oil down and it has had an effect on projects such as the Alsands.
Hon. members opposite have made light of conservation but in Canada and in the United States, and indeed all over the world, conservation has had an effect.
Energy comes from many sources, Mr. Speaker. We are beginning to see what happens when we use more coal. 1 know that my colleagues from British Columbia and Alberta are happy that more coal is being used and that more will be used all over the world in the future. That, too, will decrease the immediate need for oil in this country.
Hydro plants, nuclear powered, conventionally powered and steam powered, are coming into production and are adding to the total supply of energy. We are beginning to make much better use of natural gas, and that is a good thing.
All these things are part of the reason why the private sector has elected not to go into the Alsands project at the moment, even though they concede that the federal government and the government of Alberta have made very generous offers.

Why didn't you say that
two years ago?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
I keep hearing this reference to two years ago but although I do not profess to be as learned as my colleagues opposite, it seems to me that the implications were there then. If I were in the private sector and were going to put down so much money for such a long time I would want to know what
5.0. 26
is going on-are we bringing in more oil from conventional sources? Are we finding that offshore resources are coming in very quickly? Even more than two years ago technology was beginning to show that there was the possibility of gaining more oil from reserves that we could not get at or that were thought to be uneconomical in the past and so, with the increase in oil prices at that time, it seemed that perhaps we had better go slow on this important project. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, there will come a time when the Alsands and pipeline projects will continue. But to blame the delay on the NEP, or this government or that government, is to say that the private sector is not at work and is not the most important player in the game. I happen to have a great deal of respect for the astuteness of the private sector, and I think that thinking Canadians recognize that this resource which remains in the ground-although we would rather it was turning out all the jobs we want, and all those other things-is still there to be developed in its time. We thought its time had come, but unfortunately it has not because of a number of different reasons.
I wanted to intervene in this matter, Mr. Speaker, simply to try to give an overview which I think even members opposite recognize is the basic truth of the matter. You cannot tell me I am that far off base when we see that Exxon has cancelled projects around the world, as have the French and so many other countries. They have said, "Hold on, these projects are very expensive and we do not really need them right now because we cannot afford to tie up that amount of capital for that much time".
Why?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext:
The members opposite ask why? What they are really suggesting is that they are joining their friends at the other end of the House who are saying, "Let us do it all; if they will not do it, we had better do it for them". The whole concept of the Alsands project was to give the private sector the maximum opportunity to exercise their right in the free enterprise system to make such a development. The only other way it will work, Mr. Speaker-and if I were leading the country I would be tempted but I would certainly back off- would be to take billions of dollars out of the public coffers and make this thing work because of the spin-off effect. But that is coming out of the public purse, not the private sector, and when the private sector knows the time is right, they will make it go. We are prepared to work with the private sector and we have proven that, and so are the producing provinces, particularly Alberta.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, 1 keep hearing members opposite saying it is government policy, it is this and that. The country to the south of us has a slightly different system but they have the same problems and exactly the same thing has happened there.

Tell us about the Australian megaprojects.

May 5, 1982

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext: They do not have the same kind of plan which seems to be so objectionable to these people. I think in the final analysis, Mr. Speaker, the NEP will put us in the position we really want to be in where we are self-sufficient in energy. I know that will happen. I think we will also be able to do it in the Canadian context because we will have enough control of it to make it go the way we want it to go and make us less dependent on other parts of the world. So I hope, with all the rhetoric-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext: -which has been let loose in this House, that somewhere along the line members opposite in their private moments will recognize that basically the private sector rejected the Alsands proposal. I do not criticize them for that, I am sure they had good and honourable reasons, but the bottom line is that it was going to cost too much and take too long to get a return. With the change in the world situation they were not as certain about the project as they would like to be, and so they have backed off at this time. The oil remains and will be developed when its time comes. We on this side will make darn sure that we are prepared to work with the private sector to bring this project to fruition.

Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome the opportunity to participate in this emergency debate, but quite frankly I do not believe members on the government side really appreciate how serious the economic situation is in Canada today. About 12 years ago the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had this to say in an interview while discussing his efforts to change the course of the ship of state. He said:
One has to be in the wheelhouse to see what shifts are taking place. I know that we have spun the wheel and I know that the rudder is beginning to press against the waves and the sea . .. but perhaps the observer, who is on the deck and smoking his pipe, or drinking his tea, sees the horizon much in the same direction and doesn't realize it, but perhaps he will find himself disembarking at a different island than the one he thought he was sailing for.
We have landed, Mr. Speaker, on a differnt island than the people of Canada ever anticipated 14 years ago when the Prime Minister was first elected to office. We have landed on an island where unemployment rates are the highest since the depression of the 1930s. We have landed on an island with double-digit inflation and where gasoline is $2 a gallon and going up. At the same time, gasoline across the border is about half our price and going down. We have landed on an island where interest rates run anywhere from 17 per cent to 20 per cent and higher. We have driven hundreds of millions of dollars of investment capital out of our country. We have farm, business and personal bankruptcies. We have budget deficits in the range of $16 billion and a gross national debt of some $137 billion. The amount required to service that debt amounts to more than the entire budget for this country at the time when the present Prime Minister took office. There is a feeling of frustration and pessimism in the business community, indeed in the hearts and minds of the public generally. I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister was in the wheelhouse but he was not alone; he had the Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent) and his followers on the ship with him.
They were helping him chart the course, and they were stoking the fires to keep the engines going and move the ship towards a socialist state.
When the finance minister gave his budget speech on November 12 he filed a document entitled "Economic Development for Canada in the 1980s''. I would like to quote from page 2 of the document, which was prepared by an ad hoc committee made up of the Hon. Allan J. MacEachen, chairman, the Hon. H. A. (Bud) Olson, vice-chairman, the Hon. Herb Gray, the Hon. John Roberts, the Hon. Pierre De Bane, the Hon. Ed Lumley and the Hon. Lloyd Axworthy. The first paragraph on page 2 reads as follows:
The decade of the 1980s holds great promise, offering opportunities of unprecedented magnitude and the potential for lasting benefits from economic renewal to Canadians in every area of the country.
The leading opportunity lies in the development of Canada's rich bounty of natural resources.
The next paragraph reads:
These developments will involve massive investments in productive capability and in the transportation industry's capacity to ship bulk commodities. The recently published report of the Major Projects Task Force, for example, identifies $440 billion of potential projects, predominantly in the energy and resource sectors, which are under consideration for investment between now and the end of the century.
Energy and resources were the sectors that were to offer the opportunities of unprecedented magnitude and potential. They could have done so. But what happened? The government brought in a national energy policy, a policy that was supported by my friends on my left, the New Democratic Party. It was a policy which virtually destroyed the oil industry. Some 270 drilling and oil service rigs left Canada as a result of that policy. There were bankruptcies in service related industries. There were lay-offs, adding to our unemployment statistics, not only in Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, but in Ontario and Quebec as well.
A few days ago I spoke to a young engineer who graduated last year from the University of Saskatchewan. He and his friends prior to graduation had worked in the summer time in Alberta for some of the major oil companies. Upon graduation they were hired by these oil companies. They felt their careers were assured, that they had been hired on a permanent basis. Some of these young engineers who thought their future was assured have recently been laid off. A young engineer told me that most summers the oil companies in Alberta would hire anywhere from 1,500 to 2,000 students to give them engineering training. These summer jobs have all disappeared. The oil companies, while they had advertised for students and engineers at universities across Canada earlier in the year, have now sent letters to all these students that they would not be hiring any summer students and very few graduates. This word comes not only from the major oil companies but also from Petro-Canada. They are just not in a position to hire summer students. This is what the national energy policy has done to our young people.
May 5, 1982

In the last few days the Alsands project has been abandoned. The Alaska highway natural gas pipeline has been put on hold for a two-year period. As a result of the cancellation and the delay there has been a loss of thousands of man-hours and man-years of work across the country.
I listened with some interest to the Leader of the New Democratic Party who spoke earlier in this debate. Quite frankly, I did not know and I still do not know on which side of the fence he is.
He doesn't know either.

He appears to be straddling the fence. On the one hand he has a hatred for the multinational corporations, the large oil companies. Obviously, he would like to nationalize them and kick them out of Canada. But we can expect that from someone who is the vice-president of Socialist International. While he believes in nationalization and getting rid of what he calls the multinationals, he was condemning these same companies today for not investing the massive amounts of money necessary for the Alsands project. The Leader of the New Democratic Party cannot have it both ways. He cannot get rid of private enterprise and have Crown corporations or government create the jobs necessary to cut down our unemployment.
I was interested in an article that appeared in The Wall Street Journal on Monday, May 3, 1982. I would like to quote from that article as follows:
"The Alsands failure will reduce business investment spending in Canada by $360 million this year and sets the stage for a steady loss of real output, employment and foreign investor confidence," adds William Empey, vicepresident and director of economics with Data Resources of Canada, an economic forecasting concern. Mr. Empey sees the investment spending loss rising to $2.7 billion in 1985.	.	-
Another paragraph reads:
Adds Mr. Empey of Data Resources: "Since much of Canada's political and economic history is made up of such high-profile joint business-government ventures, this failure might be interpreted as a particularly bad omen by international investors."
Twenty thousand man-years of direct employment and
60,000	man-years of indirect employment went down the drain when the Alsands project was cancelled.
The delay in the Alaska highway pipeline project means that another 70,000 man-years of employment are gone, gone at a time when our unemployment is at an all time high and when jobs are required. 1 have been a member of the special committee on the Alaska gas pipeline since its inception in 1978. Time and time again, the minister reiterated that he had an ironclad guarantee from the Americans. On that basis the southern prebuild was carried out.
I listened to the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) earlier today. I agree with his comments when he said that there was no need for the Alaska highway pipeline if the Mackenzie Valley pipeline had been built. The Mackenzie Valley pipeline would have been built if it had not been for Mr. Justice Berger and his socialist friends to the left. If it had not been for them, the pipeline would have been built and in
operation today; our natural gas would have been moving down from the Mackenzie Valley; American gas from Prudhoe Bay would have moved across the Delta and down through Canada; and Canada would have received the benefit of a substantial amount of income, not only in the form of jobs which would have been created, but through the materials which would have been required and from taxes on the cost of transmission of gas.
I listened with interest to the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) earlier in the debate. It is interesting to note that she is the only minister who saw fit to participate, but she seemed to ignore the fact that many projects are not going ahead. For example, there is the Dempster pipeline which would have meant 6,000 man-years in direct employment and
26.000	man-years in indirect employment. Earlier I mentioned the Alaska highway pipeline. Also there was the Polar gas project which would have meant 15,000 man-years in direct employment and 45,000 in indirect employment. Kitimat was cancelled, a project which would have meant 5,000 man-years in direct employment and 15,000 in indirect employment. Also the tar sands project was cancelled with its 20,000 man-years of direct employment and 60,000 man-years of indirect employment. The list goes on and on. If we total the man-years, we find that because of cancellations and delays some
71.000	man-years of direct employment have gone by the boards as well as some 255,000 man-years of indirect employment.
What did the minister concentrate upon in her remarks? She seemed more concerned with the fact that the government developed CHIP, the Canadian Home Insulation Program. She felt that it was the ultimate because it created some jobs and conserved energy since it would cut down on the utilization of gas or oil. I just could not believe it. Until such time as Canada is rid of the man at the helm and of the first, second and third mates who sit in the front benches on the government side, until we steer a course for a new island, unemployment, high interest rates, recession and depression will continue.

Mr. Speaker, it is 3.15 a.m. on May 5 and we are debating a motion under Standing Order 26 which was introduced about three o'clock yesterday afternoon, so that the House could be placed in emergency debate commencing at 8 p.m. on May 4 because of the failure of the megaprojects to materialize.
The Alsands project would have created some 4,800 permanent operating jobs and many more jobs during the construction phase. Also there was the Cold Lake project which perhaps has been cancelled. It would have involved some $14 billion, some 3,300 permanent operating jobs, and some 28,500 jobs in the construction phase. The final project which enters into this emergency debate is the Alaska gas pipeline which will not likely proceed either. It involved a cost of some $40 billion, some 400 permanent jobs in its operating phase, and some 11,875 jobs in the construction phase. This is not counting the hundreds of thousands of spin-off jobs from coast to

May 5, 1982
5.0. 26
coast. In total, some 70,000 person-years of employment in the construction phase and perhaps 8,500 permanent jobs will be lost.
We are really talking about much more than only those three projects. We are talking about the disastrous state of the Canadian economy, about jobs, and about energy self-sufficiency which has gone by the boards. I do not think there is any possible way that the present administration governing the country can ensure that we reach energy self-sufficiency by 1990.
Oh, oh!

I ask hon. members to show some courtesy by not hollering across the floor. The Conservatives say that the Liberals are wrong; the Liberals say that the Conservatives are wrong. I say that they are both right because they are both wrong.
Take that from the top again, Doug.

They both are wrong when it comes to the stands they take on the megaprojects. Economic times in Canada are not good. In fact throughout the world economic times are not that good. This has reflected poorly upon Canada and the Canadian government. It has filtered down to other levels of government. Many people feel frustration in the country today. For example, I think of some provincial governments which have been turfed out lately, such as the government change in Manitoba and the one in Saskatchewan.
Let me indicate what happened in the recent election in Saskatchewan. Some of the NDP members who held seats in northwestern Saskatchewan either held their vote or marginally increased their vote.
Oh, oh!
They were defeated because their Liberal constituents all voted Conservative.
Hear, hear!

I think it shows, and the statistics will bear it out, that the total Liberal vote collapsed. It went from a small percentage to an even smaller percentage of around 4 per cent. That vote did not go to the NDP; it went to the Conservative party in Saskatchewan.
Another reason for the defeat of the Saskatchewan government was that it came at the hands of the many young people who were very apathetic about the current situation. Those young people believed in the Conservative promises and voted against the government in the hope of gaining something better. I believe that democracy should prevail, and I want to give Mr. Devine and his government in Saskatchewan an opportunity to make changes. While those Conservatives to my right smile, I will ask them to look at the situation in Manitoba. After the NDP premier Ed Schreyer of that province was defeated and the Conservative premier Sterling Lyon took his
place, in subsequent elections the federal NDP elected more members to the House of Commons. For that reason I do not know why the Conservatives are rejoicing as much as they are over that situation. In any event, we want to give Mr. Devine a fair opportunity to deliver on the many promises his government made during the campaign. With 57 seats in the 64 seat legislature, there is no reason for them not to deliver to the people of Saskatchewan.
The Tories are asking for an opportunity to govern the country. I wonder if they are that much different from the Liberal government. If we review the voting record since the beginning of this Parliament, the Conservatives have voted with the Liberals on 29 occasions, whereas the NDP voted with the Liberals on 14 occasions. This means that the Conservatives voted almost twice as many times with the Liberals to form a coalition.
When you review the megaprojects, you must wonder about their viability. We hear of the many benefits of megaprojects, but I think of megaprojects which have been built that have caused many problems for the environment, such as acid rain which has killed many lakes in Ontario and other areas of the Great Canadian Shield. I think of such things as the heavy oil upgrader which is to be built in Saskatchewan. Would it not be possible and more beneficial to have smaller self-sufficient communities which are more self-sufficient in energy and food production, and where people at the grass roots level usually know how to govern themselves better, rather than having a government thousands of miles away? I think it would be better to build three smaller oil upgraders at three strategic locations in a province rather than constructing one megaproject. It is questionable whether megaprojects are energy selfsufficient in themselves. There is some thought that the energy involved in creating these projects is never returned in the energy produced by them.
It seems that the three megaprojects have collapsed. These were projects which were strenuously supported by Liberals and Conservatives because they thought that this was the direction the country should go. Because of our party's environmental concerns and our suspicion about the lack of efficiency of megaprojects, we do not necessarily support them because of their size, there are some examples from which we should have learned a lesson. For instance, there is Ocean Falls in B.C., Uranium City in Saskatchewan, where people were encouraged to live and depend on an industry which would some day expire. This also happens today in some areas where there are megaprojects. Thousands of families are drawn to areas where these projects will eventually be closed down. The government will then have to deal with the social unrest which will occur in those areas.
It is asked by some why the Conservative and Liberal policies are closely related. For instance, their interest rate policies are very clearly similar. Those two parties have the same view on many energy issues. They both favour the megaprojects while not considering the conservation which should take place.
May 5, 1982

I can tell you why they are so closely related. I just have to look at some of the contributions given to the old-line parties, the Conservatives and Liberals, in 1978. It has been said that the Liberal party is the representative for big business and the Conservative party is big business-or is it the other way around? In 1978 the Alberta Gas Trunk Line contributed $15,752 to the Conservative party. That same company donated $15,800 to the Liberal party. The Aluminum Company of Canada donated $15,000 to each of the old-line parties.
How much did you contribute to the NDP?

The member for Athabasca asks how much I donated to the NDP. I donated $1,800 to the NDP last year, and I am proud of it.
The Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce donated $25,351 to the Conservative party and $25,000 to the Liberal party. In 1978 Gulf Oil of Canada gave the Conservatives $41,000 while only giving the Liberals $27,200. Does that mean they favour the Conservative party over the Liberal party? I do not think so.
If we review the 1979 figures, we see that Gulf Oil gave $53,324 to the Liberals and only $39,342 to the Conservatives. It is the same situation which might flip-flop back and forth every year. The two old-line parties are still the same and they do not represent the common interests of the people.
In total for 1978 the Conservatives received $878,839 from public corporations. They received $1,413,560 from private sector corporations. We see that the Liberals received $1,019,972 from public corporations while they received $1,234,470 from private corporations.
In 1979 the Alberta Gas Trunk Line donated $36,630 to the Conservatives and $31,600 to the Liberals. Kaiser Resources, which is a big western development company, donated $31,990 to the Conservatives and $31,000 to the Liberals. Cominco, which sounds like part of Canadian Pacific, donated $5,000 to the Conservatives and $5,000 to the Liberals. West Coast Transmissions donated $15,357 to the Conservatives and $16,000 to the Liberals. Other examples are the same, and they just continue. These parties are the same.
In order to reach energy self-sufficiency we, as a country, must very seriously consider some alternatives. We cannot only anticipate attaining energy self-sufficiency just through the development of hydrocarbons, although they should be developed vigorously. We must look at conservation measures which are so important to reduce our dependency on hydrocarbons.
The internal combustion engine can run on many things besides hydrocarbons. It can run on ammonia mixed with acetylene hydrogen, propane, a number of things which are less polluting to the environment and which could be more cost competitive. It just needs some impetus, some push from a government, a push which a federal NDP government could
give to the energy sector to make it go after alternatives in the energy-efficiency battle.
We also need to look at the jobs we need to create in Canada. As many members on all sides of this House mentioned, we have the highest rate of unemployment since the Great Depression. We in the New Democratic Party attribute most of that to high interest rates.
When we look at the amount of money which has been freed up by the cancellation of megaprojects, some $77.5 billion, maybe there is a possibility that this can have some downward pressure on interest rates. This money could be freed to do other things in the economy. I hope that is one of the positive results of the Liberals and Conservatives not wanting to go ahead with the things that are necessary in this country.
We would like to see the federal government not stifle the productivity of the people. Our gross national product is very sad when we have people who have been ingrained with a strong work ethic. They want to work. They want to help their country. However, governments like this government have held them back.
We need to increase manufacturing and processing in Canada. If you look at the manufacturing industry as opposed to the resource industry, it costs 40 times as much to create a job in the resource sector as it does to create a job in the manufacturing sector. We have to look at things that are more labour-intensive, such as manufacturing, as opposed to capitalintensive types of projects in the resource sector now and the high costs of recovery of some of the hydrocarbons.
We need an economic development plan so that people can prosper from coast to coast within an improved self-sufficient community, using the resources they have for their benefit and to fulfil their needs, and then exporting to the rest of the world. Once our needs are fulfilled, we can export beyond our borders and import as little as possible in order to have our productivity increased.
We also believe we would go a long way once the interest rate has come down a bit. Hopefully from this new money in the market, the interest rate will be locked in and not allowed to fluctuate wildly up and down. One of the frustrations of many small businesses, farmers, individuals on fixed incomes, and wage earners is that they never know what the interest rate will be from month to month when they go to the bank. They do not know how much they will have to pay on their mortgage, their car, operating capital or inventory. If they could at least plan with some degree of certainty, knowing that interest rates are going to be 15 per cent, and will be 15 per cent for a year, the people would know what they were dealing with. They could plan for their future.
We also believe that anyone who makes a large profit that is unwarranted, a profit that is beyond anyone else's in the country, should be taxed on that as an excess profit. We think there should be income tax cuts for the low and middle-income people. These are some things that can get Canadians back on the right track and back into the work force. Some of what has been outlined this evening by my colleagues and myself point

out a better way for Canada through the New Democratic Party.

Mr. Speaker, I was listening a little while ago to my New Democratic and Progressive Conservative colleagues bragging about all kinds of election results. I remind them that over the past 20 years, the results which we have seen here in the House of Commons, have been, I believe, to the benefit of the Liberal Party of Canada. If I am not mistaken, in the past 20 years, there have only been nine months of Progressive Conservative rule and God knows we were anxious to see that rule come to an end.
A byelection was held in the riding of Levis exactly one year ago on May 4, 1981. I had no idea that 366 days after that byelection, we would be holding an emergency debate on the Alsands project at 3:40 in the morning.
The motion introduced by the Leader of the Opposition seems to imply that the entire country should be in mourning because the Alsands project has been suspended. Reference is being made to famous megaprojects to indicate that these projects are important for Canada, but it seems that we would want to have the people believe that by scrapping the Alsands project, we are scrapping all important projects in Canada in the coming years. By attempting to make the people believe such a thing, they are really trying to make them forget that we have planned megaprojects worth hundreds of billions of dollars up to the year 2000, that the cost of the Alsands project was estimated at about $14 billion and that the Alsands project is not yet dead and buried, but only delayed for several months or a few years. I think that the persons directly involved can explain the situation even better and I refer to the comments made by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) last Friday, April 30. The Honourable Minister stated, and I quote:
-the suspension of construction activities at the Alsands synthethic crude oil plant means that Canada will have to put greater emphasis on its oil potential in the Beaufort Sea and off the Atlantic coast and on the development of traditional western crude oil resources, on increased oil and improved crude oil recovery.
However, we are talking about, and all parties are prepared to say it, the suspension of the project, not the termination or death as some are saying tonight. I continue with the Hon. Minister's statement, and I quote:
Fortunately, Canada has other potential supply sources-
New prospects in the North and offshore are very encouraging and we are still confident that we will reach our goal of self-sufficiency by 1990. We support exploration and development in these regions through our incentive measures and our pricing policy.
The Minister continues, and I quote:
The uncertainty surrounding the evolution of world oil prices has private investors concerned, not only as far as the Alsands project is concerned, but also with regards to major synthetic crude oil, electrical production and coal liquefaction projects in the U.S. and elsewhere.
I think it is important to note that not only in Canada have oil production programs been delayed. I continue to quote the Minister:
Clearly, this financial challenge was too difficult to overcome at the present time. Ironically, corporations hesitated to commit themselves, partly because they realized that there were excellent alternate solutions, particularly in offshore regions.
I wanted to refer to these excerpts from the statements of the Minister because in the riding of Levis and in the greater Quebec City area, and I would even say in eastern Quebec, one of the topics in the news in recent weeks has been the presence of Dome Petroleum in the greater Quebec City area. I think that when the Minister says that we will have to focus our attention on the Beaufort Sea, we must realize that Dome Petroleum, which purchased Davie Shipbuilding Ltd. in the Quebec region in June of 1981, is currently exploring for and developing oil and gas resources in the Beaufort Sea.
Moreover, at the time of this famous transaction which represented approximately $40 million or $38.6 million, Dome was presenting itself as an independent company administered by Canadians conducting oil and gas exploration activities in Western and Northern Canada. Since its early beginnings in 1950 when it had only a few people on staff as compared with the present day figure of 4,300 employees, the company has always focussed on growth and thus, in June 1981, it acquired the Davie shipyards along with its 2,300 or 2,400 employees. We must understand that Dome Petroleum purchased the Davie shipyards in 1981 in order to create new jobs, in the sense that the company had an expansion program and a shipbuilding program under way. Eventually, within the framework of the project currently in the hands of the Canadian government, Cabinet will normally have to decide in coming weeks whether this project is to be approved or not. As I was saying, a project worth several hundred million dollars is under way to expand and modernize the Davie shipyards.
I do not believe that because we are shelving temporarily the Alsands project, Canada is losing everything. Unfortunately, it is true that for the time being, in this particular region of the country, some jobs will- not be created in the near future. However, people in other regions of the country, particularly in Eastern Canada, in Quebec and the riding of Levis, will come out ahead. In fact, they will profit from the misfortune of others. Under the circumstances, the Canadian government and the government of Alberta did everything they could to carry through with the Alsands project. I do not think that they could have done much more than they did, short of taking public funds and giving them to private corporations.
We are talking about the two governments being involved as equal partners. I think that, under the circumstances, that was more than sufficient and a more than reasonable offer. The New Democrats and the Progressive Conservatives believe otherwise. The New Democratic Party would have liked to
May 5, 1982

have seen Petro-Canada take over the project and public funds used. The Progressive Conservatives, on the other hand, perhaps would have liked us to help the private corporations even more by providing them with more financial backing. However, the parties involved were unwilling to carry on with the project. And, as I said at the beginning, we have to understand that the project is only being delayed for several months or years, in view of the present state of the world economy, and that it will not be delayed ad vitam aeternum.
Two, three or even four years ago, we were saying that the Alsands project was vitally important, that it had to go ahead and that many other projects were also of an urgent nature. Given the present state of the world economy, and in view of certain forecasts which were perhaps inaccurate for all sorts of reasons, today we find ourselves in the position where we are saying: world oil prices have fluctuated, perhaps we don't need as much oil as we thought we did, perhaps we can delay the Alsands project for six months, for one year, for two years, for three years and maybe even for four years.
I think we have to live with today's crazy economy where a barrel of oil can be had for $40. We could speculate that tomorrow the price might drop to $30 or to $25, contrary to what recent forecasts indicate. All of the forecasts were based on the assumption that the price of oil would continue to increase. However, as it happens, in recent months, OPEC decided to drop its prices. Today we can even anticipate a further reduction in the price of a barrel of oil. Therefore, under the circumstances, the decision that was made by the two government to make a sizeable offer, but not to concede everything, was a reasonable decision. We will just have to wait for a few months or a few years before Alsands and all of the other projects are carried out to the benefit of all Canadian workers.

Mr. Speaker, I must say you are looking very well, considering the circumstances. You are certainly looking much better than the three members of the Liberal party who have turned up for this evening's debate and the one single member of the New Democratic Party. I am pleased to be amongst many colleagues in the Conservative party. The fact that there are many shows that the people in my party are really interested in the affairs of the nation and really concerned about what has happened to Alsands and the Alaska gas pipeline.
What we are debating tonight is not just the two projects named in the motion, the Alsands project and the Alaska gas pipeline, but a culmination of a whole series of disasters. There have been megadisasters and minidisasters, but they have all been disasters. The Alsands project and the Alaska gas pipeline fiasco was preceded by Judy Creek, which went down the hole; Cold Lake, which was shot out of sight; and various pipeline projects, including Kitimat, and the proposal to build both oil and gas pipelines down the Mackenzie Valley. They have all gone by the board. Those are the ones which have
been spectacular because the loss of jobs associated with them has been fantastic. Tens of thousands of jobs in the construction industry have been lost. Those jobs would have been directly associated with the actual physical construction of various projects.
We have heard from many speakers tonight. We have heard that hundreds of thousands of jobs have been lost from Nova Scotia and the maritimes to Quebec and Ontario and all the way over to British Columbia. Hundreds of thousands of important jobs have been lost because of the policies pursued by the Liberal government.
I do not want to dwell particularly on loss of jobs, of opportunities and of billions of dollars worth of spin-off benefits because many speakers, this evening and yesterday afternoon, have done that extremely well. However, I would like to discuss some of the minor disasters which have gone along with the major ones. In many ways these are more insidious. With respect to major megaprojects we are talking about jobs lost, but those jobs did not exist in the first place. It would have been very nice to have them in this day and age, but with respect to smaller projects we are talking about jobs which did exist but which no longer exist. They have disappeared from Canada altogether.
Let us consider, for instance, just a small well in Saskatchewan producing perhaps 20 barrels of oil a day. That is not a lot, but it helps Canada on its way to energy self-sufficiency. It provides a certain amount of employment. That is 20 barrels of oil a day we do not have to import. However, because of the policies of the government, and the National Energy Program in particular, that well has had to shut down because it is no longer profitable. The operators of that well have been losing money on every barrel of oil pumped out of the ground. My friend, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson), is conversant with this particular problem as it affects his area.
Let me discuss small Canadian exploration companies in the oil and gas business. I know many people involved in them. They had high hopes. Indeed, many of them still have high hopes of eventually becoming large corporations which might compete with BP, Shell, or even Imperial Oil. However, they no longer have that opportunity, if they want to stay in Canada. That opportunity has been denied them by the actions and policies of the Liberal government.
Let me discuss shut-in gas fields which still exist. There are quite a few in Alberta and in other places. There is one in Yukon. There is gas which people have worked to find and prove up, but they still cannot find a market for it. That gas could be used to displace imports of oil into Canada. People could be working in those gas fields, but they are not. They are not working because of the policies pursued by hon. members opposite.
Let us take a look at the service industry in the oil field business, including service rigs, hauling and specialty companies, drilling muds, well logging and that type of thing. We are no longer drilling wells in Canada because of the policies of hon. gentlemen opposite, and these people have had to leave

May 5, 1982
Canada. They have gone down to the United States in droves. This is another effect of the national energy policy and is illustrative of the insidious effect this policy has had on the Canadian enterprise stretching from Alberta and the west right across Canada.
When we add all of these small minidisasters together, as I have said before, we find that they are just as disastrous as the loss of Alsands and the loss of the Alaska gas pipeline. We must ask ourselves why has this all come about? The answer is pretty clear. It is because of a concept shared by the Liberal party and the New Democratic Party. Their view of the Canadian oil and gas industry is to see only a few people in the business, those from large companies. It does not really matter whether it is a nationalized company like Petro-Canada or whether it is a company like Imperial Oil. They want to see these few big corporations around which can then be controlled very easily from the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources.
If hundreds of small operators are mixed in with the big guys, it is pretty hard to control them. They will speak up for their rights. Bigger companies and multinational organizations seldom do. They generally stay out of what they might term local politics or national politics. They do not get involved in that type of thing. They go by the rules as they exist in a country. However, the little guys are like farmers. They speak up for their rights. They will make noises during elections. They will try to change government policies. They will get in the way of the technocrats in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. For that reason the Liberals and the NDP want to get rid of them. They want them out of business.
The government and its friends in the NDP would like to see the oil and gas business as a utility, where rates of return are strictly controlled and where there is no real point in taking any risk because one will not make any big money if one hits it. The government will tax it all away. It will allow a 15 per cent or 16 per cent return on the investment as it allows the business of generating electricity, but that is all. The government is taking the fun out of the oil and gas exploration business. Why would anyone want to become involved in the business any more? We might as well leave it up to the big guys. They drill so many wells that it is simply a matter of statistics to them. They drill so many wells and they know that they will find so much oil and gas.
It is not like the business was before and the way the business should be, with individual Canadians willing to come and invest their own capital in these projects. If they are unlucky and they lose everything they have, it is well and good. It is their money. They lost it, and they should not expect anything in return. But, on the other hand, if they do strike it rich, if they are lucky, then they should be able to make a decent return. They should be able to walk away with what my friends on this side will call windfall profits.
That is a dirty word.

It certainly is in the vocabulary of the party to my left, but it is what built the Canadian energy industry in the first place. If we want to sustain the energy industry, particularly in oil and gas, we have to bring back the profit motivation. What the Liberals and the NDP want is a strictly controlled industry. We have seen that in the national energy policy, in Bill C-48, and in the tax bills. They want no leeway given for enterprise but everything done under the dictates of the government. That is the reason for the mess we are in today. They have treated the oil and gas industry as a fabulous source of revenue-at least that is what they expect it will be. I think they are going to be disappointed because prices will not continue to escalate as they have in the past.
The agreement between Alberta and the federal government, which was two years in the making, would result in an additional $50 billion of tax revenue accruing to the federal government. If it takes that much money out of the oil and gas industry, what is left for the people who make the investment? If they drill a well and find something, they have to pay the profit over to the government, but if they vote the right way and support the right party, they might get a little bit back as a PIP grant. That is not the way the industry was built up in Canada and it is not the way it will be sustained.
The demise of the Alsands project and the Alaska gas pipeline has been described this evening as a betrayal of Canadians. It has been described as a breach of trust. One could say that it is a betrayal which was brought about by ignorance and sheer incompetence. We know that these attributes abound in the ranks of the Liberals and their western cousins, but the argument could be made that they knew not what they did when they brought in those policies. There is evidence to suggest, however, that at least in some instances it was not just incompetence that brought these things about; it appears to have been deliberate sabotage.
I should like now to deal with the Mackenzie Valley, a part of Canada that I am proud to represent. If Canada had played its cards right in the 1970s it would not have raised all kinds of obstacles to progress and we would by now not only have a major gas line down the Mackenzie Valley but in all probability we would have a major oil line as well. The oil lines that now stretch from Prudhoe Bay in Alaska to the Port of Valdez would in all probability have been built down the Mackenzie Valley. That was not to be the case.
Let us remember the Arctic gas-

Mr. Speaker, I think it is worth noting that there is only one Liberal member in the House and only one NDP member.
I was speaking of the Arctic gas proposal in the years 197374-75. About $250 million was spent by the proponents of that scheme to prove its feasibility and to do all the work necessary to show that it could be built without undue environmental effect, that the engineering was sound, and that the economics were sound.
We know what happened to that. The proposal was shut down by the NDP Judge Berger in his infamous report. He was appointed with the connivance of the Liberals, and the NDP acting in concert. The sordid history of the Berger inquiry has left Canada, and especially the Mackenzie, much the worse for wear. The NDP has consistently opposed any and all projects which would have brought energy self-sufficiencey to Canada and which in the process would have created thousands and thousands of new jobs for Canadians. It is no use crying over spilt milk, however, and it is no use crying about the fate that has been brought upon us by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the NDP in collusion.
We cannot go back to 1979 and have the vote on the Crosbie budget all over again. We cannot go back and hold the 1980 election again. But I think we all know what the results would be. The Canadian people certainly wish they had another chance and that we could turn the clock back and go through it again, but that is not to be.
We have to face the future, even if it is not what we would like. This evening we must not just describe all that has gone wrong in the past. We have to think about the policies that should be developed and adopted now so that history does not repeat itself. Let us consider what policies we should adopt to get us out of the mess into which the Liberals have got us.
Before I go into that, Mr. Speaker, there is one thing that I do not think anyone else has touched upon. I should like to know what is going to happen about the Northern Pipeline Agency. I do not have any particular sympathy with the Hon. Mitchell Sharp who has had his nose in the Liberal trough for many years, but there are many skilled and experienced engineers, accountants, lawyers and biologists who have congregated to act on behalf of the Northern Pipeline Agency. The decision to delay the project is probably the worst that could have been made. These people would have been better off had the decision been either yes or no.
I wonder if I could request the unanimous consent of the House to continue for a few minutes, Mr. Speaker.
Agreed.
I should note that I am only on page four of an eight-page speech.

Mr. Speaker, I will just complete my remarks about the Northern Pipeline Agency, and I will give you at some other time my plans for renewal and reconstruction of the Canadian oil and gas industry, should you so wish.
The question of the Northern Pipeline Agency, and it is a serious one, has not been brought up in this debate. The question is: what do we do with it? We have all these competent, capable and experienced people drawing larger than normal public service salaries because of the nature of their work, and they do not know where they stand or what they have to do. In fact they have very little to do at this time. I can think of a useful purpose for some of these people on the rather small oil line which is to be built from Norman Wells to Zama Lake. There are a number of problems similar to those which might have existed on the Alaska gas pipeline, but on a smaller scale, and it might be useful if some of those people serving in the Northern Pipeline Agency were seconded to help deal with some similar problems-
