Mr. Speaker, as I approach this debate I cannot fail to consider that the collapse of these two projects has all the earmarks of being just one more in a series of megadisasters for which this government must be held responsible. I would suggest the first megadisaster was the downgrading of Parliament. As I approach the tenth anniversary of my nomination for election to this House, I look back with sadness on those ten years which have been strewn with disasters of one kind or another, all caused by the wrongheaded policies of this government. In fact one could almost say this Liberal government has developed the knack of putting a blight on practically everything to which it has set its hand.
I think of Parliament and how it has been downgraded. It was started by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) when he said members of Parliament are nobodies when they are 50 yards off the Hill. I think we can narrow that distance now and say that, in the eyes of the Prime Minister, members of Parliament-including his own-are nobodies in this House. In fact there is nobody over there at the moment except for one body. I do not mean to be facetious about this, Mr. Speaker, because it is a serious matter. This democratic institution, which the Canadian people rely on to deal with the problems confronting them, has shown itself under the direction of this particular government to be absolutely incapable of doing just that.
Another megadisaster is the confrontation between east and west. Federal-provincial relations have deteriorated to the point where there are animosities which I find unworthy of Canadians, but they have been created by this government and

May 5, 1982
its attitude toward the other level of government. A paper came across my desk the other day, the Sunday Express from one of the eastern townships, with the heading "Trudeau has been an absolute disaster". It goes on to say:
When Trudeau first came to power unemployment was at 4.5 per cent-today we're over the double digit mark. Inflation hovered around 4 per cent back then and today it stands at 12.5 per cent. Federal spending in 1968 was roughly $12 billion, while now-thanks to the extravagant ways of a Prime Minister we can clearly not afford, it has reached $72 billion.
He preached 'a Just Society' then promptly delivered The War Measures Act. He promised to maintain Canada's "integrity" but today, members of the once proud Royal Canadian Mounted Police occupy the prisoner's dock of a Montreal courtroom-
And they are being denied documents for their defence. Everything this government touches is blighted by the contact. The military have been downgraded. The fourteenth anniversary of the Prime Minister's time in office should have been a day of mourning. In 1968 the military had about 100,000 members. It is now down into the 80,000 range. Everything, including inflation and interest rates, has become worse under this government and now we are faced with the energy problem. Hard to believe, is it not, that two years ago there was a throne speech, and we are still in the same session. It is very interesting to look at some of the statements in that throne speech. It said:
-energy development has the potential to create growth and prosperity across Canada.
No one denies that, but where are the growth and prosperity? We are in mourning today over the demise of two very important energy projects from which Canada would benefit.
I am just taking selections from the throne speech. This is the Governor General speaking but it is really the Prime Minister, and we read:
My ministers do not intend to impose an 18-cent increase in the excise tax on transportation fuels-
That, I suppose, is pretty clever. The government does not intend to impose an 18-cent increase, but instead of that the government has imposed a 52-cent increase. I still say that statement is slightly misleading, because within that 52 cents the first one third of it is 18 cents.
The Speech from the Throne goes on:
-and the made-in-Canada price will result in a lower price to consumers than the one proposed in the budget of the previous administration.
Just for fun I make a note of the various changes when I am at the gas pump where I normally get my gas. In January, 1980, for regular gasoline we were paying 23.2 cents per litre, which is about $1.05 a gallon. Excuse me for using a gallon measurement. I think I am covered by parliamentary immunity here so I cannot be taken to court for using that improper term.
You had better check that one out.

The Speaker will protect me, I am sure.
As I was saying, gasoline was $1.05 a gallon in January, 1980. But what is it in March, 1982, which I think is the last time an increase was imposed? The cost is 41 cents a litre. That is almost double what it was in 1980. It is now $1.86 a gallon. But in the Speech from the Throne of April 14, 1980, we read:
-and the made-in-Canada price will result in a lower price to consumers than the one proposed in the budget of the previous administration.
The American price is 27 per cent lower.

And as my colleague, the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gustafson) says, you can fill up your gas tank for a great deal less in the United States than you have to pay in Canada.
Let me read a little more from the energy portion in the Speech from the Throne. It reads:
In spite of Canada's large energy resources-
Which are admitted. The sentence continues:
-which put this country in the extremely favourable position of being a major energy exporter, we remain partially dependent upon imported oil.
That was April, 1980. We are still dependent upon imported oil despite that claim that we would be sefl-sufficient by 1990. We are not closer to self-sufficiency. We are receding from that goal as the evidence accumulates before us.
The Speech from the Throne continues:
-and by stimulating the production of new domestic energy supplies.
One way this government expects to cease being so dependent on imported oil is by stimulating the production of new domestic energy supplies. But what did we see last Friday, which was Black Friday? Last Friday is the Friday we are talking about, when we saw the demise of two important projects. One would be a transit project but the other one was purely domestic, the Alsands project. I find it tragic that the government should have two years ago set that as its goal but finds itself today in this particular position.
There is another matter which affects our compatriots in the eastern provinces. The Speech from the Throne goes on:
My government equally favours the earliest possible construction of a natural gas pipeline to Quebec City and the maritime provinces-
That natural gas pipeline is called the Q & M, that is, Quebec to the maritimes pipeline. I think the real name of that pipeline should be the M and Q, that is, the Montreal to Quebec pipeline, because I do not think it has even got that far in this time. The Speech from the Throne reads "the earliest possible construction of a natural gas pipeline". I do not know what has held it up. I am sure that my colleagues from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick are deeply upset because they have to pay the highest possible prices for their heating fuel, and this would relieve much of their burden.
I have a final quote from the Speech from the Throne that I would like to put on the record. It is found in the last part of the section headed "Security of Energy, at a fair price." It reads:
May 5, 1982

My ministers believe that, if given the opportunity, Canadian companies and investors would involve themselves more heavily in the energy field. My government, therefore, adopts the specific goal of at least 50 per cent Canadian ownership of the petroleum industry by 1990-
The government did not specify how it was going to do that. There were a good many Canadian-owned companies at that time. However, if we take a look at the latest issue of Canadian Business, which is the May, 1982 issue, here most graphically described on page 84 we find the state of some ten private Canadian businesses engaged in the energy field. The names may not be familiar to you, Mr. Speaker, but nevertheless here they are: Chieftan Development, Czar Resources, Dalco Petroleum, Drummond Petroleum, Francana Oil and Gas, Numac, Page Petroleum, Rupertsland, Sulpetro 'B' and Trinity Resources. Here there is a uniform history of disasters in Canadian-owned enterprises. The heading of the article is a tragic one, "Drowning in debt". I would like to quote just a little from this article. It commences:
There are hundreds of oil men in Calgary today who are watching the companies they built, carefully and successfully, drift dangerously toward receivership. There are hundreds of former employees of oil companies in Vancouver who are no longer needed because the companies they worked for cannot afford to explore for energy in Canada.
That is a direct result of the energy policy of this particular government. The article goes on and mentions a number of companies and how their situations have deteriorated as a result of this policy. True, we have to admit there is a bad business climate throughout the world and a bad business climate here in Canada. Money is difficult to come by. The National Energy Program, which was supposed to be a budget, came out as the national energy policy, and that is all it was.
One of the promises in the National Energy Program which was published in 1980 was the Petroleum Incentives Program. It offered:
For oil and gas exploration anywhere in Canada, enterprises that are at least 50 per cent owned by Canadians, and are Canadian-controlled, will qualify for an incentive payment equal to 10 per cent of approved costs incurred in 1982 and 1983, and 15 per cent thereafter.
Let me go back to the article entitled "Drowning in debt" in the May issue of "Canadian Business" magazine. It reads:
All these hopes were crushed when the NEP was tabled in late 1980.
These were the hopes of being able to maintain themselves in the market. The paragraph continues:
It introduced a complex set of new rules and regulations which offered new funding with one hand and took it away in new taxes with the other hand.
Canadian content became the crucial thing. These companies are fully Canadian. The petroleum incentive payments were offered in 1980. But let me continue with this article:
But to date not one penny of PIP grants has been received by the industry, even though companies have operated and budgeted under the new regime for one and a half years. Some analysts have estimated that over $5 billion is now owing in PIP payments, but this grant money will begin to flow into the industry only after the energy security bill incorporating the remainder of the National Energy Program-
-and associated energy changes in the infamous Bill C-94.
-is appropved by Parliament.
This is the inducement to get busy in the oil and energy business. We have heard a misleading National Energy Program. We have seen and we have received a misleading National Energy Program. We have seen the destruction of the industry, the destruction of hope and the destruction of the employment market.
Figures have already been quoted, but I think it useful to quote them again for the benefit of the two government members who are present this morning, one reading a newspaper and the other just sitting there. It is worth recalling the losses in employment as a result of the imposition of the National Energy Program. It was foreseen by the former minister of energy, mines and resources in 1978 that there would be 71,000 direct employment opportunities in a number of energy projects both in the west and in the north. As the hon. member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) pointed out, this is a northern problem as well. The 71,000 direct jobs which were foreseen included the Dempster and the Alaska Highway gas pipeline. In indirect employment 265,000 man-years were foreseen. I suppose one should say person-years, but I think in the oil industry we should stick with man-years. This indirect employment has now gone by the boards as a result of the Speech from the Throne and the National Energy Program. The government has brought this megadisaster upon Canada. It boasts about the number of jobs it created, but it ought to know the number of jobs which have been lost in Canada. Governments do not create jobs, industry creates jobs. These jobs would have been available for Canadians had the government not followed the disastrous course it adopted in 1980.
Also it was indicated in the Speech from the Throne that the government did not intend to impose an 18-cent increase in the excise tax on transportation fuel. It did not mention the tax on heating oil, which of course was one of the main points of the Conservative government budget. There was not a word said about relief for those living in the colder climates of Canada in the National Energy Program; it was tragic.
In conclusion, I should like to quote a rather significant comment of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in a 1969 interview just after coming into power. He was discussing the efforts to change the course of the ship of state. He said:
One has to be in the wheelhouse to see what shifts are taking place. I know that we have spun the wheel and I know that the rudder is beginning to press against the waves and the sea ... but perhaps the observer, who is on the deck and smoking his pipe, or drinking his tea, sees the horizon much in the same direction and doesn't realize it, but perhaps he will find himself disembarking at a different island than the one he thought he was sailing for.
That was an ominous comment, especially when we think of the fact that he used the words "I know"; but the rest of Canadians were not supposed to know. They have learned the hard way and we have seen the results of that shift in position. I find it difficult to believe that there is not a great deal of design in what has happened to the country, and it saddens me to say so.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks I should like to mention that I cannot remember ever

May 5, 1982
making a speech, be it in the House of Commons, in my constituency or anywhere else, at 4.35 in the morning. Nevertheless, this is a very important topic which we are discussing. It is of such vital concern to the entire country that we felt we could only dramatize it by extended debate in which members from all parts of the country could participate. On behalf of their constituents they could express their concerns regarding the very dramatic economic loss to the country as a result of the cancellation of the $13.5 billion Alsands project. It has literally bit the dust or has ended up in the economic graveyard of the Liberal government. Also, the Alaska highway natural gas pipeline has been put off for another two years, and perhaps indefinitely.
At the present time in the country Canadians are starting, after three of four days of listening to radios, reading newspapers and watching television, to realize the enormity of what has happened through the almost total mismanagement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Liberal government.
Some time before the end of this debate later on today, this afternoon or perhaps tomorrow, we hope that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) will return to the House of Commons, give a speech, and admit that in many ways he was wrong in the direction and the intent of the National Energy Program which he and the Prime Minister piloted through the House of Commons. The purpose of this debate is to centre upon this particular question. We hope that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources will make some constructive comments and provide some positive direction.
The project that certainly concerns most Canadians at present is the $13.5 billion projected Alsands project which would have delivered 140,000 barrels of oil per day. This would have greatly enhanced Canada's chances for energy selfsufficiency. Because this project has failed we will find ourselves more dependent on imports in the next eight years than we are now. We will be at the whim of OPEC countries in terms of who they export to and the price they export for, and we will be influenced by what happens when an international incident may arise. These possibilities are greater since the failure of this project.
Aside from this fact, Canada will lose literally thousands of jobs in the process. It is estimated that the Alsands project alone would have provided a minimum of 25,000 construction jobs, a minimum of 25,000 manufacturing jobs in eastern Canada and anywhere from 7,500 to 10,000 permanent jobs once that project was completed and on stream. Some $450 billion would have been injected into the Canadian economy over the life of that project. That is a tremendous amount of money for any country, let alone a country the size of Canada. These are some of the benefits we will lose because of the failure of this project. Of course, it would have sparked tremendous economic growth at a time when it is almost nonexistent. In my opinion, this is one of the greatest financial disasters to hit Canada in decades.
I very briefly alluded to the reasons for this belief when I began my remarks. We have a Prime Minister who does not really understand, and at times does not care about, economic activity in Canada. We have a stubborn Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who will not listen to the reasoning of MPs, Canadians and the oil industry in general. We have a Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) who does not seem to understand and grasp the enormity of the kind of projects we are talking about tonight and their impact upon Canadians. These are some of the people who are responsible for the economic insanity brought about by this government.
It all started with the National Energy Program which was and is an unmitigated Canadian disaster. We have seen this government try to repair something which is irreparable. There is no way to patch up the problems that the termination of the Alsands project and the National Energy Program itself has caused. Because the National Energy Program has made a huge grab for more federal revenue, because it certainly thrusts the government deeper into the private sector than ever before, because it discriminated against foreign petroleum companies which have worked in good faith for Canada for the last number of years, and because it has confiscated petroleum rights and unsettled foreign investors, Canadian oil exploration and drilling companies have been driven away and may never return.
Tough.

The hon. member to my left says "tough". Many of these companies which have left were Canadian companies that were owned and operated by and comprised of Canadians who have been forced to go elsewhere in order to avoid going bankrupt like many other Canadian companies. Canada has been left at the mercy of OPEC countries and other oil exporting countries. The abandonment of the Alsands project will drastically affect an already shaky economy.
I assume that the government will desperately try to revamp its economic strategy, if it ever had one. Since the government included the vast amount of moneys it would have received from the vast resource sector in its projections for the next number of years, it will somehow have to replace those funds. Therefore, two things will have to happen. First, there will have to be drastic cutbacks in programs over the next couple of years-which has not been the general rule of the government-or second, the government will have to increase its deficits to a degree which no one can imagine. I suspect the government will opt for major tax increases over the next few years.
The failure of Alsands will reduce business spending in Canada by an estimated $360 million this year. This will set the stage for a steady loss of real output in the ensuing years. As a result, we will find increased unemployment in Canada and a very shaky foreign investment climate. Companies are not interested in dealing with a country which has a government that does not have an economic strategy, that wants to become involved in industries and control private incentive. It
May 5, 1982

is a climate such as this which has brought about a stagnation in Canada's economy today.
An estimate of business losses by 1985, which is probably conservative, amounts to $2.5 billion. This is an astronomical amount for a country such as Canada. It is no wonder that Canadians are concerned and that we have ended up having a marathon debate on one of the most important economic matters that any member in the House will speak to for a good many years.
Some $7 billion has left Canada in order to purchase foreign-owned oil companies during recent years. This is one aspect of the National Energy Program which concerns many people. This expenditure has put pressure on the dollar and interest rates. Of course, it has had an effect on everyone, from small and large businessmen to farmers and housekeepers. Anyone involved in any kind of economic activity in this country has felt the indirect effect of the mess the government has made with its National Energy Program. Billions of foreign dollars have fled, making the situation even worse. It is estimated that some 330 oil drilling rigs have moved south and that 2,000 fewer wells were drilled in 1981 than in 1980. This is the kind of economic stagnation we are seeing in this country. It is a direct result of the total lack of understanding of the Liberal government and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who, at least from a public perception, has been spearheading this whole process.
More than 15,000 jobs have been lost in the petroleum industry and an incalculable number in the manufacturing sector that supplies the petroleum industry. The bottom line has been that this government has been a disaster, not just in terms of world prices but in the whole design of its economic strategy and the direction it has taken on the energy question.
Canada at one time was a great country, and it still is. The potential is there. However, to some extent we have lost our objectives and ideals. We are floundering at the present time. We are concerned about ourselves because others are concerned about us, our neighbours, other people and countries. This is having an unsettling effect on Canada.
We are also concerned because unemployment is desperately high in this country. Future generations do not have confidence. They want to work but are unable to find a job because economic activity is not being generated by the private sector, in some cases combined with the government. It is not there because those who Canadians look to in terms of leadership, politicians and government, have not given leadership over the past two or three years.
Think about the effect of unemployment on a family. When we think about the damage it creates, one has to be concerned. In some respects this debate is larger than just the question of energy and economics, although both are very serious. It embraces the whole question of the social fabric of this country and the damage this kind of government is doing to that social fabric.
We hope the Prime Minister will not be around much longer. Then maybe we can again piece together what must be done. Given the chance, we feel that this Conservative party can do that.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to speak to this motion. It is ironic that while it quite rightly condemns the Liberal policy followed by this governmment, it equally condemns the policy of the party that moved the motion. The only complaint of that party agains the Liberal government is that it is not doing more of the damaging and disastrous things that it is doing.
We have a policy of selling off Canadians resources at the highest rate without any regard for the future of the Canadian economy or the needs of our people. The fact that the policy is already on the rocks illustrates how disastrous it is for the Canadian people and raises the possibility that it might be changed, if not by one of the two antiquated parties to my right and opposite, then by a newer party.
The Alsands and the Alaska gas pipeline have failed. The government now hopes to bring the Cold Lake project back from the graveyard. No one is optimistic about that working. These projects were always doubtful. They rested on very shaky predictions of oil prices and had to run against extraordinary interest rates. It was easy to see in advance that they were very unreliable projects.
Our party pointed this out previously, yet the government chose to charge ahead. The government was willing for this purpose to cut $6.5 billion over the next five years from needed public expenditures, transfers from the provinces, money needed for our health system, education system and other necessary social programs shared by the federal and provincial governments.
That money has been taken out in order to fund the corporate welfare bums, the oil companies. The $6.5 billion, give or take a couple of hundred million, is almost the same amount taken from education, health, daycare, pensions and benefits to senior citizens in order to fund companies that have more money that any other companies in this country, if not in the world, simply to meet their blackmail claim that they need more and more. They say that 18 per cent is not enough, they need 20 per cent. If we gave them 20 per cent, they would want 25. They think that the Government of Canada is a bottomless pit.
Their real oil well is not in the oil sands, the Beaufort Sea or the Hibernia, but here in the Parliament Buildings, primarily in the frontbenches of the government. That is where they get their money. They do not have to take oil out of the ground as long as they can get fat subsidies from the Liberals or Tories, depending on which party used the subsidies to oil companies most successfully in their election campaigns.
It is still a failure. In fact, the whole policy of the megaproject system is a failure. Megaprojects are the wrong projects in which to invest. The government wants to put about $440

May 5, 1982
billion into megaprojects during the next 20 years, and yet the government's own figures show it takes about $4 million to create one permanent job in those megaprojects. That is 40 times what it costs to create a permanent job in manufacturing. At a time of rising unemployment, the government was proposing to dump $77 billion into these three projects for only
8,000	permanent jobs.
Hon. members talk much about construction jobs, but construction jobs come and go very fast and they leave very little behind. Construction jobs are necessary in any developing country, but an overemphasis on construction jobs simply disrupts family and community life and leaves ghost towns behind. Construction jobs are no substitute for building up permanent industries in Canada. They are no substitute for jobs in places like Brampton or Toronto. They could be a supplement to those jobs, but they are not a substitute.
By concentrating exclusively on megaprojects-damaging the country's manufacturing industries-the Liberal Party has done as much harm as it could, although perhaps not quite as much harm as the Tory party might have done had it been in power.
There ain't a hell of a lot of difference.
Come to Brampton and deliver this speech.

Manufacturing jobs are needed to build this country. They build permanent communities in which education and job training make some sense. Fly-by-night construction projects are here today and gone tomorrow.
This government has been killing off manufacturing industries. Its high taxes have been draining off the income people need to buy the manufactures of this country. They have been killing off the initiative of the small businessmen who have been the backbone of manufacturing in this country.
The high interest rate policy of this government has done the same harm to small business and manufacturing. The government claims it does not have a high interest rate policy, yet this government and the previous government of the Tory party have both endorsed the policy of Governor Bouey of the Bank of Canada.
They still do.

For seven years his stated policy, about which Governor Bouey brags, is to restrict the money supply in order to raise interest rates. This is the policy endorsed by the two antiquated parties in this country. It has produced high interest rates which have caused a present rate of over 1,000 bankruptcies per month. That is what is killing manufacturing.
In addition, this government has followed a policy of so-called free trade, that is, handing over Canada's manufacturing jobs to countries-many of them police state countries- which enforce low wages. Wages of $2 a day are enforced in places like El Salvador. Wages of $1.39 an hour for autoworkers are enforced in places like South Korea. The policy of this government is to dismantle Canada's manufacturing industries
in favour of industries in countries where low wages are enforced.
As if that were not enough, the government is also allowing the internal basis of Canada's transportation to deteriorate by cutting back on both the passenger and the freight capacity of VIA Rail. For decades hopper cars have been one of the basic freight capacities of Canada's rail system, but they have been allowed to deteriorate. The government refuses to make good its promise to renew and replace hopper cars. In other words, the government is not interested in maintaining the industrial manufacturing capacity of Canada.
According to the reports of Canadian and American business experts, Canada is losing out in the present western world recession. We are the slowest of all the western countries to recover or to show any signs of recovery. This is because of the policy supported by the hon. member for Brampton-George-town (Mr. McDermid) and many other members in the north end-the wrong end-of this House, that is, the policy of killing off Canada's manufacturing industry for the sake of quick bucks from megaprojects.
Canada is on the way to becoming a Third World country. It is very ironic that the person who coined the phrase "Canada is becoming a banana republic" was at one time the leader of the Tory party-which forces Canada to do what the late John Diefenbaker warned against. There is, in fact, no difference between the Liberal and Tory parties, with the exception of one small difference of degree. They alternate. They vie. At one time one says we should have higher oil prices and the other says no. Then the other one gets into office and says, "Let us have still higher oil prices". Out of office each one wants low oil prices but in office wants high oil prices. Their basic concern is to curry favour, not with Canadian voters but with oil companies, it is quite understandable that they would want that; they rely very heavily on oil companies for com-paign funds. Nearly half a million dollars is given to each of them by oil companies for campaign funds at election time. That buys a lot of election campaigns.
Where do you get your money?

The result is that they follow bad policies. It does not matter whether they are preached by the Conservatives and practised by the Liberals or vice versa; their policies are disrupting the industrial communities of Canada. They are disrupting the industrial cities Canadian workers have built. They are policies which are causing misery and unemployment in every city.

The NDP has been requesting policies which would build the Canadian manufacturing industry and promote Canadian content. That is in direct opposition to the policies of the present megaproject system because its sourcing is clearly not Canadian sourcing. This is the policy we have been advocating. This is the policy which would rebuild our manufacturing industry.
