You wouldn't understand it, anyway.
-because that is the key to the future health of Canada.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), who just spoke, does not want to export gas. He does not want to build Alsands. He does not want to build an oil and gas industry for Canada. What in blazes does he want to do to create jobs in Canada? Just what are his plans to create jobs in Canada?
We are going to capture the gas you are exporting.
Does the hon. member not think that we should use the resources that God put at our disposal in this country for the benefit of Canadians?
Hear, hear!
For whom?
Before commencing my speech, I would like to thank my colleagues for giving me the opportunity to speak tonight because I know that some of the others will not get an opportunity to speak.
Oh, yes, they ran out.
It seems kind of funny to thank someone for the opportunity to speak at 5.15 in the morning, but I sincerely do because I have some strong feelings on the subject we are discussing.
And only two Liberals in the House.

Last week I had an opportunity to speak in Belleville. After I had concluded my remarks, a lady came up to me and said, "I have a daughter and a son-in-law who are living in Stettler and I was out to see them recently". These people were originally from Ontario, from the Belleville area. She said to me, "I cannot believe the seething hatred for central Canada which is in their hearts. They have only been out there for a few years". Then she said to me, "You take your hate and go back to Alberta". I was dumbfounded. I had been giving a speech on Canadian unity, and I do not believe I had made any remarks which would have brought on such hostile reaction, so it was interesting to me.
Later that week, last Friday night, I happened to be in Pickering and I ran into an Ontario cabinet minister. I was seated beside him at dinner and he just ripped me up one side and down the other over the Alberta heritage fund.

Give us your unity speech.

May 5, 1982

I said to him, "Ontario and Quebec have their heritage funds. They are called Ontario Hydro and the Quebec-Hydro. The equity in those two corporations is roughly twice the amount of the Alberta Heritage Fund". That did not faze him one bit. He was not about to buy that. He said, "But Ontario Hydro and Quebec-Hydro are assets which are working for the people, while the Alberta heritage fund is just a big pot of money sitting out there, doing nothing for anyone". So I said to him, "I think that that is not quite true. Twenty-five per cent of the Alberta heritage fund is tied up in the Alberta home mortgage plan in exactly the same manner as the Ontario mortgage corporation. Another 25 per cent of the fund is tied up in the Alberta government telephone company. About 10 per cent of the fund is tied up or has been spent on oil sands research and technology. Another 10 per cent of the fund has been dedicated to medical research under the Alberta medical research authority".
Hear, hear!

The cabinet minister said, "Well, I never knew that before". However, the point I am trying to make here is that he, too, had a built-in prejudice and hostility toward another part of Canada.
Then later on in that same evening, I ran into a young man from Oshawa who was attending this function. He said to me, "Alberta is ripping this country apart. Alberta is ripping me off. Why should I pay the price that you are demanding for oil?" Again, the point I am trying to make is that here was another young man who was full of hatred, vengeance and hostility. This is not peculiar only to the people of Ontario; I see more of it in my own riding. I did not think that I could stand here tonight and tell hon. members the feelings of the people from my riding of Calgary South, and I think it prevails throughout all of Alberta.
Let us just forget about the National Energy Program and Alsands for the moment. The people of Alberta today have moved from a position of hostility to one of hatred, frustration and despair. I cannot identify all of the reasons which have caused this, but it is true. They do not feel they have a representative federal government. The Constitution does not mean a thing to them, not a whit. It is just a scrap of paper to them and no more than that. As a matter of fact, most of them would have preferred to live under the terms of the British North America Act, except for perhaps a few who did feel that it was worth while to patriate. However, they do not have any respect for their federal institutions. Why do they not have any respect for their federal institutions today? It is because the federal institutions, whether we like it or not, have betrayed them. They have betrayed what the people believe to be the foundation of this country-the freedom of the individual. The federal government has betrayed them. The government has alienated the people of western Canada, whether the government likes the fact or not. Alienation has not been caused only by the National Energy Program or Alsands. It has been caused by the federal government over the last ten years.
In my lifetime there has not always been this alienation. I was born and spent the first half of my life in Toronto and for the second half I have lived in Calgary. In the first 40 years of my life I never knew the Canada that we have today. In the last 15 years westerners have come to feel that they are no longer a part of this country, that their federal institutions are not responsive to their needs. The government has kept pushing and pushing them away from the mainstream of Canada. They want to be part of the mainstream of Canada, Mr. Speaker. They do not want to separate. They desperately want to feel a part of Canada, but for the last ten or 15 years the federal government has pushed them further and further away. It has isolated them and they are desperate.
Why have we got hate and hostility in Ontario and western Canada? I think some of the responsibility has to be attributed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Liberal government. What is a federal government and a prime minister for if they are not available to help heal the wounds that occur as a result of regional differences of this country? They should give people a sense of national purpose and a feeling of belonging to a country. Surely that is the responsibility of any government that is in power and primarily of the prime minister. It is his obligation to give us that sense of national purpose and to dispel regional hatred and hostility.
When I contemplated the subject of debate tonight I felt that the Alsands and the Alaska gas pipeline were not very important when compared to whether or not we are going to have a country. Who really cares about the Alaska gas pipeline or Alsands if we do not have a Canada? What is the point of building these projects? We certainly do not need them in Alberta or in western Canada. If we are thinking in terms of regionality and not considering the broader spectrum of Canada, then western Canada certainly does not need an Alsands plant.
In the past month I have had the opportunity of speaking to a large number of businessmen from Ontario and Alberta. I spoke to about 60 businessmen from almost every sector of the Alberta economy in the last week. Last night I met with several of the public affairs representatives of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and last week I talked to people in Belleville and Pickering, Ontario.
Each time I spoke to people I was struck with the same thought-that whether we like it or not we are in the midst of a crucial economic depression in this country. I am reluctant to use the word depression because it strikes a note of panic in most people. Some of us can barely remember the horror of the 1930s. I was a boy then but I know of the suffering of some members of my family and of our neighbours.
Surely we must face up to the serious situation in Canada today. I am not about to say that these problems result entirely from the Liberal government's past or present policies. Many of the problems in Canada's economy are the result of international factors beyond our control. There is absolutely no doubt, however, that the government's past and present policies have
May 5, 1982

exacerbated the problems facing the nation today. There can be no doubt about that and in particular about the effects of the National Energy Program and the budgets of 1980 and 1981.
The most serious problem that I see facing the Canadian economy today, apart from the fact that we are in a depression, is that investors and Canadians generally do not have any confidence in the economy or in their country. They do not have confidence in the federal government. They have lost confidence in the Canadian economy's ability to provide them with jobs and to assure them an income. Many people I have spoken to who might be in a position to invest in Canada are now not only not investing in Canada but are faced with the problem of economic survival. Time and time again I have heard them say "Batten down the hatches", or "If I can just live through the next 18 months, if I can survive, maybe I can fight the battle another day."
There is not a single person I have spoken to in the last few months who is prepared to invest in Canada. No one is prepared to invest in a country like Canada with its resources and with so much going for it. It is a disgrace. It is hard to believe.
I have been an entrepreneur for most of my life, Mr. Speaker, but I would not invest in one single common stock that is listed on the Toronto Stock Exchange or any other Canadian exchange. All one has to do is look at the Toronto Stock Exchange index to see the level of confidence Canadians have in their economy and government today.
The house-building industry is in a shambles; the automotive industry is on the ropes; the forest products industry is in desperate shape; the mining industry is fighting for its life; the steel industry is trying to keep its head above water; and finally, many sectors of the oil and gas industry are facing bankruptcy. That is the truth, Mr. Speaker, because I have talked to the people who are running these companies. Small and medium-sized businesses throughout Canada are falling like flies. They have been devastated by the Canadian economy and by high interest rates.
I am not about to condemn the Liberal government for all the evils of high interest rates but they need not be as high as they are. It is the National Energy Program, Canadianization and the headlong plunge into nationalizing the Canadian oil companies that is responsible. One of my colleagues says that it has cost $7 billion. Interest rates need not be as high as they are. That policy has inflicted untold damage on the small and medium-sized business sector of the economy.
I guess what I find so unbelievable is that the government does not seem to recognize the problem. If it does, it does not seem to be prepared to do anything about it. I do not know whether it is a question of pride or stupidity, but surely to goodness you can see the Canadian economy falling down around us. You have to be blind not to see it.
Yesterday in this House the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources deliberately misled the Canadian public by telling
them that the participants in the Alsands project decided against going ahead because the world price of oil was dropping. Certainly that was a factor but not the major one. Mr. Stoik, president of Gulf Canada, one of the last of the companies to leave Alsands, said:
Over the years the government has so strained its credibility with retroactive rule changes that those of us in the industry must now ask ourselves, how can we undertake to make huge investments in long-term megaprojects when we have good reason to fear that the government will come along again and pull the rug on us?
The president of Shell Canada, Bill Daniels, said:
In the current and foreseeable economic and industry environments we cannot proceed.
It was absolutely untruthful and misleading for the minister to blame it on the falling world price of oil. What a tragedy of staggering proportions for Canadians, not only in terms of lost jobs but in terms of lost opportunity for oil self-sufficiency. We are further away from that than we were in 1974.
The minister and his cabinet colleagues should be horsewhipped for what they have done to Canada. If the minister had an ounce of integrity he would resign, as would the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). The National Energy Program has emasculated the oil and gas industry in Canada. It has discouraged foreign investment, damaged our trade relationships, weakened the Canadian dollar, and increased interest rates beyond what they might otherwise have been. But does this government recognize the problem or do anything about it? Not on your life! They sit there, smug and arrogant, and laugh. Day after day in question period I watch the minister get up and laugh at his fellow Canadians' misery. My constituents are going broke, and he laughs at unemployment. Those that do not have jobs are losing their houses, and he has the gall to sit there and laugh at Canadians who are suffering because of his government's policies. I condemn them for it, and my constituents condemn them for it.
What kind of insanity is a National Energy Program which purchases 400,000 barrels of crude oil every day from Venezuela, Mexico and Saudi Arabia, while it shuts in
300,000	barrels a day of western Canadian crude? Can you imagine what the feelings of my constituents and the people of western Canada are when they see that happening? Why are we paying foreign suppliers hundreds of millions of dollars a month which could be going to Canadian producers and creating Canadian jobs, not only in the oil industry but in Ontario?
Hear, hear!

It is beyond comprehension. What kind of National Energy Program is it which drives Canadians out of their own country because they cannot find work here? A friend of mine with 31 years of experience in oil and gas exploration in Canada has been forced to move to Texas in order to earn a living. I talked to the president of a small independent oil and gas company, completely Canadian owned, with 25 employees. I asked him if he would help me with a fund raising project and he said "I am sorry, I cannot, I

May 5, 1982
am moving to Denver. I have closed the doors, 25 people are moving with me", and they are selling their Canadian oil and gas properties.
What kind of a National Energy Program is it which drives 150 trained engineers in oil well logging from Canada to the United States and other parts of the world with half their equipment? It is insanity. Wake up!

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I have to advise the hon. member that his time has expired and he should seek the unanimous consent of the House to complete his remarks.

Mr. Speaker, I did not want to intervene right away because I am one of those who still believes we can learn by listening to each other. I listened to the speech very attentively as I always do, but particularly to this one, and I am afraid I understood that the hon. member for Calgary South said that a minister has deliberately misled the House. I am still very interested in hearing the speech and I would certainly consent to the hon. member continuing, but he knows the rule very well.
I understand his feelings very well, but I would not like to have a debate later today or tomorrow over a question of privilege which can be disposed of right now if the hon. member changes his phraseology.

Mr. Speaker, I was going to suggest to the hon. member that he is perhaps premature in rising as he does on a point of order. I think in all fairness he should wait until the minister returns from his trip to the sunny south and has an opportunity to explain whether in fact he did what the hon. member has indicated he did. I would point out, Mr. Speaker, as we all know, that in July, 1955 in this House, as reported at page 6638 of Hansard, the Speaker said:
An expression which is deemed to be unparliamentary today does not necessarily have to be deemed unparliamentary next week.
Clearly, it could well be that if the hon. member feels in some vague way that the expression used by the hon. member was unparliamentary, that does not mean it would not be found to be completely parliamentary in the context of this debate tonight.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make it very clear that what was unacceptable then is still unacceptable. I think the hon. member knows very clearly that anyone can raise this point. I want to be clear, even at this time in the morning, that I do not need a minister here to tell me what I have to do.
The Speaker decides.

The rules are very clear; if you want to change them, we will proceed on that some day. I want to give consent to the hon. member so he can finish his remarks, because if you believe in Canada, you have to listen to people who have strong feelings. However, the rule is clear. I heard the remark and I ask the hon. member for Calgary South if he
would kindly change it so we can give our consent to hearing his views, which we can then reflect on.

Mr. Speaker, in the interests of expediting the debate and giving the minister the benefit of the doubt, I will withdraw the word "deliberate" and say he unintentionally misled the House. And I thank the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) for his intervention.
To continue, I have just a moment left here-
No, take your time.

The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is, I guess, laughing somewhere almost every day. When people get into a corner, I guess the best defence sometimes is to laugh. But as I said earlier, he is laughing at the suffering of fellow Canadians, suffering caused by the minister and his mandarins.
What kind of a man is this minister of energy? He is a man who has so little respect for the Canadian people that he finds nothing wrong with using Petro-Canada as an instrument to employ his public relations assistant. He sees nothing wrong in that, but I say that is misusing taxpayers' funds for his own personal benefit. I think that is wrong. But this is the kind of man the minister of energy is. He sees no conflict of interest in that whatsoever.
What kind of judgment can a man like that bring to bear on energy policy when he cannot see the moral right or wrong in using Petro-Canada, which is a Crown agency belonging to the taxpayers of Canada for his own personal purposes? What kind of a man is this?
As far as oil self-sufficiency is concerned, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources still has the gall to stand up in this House and say that we will be self-sufficient by 1990. I heard a gentleman here tonight say that there is no problem whatsoever with self-sufficiency by 1990. Again, I have to say to the hon. member, "You are misleading the Canadian people, perhaps unintentionally; but you are misleading the Canadian people if you are telling them that this country is going to be oil self-sufficient by 1990".
Neither the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, nor his department have any idea how they are going to achieve it. As a matter of fact, if any hon. members take the trouble to talk to the officials of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources or bring them before the current energy committees and ask them how we are going to achieve energy self-sufficiency by 1990, if they are truthful, they will tell you that they don't know how. What they will tell you is what the minister and others have said, that with offshore oil, Beaufort and Hibernia, along with substitution and conservation, it will be done. I think that is what the hon. gentleman on the other side said tonight. Those are words. But we are talking about replacing one million barrels of oil a day by 1990. Let me repeat that; one million barrels of oil a day by 1990 have to be replaced.
May 5, 1982

Presently we are importing 400,000 barrels a day. Our conventional oil production between now and 1990 will decline by 600,000 barrels a day. Surely, even if we substitute as much as we can in terms of gas for oil over the next eight years, and even if we do conserve, we will be consuming roughly the same amount of oil per day or we will have a completely no-growth economy over the next eight years.
We are looking at one million barrels of oil a day. Where is it going to come from? There is not one knowledgeable person in the oil industry nor even those in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources who will tell you that Hibernia and the Beaufort Sea will deliver oil before 1990. There is not one person who can tell you that. We do not have the faintest idea how we will get oil from Hibernia yet. We know it is there but we do not know how to go down through 250 feet of water 200 miles offshore, with icebergs coming down iceberg alley that are scouring the ocean floor to depths of 100 feet, and extract it. We do not know what kind of platforms we will erect. We do not know what kind of sub-sea wellheads we will instal. The Beaufort is equally as difficult. But I have taken too much of my time.
But at least you are saying something.

The Alsands and Cold Lake projects would not have solved the problem of oil self-sufficiency, but they would have provided 280,000 barrels of oil a day of that one million. These projects would have provided goodness knows how many jobs for Canadians at a time when we are in desperate need of employment. But they would have provided a stimulus to the whole Canadian economy. They would have given us something to lean on in a time of distress. They would not have been a panacea by any means, but they would have gone a long way toward helping to solve some of the crucial problems that we are facing at this time in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I did not expect to be speaking at a quarter to six in the morning in this debate in this House of Commons but there are some things to which I must reply in this emergency debate which started last night and was called by the opposition.
At the present time of soft world prices and world oil surpluses, there are many examples of development programs that are facing funding cutbacks in other countries in the world. I think that has to be noted. These examples point out that Alsands is not unique. In fact, in the United States alone the Exxon shale project has already been cancelled.
That is a red herring.

In Colorado, the Exxon Troupe lignite gasification program and certainly the Panhandle coal gasification project in Wyoming has also been scrapped. Mexico has delayed a huge project. Nigeria has shelved a $14 billion project. Falling oil prices and demand are creating uncertainty about the outlook for up to 70 potential new United Kingdom oil fields in the North Sea. Beyond project commitments already made, most further oil development in the British North Sea seem to be coming to a halt. While development in
The Netherlands sector of the North Sea is continuing, the emphasis is on small oil fields requiring minimum financial commitment. Due to falling oil prices and soaring costs, British Petroleum is turning to less costly equipment alternatives in its North Sea development. Investment costs per barrel of oil production capacity are thereby being lowered. The worsening oil markets and pricing uncertainties have led the French to shelve plans to buy 40,000 barrels per day of heavy crude from Venezuela and the French have shelved plans for building an upgrading plant in France at a cost of over $1 billion. However, like the Alsands project, if the situation changes in the future the plans can be revived. In the United States there are similar situations to those that I have mentioned.
There is an article in today's Globe and Mail written by George Linton which has rather significant news in it. It reads:
Shares of Dome Petroleum Ltd. of Calgary and of Gulf Canada Ltd. of Toronto rose in active trading on North American stock exchanges following a statement by William Richards, Dome president, that a Bearfort Sea well currently being tested "could be one of the best in Canada."
Another paragraph in this article reads:
Mr. Richards, testifying in Ottawa before a parliamentary committee, said the Tarsiut N-44 well "looks to be the best well we have drilled in the Beaufort and could be one of the best wells in Canada."
The well is producing "very interesting results" and offers an "very good prospect for being a commercial discovery."
I suggest that the cost of this oil from the Alsands project being what it is, the economies are simply not there at the present time-to proceed with this megaproject under current world conditions-not only conditions in Canada but world conditions.
Opposition members talked about operators moving to the United States in order to find work. I ask them why anyone would want to drill another gas well in Canada when there are already thousands upon thousands shut in at the present time because of the disappearance of markets. Most of the equipment left the gas fields where more than 40 per cent of the exploration work was being conducted prior to the rigs moving south of the border in September, 1981. Most of the rigs which moved south at that time were small and older ones which were not capable of reaching the depths required to bring new oil reserves within our reach.
The Alsands project was not economically feasible even if we consider the fact that the Government of Canada, working in unison with the government of Alberta, offered to guarantee not only 68 per cent of the equity put forward by the companies, but to supply 50 per cent of the total equity. Were hon. members opposite suggesting that the government should have put in 100 per cent of the equity and made it a public utility? Is this the other option? If this is what they are suggesting, I think we should look at it. They are not satisfied with what we have done; perhaps this is their alternative. I thought only one party opposite believed in nationalization. I believe there must be room for the private sector.

May 5, 1982
I have with me the 1980 annual report of Imperial Oil in which it described its exploration in the Arctic. It reads:
One of the best hopes for major additions to Canada's conventional supplies of oil and gas lies in the regions of the Mackenzie Delta and the Beaufort Sea in the northwestern Arctic.
I believe that this has proven to be correct. Turning to the 1981 annual report of Suncor, it was pointed out that new oil discoveries were being made on a day to day basis in Canada. It referred to Arctic Islands drilling and read as follows:
The 1981 drilling season in the Arctic Islands was highly successful. Three wells were spudded in late January and all three were discoveries. Oil and gas were found at Skate B-80, 18 kilometres northeast of Lougheed Island; Cisco B-66, 16 kilometres west of the Island; and Maclean 1-72, 27 kilometres east of the Island.
It went on to point out the tremendous potential in the Arctic Islands.
Turning to the 1981 annual report of Petro-Canada, it showed in detail the amount of drilling which has taken place off the east coast. It indicated that this oil will have a much lower cost than the oil anticipated in the tar sands projects. We have the reserves. It is a question of developing them within a cost frame which lends itself to economic conditions not only in Canada but in other major industrialized countries.
While we would have liked to see the tar sands project go ahead-as I believe some day that it will-we must remember that the Government of Canada and the government of Alberta made concessions. In the meantime we should reexamine the entire situation to see if we can develop other energy sources which will be lower in cost and redirect our present energies. Perhaps many job opportunities could be created in other places. If the Wilkins theory of the early 1940s were applied, the spin-off effects would benefit all Canadians.
Returning to the debate at hand, I think there are some matters which must be made very clear. There have been many different statements made about the National Energy Program, which has run into many problems. We must bear in mind that the federal government does not set retail prices, but it establishes the price paid to refiners for their crude. The blended price about which I am talking now is 70 per cent of world price as of January 1982 and the old oil price is 54.4 per cent of world price. Refiners purchase their crude oil at this price. Several costs are added to the retail price, such as 9 per cent for federal taxes.
I have heard hon. members opposite, not necessarily this morning, saying that oil and gasoline is much cheaper in the United States. I should like to give some comparative figures. I checked on the weekend and gasoline in Michigan was 98 cents per gallon. An American gallon is equal to 3.78 litres and a Canadian gallon is equal to 4.54 litres. If a gallon of American regular leaded gasoline costs 98 cents and the current United States dollar exchange rate in Canadian funds is approximately $1.22-and that was the exchange rate of the Bank of Canada as of May 4-then to purchase one American gallon of regular leaded gasoline in Canadian funds would cost $1.19. Since there are 3.78 litres in an American gallon, the cost to consumers in Canadian funds per litre of regular leaded gasoline would be 31.72 cents. Regular leaded gasoline in Ontario can be currently purchased for 37.9 cents per litre at
the Top Value station on Bronson Avenue in Ottawa. In Ontario the provincial sales tax on gasoline is 20 per cent or approximately 6.4 cents on every litre of gasoline. This means that the Canadian price is actually lower than the United States price.
What about United States taxes?

I have not mentioned the Ontario corporations tax or the lack of an Alberta tax on gasoline. For the benefit of the hon. member, let me indicate that in Alberta the price is approximately 31 cents per litre. We hear complaints about the price of gasoline. Oil companies indicate in some of their advertisements that two thirds of the price of gasoline goes to various levels of government. Perhaps this is true in the province of Quebec, but it is certainly not true in Alberta, Ontario or in most other Canadian provinces.
There are various rates of tax in the provinces. For example, in British Columbia it is 20 per cent. Of course, Alberta has no tax. Saskatchewan will be 20 per cent and 28 per cent, plus the insurance tax, which I understand will be removed. For Manitoba it is 20 per cent and gasoline at 18 per cent. Quebec is 40 per cent and New Brunswick is 16 per cent. Nova Scotia is fixed at 4.7 cents for gasoline and 6 cents for diesel fuel. In Prince Edward Island it is 22 per cent for gasoline and 29 per cent for diesel fuel. In Newfoundland it is 22 per cent and 26 per cent. In the Yukon and the Northwest Territories it is fixed.
I believe that the point which must be made is that it is just not a Canadian problem which has caused the cancellation of this megaproject. I am not even sure that we should say cancellation. I believe that temporary postponement is more accurate.
If we reflect back to the early explorers at the time when oil was first discovered, we realize that the potential of these reserves was recognized. These reserves are still there for future generations to be used as technology improves and more economical methods of extraction take place. With respect to surface extraction or open pit mining, we can only go down 70 feet in much of the tar sands area. Petro-Canada is actively involved in extensive research in order to find easier and better ways to develop and extract that oil. As well, many other companies are experimenting with steam extraction in order to find ways to go much deeper and utilize more of the oil that is there.
In the area where I come from, Lambton-Middlesex, there are many old oil wells. Some of them were the first discovered in North America. That is where Imperial Oil first began.
I am saddened at the fact that due to the lack of early technology those early drillers put down a multitude of wells without accurate records, with the result that after they became uneconomical, those wells ceased to be used and were left unplugged. Consequently, we are very limited in the ways
May 5, 1982

we can proceed to extract 60 per cent of the original oil that is still in the ground. The estimates vary as to how much is still there but certainly we have seen, through the National Energy Program, a revival of those old wells. New wells are being put into those new formations which may only yield 3 barrels per day, but under the National Energy Program and the pricing scheme, they are profitable.
It is wells such as those in Kansas that are attracting the drilling rigs out of Alberta to work areas with shallow fields in order to get oil which is less than 1,000 feet deep.
I believe that cheaper methods will be found not only to extract oil from my own area but from the tar sands as well. In fact, about 40 per cent of the wells in northern Alberta fall under the category of low producing wells. The incentives through the incremental oil revenue tax and the production in low producing wells has certainly made it feasible for the service industry to bring those wells which have been dormant back into production. These are wells which had been in production for only 20 years.
I believe there are many other areas to be considered during these difficult times. With the oil present in Canada today and as development of the Beaufort, Arctic Islands, Hibernia and the fields off the coast of Labrador continue, I believe that in the near term enough oil will be found to satisfy the needs of the Canadian people and give us the security required until such time as we have the technology required to do a better and more thorough job of extracting oil from the tar sands. It is my hope that these projects will continue and I am sure that they will. However, it will have to be under conditions which will give a better economic rate of return to the oil companies and to Canadians.
In closing, I would point out that with the oil companies as involved as they are, along with the two governments, perhaps their decision was correct in view of all the other cancellations in other countries of projects almost as large as this one. I look forward to the day when the National Energy Program will give us energy self-sufficiency. I trust that it will happen as forecast, that is by 1990.

Mr. Speaker, through you, good morning to all of those who tuned in from Atlantic Canada and to any early risers in Ontario and Quebec. My colleagues and I in the official opposition have been here all night in this wake for the Alsands project. I must say that I wish all Canadians could have heard the impassioned and excellent address given by our colleague, the hon. member for Calgary South (Mr. Thomson) about half an hour ago.
Hear, hear!

Indeed, many of our colleagues, whose eloquence obviously comes to a peak at these very weird early morning hours, gave excellent speeches.
It may be unusual for Members of Parliament to be speaking at 6.07 o'clock in the morning, but we in the official opposition not only find unusual, but critical for the economic and energy future of this country, the developments which
have clearly resulted from plain bad management by this government.
Let me say to those who have faithfully monitored the debate up to this point: do not expect any firm answers or even credible answers from this Liberal government by the time you rejoin us later in the day. From what we have heard, this government has answers to the tragedy which has occurred. It can only stand condemned for the collapse of the two megaprojects; Alsands and the Alaska highway pipeline. It can only stand condemned for the tens of thousands of Canadian jobs and dreams and for the ill-conceived National Energy Program. Without the National Energy Program I am convinced that we would not be having this emergency debate. Alsands would still be in place and the Alaska highway pipeline would still be under way.
I am an optimist by nature. I have always had an unshakable belief in the great good fortune of our country to have such a wealth of natural resources and people with an entrepreneurial spirit. But I have been deeply disturbed by the failure of this Liberal government to work in concert with the producing provinces in a national effort to move Canada toward the vital goal of energy self-sufficiency. The Progressive Conservative government set that goal for 1990. Our government, under the leadership of the right hon. member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) would have provided reasonable and orderly increases in petroleum prices over the next five years. We would have guaranteed Canadian industry and consumers that they would have continued to pay lower prices than their American counterparts. We would have produced more than $6 billion in new federal revenues for investment through a Canadian energy bank in new energy supply, substitution and conservation projects. Canadians do not need to be reminded once again why those plans ended with the federal election of 1980.
Canadians should be reminded of what has happened since the "cheaper than 18 cents a gallon" bunch rode back into power in 1980. A giant cloud of confrontation and mistrust has poisoned the relations between Ottawa and the producing provinces. Instead of agreement, the provinces were given aggravation and the National Energy Program. Instead of our programs which would have contributed so much to Canada's energy needs, economic growth and the creation of jobs for Canadians, we now see what the country bought in February 1980.
We have a National Energy Program which has driven investment, drilling rigs, expertise and whole projects out of the country or into the ground. We now have entire cities in this country on the verge of bankruptcy. We now have the collapse of the mighty Alsands project, the indefinite hoisting of the Alaska highway gas pipeline project, cutbacks in exploration and development activity, the direct loss of 71,000 jobs and the indirect loss of 255,050 Canadian jobs. That is Canada's loss. The blame for this gutting of Canada's energy future and our economy lies squarely on our perpetual Prime

May 5, 1982
Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and on the Liberal government of Canada.
There is no question that inflation has played a big part in the devastating turn of events. There is also no question that the rate of inflation was a whole lot lower three years ago and that these megaprojects would have been a good two years down the road had our government remained in power.
Let us just see what has happened to inflation. The inflation rate has risen from 9.3 per cent in March 1980 to 11.6 per cent in March 1982. In the past year alone, fuel oil costs have risen by 29.6 per cent, transportation costs by 16.4 per cent, fresh fruit costs by 28.7 per cent, processed vegetables costs by 18.8 per cent, and its goes on and on.
Wages are not keeping pace with inflation. The average wage earner in Canada has lost $285 in annual purchasing power since the February 1980 election and $635 since the fall of 1977. If you want to look at Canada's position vis-a-vis other industrialized nations, in the Olympics of economic performance, Canada is a hands-down loser in terms of trade, productivity, energy efficiency and changes in the standard of living. In terms of economic growth, in 1980 Canada's economic performance was one of the worst in the world. There was almost zero, 0.1 per cent, economic growth in Canada compared to an OECD average of 1.2 per cent growth and a European Economic Community average of 1.4 per cent. Our economic performance in 1980 ranked us twenty-first among 24 OECD nations.
In terms of energy efficiency, Canada is perhaps the most inefficient user of energy in the western world. In 1978, for example, we used energy at half the efficiency of European nations. The true picture of Canada under a Liberal government is much bigger and blacker.
Any consumer can confirm these statistics, especially those Canadians who travel a great deal to other industrialized countries in the western world. People need only drive up to a gas pump in the United States or compare prices at check-out counters in other countries to know what has happened to the Canadian economy.
I guess it is in the price of gasoline and home heating fuel where we feel most betrayed by this government. I know, as consumer affairs critic for the official opposition, that my anger is mirrored by millions of other Canadians. Consumers are going to get clobbered again as a result of this latest development.
Hundreds of thousands more barrels of imported oil during the coming years will likely result in higher home heating costs and, if this Liberal government continues in power, the next few months will definitely see higher prices at the gasoline pump. After all, governments, federal and provincial, lift 66 cents out of every dollar that consumers pay for gasoline in taxes.
The Trudeau government has continually inflicted its brand of water torture in the form of energy pricing-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: With all due respect to the hon. member, the practice of referring to hon. members of the House should either be by constituency or by function. That is a courtesy well preserved.

I apologize, Mr. Speaker. I should have said the government which is led by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), which is completely unacceptable to many Canadians. Nevertheless, I shall stick to the rules.
That government has continually inflicted on Canadian consumers its brand of water torture in the form of energy pricing. Their drip by drip campaign has been masqueraded under the metric guise of litres. The Liberals still insist on referring to the so-called odious 18 cents a gallon in the budget of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), so let us just put into perspective what has happened to the Liberals' solemn promise of cheaper gas in the last election campaign.
Gasoline prices have risen in some parts of Canada by as much as 86 cents a gallon. The average across Canada-my office recently sampled Vancouver, Winnipeg, Toronto, Montreal, Fredericton and Halifax-is 80 cents a gallon. That is 80 cents versus 18 cents, and that is just since February 1980, a little over two years.
What are consumers getting for this broken promise, this four and a half times more expensive increase in the price of gasoline than the 18 cents in the Conservative budget of 1979? Well, Canadians can see in the collapse of two large energy projects over the past few days that there are no economic benefits from this very costly increase. Indeed, there are very definite negative spin-offs, especially in Ontario and Quebec.
If the impact of the Alsands and Alaska highway are not felt immediately, future expansion plans, supply, employment and general economic development in Ontario and Quebec will almost certainly suffer.
I am indebted to my colleague, the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson), for supplying me with notes which target several key areas in central Canada which could either greatly benefit from high drilling activity and the megaprojects or which can be hurt temporarily or even permanently. The hon. member for Etobicoke Centre had this to say:
Energy is Canada's number one growth industry. The energy industry can be the primary engine for growth in employment, new technology, increased exports and new industrial development that will be drawn to this country by the promise of secure energy supplies at a price advantage relative to other industrialized countries. We in Ontario tend to think only of Alberta when we think of oil and gas. Let me illustrate the misconception of that view.
The potential stimulus for our manufacturing industry from energy development is virtually without parallel in our history. There are job opportunities in the next seven years in these industries to employ some 350,000 people throughout Canada. We cannot afford to disregard these opportunities.


May 5, 1982

The hon. member made those statements in 1980. Clearly this government does not believe in those opportunities. For some years we have been concerned, as the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre says, with the importance of developing our talents in areas where we have natural strengths. One of these areas is clearly oil sands development. The engineers and technicians working on the oil sands and heavy oil projects are developing technology which will be in tremendous demand in countries such as the United States, Venezuela and Australia. That will be no more, Mr. Speaker.
More than that, each synthetic oil project will generate economic activity over the life of the project about equivalent to the current level of our annual national income. In other words, each project will produce about $250 billion to $300 billion of economic activity over the 25-year life of the project. Of the economic activity during the construction period, about 40 per cent is generated in Alberta, 25 per cent in Ontario and 12 per cent in Quebec.
Major suppliers to the oil industry from Ontario and Quebec include Algoma Steel of Sault Ste. Marie, which supplies seamless steel casing. Stelco Canada, located in Hamilton and Welland, produces seamless tubing and continuous weld tubing. Ladish Company of Brantford supplies the industry with piped valves and fittings. Jenkins Brothers Limited of Lachine, Quebec and Mississauga, Ontario produces forged steel valves. Graphic Controls Canada Limited of Gananoque, Ontario supplies gas charts to various companies in the industry. Hawker Siddeley, Orenda division of Toronto, supplies industrial gas turbines. Farhamet of Orillia produces abrasive resistant castings used in the petro-chemical industry, and Simmons Drilling buys most of its trucks from Kenworth in Quebec.
Ontario is a major beneficiary, and would be a major beneficiary, not only because these activities produce the lifeblood of our manufacturing industry, oil, but because they also provide a major stimulus to our economy. Now, and if not immediately, down the road a few months and, even worse, two or three years from now, Ontario will not be a major beneficiary and there will not be any major stimulus as a result of the collapse of these megaprojects.
Some of my former colleagues in the parliamentary press gallery have almost been throwing up their hands and saying that from now on it is probably just a matter of good luck instead of good management in terms of our energy future and our energy security. In a philosophical column of yesterday, May 4, in the Ottawa Citizen my good friend Charles Lynch closed with this paragraph:
We must temper our expectations and put aside our dreams, and accept that the fading years of the 20th century won't be as exciting as the eight preceding decades, with their mixture of hope, peril and achievement. We know now, for the first time in the memory of the oldest among us, that some things are beyond our grasp.
I am not so sure I agree with Mr. Lynch's sad conclusion. I have not stopped dreaming dreams for this country. I do not believe the last two decades of this century should be any less
challenging or any less fulfilling than the preceding four and a half decades during which I have been around. I do not believe Canadians should abandon hope for this nation. Of all years, this year when Canada has achieved full independence and complete maturity as one of the great countries in the world we Canadians have much to look forward to, a great deal to achieve in the way of potential and a mighty part to play in the free world. If we are limited in any way, it is through the complete and utter incompetence, insensitivity, combativeness and mismanagement of this Liberal government.
Canadians have the capacity to get rid of this government in the next federal election. Canadians have it in their hands to elect a government which will regain the confidence of investors, and confidence of our massive energy industry, the confidence of the provinces and, above all, the confidence of this country's pioneering spirit. Those of us who are participating in this important debate, Mr. Speaker, fully intend to be sitting on your right after the next election, and we as the new Government of Canada will inspire that confidence in Canadian industry and enterprise. This government has proved that it is out to destroy initiative in this country, and we in the Progressive Conservative Party are determined not to let that happen.

Mr. Speaker, the government's national energy policy has now obviously collapsed in tatters around the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). If he would just stand up and resign as he was asked to do when he announced the failure of the Alsands project, we could all go home and start dealing, in the next day or so, with a brand new energy minister and, hopefully, a new federal energy policy.
It seems odd that everyone except the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources could see the collapse of the Alsands project coming, and we could all predict the postponement, once again, of the Alaska gas pipeline. Yet right up to the last minute these megaprojects remained the heart and soul of the National Energy Program. Did the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources really hope to pull off a miracle, or was he caught completely off guard?
With the removal of the centrepiece of the National Energy Program we are left with the federal government's beloved Petro-Canada and some investments in a few projects which may or may not show results in the foreseeable future.
I know that the federal government has some investments in oil and gas projects up in the Arctic, but the best estimates as to when we might see any oil or gas south of the Arctic Circle run anywhere from five to ten years to never. Judging by the government's performance since we were promised cheaper gasoline at the pump in the last election campaign, I suggest that the best estimate is never.
In its April 23 editorial, The Windsor Star predicted that the Alsands project would be dissolved by the end of April. The Star was right on, and it really is too bad that a project with a projected production of 137,000 barrels of oil per day

May 5, 1982
and a life expectancy of 25 years had to go down the drain because of government bungling.
Let us take a look at what the government has left in its national energy policy grab bag. We have Petro-Canada, as I mentioned before, the darling of the Liberal government and the NDP. The national energy policy gives Petro-Canada a free pass to the federal Treasury and carte blanche to buy up anything that comes up on the market, even if it has to pay 50 per cent to 100 per cent more than a company would bring in the private sector.
Then we have that much-touted policy called Canadianiza-tion whereby the federal government goes around buying up oil companies which are already Canadian owned. Then there is the government policy, brought in after the 1979-80 federal election campaign promises were put on the shelf, which imposes new federal taxes on gasoline at the pump every other week. These are not policies; they are evidence that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and his colleagues in the cabinet do not have any policies. They are bankrupt and tax-happy.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has the nerve to suggest that the collapse of the Alsands project is the fault of the private sector companies which were anxious to develop this source of oil just a few short years ago. They were so anxious that they have already invested tens of millions of dollars in the project. But it is smart money which goes where the action is, and the companies involved have to show a profit. When they see world prices being brought down by a reduction in demand for fossil fuels and when they see the federal government standing on the sidelines with both hands out, they run for cover. Who can blame them? They do not have access to the public Treasury. They have to answer to their investors and to their bankers, and they already know what the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) thinks of those of us who are not in his cabinet. He says that when we get 100 yards away from the House we are nobodies. Well, we have had all night and we have all day to let him know whether we are just a bunch of nobodies.
While we are talking about the increase in gasoline prices and the decline in world oil prices, I might ask the Prime Minister, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources or anyone opposite who bothers to listen whether they have consulted lately with their counterparts in the United States. I was told a few days ago that the price of gasoline has dropped slightly below $1 per gallon in some states, and the people still think they are paying too much.
Each time the price goes down in the United States, the price goes up in Canada, and it is really going up. We know already that we can expect two or three more increases in the price of gasoline and heating oil over the next few months, and the price in most places is already more than $2 per gallon.
A few days ago I was glancing through a householder sent to me last summer by my colleague, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). He had listed gasoline prices at several points in his riding. Regular gasoline was selling for $2.36 per gallon in Faro, and unleaded gas was selling for $2.43 per gallon. Heating oil cost $1.66 per gallon. These were prices in the
summer of 1981, and so I would very likely be shocked to hear today's prices. But the way things are going in my own riding, we will see those price levels down here before too much longer.
To get back to the government's tattered national energy policy and the collapse of the jewels in the Crown, the Alsands project and the Alaska gas pipeline project, I am intrigued by some of the figures that were being touted around by the government just a few days ago. My attention is drawn immediately to the number of jobs that we could expect to see created during construction. At the peak of construction there were to be almost 10,000 new jobs created, with 2,800 longterm jobs created to run the plant afterwards. Construction was to extend over the next six or seven years. Those jobs just went down the drain.
I notice that $13 billion in new money would be injected into the Canadian economy, but when I read further I see that one of the three remaining partners in the now defunct project was Petro-Canada, good old Petro-Canada, waving its key to the front door of the public treasury. Therefore I would expect that a large part of that $13 billion would have been recycled money, yours and mine.
Only the present government, with its bungling and fumbling could have struck fear into the hearts of the partners who jumped ship earlier in the game. Or, maybe they just got disgusted and decided that there was a better climate elsewhere for their investment capital. These are major players, Mr. Speaker, the big leagues, Dome, Hudson's Bay, Amoco Canada and Chevron Canada, and Shell Explorer (Houston). Of the remaining partners there was Petro-Canada, Shell Canada and Gulf. With Petro-Canada eyeballing Gulf, and Gulf looking over its shoulder at PetroCan, it must have been a very pleasant investment climate.
The Alsands collapse would have been bad enough by itself, but the tattered remnants of the government's energy program were already waving in the breeze caused by about 200 oil rigs heading south. A few days ago the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources proudly announced that a couple of drilling rigs had returned. Big deal, if any of the rigs have really come back. I feel sorry for them, because they were probably hoping to get a piece of the action at Alsands if the energy minister had pulled off his miracle, which never came about.
With the Alsands fold-up coming so close on the heels of the shutdown of the Cold Lake project last year, I do not see how the energy minister can keep his pipe dream of Canadian energy sufficiency propped up. We could have energy selfsufficiency under the minister's policies, but who could afford it? Who could afford to pay the price for energy self-sufficiency when we are already paying the highest prices in North America at the gas pumps, and drillers and investors are leaving Canada in droves?
I am absolutely appalled, and I think we all have a right to be appalled and even angry, that the present Liberal cabinet,
May 5, 1982

the largest cabinet in the history of Canada, cannot come up with a single idea or policy that will produce a single job. I think that we have a right to ask why it is that this Liberal government cannot seem to come up with anything except high unemployement, high inflation, high energy costs, high interest rates, high government deficits and a low Canadian dollar.
Our national economy is in an absolute shambles, and this is reflected in general public apathy. We see people packing their belongings and moving out of their homes in the dead of night. They are leaving their homes to the banks or trust companies, or to the Canada Mortgage and Elousing Corporation. They just do not care. They are fed up. A few short years ago the average Canadian would not have dreamed of doing such a thing as to walk out of his home and say, "To hell with it".
Canadians are fed up. They are fed up with not being able to afford a roof over the heads of their children. They are fed up with worrying about how much longer their employers will remain in business. The night before last there was a television special about a dying town, and the camera showed the types of businesses that were folding up. One was a bill collection agency. They are usually the last to go. But, I suppose, they decided that they could not get blood from a stone, so they just closed their doors.
Canadians are fed up with excuses and diversions. For almost two years the Prime Minister fiddled around with his pet project, the Constitution, while Canada burned. The government is spending $9 million to tell Canadians that they have a new Constitution, as if they did not already know. What Canadians want to know today is, what is the government going to do about high unemployment and high inflation. If they are not going to do anything, it would be refreshing at least to hear them admit it.
The collapse of the Alsands project is a serious matter. But let us not mistake it for the disease. It is only a symptom. The real disease is the collapse of the Canadian economy, and the jobs lost by the Alsands collapse will, unfortunately only be added to the record total of unemployed in Canada today.
The investment capital chased away by this Liberal government at the Cold Lake and Alsands projects will only be added to the list of investors already driven out of Canada. The real tragedy, the one thing that none of us is able to understand, is that the collapse of the economy is being presided over by 35 cabinet ministers, the largest cabinet in any country in the western world. This inflated, bloated cabinet, is backed up by no less than 114 people with the rank of at least deputy minister. What are they all doing, Mr. Speaker? What are they waiting for?
I am deeply disturbed by the collapse of the Cold Lake and Alsands projects, and the further delay in the Alaska gas pipeline project. I am disturbed by the collapse of the federal government's National Energy Program. However, my real sympathy is for the business people who are having to declare bankruptcy and close their doors, some of them old family firms of second and third generations. My sympathies are with those people who cannot find jobs, whose work ethic is being
trampled into the ground. My sympathies are with those families who cannot afford decent accommodation because of high inflation and high interest rates. I hope we can give some advice to this government which it will heed and which will stimulate our economy, put our Canadians back to work and put our Canadians back in their homes. I hope we can find an oil policy which will work and be beneficial to all Canadians.
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, 1 thank the Tories down there for their applause. It is very nice of them.
You need a hand now and again.
At this time in the morning one needs all the help one can get.
Where the hell have you been all night?

I managed to get two or three hours of sleep. I am in a somewhat better shape than a couple of people will be because of it.
I think all hon. members in this House feel rather sad during this debate because of the sorry mess caused by the continuing policies of the ding-bats and the ding-a-lings, the Tweedle-dums and Tweedle-dees of Canadian history as far as energy policy is concerned. A number of my colleagues and a number of other hon. members have discussed the single-track psychology of the megaproject and the inevitable problems which will arise later on because we tend to put all of our eggs into one basket, sometimes in a basket of a slightly different colour, but one basket nevertheless. We seem to be playing Pharaoh in this country. For at least 5,000 years, politicians have been building pyramids every time they think they are in trouble. The only difference between those of today and those that were built in Egypt 5,000 years ago is that most of the ones we are building or trying to build in this country now turn to dust even before they are erected. It does not seem to matter very much whether it is a giant oil sands project or whether it is B.C. Northeast Coal which almost seems to be on the rocks before it gets started. People are saying it is underpriced by $20. I know that the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) has no great love for what that project seems to be doing in his constituency.
There are large-scale hydroelectric projects that are shipping electricity across the line for far less than they could get for it there.
In times like these we tend to forget the stupidities that led us into the present crisis. These super-efficient oil companies that my friends to the right and hon. members opposite like to tout as being the champions of initiative and skill got us into a mess a few years ago and, all of a sudden, hundreds of years of oil reserves turned into 20 or 30 years of reserves in one fell swoop. That is the kind of leadership and imagination of which a lot of Canadians have had enough.

May 5, 1982
It is this sort of thing that has allowed the present government, among others, to create its own "Canadianization" version of the Tasmanian devil that looks like one thing, acts like another, and brays like something else, and is not particularly productive.
Other megaprojects are involved such as the coal deposits in northeastern British Columbia. There is talk of shipping this non-renewable resource across the ocean at a subsidized price to low-cost industry whose products will come back to compete with our own. That is another glorious result of the various national energy policies that we have seen in this country, one after the other. B.C. Hydro is shipping huge quantities of hydroelectric power south of the border at a price which is far lower than the market could bear.
It appears that the new nuclear station in New Brunswick is going to share its excess electric power from that nuclear plant-which has been a boondoggle all its own-down south of the line. And yet we talk about energy self-sufficiency, Mr. Speaker.
One of the reasons that I dwell on that is that Kootenay West had its own megaproject a few years ago. That was another boondoggle, Mr. Speaker. The Social Credit premier of British Columbia at that time was a man that many of us had a great deal of affection for. At least he knew a little bit about life, having gone from the bottom up, and unlike some other politicians in this country, he understood a little bit about how people and how communities tick. We could use a little more of that kind of horse sense today. He made a couple of real dandy mistakes, however. One was the Columbia River Treaty and the various and assorted dams that were "not going to cost the province a nickel." We see the same kind of economic genuis behind the National Energy Program.
A lot of people tonight seem to not want to talk about anything but Alsands, but there is another issue in this motion, Mr. Speaker, and that is the Alaska highway pipeline. I know that the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Yurko) and the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) had a little good-natured fencing match over that issue a short while ago. The issue of the Alaska highway pipeline and how we got into the sorry situation that we are in today again appears to be on the back burner. I wonder why no one has spoken about the prebuild tonight?
We sometimes talk about people being in bed together, Mr. Speaker. The Liberals and the Tories may not be in bed together but a lot of people suspect that they are going at it pretty hot and heavy somewhere behind the bushes. They just do not like to do it out in the open. They are both nourished from the same tit, Mr. Speaker. That is the way they act and it has been the same in this country for over 100 years.
I am a relatively new member of the House, Mr. Speaker, but one of the things that makes me sad is the combination of the spirit of arrogance on the side opposite and the continuing spirit of revenge that has been present in the Conservative Party ever since the kamikaze squad led them to self-immolation in December 1979. The choice that is before the Canadian people is whether the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is going
to kill them on purpose or whether the Conservatives are going to do it by accident. That is the only choice.
Tommy Douglas used to tell a story about the old cream separator. I will not go into that, but what is going on with the energy policy today reminds me of it. All these guys know how to do is how to shovel public money at people, whether it is to the oil companies or to the people who, unfortunately, have been left without jobs in this country. They always want to shovel money at people.
The Tory-Liberal policy on energy is continually to shovel money into one end of a pipe and then to call it a suitable reward for private initiative when their friends in the oil industry-who, by the way, help finance their parties and their election campaigns-grab the cash as it comes out the other end. If it does not come out the private end of the pipe, the PCs and the Liberals keep shoving it into the public end. They call that providing additional incentives. When they have shovelled so much of the taxpayers' money into the pipe that it is forced out of the private end, then the companies compete to grab the spout and take the risk of being trampled in the rush. That is about the only kind of risk that some of the friends of the people to my right and some of the more secret friends of members opposite take. They get 93 cents out of the dollar, so that is not much of a risk. It is an old story and maybe people get used to it.
I said I was saddened by the combination of arrogance and revenge that I see around here. Ever since that late evening of February 18, 1980 this incompetent kamikaze squad to my right, otherwise known as the Conservative party, has been sulking. It has been mired in a well of self-pity. When they tire of banging their heads against the wall or, more often, banging their heads against each other or engaging in some other act of self-flagellation, they rise only to vent their rage at everybody in sight, shouting, "Revenge, betrayal, conspiracy, unfair", in a useless and increasingly sad attempt to focus blame on others for their own miserable ineptitude.
PC no longer stands for Progressive Conservative, Mr. Speaker. It stands for pitiful castaways. That is what they are, pitiful castaways. Somebody ought to do a TV serial on them. They have been cast away into the garbage can of political oblivion, and the more you hear from them, the more you know that they have really earned that role.
That is what happened in Saskatchewan.

It makes you sad because they have had some pretty good people in the past, and there are a few good ones there now. One of them had to leave, and he now sits behind us over here. The hon. member for Edmonton East is one, and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) is another. There may be others. From time to time we do hear some rational thought, and whether we agree or not philosophically, at least there is an attempt to serve what we all call the public interest. There are people who are a
May 5, 1982

little bigger than the kamikaze squad over there who fell on their own swords. I wish I could find something more cheerfull to say about them, but I find it difficult.
One of the problems is that the government cannot seem to make up its mind on what it wants to do. If you are going to go the public sector route on projects which are not profitable enough or which society in its wisdom feels that for social or political reasons have to go ahead, that is fine. If you want to use the same process in those areas which are profitable so you do not have all the losers on the public purse and the winners in the private sector, that is fine. But to have a system called Canadianization, which is nothing more than a pseudonym for bureaucratization, is the worst of both worlds. It makes you think that they are trying to decide on what kind of mixed-up policy they can have to create more jobs for bureaucrats. I wish they would get their heads together because, for better or worse, they are in those seats over there and we are stuck with them probably for the next couple of years at least.
You put them there.
That was not our choice, sir.
That was your stupidity.

Whether you like it or not, the people of Canada put them there. They also put you on this side, and I know you do not like that. I think there is a sadness which pervades all of us over the events of the last little while. I was wondering whether we should not ask the Canadian Labour Congress to put on a grade-one school in bargaining strategy and make it a compulsory course for all cabinet ministers and anyone who aspires to be a cabinet minister. Hopefully, they will then learn not to repeat what they did with the pre-build. You do not give the whole package away until you get somebody's signature on the dotted line, not some phony ironclad, lily-clad, cottonball guarantees which are not worth a damn thing anywhere. It is sad that the attitude which is perceived to be typically Canadian is that you always get taken for a ride. That is the image these guys on my right and those guys on the other side have continually given to us in the international business world. You give away the store and then wonder why somebody takes advantage of you. If you sit down forever with your head in the sand and your bare rear end stuck up above ground, somebody is going to do it to you sooner or later.
I find it rather offensive, Mr. Speaker, to hear these sexist comments coming from the hon. member of the NDP. The least he could do is to offer respect to the women-

speechtext: The Chair has been listening carefully to the language, and while it is borderline, it is not unparliamentary.

It's just the romance in my soul, Mr. Speaker, but I must apologize for offending the sensibilities of my hon. friends down in the corner. It is just that they get us so excited. They are such titillating personalities. In any event, Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is any sexual innuendo in talking about their being lousy bargainers. We are going to be
in a crunch very soon, Mr. Speaker, and I hope my friends on the right and across the way take one of those elementary bargaining courses I was talking about and do a better job for the people of this country.

Mr. Speaker, I have several things which I think are quite important to put on the record and I hope they enter the minds of some members of the House. What we are debating here tonight started in 1973-74. Eight years ago we had the rise in metal and oil prices, and we saw the provincial governments tripling and quadrupling their taxes on the mining and oil industries. It went right across the country. Keep in mind that there are more culprits in this particular mess than appear on the surface. The beginning of this mess we are in today was when the provinces went hog wild in their greed and tripled and quadrupled their taxes.
In 1974, the critical act which really put us on the path to where we have ended up tonight was the decision of the federal government to retaliate against the provinces and bring in the Turner budget which made provincial taxes and royalties nondeductible. In effect, it was an interference with the federal system and was, in plain terms, stealing the property of the provinces. One mistake by the provinces was countered with a second mistake, much worse, by the federal government. That first budget was under a minority government. That minority government was defeated after two years and we went to the country. The NDP and the Conservatives worked together in 1974 to fight that budget, led by a man who is no longer with us, Mr. T. C. Douglas, who at that time was the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands. This history is important because when you find a fight between two levels of civil servants-because that is really what it was-or who could grab the most money from the mining industry and from the oil industry to go on that spending spree which all the provinces and the federal government went on, this is where our trouble began.
The key to it in these Turner budgets was the non-deductible provision. I felt just as keenly then as I do now about that horrible mistake in economic and political judgment. I spoke in the House at the end of one of the ways and means motions on the second budget on January 30, 1975. I would recommend that speech to every thinking person, not only in this House but all across the country. It was reasonably non-political. I put forward then the warning that every capital intensive venture that would be embarked upon in the future had no hope of success because of the double taxation in the Turner budget. I give credit to the then leader of the NDP for seeing the danger. He warned the House that once the government cracked down, unconstitutionally, on the mining industry and on the oil industry, the forest industry would be next in line, followed by the electrical industry. Those warnings by the two of us went unheeded. Now I can look at that speech made

May 5, 1982
eight years ago and realize what a tragedy has unfolded leading up to the last two or three days.
Canada has waited 100 years for the world to need its resources. But it is on these resources that we plan to build our industrial pyramid. But you have to get a demand to create a cash flow on which to build. That mistake of the Turner budget in 1974, because he repeated the same thing the second time around, will rank in the economic history of this nation as one of the greatest blunders ever made.
Shortly after the election, as we all know, Mr. Turner, the minister, asked to retire from his job because he had been destroyed, and he knew it. All he got from his leader as a reward was the offer of a senatorship. He has returned to law practice. We hear rumours through the press that he may want to come back. The truth is he likes it where he is now. He knows what he has to face in this House with a budget like that on his record if he comes back. He was one of the most best liked and most able men I have seen on any side of the House. I saw him destroyed by taking up the case of civil servants in finance and seeking revenge against the provinces for raising taxes, which they had every legal right to do.
I want to make one thing abundantly clear. I have spoken tonight about Tommy Douglas, an NDP member, and myself, a Conservative. We were not speaking as partisans in that debate, we were speaking as Canadians from Saskatchewan who came up the hard way. We were speaking on behalf of the future of the Canadian people. I can never forget in my own mind, as the debate ranged the second time on the second budget, hon. NDP members in this House cheered on their Liberal allies. They thought they were gouging the oil and gas companies and the mining companies and they said "That is their policy, destroy them." But they did not realize that they were destroying the jobs of the workers of Canada. Now we see the mines that should have been in Ontario are over in Minnesota where we pay a much higher price for the basic iron reserves of which we have ten times more in Canada than the Americans ever had.
I put this before you because the mistake that we are witnessing this last few days started a long time ago because some people put politics ahead of their country.
I have never blamed Turner for that budget. I knew he was concerned about it. Yet he had no recourse, without any backing from his leader, in standing up to the civil servants. That is the reason why he was through. The same thing was repeated.
All governments entered into a rash of takeovers; private enterprise entered into a rash of takeovers. These takeovers were not to increase production, just to become bigger. There was the potash industry in Saskatchewan. There was no discussion with the public. The government of Saskatchewan rushed in after the election was over in 1974 and took over large chunks of the potash industry. In British Columbia there was a great fight for the mining industry. That government brought the mining industry to its knees. Not only was this government at fault. A rage seemed to come over people. They had to smash any person or company that was in the resource field. That mistake rests on all political parties. But there were
some in every political party that warned against it. Now that the chickens have come home to roost, we should be absolutely clear what the real mistake was, people put partisan politics above duty to their country.
This was the beginning of the federal-provincial war over revenues which has existed ever since. This war has led to the most serious attack on the Constitution we have ever experienced in our history. The first bit of evidence on this was the Petroleum Administration Act, 1974. We fought it in the House all during that year, before and after the election. We were able to get nine provinces to join us in the fight. In the meetings with the then minister reponsible for mines and the then minister of finance, the legislation was not made any more acceptable. The great mistake was that the ministers used the excuse that there was an energy crisis and that it was necessary to have the Supreme Court of Canada say that in a crisis the federal government would have certain powers which it did not otherwise have. This meant that the power of the federal government could override the power of provincial governments, which is paramount, because the resources belong to the provinces and they have every legal right to do whatever they like with them. The Petroleum Administration Act is still on the statutes. It was amended only two months ago, but it is still unconstitutional. No one has ever referred the matter to the courts so that we could have the benefit of a decision on its constitutionality.
