Now that the crisis has turned around and apparently for a few short years the world will have a surplus of oil, would they rule it a crisis in energy? I do not know, but I hope Canadians realize that we are debating the mistakes of the last eight years in this all-night session. These mistakes should be branded on the flesh of politicians with a hot iron so that they will not be repeated.
We have seen the rise of separatism in Quebec and the rise of western alienation. Then came the period of fraud and scam when nothing was being done on economic issues. Politicans became involved in a program of producing great showpieces to amuse the people. There was a great cry that it was necessary to patriate the Constitution. Now that it is patriated, do Canadians notice any difference? We have the same old Constitution with the Charter of Rights and Freedoms, but the Diefenbaker Bill of Rights has not been repealed. One would think from all the screaming and yelling in the House that a battle was going on.
Also we have Tweedle-dum in the NDP and Tweedle-dee in the Liberal Party saying that the Constitution is the greatest in the world. What fraud, what scam! Is it any wonder that people across the nation are losing their respect for every party? We all suffer because of image-making politics led by pollsters, advertisers and con men. The radio, television and newspapers preach a campaign of fear rather than debate issues. For example, they told the people of Canada that they should not dare to vote for the Right Hon. Leader of the
May 5, 1982

Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) because smart Toronto had named him a "wimp". They scared the daylights out of people. Some wimp! He was the one who rose and said that because of the federal-provincial war brought forward by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the Constitution Canada would never be the same again. Any responsible person in Canada who rises and says that there is danger ahead and that the country is being changed is not a wimp. Every Canadian listened and acted. As the record shows, this man rose in the House of Commons and said that Canada would never be the same, and the population came to attention. After a two-year fight, this young man pushed an arrogant government to its knees. The government was forced to refer the Constitution to the Supreme Court of Canada and to take it back to the provinces. No man is perfect, every man makes mistakes. When a man does something which is worth while for his country, it should be noted, as I have noted it today.
The National Energy Program caused many of my colleagues to become very excited. It was a fraud from the word go. It was an exercise in pretending to Canadianize the oil industry. All it did with the energy policy was to come to the bitter truth of the last few days. It was a fraud from the beginning, and the government is paying a heavy price for it today.
During this debate we have heard about the loss of jobs and businesses. Not only eastern Canada is in stagflation, but the government has succeeded in sending the entire country into a very deep recession and probably a depression.
I well remember the debate on the budget which was referred to earlier. The budget of the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) was not too bad. It was the first budget in the western industrialized world which tried to balance the budget, not only by restraints here and there but by decreasing taxes across the line. When there are two political parties rivalling each other and claiming credit for defeating the budget of the hon. member for St. John's West, how will history deal with it? Long before President Reagan was elected and balanced the budget by reducing taxes which will become effective this summer, the Conservative government had done it in 1979. It is true that the advertisers hired by the party did not know about it. Perhaps they do not read very well, but the fact remains that it was not a bad budget.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his allotted time has expired. He may continue only by unanimous consent. Is there unanimous consent for him to continue?
Agreed.

I only have a few more comments to make. I am simply pointing out that all of us have a lot to answer for over the last eight years. I did want the opportunity to put what I said on the record. Many a fine person in the game of image politics has been destroyed in the history of his country because it all comes out sooner or later.
I would like to think that there is some glimmer of light which will emerge from this debate. I believe there are glimmers of light in this sorry mess with Alsands and the pipeline delay. As I pointed out in my speech almost eight years ago, neither of these projects should have proceeded in the manner in which they were financed.
I wrote to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and spoke to him. I wrote to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and spoke to him. I wrote to every premier in the country and I wrote to every major oil and gas company to show them my old common sense figures. It is not the cruel way of putting a company under a high interest load for a long payout period. I would just like to say that I have available hypothetical cash flow figures showing how it works. For example, when interest rates are high, you do not borrow.
Another principle which I put forward and which has been used before is increased velocity of capital flow and I will explain how it is done. Whether you buy a home, farm or capital intensive business, you must get rid of front-end loading. As a result of this type of financing, the Alsands projects can be brought onstream so that not only will the government earn money, the companies will get enough money to reward them for the risk they have taken. We should not object to making more money when everybody benefits. That is my only point.
Another reason why I am glad that the Alsands project did not proceed is that we have on the horizon three new technologies for recovering heavy oil out of the ground and removing tar sands from the sand in a much cheaper and better way than what we are doing with our present technology. This slight delay may encourage governments to try the latest technology. One can be tried and proven one way or another within a year and the other may take longer. However, it may give us a chance to avoid what I thought would be a great blunder if we proceeded with these megaprojects which had bad financing policies while not looking for enough alternative technologies which could make them better. There exists in the tar sands 1,000 billion to 1,500 billion barrels of oil. With our present technology, all we can hope to derive is 250 billion to 275 billion barrels. With these newer and cheaper technologies it would be possible to derive up to 60 per cent. The present recovery plan is about 12'/2 per cent to 15 per cent. I find it sad that we can only derive 10 per cent or 12 per cent of those resources and leave the rest in the ground. This occurs constantly with our late oils in Alberta, Saskatchewan and British Columbia, as well as in all other major oil producing countries in the world. We have recovery up to 25 per cent or 27 per cent, but I am disturbed by what is left in the ground. Technology is being developed and I believe success is very close in this particular area.

Mr. Speaker, I always enjoy hearing a good speech from the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton). I would hope that in the near future he will have an opportunity to put

May 5, 1982
on the record his suggestion regarding the financing of this project.
I was pleased to hear that he ended on a positive note. I believe that it is absurd to assume that we are discussing the total demise of the oil sands project in this country. I cannot believe that this is the case.
If we look at alternative plans in the future instead of discussing the last year or two, we will see that we need those projects very badly. The method of extraction discussed by the hon. member should be looked into in this country.
I do not entirely agree with him that what he calls double taxation has been at the heart of the problem. I believe there are other factors involved which exist today. I will deal with those factors in a few moments.
For several weeks now I have listened to the debate on this subject and the whole question of the National Energy Program. I would like to make some observations with respect to this debate. If one listens in particular to the Progressive Conservative members, one would assume that at some point the National Energy Program was guilty of drilling a hole under the earth's crust, thus allowing all our oil to leak out, and not leaving us with any. It is their attitude which makes one think that the oil will be gone forever and we should be extracting it rapidly because it will all leak out. They have the same attitude with respect to gas which is capped. They believe it will somehow leak into the air. They seem to think that if we do not explore we will not be able to find it again. It appears to be the dominant attitude of those hon. members.
Perhaps nuclear fusion or some other technology will render this particular resource useless, but I do not believe that. Those resources are there and they will become more valuable as time goes on.
I would like to put forward some of the reasons why we are not proceeding with this project. They do not have anything to do with the value of those resources. To suggest that we must develop our oil and natural gas quickly is ridiculous. Another fallacy which prevails is that if the state acquires an interest or ownership in a private corporation, it is an expense to the government. For instance, if the government is buying Pacific Petroleums it is considered to be an expense to the government and a waste of money. On the other hand, when Thompson acquires ownership of Hudson Bay it is called an investment. Thompson expects to make a profit over the years on what would be termed a good investment.
When the Canadian government buys Petrofina, it is an expense. Obviously it does not expect to make any money out of that purchase. We constantly hear the question being asked as to why we buy these gas stations. It is as though we were spending a lot of money and not getting anything out of it. I will tell you why I want us to own such a company. I want to see the inside of the industry, from the search for oil to the drilling, to the gas pump. I want to keep an eye on this. That was the reason for setting up Petro-Canada in the first place. It is still a reasonable proposition.
There is another point which seems to elude a lot of people, particularly the Tories. I find it difficult to understand the position of the NDP on this. The point is that it seems there is something dishonest or socialistic-I guess the two are used together by people who talk of socialism as some kind of evil, even though we live in a part of the world where a mixed economy is a common factor, at least for this century-about a government that would get itself into the position of trying to own 50 per cent of its own natural resource.
How is this done? How is it acquired? Do we sit and wait for it to happen? It has never happened before, and will not happen unless someone takes a step to make it happen. Someone must say this is what we are going to do. I remember a convention in about 1975 or 1976 where there was a lot of talk about 50 per cent ownership. We do not hear that any more. All we hear now is that it is a terrible thing for us to do.
I have to be very angry with the NDP on this point. I have great respect for the Hon. Tommy Douglas. In my opinion he was a great legislator. I worked with him for a long time on approximately five energy bills. When I say a long time, it was because they were drawn out for a long time, 30, 40 or 50 days.
Each time in the House when we dealt with energy bills, or dealt with them in committee, the members of the NDP, represented by Mr. Douglas as the energy critic, supported every one of those bills. The National Energy Program is the first time that party has not supported these bills. Mr. Douglas has shown interest in supporting them by talking with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and groups of other people, offering his support.
There may be some things in the bills that could be changed. They could be changed by a party that says it supports the principle but here is what it wants to do. That is not the kind of politics that party is playing at this time.
I would like to deal specifically with the problem of the so-called demise of the Alsands project. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain is correct that it is only a temporary demise. It is interesting to note that on the same day, or within a day that the announcement was made that this project would not be going ahead, Exxon in the United States announced it would not be going ahead with the oil shales project. I find it very interesting that the two projects were slowed down, stopped, terminated or postponed at almost the same time. I expect the rationale for both decisions has to be found in the global economic scene.
There are some factors we should look at seriously. The first and perhaps most important factor came into effect in the last six or eight months as a result of softening in the major markets of the world price of conventional crude oil. Prices had risen very rapidly, almost doubling, since we came into power. All of a sudden they have started to taper off. This is a very temporary phenomenon. There has not been nor do I think there will be any large increase in the world supply of conventional crude oil. There is the Hibernia and some large finds in the North Sea, but total world growth in known
May 5, 1982

reserves does not appear to be substantial. This is another reason why synthetic fuels will come onstream in a few years.
Let us look at what caused the softening of oil prices. The conservation ethic had a lot to do with prices. Prices increased from $1.50 to $2 a barrel to $34, $35, $38 or $39 a barrel, depending on the spot market. That happened in less than a decade, about nine years. It had a very significant effect on the amount of oil being used, but not much effect on the amount of oil that has been discovered. That problem must still be dealt with. However, conservation as it is related to price has had an effect on the amount of oil being used.
The second factor is the world recession. There is no doubt that with a general recession, individuals, corporations and nations do not use energy at the same rate. Things have slowed down. The growth factor is not there.
This country has gone from a growth rate of 5 per cent or 6 per cent along with a good portion of the industrialized world in the mid-seventies to almost a negative growth rate at this time. That has had a significant effect on the price of crude oil. The failure of crude oil to continue to rise in price has been one of the major factors in making this project not very desirable at this time in terms of financing and a return to the companies and governments involved.
The second factor is related to the first factor. These factors are not separable. They have to do with world inflation. This has not been given enough consideration. I spoke about it in 1973, and many times since. I refer to the inflationary cost in terms of megaprojects. Time and again with a project as large as the gas pipeline or a tar sands plant there is a built-in inflationary factor which does not seem to follow reason. The inflationary factor with the trans-Alaskan pipeline was several times the normal rate of inflation. You predict certain things will happen and the inflationary factor grows immensely. If you look at the oil shales in the United States and the two projects that are under discussion, the gas pipeline and the Alsands project, you find a tremendous inflationary factor built into those megaprojects. The argument is one I have always made; hon. members can go back and look at the record. I think this is one of the things we must consider.
1 seriously want to discuss the third factor. I think we should get into this in a real way. Some action in this area is needed in order to move our economy in total, and in order to give these kinds of projects some possibility. The matter to which I refer is that of high interest rates. We cannot ignore this factor. We can shout and say all kinds of things, but high interest rates are what really determine what in the long run, along with the other factors, will be the bottom line. What does a project cost? Anyone buying a house today must know that the real factor is not the cost of the house. The real factor is what will be paid over 20 years, 25 years or 30 years. The same is true with any project. Megaprojects have their own special inflationary problems, but still the main factor is the cost of money and the cost of investment. That is what we must consider.
We keep hearing-from monetarists, particularly-that inflation can be beaten by high interest rates. That monetary policy involves reduced monetary supply. It involves a reduced supply of money and, inevitably, high interest rates they say, will kill inflation. They have not done so in this country, and I do not believe they really have in the United States. With the inflation rate being down, one would think interest rates would also come down, but that has not happened. The effects are rather strange. In the United States today the real interest rate is somewhere between 14 per cent and 15 per cent. What I mean by the real interest rate is the bank prime rate minus the inflation rate, and the real interest rate is something in the order of 14 per cent or 15 per cent. If there were any direct relationship between inflation and interest rates, one would assume that when the inflation rate in the United States is less than 3 per cent-some say it is a good deal less than that- interest rates would come down accordingly.
I have gone back a couple of times and taken close looks at the relationship between inflation and interest rates, or the real interest rates, and I have found there is a very close relationship, but that that relationship disappeared about 1978 or 1979. In 1973, real interest rates in Canada averaged about 3.9 per cent; in 1974, about 1.9 per cent; in 1975, minus 0.7 per cent; in 1976, 0.7 per cent; in 1977, 0.6 per cent; and in 1978, 3.3 per cent. All were under 3 per cent, or in that area. The difference between the inflation rate and the prime rate was between zero and 3 per cent. I have looked into this matter back to the sixties and back to the fifties, and I have found the same pattern. The real interest rate has been anywhere from zero to 3 per cent.
All of a sudden the rate took off. In 1979 it went up to 5 per cent; in 1980, 4.8 per cent; and in 1981, 6.5 per cent. If we look at figures from July 1, 1981, to the end of February, 1982, we find that the average was 8.9 per cent. In the United States it is about 14 per cent or 15 per cent.
What used to be true is no longer true. That relationship is not holding the way it used to hold. I think this distortion in the relationship has more to do with the problem we are facing than almost any other factor, including even world recession or world oil prices. This distortion has made this kind of project almost prohibitive. It is almost impossible to go ahead with it because of this distortion.
My time is up, and I see you are ready to rise, Mr. Speaker. At a later date I would like to discuss this distortion, what is causing it, and what is the underlying cause of the fact that our economy is so stagnant at this point.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. McRae) wants to put off until another day an explanation for the underlying causes of our economic dilemma. If he had been here all night he would have heard very detailed, succinct and thorough explanations of those causes and, if he would care to stick around a little longer, we might give him the benefit of further explanations.

Right out of the eighteenth century.

May 5, 1982

It has been a long, weary night for those of us on this side who stuck it out, but for me it has been worth waiting for this opportunity to speak in this important debate on the crisis facing our nation and the incompetent leadership from the government opposite which has led Canada to the brink of a national economic depression. I wonder why it was that only two Liberals sat on the benches opposite for most of the nighttime hours and only one or two NDP members were here. This is an important time when they should be listening to the views of the opposition and contributing to this debate in a rational way instead of living in a dream world, as the hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan appears to be when he describes these problems to international factors, the provincial governments, and to all the red herrings he can dig up, and never faces up to the fact that the government opposite was elected to govern and to take advantage of certain situations in our country.
We have excess production capacity to ensure that people in this country are employed, but constituents call us on the telephone, as a young lady called me the other day. That young lady is a mother of two. She wept for half an hour while telling me that she and her husband placed their personal home on the line a year and a half ago to borrow money for a business venture, only to see it collapse because of the retrograde policies of the MacEachen budget and the National Energy Program. This couple are now faced with the government's taking away the home for which they worked several years, and losing the equity they have accumulated in that home.
A Vancouver housing developer who put a million and a half dollars into a major apartment project in Vancouver came to my office, with red in his eyes and ferocity in his heart, to tell me that he lost a million and a half dollars and that everything he had worked for in the last ten or 15 years was tied up in property he could not sell. Lie told me he was on the brink of bankruptcy. These are the circumstances which have brought this country to the point where we must hold this emergency debate and talk incessantly until the government opposite begins to realize that all this need not have happened. That is the crime of it all. All this need not have happened.
The anti-Canadian policies of the Liberal government opposite, aided and abetted by the NDP, are wrecking our beloved country, which was once a land of freedom and opportunity and is now reduced to little more than a welfare state. These people are referred to by The Globe and Mail as the demolition experts. I think that is quite an apt description of the anti-Canadian, subversive policies which are imposed upon this country by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) to such an extent that they are bringing about the economic ruination of our country and a crisis of confidence of unprecedented proportions.
Frankly, those who have money to invest in the future of the country just cannot trust the leadership of this nation. I would like to quote Mr. W. A. Macdonald of the respected Toronto
law firm of McMillan, Binch, who spoke at a special IBM conference in Banff recently. Mr. Macdonald said:
Canada is beset by political directions at the federal level that run strongly counter to strategic requirements of the country. The policy outlook and political commitments of those in charge make an early change in these directions unlikely.
Canada, with this major drag on its capacity to adjust, has lost the confidence of investors at home and abroad, and has damaged the foundations of its relationships with other countries, particularly the United States.
Mr. Macdonald went on to state:
The most difficult thing to reserve will not be the bad policies, although that will also not be easy. It will be to restore trust, within the country and outside.
That is the dilemma we are facing at a time in our history when we sit on the threshhold of massive potential and opportunity. In those oil sands in the Fort McMurray area and northwestern Saskatchewan we have the potential to produce oil for 500 to 1,000 years at the current rate of consumption, approaching one billion barrels a year. We have that potential to be tapped here and now.
You are guessing.

Although research and extracting of oil from sands has been under way since 1950, when the Alberta Research Council and the government of Alberta first initiated this research, the best known technology today requires that megaprojects and the economies of scale be used to develop that potential.
Some of the other concepts which involve solvents and steam injection and frothing to the surface of underground deposits are not viable, at least for a decade. Therefore the point we have to make is that these major megaprojects are essential and that before 1990, if we are to become self-sufficient in energy, we must have six to eight projects of the scale of Alsands in operation. That is the only way to produce the more than one million barrels a day of excess supply which we will need if we are not to be dependent on OPEC and the instabilities of world political factors. The only way we will get that is to get on with projects like Alsands here and now, and to take advantage of the excess capacity in our manufacturing sector now, not five or ten years from now.
We should use technology which has already been proven by Syncrude and Great Canadian Oil Sands to get on with extending our domestic supply by another 140,000 barrels a day, by building Alsands. In order to pay the cost of that, we need to have that northern gas pipeline under way. Our country is currently faced with massive unemployment in the steel and technological industries. We need that employment now.
That is the great tragedy of all of this matter. At a time when we need all of these things now, through government policy we have destroyed that opportunity and we are contributing further to the deterioration of our national economy.
Why is it so important that we reject the arguments of those hon. members opposite who are saying, "Well, now, there is a glut of oil on the world market, and it is just too expensive to
May 5, 1982

produce that exotic oil from oil sands even though that is our key to the next five centuries". They are saying, "Oh, no, there is a glut on the world market".
I want to remind the hon. members opposite that, right here and now, we have a war going on in the Falkland Islands, and that war is a reflection of the tremendous instability in the world political structure which could see all of South America possibly aligning itself with the communist nations. We could see Venezuela and Mexico cutting off their oil, including the cheap oil which has been contracted for Mexico, in a matter of a fortnight, or overnight. We could see the Middle East erupt into a violent crisis or confrontation. We have the potential for world war breaking out at a time when our dependency on offshore oil has increased from something of the order of 20 per cent in 1979 to almost 30 per cent now. If that foreign oil supply is cut off tomorrow, we are a very vulnerable nation. It is absolutely inexcusable, at a time when we have the potential, as represented by these major megaprojects, to ensure the internal security and maintenance of the lifestyle to which Canadians are entitled, given their decades of work to this end.
It is too late to turn the calendar back. Many of my colleagues have pointed out that had the Crosbie budget of December, 1979, been adopted, this country would be in a much better financial shape today. Interest rates would have been less than 14 per cent-probably 13 per cent. The Alsands project would have been a year and a half on stream in terms of the major financial commitments, and this disaster would never have happened. In all likelihood the Northern Gas Pipeline project would also be in production.
However, because we cannot turn the clock back and bring in the incentives to investment which are an important political principle of this party and, in fact, of our Canadian history, I want to make a suggestion at this point, because it offers the potential for an immediate solution to this problem.
I would suggest that the Government of Canada undertake to initiate Canadian oil sands investment certificates which would be issued to all those who chose to invest in private sector corporations which would then engage in financing the Alsands and future megaprojects related to securing our energy supply. These investment certificates issued by the Government of Canada would entitle the shareholders to a 100 per cent tax credit for any earnings on those investments.
If five million adult Canadians were to purchase $100 of those share certificates, we could raise $.5 billion in one year. Five million Canadians at $100 each would not be hard to come by at this particular and critical time in our history. I would suggest that if those types of certificates were made available to encourage Canadian participation by private individual Canadians, we could raise sufficient capital and produce the restoration of confidence which is required from Canadian sources to ensure that this project is adequately financed from the private sector and will go forward.
Therefore there is no excuse for the government not taking a positive and constructive initiative, even now, to save the Alsands project.
That's Social Credit.

The hon. member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan does not understand the structural problem which has led us to this dilemma. There are three key factors which have led us to this problem.
First of all, government tax policies of this past decade have punished any Canadians who would invest in securities, stocks or speculative ventures aside from their own homes. They have been punished if they chose to invest in anything other than their own homes. Therefore, what we have done has been to fuel the speculative spiral in the valuation of private residential properties, which has led to an appreciated equity in those homes of something in the order of $300 billion more than they were worth a decade ago. Refinancing that $300 billion equity each year will cost $30 billion at a 10 per cent interest rate. When the interest rate rises to 18 per cent or 20 per cent on home mortgages, we suddenly suck up another $30 billion out of our domestic economy. That is money which should be invested in job-creating ventures in productive sectors aside from home construction. That could very readily be accomplished, but for the fact that the unhealthy state of our economy, the massive government deficits and the attack on foreign investment have destroyed the economic climate in Canada to the extent that we are contending with high interest rates.
The only available cash and capital left in Canada for investment purposes are being soaked up by the government through Canada Savings Bonds and by home owners who have to refinance that $30 billion of equity at interest rates which are twice what they were a decade ago. Therefore this driving out of foreign investment, this punishing of Canadians who would invest in our country, this discouraging of private ownership and investment, is at the heart of our problem.
I might point out that the spend-thrift government opposite must now re-issue some $6 billion worth of Government of Canada bonds in the next year and a half which were formerly issued at 4 per cent and 6 per cent, and will now have to be reissued at 16 per cent and 18 per cent to refinance that portion of the deficit. In so doing, that will also soak up a big chunk of equity which should rightfully be invested, through private ventures, in megaprojects and other important, large-scale projects.
The Prime Minister is now trying to redeem himself by beginning his campaign for the premiership of Quebec so that he can continue his bitter confrontation with Rene Levesque long after he has left the national scene. He has already done much damage to our national affairs. However, after he has destroyed Canada, he now thinks he can save Quebec as premier. Would that not be interesting, and what a laugh! The Liberal party now thinks that John Turner, to whom my colleague, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Mouse Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) referred earlier as one of the architects of this disaster, might come back and somehow save the Liberal party in Quebec.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
God help us.

May 5, 1982

What a ludicrous suggestion that would be.
In the remaining few minutes of my allotted time, I want to discuss the direct impact of this Alsands decision and the termination of the northern gas pipeline, or postponement for two years. First of all, Stelco has confirmed that it has already signed a contract for some 675,000 tons of pipe, which is 55 per cent of the total requirements for the northern gas pipeline. It was to begin filling that contract in June of this year. Ipsco in Calgary and Regina was to fulfil the other 45 per cent requirement for steel pipe for that pipeline, also commencing this summer. In the case of Stelco the price would be roughly $900 to $1,000 per ton, or roughly $675 million of investment which will not now go ahead.
This contract would have kept Stelco's Stelfor mill at Welland, Ontario, going for about three years. The hon. member for Welland (Mr. Parent) is not here today but I wonder what he would have to say about the fact that 400 jobs would have been created and sustained had the contract proceeded. The $675 million would have been invested in steel which is upgraded from iron ore having a value of $50 per ton of pellets through to something like $1,000 per ton. That upgrading would have represented jobs in Canada for Canadians who need them at a time when the government is sanctioning orders for steel offshore and thus is exporting jobs to Japan and elsewhere.
Mining equipment would have been essential in the Alsands project. Only $235 million worth was produced in 1980, but in the Alsands project alone the Canadian equipment content would have amounted to about $1.2 billion. That is about five times the amount of mining equipment produced in Canada last year. It would have included structural steel, iron ore, copper, zinc, nickel and molybdenum.
The Alsands project would have involved a lot of conveyor work which would have been supplied primarily by Stephens-Adamson of Belleville and FMC of Toronto. Other Canadian conveyor suppliers are Forano of Quebec, Continental Conveyor of Thetford, Quebec, and Jervis B. Webb of Hamilton.
Canada also produces bucket-wheel loaders of 20-cubic yard capacity. These would have been supplied by Orenstein & Koppel Canada Ltd. of Dundas, Ontario.
Compressors, pumps, valves, and controls could have been supplied by Ingersoll-Rand, Allis Chalmers, and Dorr-Oliver of Orillia.
Total domestic production of machinery and equipment in Canada in 1980 was $7.1 billion. That did not involve these particular projects, and many orders in the other sectors are drying up because of the deterioration of our economy.
There was an opportunity for this country to become a world leader in developing technology in the machinery for harvesting oil sands and for producing a very much needed resource. It is an opportunity that the Steel Company of Canada and the equipment manufacturers needed to get them over a threshold.
These companies had made financial commitments and were prepared to go further. Instead of that some 25,000 people in the mining industry are now unemployed.
The mining industry of Ontario in particular supplies all its output to the steel industry of Ontario. A multiplier factor is involved, so 25,000 summer lay-offs in the mining industry in Canada will affect about 120,000 jobs by the end of summer.
If a consequence of the cancellation of the Alsands project is that we do not have the cushion that is needed to provide the employment that the project represented, summer lay-offs, and shut-downs, and early retirement schemes will be replaced by permanent unemployment. That is the spectre which faces our country. Do we want security of supply? Do we want to restore health to the economy, or do we want to continue with a proud, stubborn, obstinate and incompetent government which is devastating and destroying our national economy?
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to take part in this debate today. I must say that I join with my colleagues who are saddened by the events of the last few days which were the culmination of a series of errors of omission and commission over the years in the business and taxation policies of the government.
We are discussing this today against the background of the report of the Conference Board of Canada which was released yesterday. It indicates that every province of this country shows a downturn and projects a downturn in its economic situation. In fact it shows that Ontario, which would benefit so greatly from the continuation of the Alsands project, has one of its worst economic report cards in decades. Last week's reports are described as gloomy, and provincial assessments which have just been issued, back that up.
We are seeing the demise of a very important element of the national economic development program of the government. We are looking at the end of the underpinnings of this whole program that it has put forward. We look ahead to unemployment, failure to invest, and further hesitancy on the part of entrepreneurs to create jobs.
I should like to deal with the New Democratic Party, Mr. Speaker. Last night I listened with a sense of dismay to the leader of that party. As I did, I began to understand why the people of Saskatchewan, exercising the divine right of the people, turned the NDP government out at the last election. I had wondered why that had happened, and finally I found out.
The New Democratic Party is out of touch with reality. Historically it has denied, by its votes in this House, what Canadians have thought is important to them.
I had some responsibility in the government of the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) for the Alaska gas pipeline. The economic consequences of that natural gas pipeline were to be monumental to the country. I am one of those who does not take comfort from the fact that the pipeline has been put off for two years. That has been done in the
May 5, 1982

context of rising construction costs that will make the project even more difficult for private financing in two years time.
If the project had gone ahead on time, the construction costs, the carrying charges and all related matters would have been such that they could have been assured that the United States would look to Alaska as a reasonable source of energy. Cost and uncertainty are what have driven away the investors in that pipeline. But when this House sent a signal to the United States that there was a commitment by Canada to support the pre-build, what happened? The NDP voted against it. Why? Because they did not believe the assurances given by the U.S. Congress.
We all had difficulty with the assurance given by President Carter toward the end of his administration because we were worried about it. However, there had to be a Canadian commitment to the project. This House, acting on assurances of this government, voted for it-except for the NDP. And yet yesterday, when this debate began, the NDP lamented the loss of jobs and opportunities resulting from the delay of a project which they voted against.
Hypocrites.

My friend calls them hypocrites. I leave you to make that judgment, Mr. Speaker.
Yesterday in this House the NDP leader said something which, quite frankly, startled me. He said he was pleased that the Alsands project had collapsed under its own weight. Then, with the marvellous facility they have for talking out of both sides of their mouths at the same time, he lamented the loss of jobs from the project which he said he was happy had collapsed. You cannot have it two ways, but the NDP have had it two ways for so long that one becomes sickened by their twofaced approach to public policy.
The government has been committeed to development, Mr. Speaker. The problem with the government is that it has never understood how that development should take place in the Canadian context. That is why we are at this crossroads. The projects which have been cancelled, as cited by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, were the cornerstones of the government's approach to the economic development of Canada. All of them have gone by the board. Therefore, what other demonstrations are necessary? What costs have to be borne by Canadians before they realize that, development-oriented as this government pretends to be, whenever the Liberals get their hands on the levers of power, somehow or other they screw it up. When that happens, what do we hear? Last night the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) said there are other projects. We can look to the projects off our coasts. Yes, Mr. Speaker, there are other projects, and I am concerned as well about them when they are in the hands of this government.
Part of the problem has been that the Prime Minister's rhetoric about co-operation, sharing, about concern one for the other, about the fact that utilization of all our resources is important, and that Canada is greater than the sum of its parts, has not been matched by policies. Right at this moment the federal government is involved in a vicious fundamental
argument with Newfoundland. I see history beginning to repeat itself with respect to Hibernia, because these people never learn. If we are to get the best out of the country for its people, then the regions have to understand one another and the federal government has to understand the regions. There is a legitimate political concern in eastern Canada, and if it is not solved then we are not going to have the benefits from those projects.
Whatever the future holds, we are now dealing with the present. We are dealing with the collapse of a major and fundamental part of the government's economic recovery program for Canada. What caused that collapse? Well, Mr. Speaker, if you scratch the surface of this problem what you see at its heart is government greed. There is no more heavily taxed industry in Canada. My friends in the NDP would cheer for that-whatever it costs, keep industry down! It does not matter if it costs jobs, because their socialist philosophy is very important to them regardless of the cost. There is a limit, Mr. Speaker, to the extent to which governments generally can shoulder their way up to the table. If they move their shoulders harshly, without considering those who sit beside them, namely the investors who take the risk and create jobs, then the investors gradually are pushed off the end of the table. If you look at the energy industry in Canada, that is what has happened and we are left in the position we are in today.
The national energy policy had four major objectives: heavy taxation on oil and gas production; grants for exploration and development based upon the nationality of shareholders; suppression of prices to Canadian producers below open-market levels and the resulting extensive administration of price levels, and the subsidizing of consumer prices by keeping them below world prices through direct government expenditures. We all know now the cost of that policy which I have simplified into those four elements. The cost to our province of Ontario, Mr. Speaker, is monumental, and all this against a backdrop of depression and change in every possible way in the community. High interest rates, inflation, housing shortages, bankruptcies and unemployment, all constitute a performance which is rather frightening for those of us who look to the future of the country.
This collapse is much more than merely the end of one particular project. There is no comfort in accepting the bromide of the Minister of State for Mines who said we still have the resource in the ground. It is still in the bank, so to speak. Well, it is in the bank, but it is like forgetting about an account if you have it in the bank and cannot get it out. Whether it be for governments or otherwise, there has to be a return of some kind so that people can get it out.
So long as conditions exist as they do now and into the unforeseeable future, then we will have lost this great opportunity represented by the Alsands project. The Alsands failure will reduce business investment spending in Canada by $360 million. It sets the stage for a steady loss of real output, unemployment, and foreign investor confidence. That is what

May 5, 1982
the observers of this scene say, observers who have no axe to grind with respect to the country. Translate that to jobs, Mr. Speaker. Translate that to people, and translate that to lost opportunity. Translate that to the person who faces uncertainty in aging industries, who is looking to the new developing industries as the place to use his or her skills. It is much more than lost investor opportunity, it is lost investment opportunity certainly, but it is lost opportunities for people who want to work. That is what we face.
Why do we face that? I have mentioned one of the reasons, that governments seem to want to shoulder themselves to the table. I am now looking at the "Canadian Research Report" from the research department of Richardson Securities of Canada. In this report is an address given by the Winnipeg managing partner of Richardson Securities on April 27, 1982. At the time he was talking about then current negotiations. It reads as follows:
The current negotiations on tar sand ventures illustrate other misconceptions of our policy makers; that tar sands can provide a significant revenue return by way of royalties or taxes and that these ventures bear some similarity to "public utilities".
It has always been the case of the New Democratic Party that these ventures are public utilities. They are not, Mr. Speaker. He goes on this way and describes the projects:
Tar sand projects are in fact low grade mining operations which involve enormous initial capital and high operating costs for rates of production which are low by conventional oil standards. They involve a series of very large-scale activities done in a sequence which makes the entire operation vulnerable at every stage; pit design, ore grade, mining, conveying, separation, coking and refining. The discussions of "projected" rates of return have deluded the Energy Department as to the fundamentals of tar sand developments.
I just want to remind hon. members that he said this back on April 27:
The Alsands project is stalling at the moment partly because of economic astigmatism of the governments involved-
He says "governments". That is the plural. He continues:
-partly because of fundamental economic factors, but of equal or graver concern is the fact that the major potential participants have lost confidence in the integrity of commitments made on behalf of the federal government.
This is right back at the doorstep and the feet of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), other members of cabinet, and those who blindly support this forced march to economic decimation. That is where this analyst and many Canadians are putting the blame for what has happened. He goes on to say that the way in which this can be changed is, first, to change the architects of such a deluded policy. They have led us from this period of lost opportunities, lost jobs, lost employment, lost social advance, into a period of time that has caused this House to enter this most unusual debate on a situation which, in terms of our economic development as a nation, finds the country in a state of emergency.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this emergency debate on
one of the fundamental questions facing the Canadian economy today. As previous speakers have pointed out, the entire Liberal strategy is in a shambles. It is not only the Liberal strategy that is in a shambles, but in all our constituencies we can see the economy of local people that has just completely gone down the tube. All the Liberal government has had to offer for the past two years has been the promise of megaprojects.
This emergency is not because of the problem of energy security. The Alsands project and the Alaska gas pipeline might be necessary for Canada's energy security in the future, but this is not the reason for the emergency right now. The emergency right now is as a result of the government's entire strategy for recovery and job creation which was based on those two projects. The government kept looking toward the big ticket as a way of solving all its problems. This is somewhat like an immature high school student who had hopes of somehow winning the fairy princess if only he could do some great thing. The government kept hoping that somehow it could woo economic recovery by doing some great thing, by having some economic project that would somehow get the economy rolling again with spin-off industries and everything else. But now the entire project seems to be down the tube.
Last February Senator Olson, the Minister of Economic Development, speaking in Victoria, said that Canadians should no longer feel it necessary to move away from being hewers of wood and drawers of water. He felt that we could continue in our traditional role as being exporters of raw resources, that this was the route we should continue to follow if we wanted economic prosperity.
The problem with being hewers of wood and drawers of water comes when we run short of wood and run short of water. I can see an analogy to this and the problems which the logging industry faces in British Columbia. Loggers say every year it seems that they have to go farther and farther back into the valleys, and higher and higher up in the side hills, cutting small trees in order to get the same amount of wood. In British Columbia we have a series of mills that were designed for larger trees. Now that we are dealing with smaller size timber these mills are no longer economical. The hewers of wood and drawers of water policy was a fine policy when we had readily accessible resources. But those in forestry and mining find that our resources are not quite so accessible as they used to be. And in the energy area we find that our cheapest oil and gas sources have already been exploited and shipped out.
In December, 1969, the energy minister, Joe Greene, declared his support for a continental energy policy. At that time he committed up to 34 per cent of Canada's established gas resources for export to the United States. Of course that was at the time when he confidently accepted industry estimates that we had oil supplies that would last for 923 years, and natural gas supplies that would last for almost 400 years. By selling off our more accessible resource we have robbed ourselves of reasonably priced energy that will be needed for the future. The days of cheap energy are over, thanks in large
May 5, 1982

part to the continued sellout of these resources to the United States.
Now that our easily accessible energy sources are exhausted or becoming depleted, we face a situation where we must develop more expensive energy projects. These projects depend upon a cycle of heavy capital investment which includes extensive capital borrowing from abroad. In order to raise capital, we must export more energy. It becomes a vicious circle, a circle which does not lead to energy security or to economic independence.
I should like to look for a moment at the Alaska highway natural gas pipeline. Both the Liberals and the Tories voted for the pre-build without adequate guarantees. On July 17, 1980, the government tabled a letter from President Carter. It was really the most worthless scrap of paper since Chamberlain returned from Munich. However, President Carter made one interesting comment at the conclusion of his letter. He said:
Successful completion of this project will underscore once again the special character of co-operation on a broad range of issues that highlights the U.S.-Canadian relationship.
It is that special character of co-operation on a broad range of issues which I think the House should consider for a few moments, because it almost always involves Canadians being taken to the cleaners.
Also in July, 1980, my party pointed out that it would not be in the interests of the United States to complete the pipeline once we had given the go ahead on the pre-build and to export additional Alberta gas. There was no reason for the United States to complete the pipeline in the immediate future. It had what it wanted from us. We gave it to the United States, with Tory consent in July, 1980. From their questions and speeches at the time, we see that the Tories agreed with us. They also thought that this was a sellout, that Canada was taking a long-shot risk and that there were no guarantees, yet the Tories voted for the pre-build. I have not as yet heard a satisfactory answer on why they did. Why did they vote for the pre-build when they knew it was a sellout and that there were no job guarantees with it?
There is a phrase in the Bible which compares the nation of Israel to a wild ass braying in heat. It seems to me that the government, in its attempt to attract multinationals into going along with the Alsands project, has acted something like a wild ass braying in heat. Imperial Oil was involved in the Cold Lake project. It is an interesting example of the manner in which multinationals want to operate. Originally they requested a 17.5 per cent rate of return. Later they wanted 18 per cent. After the National Energy Program was introduced, they raised the ante once again and wanted 20 per cent. Now that project is very much in question.
The Liberal government tried to sweeten the pie for multinationals at the expense of Canadian consumers. My party very rightly denounced this as a sellout because it meant that we would put up the capital, we would take the risk, but we would not receive any equivalent equity. We have seen in the
past the irresponsible way in which multinational corporations used their capital as a lever with the government and have no hesitation about going on a capital strike.
Merrill Lynch said that in some projects the oil companies are looking for 31 per cent and 32 per cent rates of return. Last year the Bertrand commission detailed the manner in which multinational corporations have ripped off the Canadian public from one part of the oil industry right through to the finished product, from the beginning of exploration to the gas pump. The Canadian public has been ripped off with the connivance of the Canadian government and of the official opposition.
I suggest that there are alternatives. If we need projects such as Alsands, we can do it ourselves, we can receive the profits ourselves, and we can make gas and oil products available to Canadians at reasonable prices without exorbitant profits being taken by multinational corporations. When we look at the entire question of energy security, we must emphasize conservation and better utilization of existing reserves. Also we need to put more money into the development of so-called soft alternatives. Thinking in terms of megaprojects and what they would have provided in the way of jobs, we must realize that there are better returns on our money if we have an industrial strategy which looks at Canada as a whole, looks at its resources, its people and its ability, and does not simply depend upon big ticket megaprojects.
We need an industrial strategy which requires corporate responsibilities from companies operating in Canada. If these companies are to make profits in Canada, they should be investing their money here. The answer is not always big ticket megaprojects. We can obtain more jobs for our dollar if we are willing to invest in some small projects.
All members of the House have heard appeals from small businesses which are going down the drain because the government does not seem to care about jobs which already exist in Canada. We are losing jobs. The government promises that somewhere down the road it will have a megaproject which will somehow meet all our needs.
In my constituency we are in the process of losing 600 jobs at the Chemainus mill. There has been a mill there for 120 years. At one time it was one of the largest mills in the world. MacMillan Bloedel, the company which is involved there, has shown no sense of corporate responsibility to the community whatsoever. It is taking the money it made in that community and investing it in other parts of the world to exploit those areas. At present it is saying that it cannot build a new mill in Chemainus because it has to develop a new pulp mill in Alabama. It is time to put an end to the rip-off of our resources and the exploitation of our workers. We want to see companies which make money in Canada investing their money here to create jobs.
This is an emergency because the government has done nothing but look to megaprojects as a source of economic recovery and job creation. I hope it realizes that the time it has spent dreaming about megaprojects could have been better spent developing a reasonable industrial strategy. Also I hope

May 5, 1982
that it realizes its approach has been wrong and that it should no longer follow a policy of putting all its megas in one basket.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak in this debate on the collapse of the Alsands project. It is really only the tip of the iceberg when you consider what is happening to the entire economy of Canada. Whenever there was a statistic published outlining a decline in employment opportunites, or a rise in Canada's inflation rate, or any change in Canada's economic indicators, we were told by the apologists for this government that there is no need to worry, that they have a number of megaprojects on the drawing board and, just as soon as these developments take place, there will be a favourable change in Canada's economic picture. We were told to be patient, to wait, and that all would be well because the Liberals are in office.
We in the opposition waited for some sign from the government which would indicate that it knew what it was doing and that it would fulfil its promise. Finally, however, the sands in the hourglass of time, at least for the government, have run out. Its bets have been called and its hand has been found wanting. As the great evangelist Billy Graham would say, "You have reached the hour of decision." The fact that the government is incapable of governing and incapable of giving direction to our great country is causing a great sense of frustration, fear and despair among all Canadians. Today this country is crying out for leadership, direction and guidance from the federal government.
Unfortunately, this government is not fulfilling its mandate. It is not acting in a way which builds confidence among Canadians or which gives them any hope for the future. Canada has been relying on the prospect of energy megaprojects to guarantee energy self-sufficiency, to give employment to some 100,000 Canadians, and to stimulate the economy in both the resource and industrial sectors.
However, this bubble has now burst with the announcement on Friday, April 30, not only of the collapse of the Alsands project but also of the collapse of the Alaska highway natural gas pipeline project which has been postponed for at least two years. This represents an unprecedented disaster of mammoth proportions for the Canadian economy. The entire blowup can be directly traced to the National Energy Program.
Of course, Alsands is only the last of a long list of megaprojects which has been cancelled as a result of the National Energy Program. Other examples are the Esso Resources Cold Lake project, the Esso Resources Judy Creek recovery project, and the Syncrude expansion project.
The economic impact of this cancellation is profound. For example, the Alsands project was estimated to produce
132,000	barrels of oil daily; Cold Lake an estimated 138,000 barrels daily; the Syncrude expansion project 62,000 barrels a day, and Judy Creek somewhere between 15,000 and 20,000 barrels daily. When these figures are added, the cancellation
of these projects represents a total loss to Canada of something over 350,000 barrels of oil daily. Obviously, the Liberal policy of self-sufficiency in oil which was proclaimed with so much fanfare by the Minister of Finance, (Mr. MacEachen), the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is doomed. The promises of oily, gassy and greasy have ended up as little more than an oil slick on the pages of time. Is it any wonder that the dollar dropped by one half cent on the day of the announcement?
Under self-sufficiency as promised by the Liberals, the maritimes could have been expected to be supplied by Canadian oil. As it now stands, this will only happen if a miracle occurs which will bring oil to Atlantic Canada from Hibernia and other offshore developments in that part of the country.
For a time, it seemed that the lucrative offers by the federal and Alberta governments to get the stalled Alsands energy project off the ground, and under construction, was one the companies could simply not refuse. However, refuse it they did, despite substantial concessions by the two governments, including the offer to cover $11 billion of the total estimated cost of the projected $13 billion. This was to be made through direct equity participation and loan guarantees. In the end, the two remaining partners in the Alsands consortium, Shell Canada and Gulf Canada Ltd., said that the risks and massive costs involved were simply too great. The uncertainty of interest rates, combined with the two recent rapid declines in world oil prices, have made the industry increasingly reluctant to tie up massive sums of money in such an expensive and longterm venture.
There have been other uncertainties as well. One is the imperfections of the oil sands technology, and the second is the more ominous industry-held view that governments have been inconsistent in sticking to terms of previous agreements.
In other words, industry, big or small, no longer trusts this government and when a situation of this nature exists there is only one thing, in my view, to do, and that is to replace this government and give a new group of Canadians a chance to restore confidence in our nation.
With interest rates still running at record levels, and with business executives and consumers becoming increasingly convinced that things will get worse before they get better, the Alsands plant had to become not only a symbol of economic recovery for the country but consortium members had estimated that the ripple effects over the project's lifetime would have an economic impact throughout Canada of some $470 billion.
It was also to serve as a political symbol indicating that government and industry could indeed work together. This begs the question of just what happened, and it brings us right back to the basic concept, namely, it is the question of trust. In my opinion the companies believed in the financial analysis that, although the terms of the deal were acceptable, they were in something like a "Heads I win, tails you lose" situation. If the project was successful, the private concerns were in fear of being forced out by the government through broken promises and agreements.
May 5, 1982

If the project was not successful the private companies stood to loose billions of their shareholders' investments, and under today's confiscatory tax laws and the arbitrary changes being made in those laws, that was simply too great a risk to take.
As a result of the collapse of their megaprojects, our Canadian recession has been turned into a full-fledged depression. Nowhere is this more evidenced than in Sydney, Nova Scotia, my home province.
The Sydney Steel plant has closed down its operations due to working conditions and the need for higher wages. Due to the mismanagement of our economy by this government workers today need a yearly salary increase at least in the amount of the 12 per cent inflation just to survive. When the individual industry in which they are employed can no longer keep raising salaries and secure the money needed for salary increases by raising the price of the product manufactured, then the industry unfortunately collapses. This is what is happening, not only to Sydney Steel but to an entire city in my province where the workers have no other place to turn, and it is happening right across the face of this nation.
In my view, this is a depression that never should have happened in this country. I say this because we are a resource rich nation. We are rich in human resources, coal, oil, gas, uranium, copper and nickel. We have more wheat than we can eat and more fish than we can fry or sell.
I ask this House what would the good Lord have had to give us, 24 million Canadians, in order to make us, if not prosperous, at least fully employed and enjoying a healthy standard of living? The answer, of course, is a government that is willing to co-operate rather than one interested in constant confrontation, a government that will establish policies and encourage productivity, policies that will reward initiative, that will free the energies of our people rather than penalize their every move with restrictive, crippling taxes and bureaucratic red tape. That is all that is happening to this nation, and that is what is keeping us down.
This depression presently facing us was triggered and has since been intensified by a succession of federal measures and, to a lesser extent, by the provincial responses which they evoked.
The breaking point, in my opinion, came when this government established the National Energy Program. The government will never admit that it made a blunder of the worst magnitude, not even today when its energy program is in a shambles, when it has fallen down around it like the proverbial house of cards. Instead, when asked questions about the state of the economy, the various ministers at one time or another attribute the depression to the joint arrival of the developed countries on the downslide of a world-wide business cycle, or they attribute it to the high interest rates in the United States, as we have heard the Minister of Finance say time and time again. This indicates that this government is ignoring the dominant role of energy among our natural resources.
If this government, instead of establishing its confiscatory tax practices, had made provision for a competitive rate of return on oil and gas production, it would have strengthened the dollar, improved national productivity and raised the national income. At most, it could have overtaken the deterrence of high interest rates which is killing the Canadian construction industry, the housing industry, the fishing and agricultural industries as well as large and small businesses.
I have a telegram in front of me which arrived this morning, signed by Bob McDonald of Chevrolet Oldsmobile Ltd. It indicates that the domestic automobile dealers in Nova Scotia are in trouble, asking that we please act accordingly. It states that Canada has become a dumping ground for the Japanese and, while we are at it, let's keep an eye on the Russians and their Ladas. It is their opinion that these products are underpriced. The Americans will not allow them in their country. Why do we allow them in ours? No matter which way you turn or which industry you look at, they are facing horrendous economic problems.
Before the National Energy Program, the strongly rising volume of investments in oil and gas exploration and development had been driving the whole Canadian economy forward. Every dollar invested by the petroleum industry multiplied two or three times through the economy in purchases of goods, equipment, and services.
Since the National Energy Program was introduced, the industry's investment in Canada has been drastically reduced by some 30 to 40 per cent through last year, and by a similar amount in 1982. These are not now recoverable funds. They have either been committed outside Canada or gobbled up by the maw of this ever-gobbling government. The withdrawal of private investors from Alsands is symptomatic of what has happened in the industry. All that has been surprising about it is that it has shocked some of those who have been supporting the national energy policy. They have professed to be shocked or indignant that a corporation should put the interests of its shareholders ahead of the government's so-called definition of the national interest. That they should be shocked gives us some indication and goes a long way toward explaining why we have sunk so deep into our present depression and why recovery from this depression will be difficult, hard work and a long way ahead.
In the last ten years the government has been reaching out to capture the key elements in our economy, to transform them into instruments for implementing its vision of the corporate or socialist state, that is, one in which political authority is assured by control over investment and production.
In the 25 years leading up to 1971, Canada had an average real growth in gross national product of 5 per cent, the envy of all western nations except possibly West Germany and Japan which at that time were still rebuilding their war-torn economies.
I was present in this House from June 10, 1957, on up through this period, and I watched at that time the progress that was made, especially in Atlantic Canada, under that great Prime Minister, the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker. During
16990

May 5, 1982
that period, and it is amazing to think of it at the present time, we had between 350,000 and 400,000 unemployed.
I wish some of the younger members could have heard the speeches made at that time by the Hon. Lionel Chevrier, the Hon. Jack Pickersgill, the Right Hon. Mr. Pearson, and the Hon. Paul Martin. They should have heard the condemnation and vilification of the Diefenbaker government at that time by those men because there were 350,000 unemployed. Today we have 1,250,000 unemployed. Somehow this has become a norm. It is acceptable. Well, it is not acceptable to me, to Atlantic Canada, or to this nation. It is time we stood up and shouted about the mismanagement of our economy, the high inflation, high unemployment and obvious lack of interest in trying to do something about it.
Hear, hear!

What happened? In the 1970s as the dead hand of government was extended deeper into the economy, average annual growth of our nation began to decline. During the ten years since 1971, real growth has averaged only 7 per cent and in recent years it has slowed to 2 per cent. As the growth has slowed, inflation and unemployment have increased. In the ten years since 1971, inflation averaged 9 per cent a year and last year it reached 12!/2 per cent. I will be just a few more minutes, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is there unanimous consent of the House for the hon. member to extend his time?
Agreed.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I will not abuse the privilege. As growth has slowed, inflation and unemployment have increased. In the ten years since 1971 inflation averaged 9 per cent a year, and last year it reached 12'h per cent. Many explanations for Canada's fading economic performance have been given through the seventies by various cabinet ministers. One of their favourites was that, having passed through its development phase, the Canadian economy had now reached a maturity in which the policy should be established to provide a redistribution of wealth rather than the creation of new wealth. This, of course, was false doctrine based upon a false premise. What we now have is a smaller pie being cut into ever smaller pieces. That is why our people are complaining.
Growth has in fact been slowed by other clearly recognizable developments. One of these was the growing rift in confederation and enforced redirection of, first, private and then government investment in an effort to paper over the cracks in Canadian unity. In my opinion, had investment been free to flow to where it could obtain the maximum return, the benefits to all parts of our country would have been far greater than the costs incurred by present government policies.
Another growth-slowing development was the perception of an emerging nationalism as a force to be harnessed to political advantage. So successful was the government at this game that
nationalism became the principle vehicle for the transformation of Canada into a corporate state. At that, it is still not clear whether this government yet has recognized all the implications of its insistence that market forces can be subordinated to political direction. The introduction of the National Energy Program in the budget of 1980 followed by the chicanery and the flim-flam of closing tax loopholes in the budget of 1981 did more than simply cause investment to flee this country. It strengthened the government's control over the uses to which remaining investment in Canada could be put.
In the past America's recovery from a recession used to be the springboard for Canada's recovery but, in my view, stengthening American demand will not this time be enough to restore growth in the Canadian economy. What we need are infusions of new capital, and I ask: Where are these to be drawn from? Certainly not from Canadian corporations. Those which can still afford to do so are diverting their capital to the United States, and others no longer have the reserves to do anything. Taxes and inflation have taken too heavy a toll.
This government is looking to the United States recovery in the hope that it will stimulate our own, but it is forgetting the extent to which the channels through which renewed American growth that normally came into Canada have since been blocked by the Foreign Investment Review Act. More than anything else this depression was brought on by the progressive extension of federal intervention in the economy. Now the depression becomes, unfortunately, the justification for still more intervention in our economy.
I hope my thoughts will at least be given some consideration by those who have the authority and the power to run this country. Because if the government does not change direction, we will have more of the same, and we face utter and total collapse of our entire nations's economy.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, I would like to say good morning, and I hope you spent the night comfortably, listening to so many speeches on an extremely important subject. Today is Wednesday, May 5, 9.03 a.m., and since yesterday, we have had thirteen hours of speeches on energy and the fact that certain projects, which would have created opportunities in other sectors, have been abandoned. Meanwhile, there is a lot going on in the world. Alas, Mr. Speaker, the big dream has ended. The Nordiques put their hearts and souls into it yesterday until the bitter end. The papers also tell us that an English destroyer was sunk and that probably thirty people lost their lives. Argentina is counterattacking-that was the headline in Le Devoir. In Poland the government in Warsaw has reinstated a curfew and more than 1,300 persons have been arrested.
Meanwhile, Mr. Speaker, here in the House of Commons we are giving our fellow citizens the impression that we are wasting our time, while thousands of people in other countries are far less fortunate than we are, a third world war may be in the offing, and many of our fellow citizens in constituencies across Canada are waiting for concrete action by a responsible
May 5, 1982

government and an enlightened opposition that will establish sound projects and programs for job creation. What have we been doing here for thirteen hours and five minutes? We have been saying that the economic situation in Canada is bad, that it is going to get much worse and that it will soon be desperate. If the Conference Board wants to tell me that the economic situation in Canada has reached its lowest point in 50 years, all right, it is their job to analyse and assess the situation and tell us what they think.
But it seems to me that representatives of the Canadian people in this House could be expected to bring in some constructive proposals and suggestions. This debate was sparked by a press release dated April 30 and published by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), and I quote:
Today, the Hon. Marc Lalonde, Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, announced that suspension of construction on the Alsands synthetic oil factory means that Canada will have to stress development of its oil reserves in the Beaufort Sea and the Atlantic offshore, and also development of western conventional crude, enhanced recovery projects and heavy crude oil upgraders.
For 13 hours, everyone has agreed that Canada's energy resources are extremely abundant and more than adequate to meet all our needs. The programs exist, progress has always been satisfactory, and a tremendous task has been accomplished.
Now we must prepare for the future. One project had to be dropped, but there are several others. Canada's resources are immense, and what is needed now is the will to develop them. To some people, the energy resource challenge consists primarily in finding new supplies of oil, the main resource in which Canada is not yet self-sufficient. The Canadian government is aware of the considerable effort this represents, and what it intends to achieve is, briefly, energy security for all Canadian citizens, opportunity and fairness.
Since this is a serious subject, I shall try to do it justice, even at this very early hour. Therefore, as far as energy security is concerned, there is no doubt that Canada's oil and natural gas reserves have increased significantly, especially in the last ten years. Notwithstanding the turn of events in 1980 which brought the oil industry into a slump, a situation aggravated by the accumulation of unsold natural gas, the oil industry has remained very active. In fact, oil discoveries in Alberta, the province with the highest production, increased substantially in 1981, compared with 1980. Oilweek Magazine expects a substantial increase in all western provinces as well as in the Canada lands and the offshore.
There is also increasing geological activity in preparation for drilling. The news is generally good. We are making exceptional progress in reducing the demand for oil. This is one of the main goals in our fight for energy security. Oil consumption has dropped considerably, namely, from 291,000 cubic metres per day in 1980 to 268,000 cubic metres per day in 1982. Thus, our objective to conserve energy has been attained. It
means that Canadian self-sufficiency rose from 79.5 per cent in 1981 to approximately 80.9 per cent in 1982, bearing in mind that the ultimate objective is still 100 per cent in 1990.
