At the same time, income from Canadian oil and natural gas production has increased 6 per cent, from 28 to 34 per cent. We are rapidly advancing towards our goal of 50 per cent, a very minimal part of an industry that is so essential to Canada's future economic development.
Canadians are playing a new and major role in meeting energy requirements. We all know that it has always been a major concern of the Government of Canada to share this country's wealth fairly among all Canadians. That is why the government has wanted to establish a pricing and tax system for oil and gas that will be fair to all Canadians, whether or not they are living in an oil-producing area, and also a fair system for the distribution of income between governments and the oil industry.
Although the Government of Canada has insisted on a fair deal for all Canadians, I must say that as a result of certain provincial taxes, some Canadians today are less equal than others. I should like to comment on what happened in my area, Cabano, during the gas price war. The House will recall that in eastern Quebec, we had a strike among independent gas distributors which lasted nearly two weeks, so that people could no longer buy gas for their cars. But I would like to say that in our area, there is a price war between the companies, and what I am going to tell you is not meant as criticism of the government's policy of fairness. In the large urban centres, the companies maintain certain price levels and in other more sparsely populated areas, prices are a little higher. As a result of the price war, in my riding, and especially in Temiscouata, we pay 10 cents more per litre of gas. Add to this the 40 per cent provincial tax, and we have to add another 7 cents per litre. So, when I compare my province with the other Canadian provinces, I see that I am paying 17 cents per litre more than other Canadians, and as soon as the new government of Saskatchewan has removed the 40 cent tax on a gallon of gas, as they promised during the last election campaign, that will mean another ten cents per litre less for them. So, in our area, we will be paying 27 cents more per litre of gas than in Saskatchewan. I am already paying seventeen cents more than Ontario or New Brunswick and the other Canadian provinces. Something has to be done about controlling provincial taxes on essential goods such as gasoline, and perhaps this debate could serve as an opportunity for members to make suggestions on how to eliminate the imbalance in gasoline and oil prices.
So, Mr. Speaker, to get back to my subject after this short digression, I would like to say that the Government of Canada and the oil-producing provinces concluded an agreement to share income from oil and gas production. We must remember, however, that this income is used to provide equitable

May 5, 1982
financing for major projects and thus ensure energy security for all Canadians. These incentives are paid for research, off-oil conversion, grants for home insulation and a number of other programs. We are now building a sound basis for confidence in Canada's energy future by applying balanced measures that will help meet the energy requirements of Canadians in every respect. Some of these measures are: The Canada Oil and Gas Act, a new system that will encourage major discoveries so that we can expect to see renewed activity in oil and gas exploration in the north and the offshore, with new prospects for business and Canadian workers.
The Petroleum Incentives Program is now being considered by Parliament, and under the program, billions of dollars worth of subsidies will encourage intensive discovery activity and provide for better development by Canadian companies. The program also provides for a new reference price for oil. It is an incentive, at the world price level, for discovery of new oil anywhere in Canada, while remaining an integral part of a domestic oil price that is only 70 per cent of the current world price.
The Canadian off-oil program provides financial incentives for consumers who wish to convert their heating systems from oil to any other form of energy. It is an integral part of a project aimed at rationalizing oil consumption and expanding natural gas transmission and distribution networks. And speaking of the distribution of natural gas, I should like to inform my hon. friends on the opposite side that since there are no natural gas distribution networks in eastern Quebec, we greatly appreciated the agreement concluded by the Government of Canada and the government of Alberta for the construction of a gas pipeline in eastern Canada, including my riding.
There is also the expanded version of the Canadian Home Insulation Program. It provides financial grants for homeowners to help them reduce energy consumption, and is now available to 80 per cent of Canadian homes. However, I am sure that the Government of Canada will also continue to encourage development of our major energy resources.
The present economic situation, the existing uncertainty as to world oil prices and the drop in demand for oil, combined with rising costs, do not work in favour of the megaprojects that have had to be postponed, not only here in Canada but in other countries as well. Expanding Canadian oil and gas prospects have led to increased activity in the oil industry. For instance, three companies have announced major investment plans for the eighties.
Gulf Canada Limited expects to spend some $7 billion on capital expenditures and exploration within the next five years. Its program includes heavy investment in the Beaufort Sea and also in conventional light crude, natural gas, heavy crude and coal. Imperial Oil will be investing $7 billion over the next ten years, to expand its operations at Norman Wells in the Northwest Territories, while also increasing its level of activity in the
Beaufort Sea and the Arctic Islands and upgrading its commercial and petrochemical operations. Suncor Canada is planning annual expenditures of some $500 million over the next three years, twice the amount forecast in 1981. The company will be taking an active part this year in the discovery of 70 new wells in western Canada, and it also wants to take an active part in developing the Canada lands.
These multinational companies are still convinced that Canada can offer them unique opportunities. They have opted for working with Canadians and Canadian companies, with a view to creating a better energy future. Canadian companies have responded with imagination and enthusiasm. For instance, Canterra Energy, founded when the Canada Development Corporation bought Aquitaine-a French oil company-intends to spend $500 million in 1982 to expand its activities to include all western regions and the Canada lands. This year, Petro-Canada approved a budget of $450 million for discovery activity and development of the industry in western Canada. This is in addition to its principal activities in the Canada lands, especially as a working member of a consortium that is active in exploration on the Arctic Islands, and as leader of the Labrador group on the east coast offshore. The Arctic Islands consortium is continuing activity at a faster pace, producing fabulous amounts of natural gas, while it is forecasting new prospects for oil. Panarctic, a Canadian company, is the main operator for the consortium.
This increasing activity will result in substantial economic benefits for Canadians through job creation and spin-offs for companies in other sectors. For instance, Husky Oil and Bow Valley, both located in Calgary, have already ordered a semisubmersible drilling rig from Saint John Shipbuilding & Dry Dock of New Brunswick. The latter company already has an option to build a second rig. And that is only the beginning. Already more than 200 businesses have come to St. John's, Newfoundland, to take advantage of the opportunities offered by oil and gas exploration on the offshore. Development of natural gas reserves in the waters of Sable Island, located off the coast of Nova Scotia, is expected to involve capital expenditures of $2.5 billion. An impressive 8,750 workers will be hired when the operational phase reaches its peak, while about 1,100 long-term jobs will be needed when the natural gas comes on stream.
None of these developments should surprise us, because the industry's net income per barrel of new oil, after deducting operating costs and royalties, has increased 107 per cent since 1979, as a result of adjustments in royalty percentages and the reference price for new oil. If we compare the oil industry's net income growth with the forecast for all Canadian industries, spread over a period of ten years, no other sector has been more successful than the oil industry. The future is promising for the industry, since Canada has made a commitment to implement its energy programs on all fronts. The National Energy Program is truly operational.
May 5, 1982

Mr. Speaker, Canada is full of resources, in the north, in the east, and of course in the west, which is particularly endowed with them. Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker, my time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, normally I am very pleased to have the opportunity to speak in the House of Commons as I have a great respect for this institution. I am always thankful to the constituents of Okanagan North for giving me the opportunity to speak occasionally in this House. However, I do not derive a great deal of satisfaction from addressing myself to the collapse of two very vital energy projects in Canada, Alsands and the Alaska pipe line. I suppose one could take some satisfaction if one were partisan because this marks the formal collapse of a bankrupt policy, that is, the national energy policy. These two projects were much too important to the economic life of this country to take any satisfaction from their demise. The horrendous effects of their cancellation will be felt throughout Canada for the next decade or more.
This country is in a deep recession, Mr. Speaker, and it is very important for us to have some stimulus. There are almost 1.5 million people unemployed in this country, which is more than at any time in our history. We need some stimulus to help the economy recover from this deep recession. We need some aid for our manufacturing industry, our construction industry and to give the economy the boost it needs to pull out of the recession.
With the collapse of the national energy policy Canadians have witnessed the failure of three major initiatives started by the government when it took power some two years ago. That three-pronged attack was designed to hoodwink the Canadian public into believing that the government knew where it was going.
First of all, there was the Constitution debacle. That is over now but it was a grab for power by central Canada, an effort to control the future economic welfare of all parts of the country to the detriment of major parts of it. That grab for power was only defeated when the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) identified it for what it was, while the New Democratic Party started its love affair with the Liberals on the Constitution issue.
The second major initiative which has failed is the national energy policy. It was a grab for wealth. All it succeeded in doing was to completely destroy the sophisticated and successful oil industry of this country.
The third major initiative which lies in ruins is the budget. It was a disaster which adversely affected the lives of every Canadian.
These policies, which were the culmination of ten to 14 years of poor government, started in 1972 with the inflationary budget introduced by the Hon. John Turner.
Perhaps it would be wise to put on the record some statistics of the 14 years since the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) took office. In 1968 the total number of unemployed was 351,000; the most recent figure is 1.2 million unemployed. Youth unemployment was 7.4 per cent in 1968 but in March, 1982 it was 15.8 per cent. The inflation rate has gone from 4.2 per cent in 1968 to 11.6 per cent. The consumer price index has gone from 89 per cent to 255.9 per cent. The value of the Canadian dollar was $1.12 in 1968 and now it is 39 cents. Our trade deficit on current account stands at minus $6 million. Bank interest rates have more than doubled and mortgage rates have more than doubled. As the final insult, we now pay 30 cents for first class postage instead of 6 cents.
All this indicates that we are in the deepest recession since 1930. Unemployment is rife and business bankruptcies are increasing. In fact, the only growth industry in the country is that of trustees of bankruptcies. Interest rates and inflation have caused the average person to suffer deeply. I am sure all members have received telephone calls from constituents who are losing their houses, their jobs, their businesses, after a lifetime of hard work.
In British Columbia the forestry industry is in a state of deep depression. In my constituency of Okanagan North unemployment is twice as high as is normal at this time of year. We have lost furniture stores, automobile industries, lumber industries, and those which are still in existence only use part-time workers.
There are those who say that this is all part of a deep and dark design to ruin the country. I do not hold to that view but I can certainly see how others might, because if someone in 1980 had designed a method to ruin the country, they would not have done anything differently. They would have had the constitutional debate, the NEP and the budget.
This government had those things and they have succeeded in placing this country in greater dire straits than we have ever been in before. The NEP was ill-conceived from the beginning. It was put together by a group of inexperienced and arrogant bureaucrats aided by incompetent, power-mad politicians. It was not as if there was a lack of warning about the problems we confront today. Bill C-48, which was the background of the NEP, had a very long hearing before the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works, which sat in 1980 and heard more witnesses and received more briefs than the Constitution committee. Every single brief opposed the bill and warned the government what to expect. Chevron had this to say to the committee:
-we now have Bill C-48 before us-prepared without any industry consultation and presented as a key portion of the National Energy Program.
Chevron continues to believe that this National Energy Program, as modified by federal-provincial agreement, will
1)	Reduce the present remaining reserves of oil and gas in Canada because
of increased tax and royalty costs and resultant premature abandonment of
wells.

May 5, 1982
2)	Reduce exploration and development activity; therefore reducing reserve additions and will create higher unemployment in the conventional exploration areas of Canada.
3)	Reduce exploration activity and development programs in Canada lands.
4)	Reduce if not eliminate the development of heavy oil megaprojects in Canada.
What did the government have to say about it? They ignored it completely. They are now reaping the rewards of their arrogance.
On October 28, 1980, the federal government tabled its National Energy Program and the minister described it as a set of national decisions by the Government of Canada. He went on to say that these decisions:
-will impinge on almost every sphere of economic activity, on the fortunes of every Canadian, and on the economic and social structure of the nation for years to come.
How right he was. He goes on to say that the NEP will have major, positive implications for the federation itself. He was not so right there. The implications are not positive, they are very negative. The minister was right, the NEP has imposed on every Canadian. The combination of the NEP and the budget has almost ruined this country. It certainly has ruined our investment climate. A recent survey indicated that 63 per cent of investment activity by Canadian companies will be in the United States. Capital was moved out of Canada in 1981 at eight times the rate in the 1970s, or some $19 billion. The government is deeply in debt this year and will be more so next year. Where is it going to find the money it is spending? It is going to borrow in the money markets and place us in a worse position. The debt load will prevent interest rates from falling, even though American rates fall.
The deficit, along with the lack of investment, will postpone recovery from the recession. Real growth will fall this year to less than .5 per cent compared to the Minister of Finance's projection of 2.2 per cent in his budget. With the collapse of these projects the government can no longer expect to receive the $54.2 billion they had hoped to take out of western Canada to bale them out of the mess they got us into over the past 14 years. The government will be lucky if it gets $24 billion. With revenues falling as a result of the recession, with expenses rising for social welfare because of unemployment, this government is going to be even more bankrupt than it is now.
The question is, Mr. Speaker, is there a solution? I have yet to see even the beginning of one from the government or the NDP. I suggest to government backbenchers that they look at the Conservative policy in this regard as put forward by the recent Conservative government. First of all, we showed real government restraint and cut back on expenditures. The government should get out of industry and the back pockets of the people and businessmen and let the country have room to grow and fulfil the great potential it has. The government should start, as the Conservative government did, an economic partnership with the provinces and co-operate with them rather than fight them as they have done in the past two years. There should be a greater reliance on private enterprise, and certainly a greater reliance on innovation, productivity and
investment. Research and development is an area in which the government has fallen drastically behind. We should build on provincial regional strength and existing economic infrastructures. Instead of downgrading our transportation system, we should be building it up.
Finally, more attention should be paid to human resources because in the final analysis that is where the greatness of this country lies. Mr. Speaker, I can only hope that the loss of these two megaprojects will somehow not result in the unnecessary extension of this depression.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Peterson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we have heard from the opposition benches nothing but gloom and doom about the future of our country. Let us be clear: none of us is thrilled to see these two projects postponed for some period of time.
Postponed?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: On the other hand, I think Canadians must be very clear about what we are doing and have done in the area of energy.
Then you are finished.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: I think if they put aside all the flak, all the clouds of doom and gloom which have been spread over the situation by the opposition-Mr. Speaker, I see the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) is in the back corridor. I welcome the opportunity to have him come down and sit in his seat because I believe that the mood of doom and gloom presented to this House in his lead-off of the debate yesterday was unfair and not a balanced representation of the existing situation. Furthermore, when you read his speech, as I hope Canadians will, you will realize that he did not present one positive alternative.
There sure was: you guys get out.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: There are members on the other side who are not used to staying up all night in debates which they have called.
Make your speech; get on with it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
I will be happy to make my speech with the permission of this House.
One of the fundamental aspects of our energy program is to create self-sufficiency in oil in this country by the year 1890.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: I believe that our National Energy Program has set us on that course and that we have the opportunity to achieve it.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Who has been up all night?
May5, 1982

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
I said 1890? Certainly everyone realizes that it is within eight years time from now which is 1990.
I do not want to be misunderstood on this point. We have undertaken major programs in all of the energy fields which I believe show a constructive means of achieving this degree of self-sufficiency that we all seek.
Let me talk about conventional exploration and development for conventional oil. Exploration drilling for oil in Alberta, where the majority of our oil is now obtained, was higher in 1980 than in 1981.
That is nonsense.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: It was higher in 1981 than in 1980. Oilweek magazine predicts an increase in drilling this year in all western provinces as well as in the frontier and offshore regions. Geophysical activity, which precedes drilling activity, is also on the increase. I do not know whether hon. members are afraid of some more good news, but we are also making some excellent progress in reducing the demand for oil. This has been an essential part of our drive for energy self-sufficiency.
No one can afford it any longer.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: Consumption of petroleum in Canada has dropped. It dropped last year by 7 per cent or a little more than 20,000 cubic metres a day. That is the equivalent of one Alsands project. That type of conservation is an integral part of our National Energy Program. We have achieved this by helping people to go off oil on to more readily available fuels. We have over 100 years of proven usable gas reserves in this country. It is natural that we would want to encourage Canadians to switch from oil to gas, which we have in abundance and which we can export.
A new Joe Greene.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
That is part of our program, our program of helping Canadians convert. They are given an $800 grant to help them convert off oil. They have been converting in record numbers to electricity, to gas and even to wood. That is a direct result of the farsightedness of this program. Hon. members scoff at our conversion figures. Let me give the figures to them. More than 170,000 conversions have taken place. That is not bad. More than 78,000 of them have been to natural gas. The hon. member over there wanted to know that.
Let me come now to the expanded Canadian Home Insulation program. We have brought in the expansion of the CHIP Program to include another 1.6 million homes. It seems hon. members do not want to hear the good news, but I think Canadians want to hear it.
Let me talk about the propane vehicle conversion program. There are grants of up to $400 for a vehicle to get off gasoline and on to more readily available, cheaper fuel.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: How do you buy one if you are unemployed?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: We have a tremendous program of compressed natural gas that is being sparked by a Canadian company which will be the leader in the field. Over the next short term we will have compressed natural gas filling stations right across the country.
Depressed interest rates is what people want.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: It is a major western company and it is Canadian owned. It will be developing the technology. I would encourage members to take the gas with which they are filling this chamber and put it into their cars, because they will have government support to do it and they will find it is a lot cheaper. They will be buying Canadian. Another major program of which I am sure hon. members are aware is the Q & M Pipeline. It is going ahead. The Q & M Pipeline is a major megaproject to help bring natural gas from the west to the east.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: When is it going to start?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: It is a major program. The program that we have put forth calls for energy self-sufficiency by 1990.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: If hon. members opposite would just listen, they will see that we are well on the road to achieving that type of self-sufficiency.
We are well on the road with what?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: The Q & M Pipeline.
Your own colleagues do not believe you.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: Let me come to research and development. Between 1980 and 1983 we will have spent a total of $260 million on research and development projects, in co-operation with the private sector, along the road to achieving selfsufficiency.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why did you bring down the target?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: Hon. members talk about gloom and doom in the private sector.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext: Reaganomics cancelled the project in Colorado, and that is the kind of policies you guys want to pursue.
Go to the west and look around.
What about the rigs that have gone south?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: Yes, some rigs have gone south. It has killed the impact according to Oilweek magazine. There will be increased exploration and development in Alberta this year over last year. If hon. members do not believe that, all they have to do is look at the Oilweek magazine.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
speechtext:
Listen to the voices of the oil companies over there.

May5, 1982
Puppets.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. I do not know whether it is because it is late in the day or early in the morning but I cannot seem to hear what the hon. member is saying. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Minister of State for Social Development (Mr. Peterson).

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do not mind a few interventions from the party opposite, but so many of them have had an opportunity to speak, it is obvious to me that they did not make the points that were really the important ones because now they want to intervene. But the fact is we can achieve energy self-sufficiency.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext: You know all about intervention.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: What is happening in the private sector? Gulf Canada Limited has announced plans to spend a massive $7 billion in capital and exploration over the next five years. Imperial Oil Limited has announced that it will spend billions in the Beaufort Sea and the Arctic Islands. Suncor Canada Inc. is spending SI.5 billion over the next three years. These are multinational companies. How about the Canadian companies?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: They are all gone.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: These include Canterra Energy Ltd.; Norcen Energy Resources Limited and Petro-Canada. These are Canadian companies that will be spending a lot of money on new exploration and development.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: If hon. members opposite want to make speeches, I hope that you will allow me to encroach somewhat on their time, Mr. Speaker. They have been occupying a fair amount of my time. I do not think hon. members opposite want Canadians to have a message of hope brought to them.
You gave it to them in 1978. I have it here. It is Mr. Gillespie's message.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: I do not think they want to hear a message that has realism in it. Their future is filled by spreading a cloud of doom and gloom across this country. They want to deny hope to Canadians.
This is Mr. Gillespie's message, not ours, and it was 80 per cent wrong.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
What about the spin-offs from the projects that we are creating? More than 200 new firms have settled in St. John's, Newfoundland, to take advantage of the new opportunities created off the east coast for oil exploration. What about the gas potential around Sable Island? As many as 8,750 workers will be needed during peak phases to work on the tremendous gas potential around Sable Island.
The Alsands project has been postponed for the moment, but there are other incredible reserves. Our program has been flexible enough to embrace utilization of these reserves. If hon. members opposite from the east coast do not think that we should be going ahead and exploiting these reserves, I should like to hear more from them. They are the ones who seem to be talking so much this morning.
There are many other options for achieving a degree of selfsufficiency. For example, there are alternative energy sources. We could look at hydro, the potential of the Lower Churchill project, electricity, the Polar gas project, gas conversion, and coal in British Columbia. We have an incredible resource there. We have new alternative sources of energy, such as solar and the others outlined by the excellent work of the task force on alternative energy which was chaired by my colleague the hon. member for Pontiac-Gatineau-Labelle (Mr. Lefebvre). Also there are the opportunities for Canadians to convert to biomass, or to renewable energy from our forests.
Also we have incredible spin-offs envisaged by the National Energy Program. If hon. members opposite want to hear some more good news, Canada is a world leader in the production of hydraulic generators-hydroelectric generators.
Hydraulic or hydroelectric generators?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: They are produced in Peterborough and in Scarborough. They have a world product mandate. These generators are exported around the world. We are world leaders in that area, and this is part of the program.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext: You buy coal loaders in Japan.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: In case the hon. member does not know, the last four generators purchased by the Grand Coullee dam project in 1980 in the United States came from Peterborough, Ontario. I am very proud of that. Hon. members on this side of the House should be proud of that.
All one of them!

speakerposition: Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
speechtext: I am proud.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: We have advance technology, long distance transmission and high voltage d.c. transmission of electricity. If the hon. member from the east coast does not want to hear good news, he should not listen to it. The people who elected him will be delighted. Husky Oil and Bow Valley of Calgary have ordered a semi-submersible drilling rig from Saint John Shipbuilding & Dry Dock in New Brunswick, with an option for a second one. That is responsible activity carried out under the umbrella of the National Energy Program. Just because there is a momentary setback-

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext:
Is 1,250,000 unemployed a momentary setback?
May 5, 1982

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: I want Canadians to know that the heavy oil in the tar sands is still there. It will be there when world prices rise.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: Has one member opposite stood up and said that we should pump public dollars into a project which at present world prices is not economically feasible? Should we foist that burden upon the backs of Canadian consumers? If that is what they believe, if that is their alternative, I ask them to stand up. Even with the tremendous guarantees of the federal government, it was not considered viable by the private sector. Why should we as a government walk in and pump billions and billions of public sector dollars into a project in order to make it work? Hon. members opposite should talk to consumers in Ontario or to consumers in all provinces. I have not heard an hon. member from that side say that he is prepared to pump public dollars to a greater extent than was offered by the province of Ontario and by the federal government to make those projects work.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
Those projects will be there and they are part of our program. When conditions change we will be prepared to continue our efforts. I welcome and compliment the efforts of the province of Alberta and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) in attempting to work with the private sector to find a way of making it viable. Unfortunately, it did not work.
I believe that confusion reigns supreme on the Tory side of the House. Members of that party have criticized us for government spending in the past. They criticized us when we established Petro-Canada. They criticized us when the federal government wanted to increase its share of energy revenue from 10 per cent-and Alberta had 40 per cent-to something more reasonable. They criticized government involvement in this sector. Now they criticize us for not bailing out the Alsands project, for not bailing out a private sector enterprise. That is hypocrisy.
No, no!
You deliberately killed it two years ago.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: The hon. member said that the federal government killed the project.
There is no doubt about it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: The facts are clear and they are on the record. We offered a 50 per cent joint venture of public money and private money. We offered guarantees on the loan. We offered tax holidays until the capital was repaid.
Too late.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext:
What more would the hon. member want us to do on the backs of Canadian taxpayers at this time? I challenge hon. members opposite to rise and say what they would do today. They are like the people who are looking
forward with optimism to the nineteenth century. They should get their heads out of the sand.
There are opportunities under the umbrella of the National Energy Program which are being exploited. We have those opportunities. Canada has the possibility of a bright energy future, an energy future in which we can and shall be selfsufficient in all forms of energy by 1990. I look forward with optimism to achieving that under the umbrella of the NEP. This is not the time for doom and gloom. This is the time for the spirit of frontier development and the spirit of enterprise which Canadians have always displayed in the past. I am confident that they will recognize the challenges and the opportunities which are there.
Oh, oh!
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it certainly opens one's eyes to how flexible people can be when one listens to the hon. member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) who just sat down. He certainly showed that he can spout nonsense with a straight face. That would naturally make him a favourite in the stakes, in the cabinet shuffle which will come very shortly. The hon. member said that we have opportunities. What he meant is that we had opportunities before the Liberal government bluffed its way back into power in February, 1980, and laid waste and devastated the Canadian economy.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), the new energy policy and the budget have done more damage than was done by the plague of locusts in Egypt. They are the devastators of the Canadian economy and of the Canadian energy scene. They are the wreckers of confidence. They have wrecked confidence in the country. They have imposed a pestilence, a plague, a famine and a blight on the Canadian economy. The results are the closure of the Alsands project and the Cold Lake heavy oil project.
The hon. member had the gall and the audacity to refer to the report of Gulf Canada. Here is what the president of Gulf Canada said in December, 1980:
Over the years the government has so stained its credibility with retroactive rule changes that those of us in the industry now must ask ourselves, "How can we undertake to make huge investments in long-term megaprojects when we have good reason to fear that the government will come along again and pull the rug on us?"
That is what Gulf says and that is what hon. members have done. They have pulled the rug from under the industry.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Social Development
speechtext: That is your positive alternative?
The hon. member wants to know what the positive alternative is. We are the positive alternative.

Hear, hear!

May 5, 1982

You sabotaged the government in your greed for power because you could not stand to have anyone else in power. In 1979 the Liberal party wormed its way back by confidence tricks with the co-operation of the NDP. The Liberals got back into power. They have betrayed the Canadian people ever since.
The minister talked about how wonderful it was that the consumption of oil dropped in Canada last year. It dropped in Canada because the government tripled the energy taxes that it defeated us on, the 18 cents a gallon. They tripled it. Prices have gone up a dollar a gallon in the last year.
As for heating oil, which we were not going to tax at all, the government has placed a crushing burden on the people of this country. There is no energy tax credit for them. Canadians are taxed to death by this government which got into power by saying that they would not increase taxes in the energy area at all. People have been converted off oil involuntarily. They are now being converted off Liberals, and that is what they will do when the next election comes.
The hon. member had the audacity to mention the east coast. This government is attempting to wrestle away from Newfoundland, the poorest of the ten provinces, the right to exercise control and management over the oil and gas that is on our shores, that we brought with us into confederation in 1949-the Hibernia oil field. The greedy-gut centralizers of this Liberal government have stopped development on the east coast because they are attempting to grab that from the province. Sixty-one per cent of the people from Newfoundland just devastated the Liberal party in Newfoundland who they hold equally responsible with the federal Liberals. They will devastate the hon. members opposite when the next federal election comes unless their policy reverses 180 degrees.
They will not have an east coast oil development to go ahead with until that matter is settled. There will be no oil ever coming from the Hibernia oil field until the province of Newfoundland and the provinces that have resources under the water off their shores are recognized as having control and management of them. That is another disaster in which the government is engaged now and which has not been concluded yet. I do not think the hon. member had anything else to say.
Let us just see what has happened and how important this matter is. This is a report of the Economic Council of Canada. They were appointed by the Prime Minister. They advised the Prime Minister on economic policy. I refer to Volume II, No. 2, in their magazine in 1981, at page 10. They said:
Although economists are often accused of not being able to agree on anything, there is virtual unanimity in the profession right now that the future of the Canadian economy over the next decade will depend on energy.
The Economic Council itself, in its 1980 annual review described energy investment as about the only good thing the economy has going for it.
It is about the only good thing going for us in the 1980s and energy investment is now declining and energy projects are being slaughtered, suspended and cancelled all over Canada. The report went on to say:
What will it take to make Canada self-sufficient in oil? If this country's needs for oil are to be met exclusively from oil sands production, there would have to be
five new oil sands plants in operation by the end of the decade-and that would be in addition to the Alsands and Cold Lake projects which is now on the books.
The government has killed the confidence of the investing sector here in Canada.
When we review what has happened in the last two years, we see a government that has imposed a new energy policy, that has destroyed confidence in the country. We see a government that now has the highest interest rates in our history. They are unecessarily high. Why? Because over the past eight years, under their stewardship we have had $34.5 billion in deficits in the balance of payments. We have a weak Canadian economy, a weak Canadian dollar, and instead of doing something to help strengthen the Canadian dollar, instead of having policies to attract foreign investment and loans to Canada, instead of having a policy to entice private investors and encourage them here in Canada, the government has exactly the opposite policy. It has thumbed its nose at the foreign investor and has threatened the private investor.
The hon. member for Willowdale mentioned Petro-Canada and investment. He said that the government was not going to put public finds into the oil sands project, and why should they? The oil sands project would have provided hundreds of thousands of jobs across Canada and helped us to make ourselves energy self-sufficient. It would have produced 137 barrels of oil a day, on into infinity. What would this government sooner do? It would sooner spend $1,750 million of the taxpayers' money without their consent by having Petro-Canada buy Petrofina, which did not add one cup of oil to Canadian supplies. It added nothing. It did not add any natural gas. It took over existing assets and paid three times their value. That is 4 cents a gallon every Canadian driver today contributes. When he drives 20 miles he is contributing 4 cents a gallon to that purchase. Can that be compared to the oil sands project or the Cold Lake project of Imperial Oil or the Judy Creek project, or any other project that would give us new resources?
Where is this western development fund which they talk about? Here is what the Minister of Finance said to Canadians on September 9, 1980, in Halifax. He said that it was to create jobs, improve living standards and promote greater equity that he took on the position of Minister of Finance. If that is the reason he took on the job, why is he still here? We have the highest unemployment in our history, the highest unemployment rate since 1940. We have over 1.5 million people on the bread line. Where are the jobs that this Minister of Finance has created?
He says that he is improving our living standards for the fifth year in a row when we have a loss in real wages. People's real income and real wages are going down. He has not improved living standards. He says that he is promoting greater equity. What is his greater equity when we have had all of these increases in energy prices, the taxation of life insurance policies, the attempt to make it less attractive to invest by taxing interest on investment, the taxation of employer contributions to employee dental and health plans. Is that
May 5, 1982

the great equity that this Minister of Finance is promoting? If the man had a shred of conscicence or a shred of decency he would disappear into thin air so that we would not have to be bothered with him again.
What was it that the Prime Minister said? He told the Canadian people on January 12, 1980: "We have an economic program for the eighties which will enhance dignity, create opportunities and provide security". The only opportunities which have been provided in the last two years by this pestilential Prime Minister has been opportunity for trustees in bankruptcy. They are the only people who are being given increased opportunities. The trustees in bankruptcy cannot handle the business. Have you seen one Canadian with his dignity enhanced in the last two years except for these puffed up cabinet ministers in their jump jets and their Canadair jet Challengers that they are spending $23 million on this year, while the government cannot find a cent to spend on search and rescue facilities in Newfoundland? They can buy two jet Challenger aircraft with the most luxurious of appointments to take them around the country in their dim-witted and fat-lotted ways. They are the only ones whose dignity has been enhanced.
Have you seen anyone who has had their security increased in the last two years, Madam Speaker? You have not. That was their economic program. What has the government done? Interest rates are 4 per cent or 5 per cent higher than they ever needed to be because the government, instead of helping to strengthen our dollar, brought in the new energy program that attacked the dollar. It drove $10.2 billion in capital out of this country last year. Canadians are moving their money out and foreigners are refusing to invest. They have no confidence in this government. They know that this government does not support the private sector and they know that it believes in government ownership and control. They know that this government disdains them and has attacked and criticized them. As Mr. Stoik of Gulf said, they have strained their credibility. That is why the dollar is so weak.
The government will change its FIRA policy. It is a government of Tarzans beating their chests, they say, because they are such Canadian economic nationalists. Having allowed our economy to be completely dominated by the Americans over the last 30 years or 40 years of their stewardship, the government is now an economic nationalist beating its chest. It has beaten the Canadian dollar down so that it only has high interest rates to protect the Canadian dollar. That has been the cost of those policies. It has cost Canadians billions and billions of dollars, Canadians who are losing their homes and businesses across this nation. They are responsible and no one else, not some outside force, not the United States. It is not the stars in the sky that have caused this. The Liberal government of Canada caused this devastation. Their whole strategy is now gone. The strategy was in the budget speech, such as it was. Expanded world markets, massive resource projects involving major expansion in manufacturing and transportation, are all gone. This document entitled "Economic Development in the
1980s" had that strategy. How can they explain their new reorganization?
On January 12 of this year the Prime Minister proudly announced a new reorganization of his government in respect to economic development. Only Alice in Wonderland could have done any better than the Prime Minister. He has created a Ministry of State for Economic and Regional Development, MSERD, headed by Senator Olson. "MSERD" rhymes with "absurd".
It is going to have regional offices in every province. It is going to have a federal economic development co-ordinator in every province of Canada. We are going to have a federal gauleiter in every province because we no longer have cooperative federalism. Co-operation is at an end, the Prime Minister says. The Prime Minister is going his own way in economic development. He wants to be sure he wrecks every individual provincial economy by putting in each province a regional office with a federal economic development coordinator. What else is he doing? Why, we are going to have a project director for megaproject development in every province. This is the great reorganization!
Why have megaproject development co-ordinators when you have no megaprojects? As I told the people in Prince Edwward Island on Monday night, keep your eye on the Gulf of St. Lawrence to see if there is a megaproject floating by which the Liberals have destroyed and cast off. I told them to see if an oil sands or a tar sands plant floats by, and if so, to grab it because they have a megaproject co-ordinator in Prince Edward Island. Perhaps they will see an Arctic pilot project or a Cold Lake heavy oil project float by. They should not forget to grab it because the federal government will now have a whole series of project directors for megaproject development. If there are no megaprojects, why does the government bother to have the Prime Minister make this proud announcement about his megaproject developer?
They set up a Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, DRIE, as compared to the old DREE. In charge of that department is to be the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) who, when asked questions in this House, goes berserk. He is like a lawnmower going berserk when he is asked a question in this House, trying to avoid answering it. To appoint that gentleman from Windsor, Ontario to be head of DRIE to battle against regional economic disparity in this country is the equivalent of the Red Cross making Dracula their blood transfusion co-ordinator. Why have all this reorganization if the government is unconcerned about them? It does not care that its only two big megaprojects are gone. Why have megaproject supervisors if it does not care about megaprojects?
There is a lot more I could say about this reorganization because there is now a minister for external relations and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan), both doing the same work. The Minister of State for External Relations (Mr. De Bane) is wandering around looking after

May 5, 1982
foreign relations. He must have a large family that lives overseas. I do not know what else he could be doing. We now have two ministers in charge of external and foreign relations, but I will leave that for another occasion.
If megaprojects are not the strategy of this government, if it is uncaring about the fact that the Alsands plant is gone, I presume we will have an announcement that we are no longer going to have megaproject co-ordinators.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) is not here today. Whenever he gets up in this House with his arrogance, superiority and destructiveness, he confirms to me that the Dracula legend is true. The other day he said not to worry about Alsands, that we are going to have the Cold Lake heavy oil project. He said we are going to resurrect that. However, when we look at The Globe and Mail of May 4, we see that Esso spokesman Glen Rainbird said:
Even if we had been offered the same terms we would have made the same decision as Shell and Gulf ... We have taken it out of our three-year planning horizon.
Imperial Oil is taking Cold Lake out of its three-year planning horizon. That is gone. Even if it can ever be resurrected, it will not be looked at again by Imperial Oil for three years. This is the government that prefers Petro-Canada to take over Petrofina, rather than create an economic atmosphere that would enable Imperial Oil to do the Cold Lake project on its own or Alsands and its partners to do the next tar sands project on its own. We have had in this Minister of Finance not only incompetence, but deceitfulness, duplicity, dinginess. He is diminished and defeated by his job. The member for Willowdale (Mr. Peterson) and the rest should go to their caucus and make sure that that minister is taken from that job and put somewhere else. They can give him any kind of job they like. Make him super Deputy Prime Minister, but put him out of harm's way. Take him out of that job.
He is left by the Prime Minister slowly twisting in the air. No one would mind that but the whole Canadian economy is twisting with him. We do not know whether his budget will go into effect or not go into effect. He has made eight changes and God knows how many more there will be. While he twists, he twists our economy into disastrous shape.
They are the Neville Chamberlains of the Canadian economy. They are the Munichers. They are also going in that direction in so far as international affairs are concerned.
The Prime Minister, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce are the four horsemen of the Apocalypse, the four horsemen of our economy, the four horsemen of the economic Apocalypse. They represent only one end of the horse, and that is not the head. The four horsemen of the Apocalypse were war, famine, pestilence and death. This government is warring on the Canadian economy. It is starving Canadian entrepreneurs and risk-takers. It will not give them any incentive. They are like pestilence across this land.
A week ago I was in the Northwest Territories and Yukon. Mineral exploration is down 40 per cent this year. Bush
aircraft companies are going bottoms up, going into receivership all over the place. The north is devastated. Mines are closing everywhere. They are damaged coast to coast. It is unbelievable.
In my own province of Newfoundland, the economy has never been worse. There is no construction and the highest unemployment in our history. The people of Newfoundland know who caused that. They demonstrated that on April 6 by voting 61 per cent for their Conservative government of Newfoundland.
The four ministers I mentioned are the dire straits quartet. The one positive thing they could now do for Canada that is still possible for them to do is resign, take themselves out of office, and give the Canadian people the chance to judge again. They know what their performance has been like for the past two and a half years. They have this Prime Minister who now thinks that he is God. Caligula could not have done any better. He is going by his personal fiat and he is going to do what he likes for the next several years. Let him put that on the line. Let him see whether the Canadian people want him or the positive alternative that we represent. Not the New Democratic Party; they are no alternative. They are hand in glove with this group opposite. Give the Canadian people a chance.
Give the policies that we introduced in 1979 a chance. Had they been continued, those projects today would have been under construction. The Canadian economy would have been vibrant. Interest rates would have been lower. Canadians would have had confidence. They would not be having their hopes crushed and destroyed by the hon. gentlemen opposite who no longer have a purpose. They no longer have any plan. They just want to cling to power no matter who it hurts, who it damages or what happens to Canada. They are in this conspiracy to stay in power. They are now twisting and wondering how they can get rid of their Prime Minister and bring in some saviour. Well, they are not going to get rid of the Prime Minister. He is not finished with Canada. He wants to leave us with an East European economy before he goes. He is an admirer of the "success" of the Polish economic system and he will not leave us until he has done us the same favour.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry, but the hon. member's time is up.

Madam Speaker, I listened to the previous speech with a great sense of horror, and I wonder what the people in the galleries and those at home who watch this debate think when it can sink to such levels. We have listened to a verbal attack on Canadians and a verbal attack on members of my party who evidently do not share the view of the hon. member who has just spoken but nevertheless have a belief in the future of this country and do their duty. I wonder what impression people listening to this debate have when they listen to performances with so little content and of such low quality. It is shocking to listen to such a deliberate attack on the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and to such a deliberate attack on ministers of the Crown and elected representatives, who represent Canadians as well as
May 5, 1982

hon. members opposite. This attack was by a member who is really a master in verbiage but whose credibility is very much in doubt.
The hon. member is a member of a party which, in December, 1979, was not even able to count to make sure it would have enough members present to win a non-confidence vote, and now the hon. member comes here and cries because his party lost an election. It lost an election because Canadians did not, and still do not, have confidence in it. The hon. member has forgotten that fact, but Canadians know they cannot trust a party which cannot even count up to 141. That is what happened to the Tory party in December, 1979. Hon. members opposite have not recovered since, and because they have not recovered and because they have a psychological problem and their egos are hurt, we have listen to this kind of speech, which was the worst performance I have seen in this House in many years. On behalf of those who have to listen to this kind of junk, I regret that very much.
If there was a gold medal given for running down one's own country and its government, surely the hon. member would win that gold medal, and surely he would exhibit it. It would be sad if he were to take pride in this kind of performance, but I wonder what pride one can take in casting doubts and distorting facts deliberately, as the hon. member has done for the past 20 minutes.
speakername: Hon.   Chas. L. Caccia@Minister of Labour

speechtext: Why don't you tell us about the 1.5 million unemployed?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: The hon. member deliberately distorted facts from one issue to the next. He did it so professionally that all I can say is the hon. member could win a medal for running down his own country.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Caccia) is entitled to say whatever he wants to say as long as he stays within the rules of the House. You no doubt heard, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Labour accused my colleague, the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), of deliberately distorting facts, and that clearly is a breach of parliamentary rules. That onus is on you, Mr. Speaker, to request the minister to withdraw that statement.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member distorted facts all the way through his speech.
You said he deliberately distorted the facts.
Withdraw.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Well, evidently. I imagine he made his speech in good faith and knew what he was talking about, and therefore it was deliberate.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext: Make yours in good faith and withdraw.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: The hon. member can believe I will do my best.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. My colleague has raised an appropriate point of order. We presume Your Honour will be able to rule on it. The minister said
"deliberately". A number of us in the House heard it. He has had an opportunity to withdraw but has chosen not to do so. Therefore, we ask Your Honour to fulfil the responsibilities of the Chair and ask the hon. member to withdraw that statement, which clearly was unparliamentary.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: "Deliberately" is not an unparliamentary word. It depends on what is attached to it. Unparliamentary expressions include "deliberately misleading", "deliberately misled" and so forth. I did not hear the minister being charged with saying that. I do not see "deliberately distorting" referred to in the rules.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext: Deliberately distorting.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: "Distorting" is not listed, as far as I can see, and if the hon. member wants to cite a page from Beauchesne, that might help the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-
Show some honour, Charlie, and withdraw. Show some integrity.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: This government has asked the provinces to act responsibly with taxpayers' funds. This government has dealt with the provinces over the past two years in a very constructive manner. There have been meetings here in Ottawa with the provinces on a number of occasions. Last summer we finally arrived at the point where the unthinkable took place; nine provinces and the Government of Canada arrived at an agreement which allowed us to conclude the constitutional exercise in a successful manner. Does the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) include that on his balance sheet? Does he include the fact that the Government of Canada has been able to arrive at an agreement with the province of Alberta on energy? Does he consider that a plus or a minus? Does he consider the fact that today we have in Canada the best federal-provincial relations we have had for many years? Does he consider that a plus or a minus?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: The economy is in a shambles.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Then the hon. member for St. John's West went on and engaged in that old chestnut about which many of us have heard many times. He spoke about the deliberate high interest rate policy of this government, knowing very well what he said was not so. The hon. member knows very well the source of our high interest rate problem. We are part of the economy of the western industrialized world, and we cannot insulate ourselves from what happens south of the border. We cannot establish our own interest rates without being aware of what is happening in other major markets and to the American dollar, and to blame the government for high interest rates is really to ignore what has been said over and over again in this House and what has been said by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) in the budget.

May 5, 1982
Blame the United States. Blame the sun god. Why not blame the Japanese?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: The hon. member is a master at blaming. I am glad he is responding to what I am saying. Evidently he does not like to hear what I am saying. It is getting to him; otherwise he would not be here in the House to hear my comments on what he said.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: You are deliberately distorting him.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: He knows very well that the high interest rates in this country are not manufactured by this government.
Yes, they are.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
We have to bring inflation down in order to bring down interest rates, and we also have to watch what is being decided in Washington with respect to the large deficit down there. That will also determine the confidence of the money market in the U.S. dollar. The hon. member knows very well the forces which come into play. He knows very well what the facts are, and that is why he is walking out of the chamber right now.
Despite the difficulties we have encountered so far, we have used unemployment insurance funds successfully to absorb the shock of difficult economic times and high unemployment. Hundreds and hundreds of unions have come forward and signed agreements with the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Axworthy) to make sure jobs are not lost. Why does the hon. member for St. John's West not make reference to the tens of thousands who are benefiting from this program? Why does the hon. member for St. John's West not recognize the fact that despite economic difficulties this government has maintained and protected the socialinsurance scheme we have? We have not done as the Americans have done. We have not cut them down. We have kept social protection for Canadians. That is a great plus for a country which is going through difficult economic times. Why did the hon. member for St. John's West not say that?
Canadians are also entitled to see the positive side of the coin. Canadians should also know what is going well in the country. The country should not be run down by hon. members like the hon. member for St. John's West who make a profession of doing that. That is not right or fair, and the hon. member should not do it. Why does the hon. member for St. John's West not speak about the program of expansion of railways in the west and the investments which will be made in the months and years to come? There will be investments in the billions to improve our railway system to permit the movement of our energy resources and natural resources to the west coast in order to improve the economic standards of the people on the prairies and in British Columbia. Why does the hon. member for St. John's West not speak about that, as well as about the performance of the government?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: The minister is a disgrace!

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: We heard a lot of criticism this morning-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Why do you not resign, Charlie?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: I am delighted to have such an audience. I have not had such a large audience in a long time-
Certainly not on your side.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: -of such fine parliamentarians.
The only minister in the House!

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: It is very simple, because they are looking after the affairs of the government by having a caucus right now, because that is what we do every Wednesday morning, do we not, Mr. Speaker? Right.
You need a caucus, Charlie! You'd better figure out when you are going to have an election!

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Why does the hon. member for St. John's West not tell the audience here and at home that we have achieved a good energy policy in this country despite all the criticism that we hear?
Come off it. I am not going to be a diabolical liar. You are doing the lying for the government, not me.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: We hear only the negative part of it. But the hon. member would not speak about the fact that the Canadian ownership of energy resources is being increased. Why does he not talk about the pluses of this policy? It is certainly good for Canadians to own a good portion of their energy resources. Why does he not mention that in his speech? When he talks about large projects, he tells listeners here and at home that two projects have defaulted. It is true that two projects have not got off the ground. However, why does he not also tell Canadians about the fact that we do have projects which are going on? We have Dome Petroleum's project of oil and gas exploration in the Beaufort Sea, amounting to $500 million. Why does the hon. member for St. John's West not mention that in his speech? Why does he not mention that the Norman Wells oilfield development for $600 million is going ahead? Why does the hon. member not say that? Why does he only bring the bad news here? There is also good news for Canadians to hear.
What?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Name one!
You get 40 weeks of UIC! Is that the good news, Charlie?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Is he engaged in the job of demolition or is he engaged in the job of construction? That is the difference between them and us. We are engaged in a job of construction and they are trying to demolish the government. We had better put them back in their places before it is too late.
May 5, 1982
You demolished the Canadian people! You are professional deceivers!

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: The hon. member for St. John's West is now unsuccessfully trying to read the newspaper. Why does he not speak about the Revelstoke hydro project in B.C., a project that is going on to the tune of $1 billion? Why does he not mention that to those who listen to him at home?
How much did you put into that one, Charlie?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: They would be glad to hear that, because what is good for British Columbia is also good for Newfoundland, or does the hon. member think that what is good for Newfoundland is only good for Newfoundland?
They know what is good for them, and it is not the Liberal Party!

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: It is good for the whole of the country, is it not? Why does the hon. member not tell us about the Trans Quebec & Maritime PipeLines?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: When is it going to start?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: It is going ahead.
When, when?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: It is a large project. It is a $1 billion project, and it is going ahead.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Tell us when, Charlie!

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Why does he not tell us about the coal development project for $700 million?

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Tell us when, Charlie!

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: That is going ahead and you know it.
When?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: He did not mention that project in his speech.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: You have been talking about it for three years!

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: And what about the Ridley Island grain terminals in British Columbia?
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: That is an investment of $400 million.
When, Charlie, when?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Why does the hon. member not mention that? You will see-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please.
It makes no difference! You killed that one, too!

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole

You are not a minister of labour, you are a minister of miscarriages!

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: But I was really struck and concerned by the fact that the hon. member for St. John's West would engage in such a demolition job which was intended to demonstrate that everything in Canada is going wrong. That is not a fact, and hon. members opposite know it.
Yes, there is a Conservative Party, and that is all right!

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: There are a lot of good things going for us in this country, and the opposition had better realize it, because it is important that we maintain the confidence of Canadians in their own country.

Mr. Speaker, I was told that coming to the House of Commons would be a learning experience, and after two years, I have learned something. I have learned that when it comes to basic policy or basic philosophy on how to run the country, there is no difference between the Liberals and the Conservatives, the so-called Progressive Conservatives. The fact is, the two old-line parties are really two parties fighting for the same position.
This whole process of debate today is aimed at doing exactly that. Two parties are fighting for the same position. The fact that they are fighting for the same position has been proven over and over in this House. It has been proven by their blind support of Reaganomics. Every day in the House we hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) telling us that the

May 5, 1982
policies of the Reagan government will save us from inflation, while our friends in the Tory party cajole us with pleas that if we would move a little closer to the great United States President, we would not have all the same economic problems as the United States. I know that this does not sound very logical, but logic is not one of the strong points of the official opposition. I suppose that the greatest proof of the similarity between the Liberals and the Conservatives was shown in the 29 times they voted together in this House in this session. The Liberals and the Conservatives have voted together 29 times on issues such as how the government should handle Governor Bouey.
Consider their support of the grain embargo. Both the Conservatives and the Liberals supported the embargo which the United States put on the movement of grain into Russia, an embargo which the United States immediately dismissed or circumvented, but which hurt the farmers and the grain producers of Canada. Both the Liberals and the Conservatives supported that embargo. Here we are again, speaking on a motion put forward by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), a movement designed to put some distance between the policies of the Conservatives and those of the Liberals. That is why it was brought forward. It is because their policies on these issues have been very close together ever since they were in power. Again, for proof of similarity of the policies of these two parties we can look to their voting records. One of the projects which has collapsed, or at least has been delayed, is the pipeline. There was another case in Saskatchewan where the Liberals and Conservatives voted together.
You know why you were defeated in Saskatchewan.

On July 22 of 1980 the New Democratic Party attempted to ensure some guarantees. On that date the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) presented the following motion to the House:
That before the House adjourns for a summer recess, the House calls on the government to declare that it will not proceed with the construction of the prebuild portion of the Northern Gas Pipeline until complete financial guarantees for the whole pipeline have been obtained and an agreement has been reached between the Government of Canada and the Government of the United States that the Canadian gas exported through the southern portion of the proposed pipeline will be replaced by Alaska gas at an equivalent price.
In a speech on the same day he said:
Indeed, I have been raising this issue in this House ever since April 17, namely, that we in the New Democratic Party believe this prebuild should not go ahead unless Canada is guaranteed that later on there will be gas swaps of amounts equal to the gas we sell now at approximately equivalent prices, along with guarantees, ironclad, signed, sealed and delivered, that the whole pipeline will go ahead. That is the position of the New Democratic Party.
Later in his speech he said:
