The main issue is that the Liberal Party is gambling with the future of this country in going ahead with this pre-build. Hon. members on the other side obviously do not see this, but I believe the jury in the country is beginning to understand what is really at stake and just what the Liberal government has done.
The Liberals and Conservatives voted together on that motion in order to make sure we did not have guarantees of swaps or guarantees that the pipeline would ever be built. They gambled and lost, so today we are faced with the motion of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and with the collapse of the pipeline. All the spin-off jobs in manufacturing and related industries have collapsed or have been postponed. This was made possible by the fact that those two parties would not support some guarantees and voted together to kill the NDP motion for guarantees.
Let us examine the government's position on megaprojects and on energy. The government pinned its economic and industrial recovery strategy on the development of resource megaprojects. The leading opportunity in the development of Canada's rich bounty of natural resources is outlined in a statement taken directly from the economic development document of the November 1981 budget. This sounds very much like a continuation of past policies which have promoted the export of raw materials and the potential jobs that would have occurred had the resources been processed and manufactured in Canada. The government sees this resource development policy as an opportunity to benefit all regions of Canada concurrently if it is managed properly with respect to funding and promoting indigenous manufacturing and service industries.
If the Liberals were serious about managing and developing megaprojects in order to build an enduring and diversified economic base, they would need to take the interventionist approach along the lines of promoting Canadian ownership and control as they attempted to do in the National Energy Program. However, they clearly state in their economic policy document that they do not consider this approach appropriate for any other sector, such as mining or forestry. Moreover, they have abandoned their throne speech promise to strengthen FIRA. The Liberals seem to be content to let others write the rules while they remain the referee.
Another weakness of the Liberal strategy is that it assumes our resources are for sale and that we will use them as a lever to gain access to larger markets for our resources and manufactured goods. Unfortunately, the government has been a poor bargainer, and in recent resource and trade deals with Japan and the United States that has been evident. All too often foreign governments and companies have been able to play on the need of this country to export raw products, which does not allow us to develop our manufacturing industry.
The economic viability of many of these megaprojects has been seriously called into question when the factors of prices, taxes, inflation, interest rates and financing are examined in the light of what is happening in the changing world today.
Claims of job creation and industrial spin-offs were exaggerated, and they were not cost-effective when compared with manufacturing investment. In all the megaprojects the Canadian content guarantees were weak. The fact that these energy companies withdrew from these projects proved that the projects are really not cost-effective. There are cheaper
May 5, 1982

alternatives to costly oil sands development. For example, enhanced conventional oil recovery or even alternative energy forms and conservation are available.
By committing themselves to megaprojects the Liberals inevitably committed themselves to massive public subsidies through tax concessions, grants and loans. The benefits are not worth the costs, and the projects have died.
The Liberal resource megaproject plan was simply to change our past economic pattern. As someone put it, we were drawers of water and hewers of wood. That has been changed to diggers of coal and pumpers of oil. We deserve better.
The NDP position is that where resource megaprojects can be demonstrated to be necessary to help achieve some defined national goal which is realistic, they should proceed with public subsidies and maximum public equity. The key words are "public equity". Moreover, maximum Canadian content must be guaranteed in terms of equipment and employment. Very little Canadian content was guaranteed with respect to the pre-build, according to those involved.
A reliance on resource megaprojects to stem the tide of the deindustrialization of Canada has proven precarious because of the uncertainties about the economic viability of these projects and the danger of perpetuating resource sellouts along with the export of jobs. The NDP has explained its policy in a statement entitled "A New Employment Option for Canada" which was released in February, 1982. We have shown a preference for concentrating on the development of our manufacturing sector by processing most of our raw resources here in Canada to create jobs for Canadians. This is a particularly important decision as far as western Canada is concerned. We have the resources; if we ship them away we limit the increase of jobs which are possible in western Canada.
With regard to some energy megaprojects, the NDP believes that we should develop, where feasible, less costly alternatives. For example, instead of a series of costly oil sands plants, enhanced oil recovery projects may be more economical and produce an equivalent amount of oil. Conventional heavy oil upgrading or even coal gasification requires less capital investment than oil sands plants. Alternative energy projects to make gasoline from natural gas, and methanol from wood waste, are also becoming economically viable. Investment in conservation is also less capital intensive, creates more jobs, and reduces the need for costly energy developments.
The NDP believes that only through strong government presence can we give direction to resource development and provide guarantees to maximize Canadian benefits. If the policy is wrong, the government should change it, but the presence I speak of must be sensible and in the right direction. The lip service given by the Liberal government until now has proven to be a disaster. Coupled with a plan to restore our manufacturing sector, this will enable us to revitalize the Canadian economy.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, upon checking the procedural books it turns out that using the words, as I did, "deliberately misleading" is unparliamentary. Therefore, I wish to apologize
to the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie), and I wish to thank you for your guidance.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak to the motion concerning the crisis in the oil industry brought about by this so-called Liberal government supported by the western Liberal Party, otherwise known as the NDP. I must say it comes as no surprise to me considering the current Liberal government's track record on fiscal responsibility. Furthermore, the National Energy Program is a cruel joke on the Canadian people.
It is no surprise that it is the Liberal NEP which has caused the failure of the Alsands project. Canadians now know that what is needed is a government prepared to work with the private sector for the betterment of all Canadians. This necessarily involves developing a feeling of trust between business and government. Progressive Conservatives place more emphasis on the creation of wealth, for we know that as more wealth is created there will be more to distribute to those social programs currently underfunded by a debt-ridden federal government. Business requires flexibility in the marketplace to pursue programs which will benefit Canadians.
The NEP has caused the industry to cut back on its capital expenditure plans, its research and development, and its participation in the Alsands project, in order to generate sufficient capital to finance projects currently in progress. The minister tells us the slowdown is a result of a worldwide economic recession. The petroleum industry has always been a strong performer in the Canadian economy, and the Alsands project was a recognition of the role energy would play in Canada's economic development. It could provide the vital initial impetus to get Canadians back to work and business into gear. The industry could play a pivotal role in our economic development in the years to come. For every billion dollars it spends, it can generate between $500 million and $1 billion in further business activity across Canada, in addition to contributing to our energy security. One can sense the extent of the failure of this government from the failure of the Alsands project.
The major oil companies are not the only ones suffering from the NEP. I find it unbelievable that as a result of oil import compensation charges Canadians will pay more for gasoline and home heating fuel when they conserve fuel. As we use a higher percentage of foreign oil, it is Canadian production which will suffer. There will as well be a loss of jobs and a negative effect on our balance of payments.
Our neighbours to the south are benefiting from a worldwide oil glut. However, the Canadian consumer realizes no such benefit. In my riding, the tourism industry supplies much needed employment. The high price of gasoline will have a detrimental effect on the number of American tourists who come to that region, and that will continue for as long as there is that difference.

May 5, 1982
In the rural areas of Ontario, where a car is more of a necessity than a luxury, residents are feeling the effect of high gasoline prices eroding their standard of living. The government-forced metric conversion program has cleverly masked the layers of tax increases being shoved on to the Canadian consumer. The $2 a gallon price for gasoline has become a fact of life for Canadians in central and eastern Canada. The small independent businessman who operates a service station bears the brunt of criticism from consumers about rising gas prices, but he has no power to control those prices. We know, thanks to the report on the state of competition in the petroleum industry, that when you squeeze out independents, the price goes up. In this case, it goes into the hands of a government pricing monopoly. These businessmen are entitled to a fair return on their investment, but with decreasing profits and rising costs the future looks dismal.
Canadians have recently witnessed the realization of a made-in-Canada Constitution. They have prided themselves on their association with Great Britain and the democratic tradition inherent in parliamentary institutions. I would have hoped this would have allowed us to carry the British democratic legacy honourably. However, I have observed that the British parliamentary democracy is not only mature, but more responsible in government. The Falkland Islands dispute provides proof of that assertion. In that dispute a senior cabinet minister, as well as two junior cabinet ministers, accepted responsibility and did the only honourable thing: they resigned. They accepted responsibility and demonstrated their belief in responsible government by resigning. However, in Canada, we have a Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) who introduced the National Energy Program in 1980 and then in 1981 introduced a budget that was so obnoxious his own party rebelled, not to mention the Canadian public as a whole. This budget, which is still in the process of amendments, is the ultimate in incompetence. Clearly, parliamentary democracy demands and rightly expects his resignation. The fact that the Minister of Finance has not changed indicates that the current government's concern for parliamentary democracy does not exist.
Now we have a Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) who also must concede defeat. Under his stewardship, the collapse of the Alsands project has worsened an already bleak economic situation. The minister is quick to avoid blame by transferring it to external factors. The minister should do the only honourable thing; that is, take responsibility for the failure of the Alsands project and resign.
It was not external factors which led to the demise of the Alsands megaproject. Clearly it was Liberal mismanagement. The budget and the national energy policy complement each other. They both stink!
To talk of oil self-sufficiency as well as to promise exploration in other areas does nothing to alleviate the anxiety of Canadians over their future financial prospects. The tax regime imposed by the National Energy Program has reduced
the industry's cash flow and earnings from oil and gas production to the point where its ability to generate investment capital is seriously impaired.
Investor confidence in the industry and in the economy has also been badly shaken, especially in the case of foreign investors. The combination of a severe reduction in internally-generated funds, which, in turn, affects the companies' ability to borrow, as well as weakened investor confidence, make the accumulation of large-scale funding, either through equity or debt, extremely difficult. It is obvious any fiscal terms that could have been struck between industry and the government had become academic, no matter what rate of return the terms created, because the petroleum industry simply does not have the money to invest on the scale required. For the same reason, and also because of a general lack of investor confidence, it is unlikely to find new participants in the near future for the Alsands project.
Investor confidence in Canada by foreigners is now restricted to bond sales and bank deposits, which have become particularly attractive to non-residents because of the high interest rates. This represents an outflow of between $4 billion and $6 billion in interest. As the federal government must float more bond issues the situation simply gets worse.
Government policies which cause the amount of capital outflow that is now occurring are policies exacted at a tremendous cost to all Canadians. The Petroleum Monitoring Agency tells us that the cost of Canadianization was $6.5 billion in the first six months of 1981.
This government must ask itself whether Canadianization costs exceed the benefits. Can we still afford the national energy policy? Of course not. There was a net direct investment drain of $10.2 billion in 1981.
While there is an element in the government which holds Canadianization above all else, the cost that is being imposed on the Canadian economy is horrendous. The name National Energy Program has a nationalistic ring that makes it sound appealing. It is, however, ill-conceived legislation that is beginning to backfire. In financing the current account deficit, together with the outflow of direct investment capital and unidentified outflows of funds, Canadians had to borrow $13.6 billion in 1981 through new security issues outside the country. An additional $14.9 billion was required in short-term capital imports.
The sharp rise in interest charges on the foreign debt is a visible legacy of the National Energy Program. The crippled dollar is another. The federal government has serious fiscal problems with little room to manoeuvre. The solution is clear. Relax the National Energy Program. Allow industry to keep a sufficient share of the oil and gas revenues it generates. It does not need handouts. It will then have the funds and the incentive to undertake a wide variety of projects. This action will also encourage outside investment.
The federal government needs to reassess its taxing and pricing arrangements for the health of the industry and the economy. While there may be initial pain from reduced
May 5, 1982

petroleum taxes, the creation of new jobs and increased profits in many sectors of the economy would generate considerable additional tax revenues.
The current period of softness in the international oil market will allow the government the opportunity to reassess our crude price position as well as our tax position. One alternative would be for domestic production to track the price schedule agreed to by Ottawa and the producing provinces, but not to allow the price of domestic crude ever to exceed that of imports.
There are other steps which could be more appropriate as federal government objectives that would allow for tax changes that could result in additional industry revenues comparable to those initiatives that have been currently implemented by the Alberta government. What is important is to provide sufficient funds to revitalize the petroleum industry in a manner that would provide the industry and investors with a badly needed assurance of some long-term stability.
The National Energy Program has coincided with one of the worst economic periods this country has experienced for a very long time. Coinciding as it did with a depressed economic environment, the effects of the national energy policy are devastating.
In Saskatchewan, Grant Devine spoke not at but to the people. He responded to the voters' wishes and struck a responsive chord, particularly with young people who are worried about their future financial prospects.
The role of government in the economy is to provide a framework for private sector growth. Creation of wealth is what government does best. Governments which become directly involved in commercial activity are not operating in the best interests of Canadians. There is still the opportunity to correct this state of affairs. If the federal government acts to provide relief on the scale that the gravity of the situation dictates, the country will see a significant turnaround in the industry and a new spirit of confidence will emerge in the future of this country.
I sincerely hope that the Canadian voter will not be fooled by the "prince-in-waiting", John Turner. The mad money policies of the current Liberal federal government were started by the former finance minister back in 1974 much to the detriment of the Canadian public. Somehow I believe the Canadian voter is fed up with being lied to.
The national energy policy, a policy of socialism with its high degree of intervention, is a 50-year-old policy that may have had some benefit during the last depression, but it is killing us now. People are rejecting the promise of next year. Temporary shutdown, it is called.
People in Saskatchewan have clearly indicated with their vote that they want relief from high interest rates, inflation and lack of opportunities. If the current government does not have the intestinal fortitude to make the hard decisions needed for these difficult times, let it put the question to the voters. Then we can get a new government that will put the state in its place and get Canada working again.
Even now, this government is telling Canadians that it is not the fault of the national energy policy that the megaprojects are failing. It is apparent this Liberal government is assuming that if you continue to repeat something often enough, hopefully, Canadians will actually believe it. This is why Trudeau and his government have launched a $5 million ad campaign proclaiming that it is "helping Canada work". Besides promoting job training and skill development, the campaign is intended to suggest that whatever its problems, the Canadian economy is working. Taxpayers are actually revolting at this waste of money. Times have changed and people no longer believe slick media slogans-the just society in 1968, the land is strong in 1972, win the ethnic vote in 1974, trust the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in 1979, and gasoline increases below 14 cents per gallon in 1980. This type of advocacy advertising is now backfiring because 1.2 million people are officially unemployed, along with students looking for work, struggling businesses, farmers and consumers trying to make ends meet with high interest rates and inflation. They all have trouble believing this b.s.
Oh, oh!

Canadians by the thousands now know this socialist party as a tired old government lacking proper representation across Canada, devoid of ideas to fit the crisis, pork-barrelling and pouring out tax dollars as a screen for inaction and incompetence. This political bankruptcy is a result of many good Liberals abandoning a sinking ship over the past few years. All that is left is the philosophy put forward by a Liberal backbencher on January 29, 1982, when he said:
If, in order to promote our development the Liberal Party thinks we have to be communistic, we shall be communistic. This is what it is all about to be a Liberal.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have an opportunity to say a few words on the motion of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) concerning the cancellation of the Alsands project and the postponement of the completion date of the northern gas pipeline project. This is not the first delay we have seen with the Alaska gas pipeline project. Certainly during the 1970s, when we were in power, we moved expeditiously to see the northern gas bill passed so that we could put in place the regulatory procedures and the agency to see the project go forward. The project is a private enterprise in which most of the funds are being raised in the United States, as they should be, because it is American gas in Alaska which will be transported to the southern 48 states. The delays are regrettable, but they are due to circumstances in the United States. We moved rapidly to put in place the agency during the 1970s. I served as chairman of the Northern Pipelines Committee. If there was any delay at that time, it certainly would not have been caused by us.
In its announcement last week the Alaskan company indicated that there were a number of factors in the United States which were affecting the project. For example, there

May 5, 1982
was the short-term excess oil supply; depressed prices of crude oil, which, incidentally, cancelled or postponed other projects in the United States like the oil shale project; low levels of economic activities; and the general uncertainty of United States financial markets. All these were factors in postponing the start-up and the completion date of the northern gas pipeline.
However, that is not to diminish the disadvantage to Canada. Most of the pipeline will be built in Canada, from which we will receive many spin-off benefits. Also there will be the foreign exchange advantage and the balance of payments advantage in the cost of transporting Alaskan natural gas to the lower 48th parallel.
It is interesting and significant that the sponsors and natural gas producers in Prudhoe Bay indicated that they are still committed to the project and will continue with the expenditure of money for the planning and development of the project. Likewise, Foothills Pipe Lines Ltd., indicated that it would continue with the pre-construction work or Phase II so that the project can go forward even though it is delayed for a couple of years.
It is important to remember that the western leg of the prebuild was completed last fall and that the eastern leg of the pre-build will be completed this fall. Certainly this will mean that something like one third of the total length of the project will have been completed. The waivers given last fall by the United States Congress, the Senate and the House of Representatives, were largely due to the completion of one third of the length of the project itself. Even the economic benefits of the pre-build are of significance to Canada. For instance, the National Energy Board estimated that the net economic benefit of the prebuild to Canada will be some $4.5 billion, and that over the lifetime of the line some $17 billion worth of natural gas will be sold in contracts to the United States, which should give us a balance of payments benefit from the pre-build of some $2 billion. Although the project has been delayed by some two years, there is no doubt that we will derive a great deal of economic benefit from the pre-build of the gas pipeline. This is especially significant at a time when we seem to have a surplus of gas in western Canada which is shut in.
With regard to the cancellation of the Alsands project, the House will recall that when the National Energy Program was announced on October 28, 1980, the Premier of Alberta indicated that he was putting a hold on the Athabasca tar sands project, on the Alsands project and on the Cold Lake project. This was especially regrettable; I am sure the premier of the province now believes that that decision was most regrettable.
On November 12, 1980, I directed a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. I indicated that the Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works had been studying these massive projects which would have an immediate influence on the amount of oil, but that over the period of construction they would be of great economic advantage to Canada. Also I indicated that in the end they would
certainly provide a great deal of oil supply and security. I asked the minister the following question:
-will the minister be seeking an agreement with the Alberta minister of energy to have the province's hold on these plants lifted and this issue separated from the over-all disagreement on oil pricing and revenue sharing from conventional oil, so that these projects can go forward without delay?
In his response the minister said:
The one suggested by the hon. member is indeed one we would welcome.
He went on to indicate that he would talk with the Alberta minister of energy. It is most unfortunate that the whole question of tar sands plants could not have been separated. If we look at it realistically, we realize that the federal government was trying to get its share of revenues increased from some 10 per cent, as it was before October 28, to something like 25 per cent or 28 per cent. That kind of disagreement will take many months and, in fact, it took about ten months to reach an agreement. There was no illusion. When you think about trying to increase the federal government's share of revenues and taking on the multinationals and provincial governments, in an issue like that, you realize it will not be easy. It will take a number of months to accomplish.
It is unfortunate that this project could not have been separated from an over-all agreement on oil pricing and revenue sharing of conventional oil. I believe if that were the case it would probably have gone ahead. The companies clearly indicated that in their testimony before the committee in the fall of 1980. We can never be 100 per cent sure. There was an agreement in early September, 1980, which was made with Alberta, but the project still did not proceed immediately at that time. Negotiations preceded that and clearly there has been the utmost co-operation between the two levels of government. They have been willing to put up half the equity-about $6.5 billion-of the $13 billion required for the project. They were willing to guarantee a return of some 20 per cent on the investment of the private shareholders of Gulf and Shell. Even with the co-operation between the two levels of government, the guaranteed return on investment, and equity participation of 50 per cent, the companies were still unwilling to proceed with the project. The problems that the United States investors faced on the northern gas pipeline were the same problems facing the private investors. I believe that it is their prerogative. It is a private-enterprise project, even though governments were willing to guarantee rates of return by granting concessions in royalties and taxes. Whether or not to go ahead is still a private-enterprise decision.
I recently spoke to a senior official in a large company who was studying a massive expenditure in the development of his company. He said, "When we sit down to look at these maga-projects we know that if we make a bad decision we can effectively wind up the company." I believe that with the uncertainty as to the interest on money, oil prices and so on, the responsibility and difficulties faced by large corporations are considerable.
May 5, 1982

The Energy Legislation Committee during this past few weeks heard a great deal about the delay in exploration and development activities in the oil and gas industry in Canada. I think it is rather interesting to note that a recent report of the United States department of commerce forecast of projected capital expenditures abroad for foreign affiliates of U.S. companies estimated that Canadian affiliates of U.S. petroleum companies plan a 28 per cent increase in exploration in Canada in 1982 over 1981. I believe that it is a significant figure because exploration by United States affiliates on a worldwide basis is estimated to be only approximately 18 per cent.
Therefore, in spite of all the rhetoric we hear from the other side and complaints about the National Energy Program, the fact is that American-owned affiliates are making capital investments at a much higher rate in Canada than they are in other countries.
We are told that a report will be coming out very soon. I believe it is the next report of Oilweek in which it is indicated that of something like 170 drilling rigs which moved from Canada to the United States-supposedly because of much better returns there-only 20 are operating. I think we would want to take all those arguments we hear from the other side with a grain of salt. It is clear that the economic uncertainties are faced by all countries around the world and not just by Canadian oil companies.
For instance, during the past couple of weeks in the United States, Exxon Colony in Colorado had planned a 47,000 barrel per day shale oil project costing $5 billion. It is my understanding that this project has been cancelled because of the very same problems that face the private sector with regard to the northern gas pipeline deferral and the Alsands cancellation. Likewise, Exxon Troupe in Texas has a gasification project worth $4 billion which has been deferred recently. Similarly, Panhandle, which is a company in Wyoming, had a coal gasification project involving some 49 billion cubic feet per year of natural gas which has been cancelled. In Nigeria, a liquefied natural gas project costing $14 billion was recently shelved because of the problems that face all megaprojects, wherever they may be in the world.
Naturally, we are all disappointed that the Alsands project was scrapped. However, I believe it is rather ridiculous to accept the argument from the other side that Canada's prosperity depends on a single project like Alsands. Its own private sponsors have indicated that it is unprofitable under the present economic conditions, in spite of the generous offer by Alberta and the Canadian government which would have covered fully the 84 per cent of the cost of the suspended project. Hon. members opposite have no faith in the economic drive of Canadians. Are they suggesting, despite their continued pleas, that the private sector should do more in the Canadian energy field and that the federal government should saddle the Canadian taxpayer with the total cost of Alsands, amounting to some $13.9 billion?
I would like to give a short report on the economic benefits which megaprojects are providing to Canadians. The number of projects, other than Alsands, to which I can point is a tribute to the diversity of the Canadian resource sector and the
potential which exists there. For example, there is the development of the Hibernia oil and of Venture gas off the shore of the east coast. There is the exploration and development of our oil and gas resources in the Beaufort Sea. There is the Trans Quebec & Maritime PipeLines which is now getting ready for construction.
Let us review some of these projects briefly. Since the National Energy Program was announced, work has progressed steadily on the work on Hibernia. Four delineation wells have been drilled. As a result, the Canadian Petroleum Association has recognized new proven oil reserves amounting to over one billion barrels. Our expectations for the area are even greater. This development means jobs for people in Newfoundland, in Atlantic Canada and across the country.
We have the Venture gas field near Sable Island. Petro-Canada had an important role to play in the discovery of this field in 1979. Since the National Energy Program two delineation wells have been drilled at Venture, resulting in an estimated proven reserve of 1V2 trillion cubic feet of natural gas.
The Venture gas field lies within the offshore region covered by the recent agreement between the Government of Canada and the province of Nova Scotia on offshore resource management and revenue sharing. Under this agreement, the government of Nova Scotia will exert a large degree of control over the development of these resources and receive the lion's share of potential offshore revenues.
What is more, the offshore administrative regime established under this agreement and the new oil and gas act which was proclaimed on March 5, 1982, will ensure that Canadians participate more fully in the accelerated exploration and development activity which will now take place in the Canada lands on the east coast.
I could go on and mention the Beaufort Sea development which is estimated to cost some $44 billion and will create
10,000	jobs, some 4,600 permanent. I could also mention the Trans Quebec & Maritime PipeLines project which will cost some $2 billion and create 12,000 jobs. There is also the heavy oil upgrade in Saskatchewan which will cost $2 billion and the Dome Petroleum project to explore liquefied natural gas which is expected to be completed by 1985. It represents $2 billion in investment and 8,200 jobs during construction. The rim gas project, also to be completed in 1985, will cost about $1.5 billion and mean 2,000 jobs in construction.
I could also mention the new methanol plant in Kitimat, British Columbia, to be completed in 1983 at a cost of over $140 million, the ethylene plant II to be built in Joffre, Alberta, by 1984, costing $500 million, expansion of the Trans-Canada PipeLine in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario which will mean an investment of $237 million this year, and the truck construction of a new TransCanada PipeLine from North Bay to Morrisburg, Ontario, which represents an investment of $408 million.

May 5, 1982
It is clear from these comments that although we are all disappointed that the Alsands project is not going ahead because of economic circumstances, we recognize there are many other projects going ahead which will help to move us toward energy self-sufficiency during this decade. I think these few comments indicate a great deal of movement in that direction.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to quote as follows from the document entitled "Economic Development for Canada in the 1980s", which was tabled with the budget introduced in this House in November 1981:
The decade of the 1980s holds great promise, offering opportunities of unprecedented magnitude and the potential for lasting benefits from economic renewal to Canadians in every area of the country.
The leading opportunity lies in the development of Canada's rich bounty of natural resources.
It goes on to point out the importance of massive megaprojects. It identifies $440 billion worth of potential projects, predominantly in the energy sector. It talks about the tremendous opportunity this will provide in terms of manufacturing activity, both to supply machinery, equipment and materials needed for resource development and to extend the further processing of those resource products beyond the primary stage.
It goes on to talk about the massive investment that will be required and about the opportunity for utilizing Canada's innovative resources in the development and exploitation of advanced technology, about increasing the productivity, providing the necessary goods and services, creating a climate of innovation and creativity in manufacturing, about engineering, technological communications, and electronic opportunities. It then points out the following:
It is equally clear that we must build upon and strengthen our technological infrastructure. Innovation is a major key to success in the market place and to the achievement of the productivity growth that is so essential to the real growth that underlies our expectations of rising standards of living.
Those are lofty, credible objectives, but analysed in the context of the reality of what is happening, these words are nothing but empty, shallow, meaningless rhetoric. It clearly points out once again the misleading nature of this government. What we have in this document is nothing but a bunch of rhetorical fluff. It resembles in great part the platform that was presented to the people of Canada during the 1980 election.
I am not sure how much longer the people of Canada will be in a position to swallow this kind of phoniness and deception. The policies of this government are such that they mitigate against the achievement of these goals and objectives. They mitigate against achieving a stable climate that is conducive to investment and has some semblance of confidence.
The people of Canada and Canadian industrialists have no confidence in the management of this country as it is now provided by this government. They believe this country is being steered by a group of economic misfits.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext: It is being castrated.

My colleague says it is being castrated. That may be an appropriate word. Suffice it to say it is being steered by a group of economic misfits which industry does not trust. It changes the rules in the middle of the night. That is why Alsands is not going ahead.
This government has developed a policy of redistribution of wealth rather than the creation of new wealth. It discourages investment, creativity, innovative abilities of Canadians, vitality and the creative instincts of Canadians.
We are living in a society, an economic climate that is sterile rather than vibrant. Moreover, the on-again-off-again policies of this government, the budget, the National Energy Program, the attitude of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the manner in which they govern in a climate of confrontation and unilateralism has created chaos and uncertainty. The budget and the National Energy Program have created confusion, the result of which has created hardship and heartbreak for many thousands of Canadians.
Since the 1980 election, this government has had essentially one objective in mind, that is, to get even with the west. I have a cartoon here which appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of June 9. It is rather interesting that it should appear in a newspaper in Canada's capital. It illustrates the picture of the Empress of Venezuela supertanker which is obviously carrying oil to Canada. At the same time there is a box of Canadian dollars being lifted by the crane. The picture shows our Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) with a caption that states: "Consider yourselves lucky, this money could be going to Alberta."
In a nutshell, that really puts this whole debate into perspective. There is an insane jealousy along the benches of this government for any potential development and growth that may take place in western Canada, particularly in the province of Alberta. There can be no question that, in the interest of national security, in the interest of the advancement of our technology and maintaining world leadership in oil sands technology, in the interest of fuelling the engine of economic growth and development at this critical time, and providing jobs, and in the interest of bolstering the manufacturing sector of Canada, this Alsands project should be going ahead. There can be no question about that. It could have been under way and it should have been under way. There is no question that it could have been under way, but unfortunately it was doomed. It was doomed, Mr. Speaker, the moment this Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources assumed his responsibility in charge of energy in this country.
To back that up, Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote from an article which appeared in the July 10 edition of the Toronto Globe and Mail. It is an article written by Mr. Ronald Anderson, a very perceptive individual in terms of economics and energy policy in this country and indeed throughout the world. He stated, back on July 10, 1981:
May 5, 1982

Mr. Lalonde does not care much any more about the oil sands. He continues to say that the Government wishes to pursue all options in increasing the domestic supply of oil; but the National Energy Program largely wrote off the supply of conventional oil in Alberta-
We know that because we have 300,000 barrels a day locked in right now in the province of Alberta and probably 50,000 barrels a day in the province of Saskatchewan. So that has been proved. He has been right on that. I quote again:
Mr. Lalonde now seems ready to write off the oil sands.
That was stated, Mr. Speaker, by Ronald Anderson in the Globe and Mail of July 10, 1981.
So the mould was cast at that time. The mould was cast, and so for hon. members opposite to stand up and blame Alberta, blame the private sector, blame the oil companies, blame the opposition, is totally false and inaccurate. The mould was cast, Mr. Speaker. This Alsands project was doomed by this government, by this minister, when he assumed the responsibility of his portfolio.
The article goes on to read:
Mr. Lalonde, after a tour of Dome Petroleum Ltd. drilling operations in the Beaufort Sea, is reported by The Canadian Press to have talked confidently about the possibility of an oil surplus in Canada by 1990.
The Energy Minister indicated that he regards development in the Beaufort as an alternative that is at least as attractive as oil sands development. He said it now appears that Canada can be "pretty confident of production coming out of the east coast and the Arctic."
That again demonstrates and illustrates the naivete of a man in charge of the energy future of Canada. We know that it will take years to overcome the regulatory hurdles, in terms of building a pipeline from the Beaufort Sea or any other mode of transportation. It will take years to develop that system to get oil out of the Beaufort into the lower part of Canada. We have the ongoing jurisdictional dispute between the province of Newfoundland and the Government of Canada.
Furthermore, I would venture to say that in the end the oil from the Hibernia or frontier source will be as expensive as the oil out of Alsands. It seems to me that any deliberate policy shift to reliance exclusively on the offshore and the frontier represents a very high risk. That is where we are today, Mr. Speaker.
The members opposite cannot try to weasel out of this, the responsibility for the failure of this project going ahead lies at the doorstep of the treasury benches. The responsibility also lies at the doorstep of the members who support this government and keep it in office, and that applies also to the red rump to my left.
The fact of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources chooses to do what he does, he is not only hurting the economy of western Canada, he is in fact hurting the whole nation. That is what the National Energy Program has done. It will go down in history as the major man-made disaster of the 1980s.
We talk about Canadianization. And who is not in favour of Canadianization? We all want to see our energy industry controlled and owned by Canadians to the greatest extent possible. The fact of the matter is, whether or not we have a
large degree of foreign ownership, we will have the regulatory abilities to develop those resources in a manner that meets the national public interest. We still have that freedom, surely.
Therefore, I do not get overly excited about the fact that we have a high degree of foreign ownership, because we still have ultimate control. But what does Canadianization cost us? It cost $6.5 billion in the last year, and that is money that has not produced one barrel of oil. It has not added to our ability to achieve greater self-sufficiency.
What else has the National Energy Program done? It has seen the exodus of $10.2 billion of investment capital out of this country, about $5.3 billion worth of foreign capital and $4.9 Canadian. We have massive government intervention in the energy industry, and we can expect more.
I notice that the Financial Times of April 19, says:
According to an internal energy department study obtained by the Times, officials are probing the refining and marketing segments of the oil industry, looking for rationalizations for new interventions. There is talk of "carrots" and "sticks" to promote different objectives ... We can see possibilities involving forced Canadianization, price controls, profit restrictions, production directives, and continuing erosion of private control of the industry.
So Canadianization is not really the ultimate purpose here, it is nationalization and greater centralized control, so that the bureaucrats and the politicians here who occupy the treasury benches can determine who the winners and the losers are going to be, who will get a grant and who will get a subsidy and where and in what part of the country. And by doing so they will be dividing rather than uniting this country. We have had too much of that. What we need in the country is a renewal of our economic and political partnership. We need co-operation. We need co-operation with other governments, we need co-operation within industry. That has been lacking. We have had division, chaos and confusion. That must stop.
I will quote now from a freelance writer who writes for the Edmonton Journal. He has observed this massive government encroachment, this massive government intervention. He has been noted as not being a Conservative or a Liberal, but rather he has been noted as being in line with the New Democratic Party. This is what he had to say:
When I look at the Ottawa crowd today, I have visions of Lenin, Trotzky and other assorted personages of the Russian revolution of 1917 ... First the government instigates inflation by being spendthrift and by being overly generous in the settling of its own labour disputes. Then it goes after inflation and hurts many people.
Much of the inflation we have in this country today was and is caused by government irresponsibility. Even now, when everyone is supposed to hold the line, Ottawa's spending is up by more than 20 per cent.
He goes on:
Federal and fiscal monetary policies affecting directly and indirectly Canadians' ability to afford housing, are other examples of Ottawa's anti-middle-class sentiment. Fewer people than ever before are in the position to own homes of their own. A nation of home owners is becoming a nation of tenants. This is bound to weaken society severely.
Coming from an individual who has leftist tendencies-and he is horrified by the tendencies of this government-one would certainly assume that the average Canadian, too, is horrified.

May 5, 1982
I have in my hand an article from one of those average Canadians, a man by the name of John B. Witchell. He refers to the writings of the Prime Minister in the book entitled "Federalism and French-Canadians" in which it is stated:
Federalism must be welcomed as a valuable tool which permits dynamic parties to plant socialist government in certain provinces, from which the seeds of radicalism can slowly spread-
If the whole of the Canadian electorate could miraculously be converted to socialist ideals at one fell swoop, there would be no reason to discuss strategy-
In his article, Mr. Witchell says:
By now, if we are willing to accept the clear intent of Trudeau's words, we begin to realize that his "Federalism" is merely a stepping stone to socialism- socialism as in China, Russia, or the Cuba toward which he once paddled in his own canoe.
That is the major concern in Canada, over and above the fact that we face the highest unemployment rate in history, the highest interest rates, the highest rate of inflation, and the highest level of bankruptcies. People are concerned about what this man and this government, his cabinet colleagues and his supporters in the back benches, will do to them. They are fearful when they hear that the government is contemplating the taxation of the imputed rental income from the homes which individuals own, another $4.5 billion. It is there. We as members of the opposition must draw this to the attention of the House and the country, day in and day out. There can be no question.
Referring back to the National Energy Program, 1 have heard much from hon. members opposite about the fact that this Alsands project has failed because of the private sector. I have also heard hon. members opposite and those in the NDP say, "Well, those boys in the Conservative Party are in the pockets of the multinationals". The National Energy Program has not hurt the multinationals. It has crippled small Canadian industry. Exploration is down by 40 per cent since this disastrous policy came into effect. Look at the headlines which state, "Exodus of oil rigs increases", "Budget may throw 200 rigs off the job", "Small firms suffer". The small Canadian firms suffer. Another headline states, "Oil service, a lot of red ink, a lot of pain". Referring to trucking companies, about 25 per cent of Alberta's heavy-haul truckers went out of business during 1981, according to the industry's trade publication. Ontario loses too. The fact is that when this megaproject was worth $7 million, as the Hon. Larry Grossman indicated in the study-although it has doubled to $14 million-it creates $800 million in business for the Ontario iron and steel industry. That would amount to $1.6 billion, $370 million for Ontario metal working firms, and if we double that it amounts to approximately $700 million. The Ontario transportation industry amounts to about $650 million. There is another $1.5 billion for other manufacturers and processors in Ontario. There is another $1.6 billion for the Ontario trade and service sector. If we look at what Syncrude has provided, we find that out of the $2.2 billion Syncrude project, roughly 20 per cent of the labour force came from Ontario and 20 per cent to 25 per cent of the equipment it needed came from Ontario. Syncrude
officials calculated that, by 1976, more than $100 million worth of machinery and equipment was ordered from Ontario.
So here we are. We see firm after firm going out of business,, yet the government has the audacity to deliberately kill a project which will kill industry in Alberta and in Ontario. For every job created in the oil industry in Alberta, two jobs are created elsewhere in Canada. This government's attack on western Canada is really in effect an attack on the central manufacturing heartland of Canada and, indeed, is causing chaos and confusion and is creating further dislocation, hardship, hopelessness and despair in this country. I can say to Your Honour that not only should this government resign, but it should also leave. It should get right out of the country because it is a menace to Canada and to the free society that we enjoy.
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, I want to begin my remarks by telling the House and Canadians how disappointed I am in the hon. member for-is it Vegreville?
That is close enough.

The hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). He was the former distinguished minister of transport who, in normal times, enjoyed the full respect of all hon. members from all sides of this House and in committee. However, to see him come into this House and stand up and try to sow the seeds of disruption and separation within this country the way he did this morning gives us cause for concern. I am sure he will want to reflect on his contribution.
You have destroyed the country. I have not been in charge of that.

The hon. member will want to reflect on his approach this morning. As I said, the hon. member for Vegreville has obviously been drawn over by his leader, not to the right or to the left, but beyond any semblance of reason. In recent times the hon. member has given utterances to the press to the effect that he was not sure whether he would support his leader in the next leadership review. However, this morning he gave us a demonstration that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) has drawn him beyond any semblance of reason.
"Beyond Reason". I have read that book.

Last evening, the Leader of the Opposition took it upon himself to take advantage of the fact that he was leading off in debate to draw in hon. members from this side. I must say that he did it in a very unfair manner. It was found that he did not even know what he was talking about, because when he made reference to the riding of Restigouche, he did not even have one bit of information as to the economic development taking place in northern New Brunswick. However, I am delighted that yesterday the Leader of the Opposition brought forward this motion to adjourn when he asked leave to move the adjournment of the House. Now there is a party which is interested in the future. There is a party which
May 5, 1982

is interested in the country. However, what do its members want to do? They keep the bells ringing for two weeks.

speakerposition: Progressive Conservative Party Caucus Chair
speechtext: To stop this wave of socialism.
Now they come to the House to ask the support of the Speaker. They lean on poor Madam Speaker-
Oh, oh!

-to help them out of the disarray that they are in today. That is the problem. In any ordinary democratic system, there must be a good opposition to give good government. What do we have here? The reason this institution has had its problems since the beginning of this year, 1982, is facing us right here in the benches of the Official Opposition.
Order, please.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Nepean-Carleton rises on a point of order.

Mr. Speaker, I know it has been some time for the hon. member for Restigouche (Mr. Harquail), but we are debating a matter of urgency. That was the finding of the Chair. That is why we are here. I think the House would appreciate it if the hon. member would direct himself to the emergency which has occurred as a result of the failure of the Alsands project and pipeline.

This is another indication of some of the tactics of hon. members in the opposition. They are so interested in democracy that they are not even willing to allow elected representatives in this House to have their fair time in which to speak when they have the floor. But notwithstanding their belligerent attitude, let me just go on to tell my friend, the hon. member for Ottawa-Carleton-
Nepean-Carleton.
-Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker), that I will be coming to the subject in very short order.
I am waiting.

1 just want to take the opportunity to address myself to some points which were brought into the debate, in case the hon. member was not here. As a matter of fact, he was here. That is how he was able to mention my riding. The Leader of the Opposition was looking through his briefcase and he could not find his notes. That is how prepared he was. He asked the hon. member for help in locating his notes. The Leader of the Opposition got exercised about the fact that I said, "Give him a helping hand. He needs all the help he can get". That is when he decided he would try to attack me, that he might take that approach. Where was the concentration and dedication of the hon. member's leader to the subject that he had brought into the House, the Alsands project, when he started to talk about my constituency? The evidence was very clear, but hon. members opposite do not want to hear about it.
Let me then tell hon. members about the economy of northern New Brunswick. Since the Leader of the Opposition
does not know about it and since he asked for information last night, I am here today to tell the world, the House of Commons and the citizens out there who are listening just exactly what is happening down there. I will be mentioning oil exploration off the coast of Nova Scotia and Newfoundland when I get to the subject of Alsands. There is a number of other items about which hon. members opposite do not want to hear, but I will put some facts on the record so that all Canadians will know.
The Leader of the Opposition is not aware that in recent months, because of very substantial support and co-operation from the federal government, three major companies have decided to modernize pulp and paper mills in northern New Brunswick. One is located at Atholville. One is at the town of Dalhousie, and one is at Bathurst. There is in total in excess of $600 million of capitalization as a result of approximately $60 million of federal incentive money. That is one aspect the Leader of the Opposition inquired about last night, and I thought I would bring that information forward and clarify it today.
In addition to the modernization of pulp and paper mills which will secure permanent jobs for the next 40 to 50 years there will be, of course, spin-offs for the economy in the region, and the number of new jobs created during construction will be very significant. I underline the importance of that.
In addition to this, the Brunswick Mining & Smelting Corporation of the Noranda group has decided to proceed with the construction of a new zinc plant within my constituency at an estimated cost of $360 million. If we combine the capital investment and the modernization of the pulp mills which is under way now, which amounts to upwards $600 million, and the commitment to incentive grants of $21 million plus the 50 per cent tax credit on new construction of over $360 million, I am happy and excited to be able to stand here and tell hon. members that upwards of $1 billion of capital investment is going into northern New Brunswick. As far as I know, northern New Brunswick is still part of Canada. Let us not forget that.
Thank God for the provincial government.

Now that through our democratic process I have had the opportunity to set the record straight on that point, I want to refer to the matter which has been brought before the House. I am sure all interested Canadians will want to ask themselves why the opposition has adopted this strategy and this tactic at this time. Why would the Leader of the Opposition want to delay the proceedings of the House? Why would the Leader of the Opposition and his party want to bring in delaying tactics? Why would they want to holler and whoop and yell when we bring forward points which are not quite in agreement with the foolish attitude they have to our approach to trying to operate this country?

May 5, 1982
Another thing which strikes me but which has not yet caught hon. members opposite-this was referred to by the previous speaker-is that in 1980 the Canadian people made a decision. That decision was made as a result of the democratic process of going to the polls.
Based on a whole bunch of deceit.
What hon. members opposite have not yet accepted-they have not had the intestinal fortitude-is the democratic decision of Canadians.
Not in western Canada.

Canadians were very clear in their decision, and who got the mandate? The economic policies of hon. members opposite were put before the people in that democratic process, and they got their answer. The answer of the Canadian people to the Progressive Conservative economic approach was no. The answer was a pure and simple no. We have accepted the responsibility to govern.
You haven't any mandate from the west to govern.

Now we hear from the little fellow from British Columbia. He just woke up. He is back in the House screeching and yelling. Yesterday the NDP member from British Columbia got into a screeching match with the House leader for the official opposition. That is his mental attitude and approach to good debate in the House. The hon. member who is trying to interrupt my speech now, screeched and yelled yesterday. The energy critic for the New Democratic Party engaged in a violent exchange with the House leader of the official opposition.
If we were to listen again to everything said in the last 12 hours or more, we might begin to wonder if there is nothing positive going on in Canada. Is everything gloom and doom?
Yes.

Is there nothing positive happening in terms of economic development in the country? Let us hear the catcalls when I enumerate some of the projects under way in Canada. Under active construction is the Dome Beaufort Sea oil and gas exploration phase involving over half a billion dollars.
Dome is going bankrupt.

The Esso Beaufort Sea drilling system involves SI30 million. The Gulf Beaufort Sea drilling system in the Northwest Territories involves $700 million. The Norman Wells oil field development involves $600 million. The Trans Quebec & Maritimes PipeLines involves $861 million. The Revelstoke hydro project in British Columbia involves $1,115 billion. The Pickering "B" generating station involves $1,805 billion.
That is a provincial project.
That is part of Canada.
Oh, oh!

Are hon. members suggesting to me that the Pickering "B" generating station is not part of our economy? I have heard the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) yell in the various committees, but I thought he would show some respect in the House of Commons. He is not in a committee now.
Poor little fellow.

Let me tell hon. members about some of the other things they do not want to hear about. There is a commitment to the CF-18 Hornet fighter aircraft project amounting to $2.99 billion. I am sure hon. members opposite want me to go on. The Ridley Island coal and grain terminals involve over $400 million. That is close to half a billion dollars.
Stalled.
The synthetic crude oil refinery and benzene plant in Alberta involves $600 million.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: That is stalled.

Do hon. members opposite want me to go on? They shake their heads. They do not want to hear this. Canada is still a great country. Canada is one of the best countries in the world, and hon. members opposite should not forget that. They should not try to drag it down and give the impression to Canadians that it is in such bad shape. They are only causing a negative division in the country, and I suggest there are some positive things going on.
Let me talk about advance planning and design stages of other projects. The Lower Churchill Falls project involves $1.65 billion. The Canadian patrol frigate program involves $1.89 billion. Sable Island offshore gas in Nova Scotia involves $2 billion. The Norman Wells oil pipeline involves $400 million. La Grande Phase II at James Bay involves $3,487 billion. The Hibernia oil development project offshore Newfoundland involves over $4 billion.
Where?
It is not even started. You have it stopped in its tracks.

Hon. members are concerned about what we would do to offer alternatives. We have stated what we would do, and there have been agreements. It is not good news at any time to hear of a project which has faltered. I would be among the first to join my colleagues who have said here in this debate on this motion that we are not happy about the fact that these private companies have decided that the risk is too great. However, let us not forget that we had the courage of our convictions to go ahead and offer financing for this project. We are not happy about the fact that it has been postponed. I am sure the government of Alberta is not very happy. Mr. May 5, 1982

Lougheed is not too popular these days out west, and I am sure he is not pleased. What does the Leader of the Opposition say about that? He is very careful not to bring Alberta in when he talks about the demise of Alsands. Alsands is always the problem only of this government. Alsands is all a Liberal problem. How naive can hon. members be? Under what illusions are they operating? Do they think people are so gullible that they believe that kind of hogwash?
We certainly don't believe you.

I sat here and listened to the hon. member for Vegreville a while ago, and 1 hope he displays to me the good spirit he displays most of the time. Hon. members opposite become very upset when someone else speaks in the House because their leader allows only a few of them to speak. I do not understand that logic, but that is a difficulty hon. members opposite have. They do not want to hear the truth. They do not want to hear the facts.
I would like to go on and speak about alternatives to Alsands. I mentioned the Beaufort Sea, and I would like to mention others. The Dome project in the Beaufort Sea involves $500 million in investment. The Esso project involves about $130 million. I mentioned the Gulf drilling system project in the Beaufort Sea, the Norman Wells oil field, Hibernia, and the natural gas pipeline into Atlantic Canada, something we are very happy about. In British Columbia we have a coal development project which represents some $700 million, and I have already mentioned the Ridley Island coal. There is the Carmont upgrader in Montreal which represents an investment of over $1 billion. There is the upgrader in Saskatchewan which is another billion dollar investment. These are some of the projects which have not been mentioned here once.
It all becomes very clear. People stop and ask themselves why do they play this kind of political gamesmanship? We have an opposition in such disarray that it has to come back to the House with delaying tactics, where the House was hijacked, and then they have the gall to come in and say with a happy face that they are all good men and women who are sincerely interested in democracy and they want our country to work. As the worn out expression goes, you cannot have it both ways.
You cannot say the country is having all sorts of difficult problems just because one project was cancelled. We have admitted that it is regrettable the project is not going ahead at this time. Perhaps it will at a later date and we will be ready to support it. It just happens that the world economic situation today is such that it does not permit the project to go ahead. Reference has been made to the reasons why. We here in Canada are not an island unto ourselves; we deal in the international marketplace.
There are other countries with similar problems, not the least of which is the United States which had to cancel the $5 billion Exxon project in Colorado. A $4 billion project in Texas has been deferred. The Wyoming Panhandle coal gasification
project, $49 billion, has been deferred. A nuclear energy project of over $30 billion in Mexico is delayed. Liquefied natural gas exports from Nigeria in excess of $15 billion have been shelved. The list goes on and on.
We can talk about the situation in France referred to by the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey) last evening, which represents a very significant amount of money and which has been postponed. In the U.K. falling oil prices and demand are creating uncertainty about the outlook for up to 70 potential new fields in the North Sea. These are some of the facts which sincere Canadians would be interested in knowing. But that is not to say, as is being put forward, that it is all doom and gloom. There are many exciting things taking place in Canada.
While we have suffered for years in eastern Canada, specifically the Atlantic area, we are at long last over and above the seasonally adjusted unemployment situation which is constantly with us in the forestry and fishery industries. We now see some hope in New Brunswick because of the modernization of their important pulp and paper mills and the proposed construction of a new zinc plant which will cost in excess of $360 million.
I have put forward, Mr. Speaker, some aspects of this government's position with regard to projects, ongoing and proposed, costing from $500 million to in excess of $1 billion. These are all the direct result of decisions taken by this government in a spirit of co-operation with private enterprise to secure jobs for the future, and create jobs now.
There are other aspects which I would like to draw to the attention of the House during this debate, but of course time is limited and I would be the last one to want to delay the business of the House. I for one, if members opposite were prepared to tell the whole story, would be in a better mood to accept it. But they do not want to talk about anything positive.
What we have seen here lately is an attitude of character assassination, attacking people personally, with no consideration for the traditions of the House, and they are trying to break down the country. And I think that is an outright shame. We know why! The answer is in the Gallup poll. When they should be on the crest, the polls show they are dropping. The Canadian people have no faith in the opposition parties, but we are going up in those polls. Then, when you look at the leadership, our leader far outstrips the Leader of the Opposition in the polls, and even the Leader of the NDP (Mr. Broadbent) is running second behind the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). It is a desperate party, a desperate opposition in disarray, with a desperate leader.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the hon. member presenting a list of all the good news, most of which had nothing to do with this government and was in the works in spite of, not because of the government. I was particularly interested to hear him mention the heavy-oil upgrader in Saskatchewan. That has been in Liberal speeches for the last eight years, and we still cannot find it. It

May 5, 1982
has just dropped out of sight. Then there is Prince Rupert. I was reading the Western Producer the other day, and the hon. member should subscribe to it because Prince Rupert is not off the ground either. Oh, the National Harbours Board has a couple of bulldozers running around pushing dirt up to the shoreline, but that is all.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, there will always be investment in projects going on in many fields of endeavour in any country, but when it remains unplanned and unco-ordinated, and when it is subject to high interest rates, just like the home owner, investors will go broke. All the experts told us what we have to do. I have a figure here totalling some $77 billion just on three projects. Of course, now that we have lower world oil prices there is not as big a buck in it as there was, so the industry is going home. The private investors are not interested because the bucks are not going to be as big as they would have been had those projects been in place one or two years ago. So much for our great corporate citizens and their grand plans for private enterprise to make Canada self-sufficient in energy. The Liberals keep running around trying to be half pregnant. But there is no such thing. On the one hand they say they are all for free enterprise. They make just as good speeches as the Tories do about their versions of free enterprise. Then they say, "We are going to go down the middle of the road." But the problem is that all the action happens in the middle of the road. My hon. friends on the government side have been running around for the last several years trying to be all things to all people. They cannot make up their minds what to do. I will say that the Progressive Conservatives decided which way to go, but they could not count.
Tell us how you do it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: Tell us how Blakeney counts.

Keep your cool, fellows.
I never gloated over eight elections in which the Tories got wiped out.
If the megaprojects are worth while, then there has to be built-in protection of Canadian companies and Canadian governments. These projects are not built just because we can make a fast buck outside our borders when there are areas in our country that do not have gas or have to pay exorbitant prices for fuel to heat homes, drive cars, run farm machinery or run industry.
What I consider to be traitorous-and I hope that word is not unparliamentary, because I believe that the traitorous attitude of the Liberal government, supported by the Conservatives, is to go again into supine acquiescence at the request of the United States government-is to agree to another four trillion cubic feet of natural gas going outside our borders and that we are going to build a pipeline in the southern part of Canada to get rid of that Canadian gas. We had nothing but a telex which the U.S. ambassador delivered here. It was not signed by the President of the United States. There was no legislation by the U.S. Congress. But every time
Genera] Haig hollers "Jump," these fellows ask "How high?" The Liberals do the same thing when it comes to our resources. They pander to corporations who can make a lot of big bucks. They even pander to making some bucks for their own particular government. It is a policy of "Ship the resource out of here." We have been had again.
The delay of at least two years about which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) is complaining will last exactly as long as it takes for the United States to decide that it has to have its own natural gas extracted from the North Slope of Alaska, and until then, as long as the Americans can have our gas, they will take our gas.
I get annoyed with those who say that there is a surplus. There never has been a surplus. There never will be a surplus of natural gas in Canada in terms of what Canadians need.
Not as long as we have the national energy policy.

Whether it takes 20 years or 200 years, Canadians need and will use up all the present and the proven reserves that we have.
We are finally building a pipeline to Atlantic Canada, which should have been in the works many years ago. But it is finally happening. While we were running around on hands and knees dealing our natural gas with yankee traders and pre-building a pipeline that will carry and sell Canadian gas, 4.1 trillion cubic feet of it, our fellow Canadians in eastern Quebec and in the four Atlantic provinces are paying exorbitant, unconscionable costs to keep their homes warm. That 4.1 trillion cubic feet of natural gas would have heated every home in the four Atlantic provinces for 25 years. But in order for the owners, the so-called owners, the private enterprisers, to make bigger bucks, we sell it off.
I invite my hon. friends to read the debates in this House in 1973, 1976 and 1977. While I hate people who say "I told you so", what the former member for Nanaimo-Cowichan and The Islands had to say, and what my leader, the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) had to say, has turned out to be completely correct. Here we sit with several hundred miles of pipeline running through Alberta, part of Saskatchewan, into the United States and up into B.C. Our Canadian gas is being used by Americans.
The demand we made in 1973, 1976 and 1977 that every cubic metre of natural gas we provide the Americans be returned to us whenever we need it, whether it is five, ten or 25 years down the road, is not met. Unless the line is completed through to Alaska, Canada will not be able to construct the Dempster branch to bring Canadian gas to Canadians. This frantic effort to sell off more of our resources that we need ourselves is something that should not be done. There is no such thing as a surplus of natural gas, and there never has been. This resource is something which the Canadian population will use up no matter how many years it will take.
The Leader of the Opposition complains about this two-year delay. We will be lucky if it is only two years. I predict that it
May 5, 1982

will be much longer than that. But he complains. Yet he and his colleagues voted with the Liberals for the umpteenth time on the pre-build. The Liberals and the Tories were dancing together at night at Canadian Petroleum Association receptions.
1 do not know why the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition should complain in his motion. He said that this was an emergency. He helped cause the emergency. He and his colleagues aided and abetted the so-called emergency. In the meantime Canada has been stuck and "had" again.
When we are dealing with megaprojects we should remember that many megaprojects could be carried on other than those involved in oil and gas. If there is the political will to challenge investors, workers, businessmen and people generally, many megaprojects could be developed. If we took only $2 billion out of the $77 billion supposedly lost, we could put it into the construction of well-insulated and energy-efficient housing units. The side effects of that $2 billion investment would be public investment, plus whatever private investment would be involved. We could return the forest industry to work, we could return the appliance factories to work, we could provide roofs over the heads of tens of thousands of Canadians. They would be megaprojects which would not worry about whether or not someone in Texas or Denver is happy with the Government of Canada.
For less than half the cost of the Alsands project over the next eight to 12 years, depending upon how fast we want to do it, we could electrify 300 miles of urban transit in Canadian cities. We could electrify 10,000 miles of railway track to carry 75 per cent of the traffic, which would be only 10 per cent of the trackage in the country. That is another example of a megaproject which would save more diesel fuel than could be produced by oil sands plants. We could transfer 36 million gallons of diesel fuel per year from running trains to producing food. It would be equivalent to producing two crops in the three prairie provinces in one year.
From where will we get the electricity?

We are up to our backsides in electricity, and we are in the process of developing electrical expansion in at least five provinces, some of which is designed for export to the United States.
Other countries in the world of all political stripes have been doing this since World War II. Here we sit like a bunch of dummies. The railways are putting tens of millions of dollars into reducing grades in the Rocky Mountains when they could have electrified the track for less money. Getting such outfits to change their mind set would show some imagination. I have mentioned only two examples of megaprojects. The first one involved the expenditure of $2 billion more on housing than we are presently spending. It could result in interest rates geared to income. The second example was the electrification of urban transit, our main high-density railway lines. It would create more employment and conserve energy. Also it would transfer energy into more useful purposes such as food production. It
would cost a lot less than the Alsands and Cold Lake megaprojects.
Operations such as Alsands are there for the country to use as and when it requires production. I do not see why it must be done yesterday or tomorrow, in view of all other available alternatives. The day will come when the nation will have to invest billions of dollars into Alsands, but it does not have to be done in a panic, especially if we were working on other megaprojects.
I hope the government will take a good hard look at its policies and that it will reverse them.
