I hope the official opposition will quit supporting the government on losing propositions which get rid of natural gas, so that some pipeline companies or oil companies can make more bucks by sending it to the United States, when we need it here in Canada, particularly in Atlantic Canada.
I am glad Madam Speaker approved this emergency debate. I think the debate concerns the fact that the national government should come to the House with a completely new program which goes in a different direction. It challenges Canadians. It is something like a declaration of war but is more like a declaration of peace. We can do what needs to be done because we have the people, the resources, and the money. All we need is the political will to do it.

Madam Speaker, first I should like to congratulate you for approving this debate. I think it has been a good one. It has provided me with a certain sense of deja vu, particularly since I am taking part in it along with the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) and the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazan-kowski).
I remember the first speech I made in the House of Commons. It was during the course of an emergency debate when the then minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, Mr. Otto Lang, disregarded the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act and touted the grain stabilization act. I remember well the excellent speeches made at that time by those hon. members. I am feeling a sense of deja vu because at that time hon. members from western Canada were castigating Otto Lang for his LIFT program-Lower Inventory For Tomorrow-which paid farmers not to grow wheat. Now we have the spectacle of the present government paying oil companies just to hang around, paying Imperial Oil $50 million just to wait around for a few more months to see what would happen because these economic illiterates were not able to make up their minds, paying the Alsands consortium a few more millions of dollars just to hang around a bit longer, until finally the whole thing collapsed because of the pernicious inertia of the government in its applied energy policy.
Also 1 remember well two or three years ago speaking with officials in my department about the glorious future of the country in terms of regional disparity relief because of the Saudi Arabia which they claimed we had in the country. The province of Alberta was to be the great instrument for developing the kind of wealth which would allow Canada to reduce its

May 5, 1982
foreign commitments, to carry out the dream of economic equality in the country, and to fuel the recovery of the Altantic region.
Now we find out that the former American president, Abraham Lincoln, was correct when he said, "You can't strengthen the weak by weakening the strong". The government has killed the initiative of this dynamic sector upon which all Canadians were counting for the benefit of their country.
Another reason for my feeling of deja vu was the national energy policy of Donald Macdonald,a former distinguished member of the chamber, of whom I am sure Madam Speaker has fond memories. He was a good minister who brought forward a policy which at the time seemed to be reasonable after the first Arab oil shock, as it was then known.
There was also Douglas Fisher, another distinguished member, who pointed out at the time that this particular national energy policy resembled in many ways the same kind of objectives the present minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) so proudly proclaimed when he brought it into the House after the election of 1980.
Mr. Fisher said in an article in The Toronto Sun that:
-Mr. Trudeau addressed the nation on TV to outline Canada's immediate responses to the oil crisis. He wanted Canadians to know his government had been working on "both immediate problems and also putting in place the elements of long-range energy policy."
Then on Dec. 6, 1973, he set out in the House his first "National Energy Program." Its "prime objective, to be reached before the end of the decade (i.e. 1980) is self-sufficiency in oil and oil products."
As Douglas Fisher wrote that was in 1973 and the target was 1980. Now, in 1982, with the whole National Energy Program coming down in ruins around us, this government has the audacity to say that we will have energy self-sufficiency by 1990. What a lot of hogwash, as someone said, you cannot accomplish "vast" projects with half-vast ideas. I think that that was never more true than at the present time.
When 1 heard the speech of the hon. member for Restigou-che (Mr. Harquail) I was reminded of Ogden Nash's famous dictum which could be transposed like this, "Perhaps modern Canadian politics would be very much the better for a more restrictive use of simile and metaphor." The examples he was using, as the hon. member from Regina quickly pointed out, were recycled and recooked projects that were existing in many cases, as the member said, despite the government's efforts and not because of them. The hon. member for Vegre-ville did not have an opportunity to point this out-although he deserves a great deal of credit for it-the Prince Rupert grain elevator project, a $300 million project for which the government is taking credit is very important to Canada. It was dead in the water when our government took office, but the hon. member for Vegreville revived it. Now the hon. member for Restigouche and others like him are taking credit for it.
The whole problem of the government's National Energy Program which has had such terrible effects on the country, particularly in the Atlantic region where we were depending upon its revenues to help develop our economy, relate back to the 1980 election campaign. If there is not a proper foundation of credibility to support your policies, it becomes an exercise in futility because the public will soon see through it and no longer trust you.
I happen to have with me a famous election campaign advertisement published by the present Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). He published this ad with great fanfare. It said, "Would you let the Tories raise the gas price again?" He went on to say that because he spoke up for the people of Canada and the motorists of Cape Breton, the price would come down. He said "Vote Liberal and the price would stay down." Anyone who would make a statement like that must have known, if he had the knowledge people gave him credit for, that what he was saying was not true. This matter was later compounded in the House, after the Liberals came back to power, when the Minister of Finance, along with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), began to play games about what was happening in terms of what the Canadian consumers and the Canadian producers were getting.
In November of 1980 the press printed an excellent article which had a picture of the Prime Minister and of the Minister of Finance. This article, written by John Ferguson, had the headline, "Is Ottawa Intentionally Misleading the Public?" The article quoted the Prime Minister as saying, "Let us look at the budget to see if it is fair to the provinces. The western producing provinces will be getting exactly the amount that Mr. Clark's December budget said they will get; $40 billion between this year and 1983." The Minister of Finance was then quoted as saying, "The energy pricing burden placed upon all consumers in Canada, including low-income people, is $40 billion less in the budget than the budget last December." That was our budget, the Crosbie budget.
Mr. Ferguson wrote that the two statements were flatly contradictory since it was impossible for the producing provinces to get the same amount of revenue under the Liberal pricing proposals if consumers are paying less than they would have under the Conservative budget. When this was pointed out to the Minister of Finance, he said, "Your point is correct." But he said that he did not think there was a contradiction. Mr. Ferguson went on to write that while the minister was smiling after looking at a transcript of the Prime Minister's speech, he thought that there was clarification needed. That is clearly a $40 billion clarification.
While I have been in the House for a good portion of the time since that statement was made, I do not recall that it has ever been clarified. It is just another example of unclarified statements that the people of Canada had to put up with since this government returned to power.
I will admit that when our party was in power we did not do everything correctly. However, at least we did not put our party ahead of the country. We kept our commitments and attempted to pass a budget which embodied some relief for
May 5, 1982

people with low incomes who could not afford to pay the very modest increases in petroleum products which we proposed to impose. We also showed some pity for senior citizens who we knew could not afford to pay high prices for fuel oil. We also realized that home owners would need some help with their taxes and mortgage payments.
Of course, none of these provisions were introduced by the present government. In my estimation the reason these provisions were not introduced was that the government thought it would be able to derive enough revenue from Alberta, that great engine of economic growth, and apply that money to implement those programs which our party had envisaged. I suggest that our program was much better and would have had more humane results.
Another cause of our economic malaise is the intense preoccupation of this government which it has shown during its term of office for sociological, philosophical, linguistic and other policies. Some of these policies are very good and constructive, but the government has forgotten entirely about the need for good constructive management.
People talk about the Prime Minister's brilliance and eruditeness, but forget that if those qualities are not grounded in solid common sense and managerial ability, he is not able to govern the affairs of the country. As many people know, under his stewardship we have seen a dynamic country which was number three in the world sink to very low depths among the industrialized nations of the world. Unfortunately, this latest debacle indicates that we are not about to make any dramatic recovery. Billions of dollars have been wiped off the stock markets of this country and it is not just the profits of rich industrialists. It is the profits from investments of ordinary Canadians also. The whole perception of this national energy policy has soured our relationship with our neighbour, the United States.
I believe it was John Kennedy who said in this Chamber that "history has made us friends, geography has made us neighbours, and economics has made us partners." What we should be doing is entering into bilateral arrangements with the United States in certain areas for our mutual benefit. We should not be fighting with them over a diminishing resource. Ultimately this will do neither country any good because it has destroyed the potential which this country used to have to cooperate with the petrochemical industry and to use that great wealth for the benefit of the entire country.
We are told by some members opposite that things in the Maritime provinces are all right. My own constituency is a case in point. Not too many months ago things were not too bad in the constituency of Central Nova. We had the Hawker Siddeley railway plant in Trenton, we had a shipyard in Pictou called Ferguson industries as well with full employment. We had other industries also upon which families depended for their future. Since this economic malaise has come over the country, and since we have now had a realignment of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, and since there is apparently no money left to fund economic relief, there are
nearly 3,000 people unemployed in Trenton and 300 people unemployed in Pictou. There is a great sense of alarm felt by my constituents.
I am glad to know that things are going so well in the constituency of my friend from Restigouche. I can assure him that is not the case in my constituency and in many others in Atlantic Canada. He talked about the Q & M pipeline. I would like to talk about the pipeline too. In 1980 the Prime Minister in a speech to the Board of Trade in Halifax set out the Liberal energy policy. There was no mention at that time about the Constitution or all of the subsequent things. He was going to do something about energy to help Atlantic Canadians. One of the points that he emphasized was the need to switch to alternate energy sources. The Prime Minister said on January 25, 1980, that in order to switch:
People must have access to gas. Nowhere is access needed more than in eastern Canada and I am announcing today as part of our program the Liberal government will take immediate action to ensure the full co-operation of all parties in the construction of a natural gas pipeline to Quebec and the maritimes. The pipeline will have reversal capacity so that maritimers will have the opportunity both to use western natural gas now and to send offshore gas to central Canada later. Like the railroad in the 1880s, energy pipelines in the 1980s have the potential to be a steel link uniting the nation.
Some steel link. It is 1982 and the pipeline is slowly inching its way down. The sad part is that it is not a truly reversible pipeline. It looks to me like the Prime Minister, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and this government are deliberately delaying it. I hate to say this, but I may as well, as the saying goes, speak the truth and shame the devil-it looks as well as though the fix is in. Instead of the Atlantic region, specifically the Strait of Canso, getting the liquid natural gas terminus that would provide us with the wherewithal for a petrochemical industry, that will go to Gros Cacouna. As well, I do not think the pipeline is designed the way it should be. I believe that the whole national energy policy as far as Atlantic Canadians are concerned is highly suspect.
I hate to say it, but I think that all members of this House and all Canadians are justified in expressing this kind of view, going right back to the time when the Minister of Finance made his obviously misleading statement in order to get reelected. When the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources indicated his desire for untrammelled power, passed the national energy policy, and in the process alienated our relations with the United States, at the same time the constitutional machinations were alienating us from the United Kingdom.
A lot of people are concerned now that the national energy policy is to all intents and purposes ensconced in the kind of statutory form that will be hard to correct considering the great power and the great amount of discretion that the minister has. I read somewhere today that the Canadian Bar Association is nervous about the kind of discretion and unrestricted power of this minister.

May 5, 1982
1 made a few notes about some of these sections on an earlier occasion. It may be reasonable to put a few of them on the record now. The minister may enter into an exploration agreement under this legislation, without notice. He has the sole discretion over the production licence. The minister has the discretion of renewing the production licence. He has the power to direct that the Crown's share be transferred to a designated Crown corporation without any input from any partners or anyone else.
He can veto the transfer of Crown shares for any interest acquired by Petro-Canada. One section provides for in camera proceedings in any appeal to the Federal Court of Canada. The sections go on and on.
I ask you, Madam Speaker, if you were a farmer, a lumberman or small business person, would you like to do business in an environment where the Crown can come in and say, "Congratulations, we now own 25 per cent of your business. Here is some more good news. We will tell you exactly where you can sell your product, how you can market it, and what kind of a price you are going to get for it." 1 do not think you would be very happy. I do not think it is any secret that the petroleum industry, whether it is American, French, Canadian or any other nationality, welcomes this kind of restrictive environment in which it is prepared supposedly to risk hard-earned dollars.
This psychology of the government of taking money from people, recycling it, and giving it back in grants is just not working. How could it work? It is wasteful. It is not in accordance with good business practice or human nature. Basically, that is what is wrong with our country.
This government has manipulated and intruded itself into many areas. It is not as though it has any competence. That is the sad part. Winston Churchill, writing a book in the 1930s called "Great Contemporaries", made a very poignant remark about a contemporary. I think his name was Lord Rosebery. He said that it might be said of Lord Rosebery that he outlived his future by ten years and his past by more than 20.
I believe when we look at the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and the Minister of Finance we will come up with a similar judgment. I remember when the energy minister gave that famous speech in the House when he was the minister of national health and welfare, about keeping the NFL out of Canada. I thought at that time he was on the downhill slide, and I think he still is.
The Minister of Finance, a native Nova Scotian of whom many people used to be proud and gave a lot of credit for sagacity and shrewdness, is now, I am afraid, not exactly on the same pedestal as he was. I have heard more jokes about him in the last month in Nova Scotia-
Tell us about the swimming, do.

No, I couldn't tell that one. To get back to the matter of the emergency debate, my party believes, and I sincerely believe, that if we as Canadians could stop bribing people with their own money, if we could imbue Canadians with a sense of initiative once again, and bring in some of the
policies that would reward people and companies, we might offer Canadians a bit of hope for the future. We should go back to doing what we did a few years ago. At least we were making economic progress then. The emergency we are facing today indicates that this government and what it is doing are a dismal failure.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity of participating in this debate. I should make the observation at the outset that this debate was precipitated based on your ruling that there was a matter of national urgency which demanded that we in the House of Commons turn our attention to matters of energy policy and the economic future of this country as a result of the collapse of the two major projects.
Implied in that ruling, I suggest, was a recognition that although the two projects were mentioned in the request for an emergency debate there were many other factors of importance to which we in the House of Commons should turn our attention. We should discuss alternatives so that the government could take some advice and change the course of its policy for the purpose of bringing Canadians to the position they are entitled to expect, that is, a position of reasonable security in terms of energy and in terms of our economic future.
It is unfortunate to observe that in the course of this debate the government party thinks so little of discussing in an open forum such as we have in Parliament our energy future and economic future that there are no more than three government members now sitting in the House wishing to be involved in this debate. The fact that there are only three members out of 140-odd government members in the House at this time demonstrates very vividly the lack of interest and the arrogance of this government with regard to these issues.
It may be that they are embarrassed.

They have every right to be embarrassed under the circumstances.
What are we talking about? We are having this emergency debate. People may be asking about it. This debate has already lasted for a considerable period of time. It is going on because we on this side of the House feel very strongly that a change in direction is absolutely essential. This government has shown by its past activities that it responds only when blunt instruments are applied to it and its policies.
We recall very vividly what transpired when the government brought in this latest energy bill. It was necessary at that time to take a stand on the form of that bill. An omnibus bill was brought forward. We on this side of the House in the Conservative Party took a firm stand. In the final analysis, after a great deal of pressure was exerted on the government, it capitulated and accepted our most reasonable proposition
May 5, 1982

which was put to it some months before the bill was introduced. The government has the responsibility of holding up the business of the country.
You may ask what was so wrong with that bill. Madam Speaker, the Canadian Bar Association has made a representation to the special committee on energy and has said in its representation and its petition, put forward impartially, what it thought of the energy legislation. What they have said to that committee of the House of Commons is simply this. The government's energy legislation is arbitrary, it is contrary, they say, to the rule of law and it is in fact contrary to the principle set forth in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. This is an independent assessment made by the Canadian Bar Association. They are not involved in any political issue but they look at the legislation from the point of view of the application of the rights and freedoms of the average citizen. This is their assessment of the energy legislation in Canada. This is their assessment of the attitude that this government takes toward energy legislation, as a government.
They say that the bill which allows the federal government to assign billions of dollars in exploration, in incentive grants to Canadian-owned companies, gives so much discretion and regulatory power that it will significantly impair the rule of law. That was the view of the Canadian Bar Association. It says that the legislation also contradicts the new Charter of Human Rights and likely will be challenged in the courts if it remains unchanged. This was the attitude taken by the Canadian Bar Association. It is an important point of view which enters into the discussion of this particular government's energy policy.
This policy has been a disaster. It has left Canadians with a future of insecurity. It has done away with any real prospect of oil self-sufficiency by 1990. I have only to refer in that connection to the last annual meeting of Texaco Canada Incorporated. The president of that corporation, reporting to the shareholders of the company, indicated:
It now appears that oil self-sufficiency is not a realistic objective in this century, notwithstanding the reduced demand for petroleum products.
Madam Speaker, what is the situation we have today as opposed to the situation that I think obtained in this country almost two years ago? At that particular time, Madam Speaker, two years ago, the Canadian oil industry was driving swiftly toward the goal of national self-sufficiency by 1990.
Right on.
Hear, hear!

I was proud of being part of the government that understood the essential importance of striving for that goal by 1990 at a time when we were making very substantial progress. Look at what has happened. In fact if the policies which were initiated by our government had been implemented at that time and carried on, we would have been in a position today where our economy, I suggest to you, would have been flourishing as a result of the initiatives we had taken.
Rather than that, what we see today is a disaster, a country with the potential we have here, faced with economic ruin. That is putting it very mildly. We are talking about the loss of jobs in this particular project-100,000 jobs in terms of primary jobs relating to this project alone; we are talking about 90,000 jobs in secondary capacity, flowing out of these particular projects. These are only two of the projects we are talking about.
We have to recall that these megaprojects were the fundamental cornerstone in the budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen). The minister predicated his forecast of megaproiects going ahead in terms of energy selfsufficiency, of economic development in our country. It has come to the point now, Madam Speaker, where today we have to redefine the term "megaproject". Now, a megaproject, according to this government and this Minister of Finance, means any project of a value of $500 or more. This is precisely because the minister goes around and tells us now that rather than having the larger projects we will have to be satisfied with a multitude of smaller projects.
Minis.

What are these projects that are going to resolve our economic circumstances? What are these projects that are going to restore us and our country in terms of energy self-sufficiency? There is very little precision, only some generalization about the projects going ahead that will take the place of the megaprojects.
Self-sufficiency, Madam Speaker, is an objective that we in our government had as the highest priority. It had its economic advantages and benefits. People in the country now, looking back at the proposals we put forward, I suggest to you, Madam Speaker, look back with fond recollection. I can tell you that in the time of another election, if this government goes forward to the people, that point will not be lost on the electorate, especially in view of the promises made, as pointed out by my colleague, the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay), by the Minister of Finance in particular about keeping oil prices and gas prices down below what they were under our projections.
Madam Speaker, the federal government, when we look back at the promise made in the last election, has deluded the people of Canada with respect to the energy future. I recall one of the first initiatives taken by this government. It consisted of a very elaborate and extensive advertising campaign initiated by the minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde). We have all seen this campaign on the television screens and in the newspapers. It was an expensive, slick advertising campaign. What we were told was that our energy future was in good hands with the federal government.
Madam Speaker, we know that the federal government is not subject to the Combines Investigation Act, because it is a part of the Crown and cannot be prosecuted. We know that it cannot subscribe voluntarily to any association that deals with misleading advertising. It is a good thing for them because if they were subject to the law and to voluntary constraints they
80114- 19

May 5, 1982
would have been prosecuted for misleading advertising to the Canadian people.
Right on.

What do we find today? When this party's government was in place, we were able to reach an agreement with the province of Alberta in terms of pricing arrangements. We had the Alsands project ready to go. We were close to closing the negotiations with Imperial Oil on the Cold Lake project. These projects were ready to go with the co-operation of the province of Alberta and the government of that province. These are the facts. These particular projects to give work to the people were in place. I can tell you, Madam Speaker, that the energy benefits from that particular project would have been very substantial.
I hasten to point out, Madam Speaker, that at that time the cost of the Alsands project was some $5 billion. That is a much different figure from the figure we are faced with today, that is, $14 billion to $15 billion. It is no wonder the company finds it absolutely impossible to go ahead, after the delay and the confrontation it has had with the federal government which has delayed purposely the development of these projects in western Canada. They are paying a political price in western Canada. That price is going to spread to central Canada and to Atlantic Canada at the time of the next election. This process has been in operation for two years. It would have involved production of 140,000 barrels of oil per day, or roughly 8 per cent to 10 per cent of Canadian crude oil production. It was estimated that there would have been over 20,000 man-years of construction work, but 6,500 permanent jobs in Canada, of which 2,800 would be jobs directly connected with the project. However, technological advantages and advantages respecting our ability to develop projects in Canada and to train people to do these jobs in our own country have been lost. There was also the potential for increasing employment opportunities for Canadians and, specifically, to provide training and job opportunities to the native people in the region surrounding Alsands. These things would have been in place. But no, this government had a different slant to its energy policy and brought in what it calls the National Energy Program. What has been the result?
I want to talk about conventional oil exploration and development. The program has been an unmitigated disaster. I am sure you realize, Madam Speaker, that during the past year over 200 oil rigs have left Canada for the United States. Of those remaining, at least 40 per cent are standing idle. That is the result of the energy policy of this government, and that has had a very deleterious effect on the industry and the future of energy self-sufficiency in our country.
In very simple terms, the energy policy is a massive tax grab by the federal government. That is the simplest way to describe the energy policy of this government. It is a massive tax grab, and it affects us in western Canada more than it does
people in any other region. I can assure hon. members of that, and that is understood and resented very much.
The National Energy Program has had the effect of reducing the earnings of oil companies. This applies not only to large oil companies but to small Canadian oil companies in Canada as well. Earnings have been reduced to the point where it has become impossible for companies to generate the investor confidence and the investment in their own companies which is needed to acquire funds with which to invest in the megaprojects which are absolutely essential to our energy self-sufficiency.
The earnings from operations of Imperial Oil, the largest oil company in Canada, fell from some $600 million the previous year to some $450 million this year. That has been repeated by large and small companies across the country. This massive transfer of oil and gas revenues from the industry to the government treasury has severely curtailed the ability of the private sector to finance exploration and development. We are bringing conventional oil exploration and development to a standstill. Hon. members opposite should go to southern Saskatchewan and see the rigs standing idle. They should go there and see all the supply people going out of business. These supply people are the people who service rigs.
Wells are not producing.

Wells are not producing. What are we doing with the potential we have in this country?
In terms of frontier development, there has been chaos in the management by this government of our Canada lands. Because of red tape the industry has curtailed its plans to explore and develop in 1982. The best information I have is that reductions will continue into 1983.
I should refer to the offshore. This government feels that somehow Hibernia will solve all our energy self-sufficiency problems. We have seen the way this government has handled the offshore situation. Confrontation is the hallmark of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his government. It has been that way since the Prime Minister took office. It has been that way with the province of Newfoundland, to the point where there is absolute reluctance on the part of the industry to move to the offshore or to make the major investments required to bring Hibernia and the potential which exists there into production. Would anyone in the House be prepared to invest the kind of money necessary when there is no understanding between the federal and the provincial governments with respect to jurisdiction, not only in terms of drilling but also in terms of manpower and other related matters?
No way.

No way at all, as my colleague says. Conventional development and production today is virtually shutting down, and the minister says this is a worldwide phenomenon. What he does not tell us is that in the United States oil and gas drilling is up this year 31 per cent from
May 5, 1982

1981. I would like to quote from an article by Diane Hill in The Calgary Herald of April 28 as follows:
This year is shaping up to be another record-breaker for oil and gas activity in the United States-thanks in part to the work of Canadian petroleum companies which have set up southern operations.
According to the Denver-based Petroleum Information Corporation, drilling for oil and gas in the U.S. during the first three months of 1982 was up 31 per cent from 1981.
Diane Hill went on to point out the following:
And 1981 was the industry's busiest year ever.
I have only started, Madam Speaker. I beseech the government to listen. I beseech government members to put extreme pressure on the treasury benches in this regard. We are facing potential disaster in terms of our economy and energy selfsufficiency. 1 say to the government that now is the time and the opportunity for it to reconsider its energy program. Let the government withdraw the energy program and reconsider it. We on this side of the House would co-operate and give the government the best advice we could because we believe in Canada. Let the government withdraw the budget. Calls on the Minister of Finance to withdraw the budget have come from every walk of life in Canada. I say to the government that now is the time to show political courage and leadership. We would support an effort to bring Canada back to its rightful place in the world, and we would offer the government constructive alternatives.

speakeroldname: Mr. Carlo Rossi (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Multiculturalism)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a pleasure to be able to take part in this debate, which will be a welcome opportunity to recall certain facts. As we all know, Madam Speaker, during the last few months, the Governments of Canada and Alberta were making every attempt to keep the Alsands project afloat. Notwithstanding the, in my view, extremely generous offers made by the federal and provincial governments with respect to tax provisions and financing, the other private sector members of the Alsands consortium decided that conditions were not favourable for carrying the project. Naturally, I share the disappointment of all Canadians who were looking forward with enthusiasm to this project, which would, in time, have become a source of oil and economic benefits as well.
Madam Speaker, we all know there are limits to what a government or several governments can do to improve the terms under which a project is to be carried out. In any case, Madam Speaker, we certainly do not need any advice from the Conservative Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). Speaking of advice, Madam Speaker, this morning on the radio I was listening to a program on CKVL called "En premiere page", which is hosted by Mr. Yves Ryan, the Mayor of Montreal-North-my municipality-and Pierre Leroux. I was saying that we do not need the advice of the Leader of the Opposition, and on the program the Leader of the Opposition was asked what the price of gas would be if he and his party were in
power today, May 5, 1982. The Leader of the Opposition answered that the difference would be 2.5 cents per litre or 18 cents per gallon. His host quickly corrected-
That is right.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
speechtext:
The member opposite says, "That is right". 1 would suggest he do some arithmetic, because he is making the same mistake as his leader. According to the program's host, 2.5 cents a litre would mean ten cents per gallon, and from the answer given by the Leader of the Opposition it was clear he had no idea how the metric system worked, and he was letting his host do the arithmetic. Then, the Leader of the Opposition, who does not have a clue about the metric system, was asked what he would do about inflation. He said: "The first thing 1 would do to control inflation would be to get interest rates down". Madam Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition was contradicting what he had said not quite twenty-four hours before. I shall quote from La Presse of May 4:
In an interview with the reporter, the Leader of the Opposition, Joe Clark, made the most astounding and disarming statement ever made by an Opposition Leader.
These are not my words, but the reporter's. Acknowledging that his party had not come up with an alternative to the Bank of Canada's economic policies, he continued as follows:
We have looked for a solution different from the government's, but we have no alternative. Today, I cannot come up with a better solution.
Those words were spoken by the Leader of the Official Opposition. This means that the Progressive Conservative Party and any government it might be called upon to form have no magic solution to the problems caused by inflation, the recession and especially by high interest rates. Within twenty-four hours, the Leader of the Opposition had contradicted himself, as he usually does.
Further on, still on the same program-I am a fan, and I listen every morning with great interest-the Leader of the Official Opposition was asked whether he was aware of the fact that Mr. Mulroney was travelling around the Province of Quebec. Mr. Clark's answer to the radio host was that Mr. Mulroney-and the Official Leader of the Opposition was aware of the fact-was travelling around Quebec to raise funds. He said that Mr. Mulroney was very active in that field, and that he was going to do what everybody else did before getting into the House, namely, become a Member of Parliament. For the time being, he was doing very well as a fund raiser.
Coming back to another one who claims he is always defending the right of Quebecers-they do not appreciate the truth on the other side, Madam Speaker. They do not like hearing it. There is another one who rises on the other side, in order always to defend the rights of Quebecers: I refer to the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle). That hon. member is

May 5, 1982
the main architect of the Union Nationale's demise, as leader of that party. Do you know what he promised Quebecers? To abolish the safety belt. What a program! To abolish the safety belt, because his wards in Quebec see that as dictatorship, being forced to use safety belts. 1 will not fall for that. His same Progressive Conservative Party, when the hon. member for Joliette was in the government, as he will recall, raised the embargo on chicken. In his constituency, in Saint-Felix-de-Valois close by, people do not feel like congratulating him, the self-avowed protector of Quebecers.
It will also be remembered that before the Progressive Conservative government in 1979, the Liberal Party granted $3 million every year for the building of produce warehouses, which allowed Canadian and Quebec farmers to hold the domestic market longer. As soon as the party opposite became the government, those grants were abolished. Fortunately, Quebecers and Canadians soon woke up, the Liberals were reelected and the same grants reinstated.
As I said, Madam Speaker, we have no lesson to learn from our friends opposite. And in spite of those promises, and although there was a Progressive Conservative government in Alberta, the Clark government never could sign and agreement with Alberta. We, the Liberal Party, succeeded in this. In the case of the Alsands project, the Canadian government and the Lougheed government gave up for the time being the idea of going ahead. Indeed, Madam Speaker, there is a point where the sum of all estimated benefits from a project, either financial, economic or psychological, are exceeded by costs and the risks involved. In my view, the Canada and Alberta governments got as near as they could to the balance point in their effort to promote the Alsands project. But even if we wanted to, we could not require from governments that they create the conditions which would have allowed the project to proceed without the private participants having to take some risks. In the final analysis, both governments were ready to assume the majority of the risks involved in front-end investments, through direct involvement and loan guarantees.
Because of the uncertainty of future world oil prices and interest rates, to mention only two of the major factors, the participants from the private sector did not think that they would be able to proceed even in present conditions. By offering guaranteed loans and special provisions for reimbursement, the federal and Alberta governments tried to find an answer to alleviate the concerns expressed by the participants. One of the concerns of the companies from the private sector was that they could not benefit from tax write-offs in a current manner. The offer of the government provided equivalent benefits. An area of concern involved the cash flow requirements and the risks involved. In this regard, the federal government included in its offer a guaranteed loan and shortterm participation at a rate of 50 per cent. Finally, the companies were worried about the risk that oil price increases would remain low. To alleviate this concern, we proposed loan repayment conditions providing, in the case of lower than
expected price increases, an extension of the period during which the project would not be subject to full taxation.
Madam Speaker, the government therefore put together a package which, while not providing for an excessive return, was very generous in reducing the risks of the participants. The companies involved could not expect an excessive rate of return, but they were to be protected against a decrease in revenue.
In view of what I have just said, it therefore seems that the Canadian government not only met the particular concerns of the companies involved, but also that it made an attractive general proposal which could have led to the completion of the Alsands project.
I want to underline that despite what the Progressive Conservatives are trying to suggest, the government is not closing the door definitely on the Alsands project. Let us not forget that, in these particularly difficult times for the world economy, important energy development projects have been postponed throughout the world, including of course our neighbouring country, the United States. It would be foolhardy to assert that these conditions will not change during the coming year. Indeed, we know from experience that rapid changes in the economic situation are the rule rather than exception. Economic conditions could very well become favourable for the Alsands project sooner than we would expect.

Madam Speaker, the Government of Canada and the government of Alberta have made repeated efforts over the past several months to encourage the Alsands project to go forward. The opposition is blaming the federal government, but in doing so they are condemning their Tory counterparts in Alberta.
We must acknowledge that despite an extremely generous offer from both the federal and the provincial governments in terms of the tax regimes and other financial matters, the remaining private sector members of the Alsands group have decided that the time is not right to proceed with the project.
I share the regret of all those Canadians who looked forward to this project as a source of both oil and economic benefits in the years ahead. But we all know that there is a limit to which any government or governments can go on making the conditions right for any particular project. There is a point at which the sum of all the expected benefits from a project, financial, economic, even psychological, are exceeded by the costs and risks. I feel, Madame Speaker, that the Governments of Canada and of Alberta went as close to that balancing point as possible in the effort to encourage the Alsands project to proceed. As it stood in the final analysis, the two governments were prepared to assume the vast majority of the upfront capital risks through direct participation or loan guarantees.
Because of uncertainty about future world oil prices and interest rates, to name two crucial factors, the private sector
May 5, 1982

members of the project could not see their way clear to proceeding, even under this reduced risk situation. The Alsands companies were concerned about their projected rates of return and their cash flow positions as the project went ahead. Both levels of governments proposed an offer which, in my view, provided a good rate of return and maintained that rate even with lower than expected rates of growth in world oil prices. The minister has already tabled the details of the offer. Let me note, however, that the rationale for the degree of support offered was to ensure that the project would receive benefits equivalent to those implicit in Alberta's earlier promise of a 20 per cent loan guarantee and, as well, to those of a fully taxable firm which can use conventional tax writeoffs on a current basis.
With the government guaranteed loan offer and the special features for repayment which are incorporated in it, we addressed directly the concerns which the project sponsors had expressed to us earlier. One such concern was their inability to use tax write-offs on a current basis. Our offer guaranteed them equivalent benefits. The second was their cash flow problems and risks. The government offer addressed this with a guaranteed loan and and a 50 per cent joint participation. Finally, the companies were concerned about the risk of low rates of the oil price increase. This we addressed by designing loan repayment terms which would, in the case of a lower than anticipated oil price growth, have delayed the time when the project would become taxable.
Of course, if oil prices escalated rapidly, the loan would be repaid more quickly and advance the date at which the project would be subject to full taxation. Thus, the government presented a package which did not provide an excessive rate of return but which was very generous in terms of reducing risk for the participants. They could not anticipate excessive rates of return but they would receive protection on the downside.
It should be clear from the terms I have outlined that we have not Only addressed the specific concerns of the companies, but put forward an objective total proposal under which the Alsands project could have gone forward.
The minister has made it clear that he was not closing the door to a renewal of the Alsands project at a later date. Delays in major energy projects are being encountered throughout the world in this particularly difficult time for the world economy. It would be rash to say that these circumstances will not change in the next year or two. Indeed, the record suggests that rapid changes in economic conditions are more the rule than the exception. Economic circumstances may well favour the Alsands project sooner than we might expect at the moment.
[ Translation]
As I said, Madam Speaker, both governments went as far as they possibly could on the financial aspect. We cannot alter indefinitely the incentives intended for particular supply sources, in view mainly of the wide range of opportunities. In
addition to the potential from frontier regions, we are taking into account the increased recuperation of oil and the upgrading of heavy oil in Saskatchewan and Alberta.
In our quest for oil self-sufficiency, Madam Speaker, we want to proceed in the manner that will prove the least expensive for Canadians. The industrial economic fallouts would have been useful, but we hope to recoup them through other means. Some have wondered why this project was not entirely financed by the federal government. Madam Speaker, I reply by saying simply that the Alberta government insisted from the very beginning on a major involvement on the part of private industries, a concept that we support fully. As soon as the National Energy Program was announced, the Government of Canada indicated that it was desirable for private industries to be more involved, although still to a limited extent, in the direct ownership of the oil industry. I will conclude very shortly, Madam Speaker.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member's time has expired.
Keep on talking!
Take 20 more minutes! Take all the time you want!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think that the hon. members would like the hon. member for Bourassa (Mr. Rossi) to complete his sentence.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Multiculturalism)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I certainly want to thank my colleagues opposite, and they know that we always do this when trying to end a debate.
I conclude, therefore, by saying that we see no reason to change our position. We want to emphasize the opportunities to co-operate in the development of major energy projects and the Alsands project provided a tremendous opportunity in that regard.
Again, it is unfortunate that we could not seize this opportunity at this time, but there will be others. I am sure that before long, we will have again the possibility to develop our oil sands and achieve our long-term objectives in the field of energy.

Madam Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to participate in this emergency debate. I think it is important not only to look at what the implications are for these two major megaprojects as a result of their demise, but what the implications are for Canada as a whole. What is at issue in this debate is the demise of the Alsands and the Alaska gas pipeline projects. They total close to $63 billion, and perhaps much more by the time they come on line. The questions we must address are: why did they collapse, and what does it mean to the average Canadian taxpayer, something which has rarely been addressed in this debate so far.
The hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) described the collapse as a result of madness rampant in the Liberal Party, particularly in the front benches. A Liberal said it was due to

May 5, 1982
the undermining influence of the Conservatives. There may be a little bit of truth in both, but not very much. I think it is time members of the House and members of the public faced the facts. The projects have collapsed, which has meant the loss of hundreds of thousands of man years of employment across Canada. We in this party say the collapse of the Alaska gas pipeline is a direct result of the gutless attitude taken by the Liberals and Tories for failing to obtain financial guarantees for the northern section of the Alaska gas pipeline some five years ago.
Canadians cannot help but wonder why this House is endlessly debating the oil and gas industry. One day we are told that the industry has ripped off the average Canadian consumer for $12 billion, but then no action is taken by the House of Commons. That leads to a very cynical attitude, particularly when one realizes that so much of government policy is based on opinion polls. When the public is angry about something, the government releases a report hoping that it will turn the consumers' attention away from what is really at issue. The next day we find out, for example, that the oil companies will get 93 cents on the dollar in subsidy for exploration. That perhaps came as a perk to angry oil executives after the public had been informed that the oil companies had ripped off $ 12 billion before that.
On Alsands, we now find that a guaranteed rate of return of 22 per cent is simply not enough. We have to ask, Madam Speaker, what do they want? It is quite clear they want Canada's economy on a platter for surgery as the monopolies see fit. That is why we in this party say that if the Liberal-Tory coalition must pander to the dinosaur mentality of most megaprojects, then we must, through this House of Commons at least, make those projects work for the benefit of all Canadians. But more than that, we should use some imaginative and creative developments of our national options. Where do we go from here?
The most recent piece of legislation indicating where the government intends to go was Bill C-48. In this bill the government has indicated its intention to spend about $300 billion over the next 15 years north of 60 and off the east and west coasts drilling for gas and oil. These are major megaprojects. But we can see already that with the Canadian economy in the shape in which it is and the global economy going the way it is with oversupply, particularly in the oil and gas sector, that approach may well and predictably be inappropriate to get Canadians back to work and our economy going again.
On the other hand, we have the Conservative position that has been put forward very well in the last 24 hours. That is simply to give a better deal to the oil and gas companies, which may well lead us deeper into the mire in which we find ourselves already.
The Conservatives say the Liberals killed these projects. But what do the Tories really say? Are they saying that Peter Lougheed and the Liberals should give more to Alsands, that
the 22 per cent rate of return is not enough? Surely, these are the original parties to the selling out of Canadian interests. It is a quick fix always at the cost of our children and the future of our country. What we should be doing is going into small-scale oil and gas projects, wind, tidal, low-head hydro, biomass, solar, geothermal and conservation.
What about the example given by my colleague, the hon. member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin), this morning, that of the electrification of the railway, particularly in dense urban transit areas which, at half the cost of the Alsands project, would release the same volume of diesel as will be created by Alsands? So why put $13 billion into Alsands when there is an option to provide through conservation the same volume of oil to Canadians at half the cost? I think the Canadian People have a right to know what is going on behind the scenes in the boardrooms.
We could have more jobs and a much more stable economy. We could develop export markets for world-leading technology in almost all of the alternates because we have one of the most highly educated and technically skilled societies in the world. Why Alsands? Sure there are jobs, Madam Speaker, but at $4 million per job, while alternatives, conservation and manufacturing can be brought in for less than $100,000 per permanent job, it does not seem right.
The facts surely lie in the dinosaur mind set of the two major parties in this country, the Liberals and the Tories. Their roots, especially their election funds lie deeply in the bank accounts of the oil and gas companies.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is a falsehood.

That element has more to do with this debate than most Canadians appreciate.
The Liberals and Conservatives even at this time vote together on policy day after day. In this session alone, the Tories have supported and voted for Trudeau 29 times. This party has voted for government bills only 14 times.
The collapse of Alsands is due to three important and reasonably obvious factors. First come the high interest rates which are supported by both the Liberals and the Tories. Second, the rising construction costs. I think all members in the House know that energy projects are prey to a kind of inflation that is quite separate from the consumer price index. Third, dropping fuel prices caused by a recession and high interest rates. These dropping fuel prices are also caused by an oversupply in both OPEC and non-OPEC nations, something that has not occurred generally in the past. Even with the Liberal and Conservative guarantees of a 22 per cent rate of return, the economics simply do not seem to fly.
Let me deal with the Alaska gas pipeline, Madam Speaker. It is a very serious issue. We have seen the federal government's never too specific industrial strategy. We have seen it now that it has collapsed. We have seen Alsands go down, which really was the cornerstone of the Liberal's policy. We have seen Cold Lake and Shell. We have seen the Norman Wells pipeline delayed for two years. We see the Quebec and
May 5, 1982

Maritime line for gas which may well run into serious problems with Nova Scotia ambitions to bring its gas onshore. As for double-tracking in the west, I do not think that was anything other than a campaign promise never to be delivered. We see now the very likely prospect of the collapse of the nuclear industry in Canada which will see the loss of 40,000 jobs. Then there is the Alaska gas pipeline which would have provided hundreds of thousands of man-years of work if this House had had the guts to put together a piece of legislation which required the kinds of financial guarantees that we talked about in the House five years ago.
I would like to quote from a recent article appearing on the editorial page of The Citizen for May 4, 1982. It reads:
The Trudeau government made the stupid mistake of committing Canada, in 1980, to "pre-building" the southern portions of the line so that the link to U.S. markets would be ready when the upper portion was completed by the U.S. partners.
In July 1980, Energy Minister Marc Lalonde warned that if the U.S. reneged, it would be the greatest breach of faith in 200 years of Canada-U.S. relations.
We have had that now and not one member of the government has even stood up to talk about it. The article continues:
The two-year delay may be claimed by Lalonde to be something less than a complete collapse of the plan, but any realistic appraisal of the situation must conclude that a $50 billion pipeline initially projected to cost less than $10 billion is a non-starter, especially in today's high-interest-rate, reduced-oil-price economy.
I would like to comment on the Conservative position on the Alaska highway natural gas pipeline because I think the Tories have played a vital role in selling out Canada's interest so that we now have trillions of cubic feet of gas essentially going out of Alberta at a door-step cost, cheaper to U.S. consumers than to Canadian consumers. So here we have these two parties which vote together but do not have the financial guarantees for the northern end of the line, yet we have gas companies in Alberta and Saskatchewan saying that they need subsidies so they can have cash flow in order to drill for gas. They drill for it, they get it but they cannot sell it because we have a surplus in Canada. But what they do then is to come to the Liberals and Conservatives and say, "You have to build a pipeline. We have to export it to sell it to the United States." We build the bottom part of the line. Then we export gas to the United States cheaper than Canadians can buy it. Of course, the Americans are not going to build the northern end of the line as long as they can get our gas cheaper then they can get their own. They never have to build the line. It is an example of Canadian lunacy where the Liberals and Conservatives are so tightly interwoven with the gas and oil companies that they are always taking another step and always needing more cash flow. Always one more step is taken to sell out Canada.
In 1978 the Conservatives supported the Liberals on Bill C-25 which established the northern pipeline agency. It gave effect to the agreement between the U.S. and Canada to build a pipeline. Led by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), their northern pipeline spokesman, the Tories opposed the NDP position and our amendments regarding the maximizing of Canadian content in jobs and material, protecting native rights and the environment, and ensuring there would be no
Canadian government financial backing or liabilities for the construction of the line.
The Tories also supported the pre-build concept. In December, 1979, the Conservative government authorized an additional 3.75 trillion cubic feet of natural gas for export, thereby strengthening arguments for the construction of the pre-build and using it to export Canadian gas. It is interesting to note that only 40 per cent of the possible throughput of that prebuild is being used. The Americans are dealing with us in a very interesting fashion. They will not finance or build the northern end. They will take what they want out of the line when they want it. They will not even abide by the contracts which have been put in place.
The Liberals, led by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde), opposed these exports when in opposition. The minister called for "ironclad guarantees" that the entire line would be built and said that there should be future gas swap arrangements with the United States in return for the exports. Of course, once he was in office he never followed through on either of these demands.
In July, 1980, the Liberals, by order in council, not through Parliament, subverted the intent of the original act which authorized the construction of a gas line to export United States gas to United States markets by authorizing the export of gas through the pre-build section. During this debate the then Tory energy spokesman, the hon. member for Perth (Mr. Jarvis) stated:
I did not talk about ironclad guarantees, nor did our minister of the day, because it is absolutely impossible. If the hon. members there demand complete ironclad guarantees, I say to them that they are against the pipeline. It is as simple as that. If you are for complete ironclad guarantees from industry, you are against the pipeline, and I say to you that you have to make up your minds.
That was the Tory position in 1980. Both the Liberals and the Tories voted together against the motion put forward by my party which would have preserved and ensured that the guarantees were in place so that we would not be here debating this today. They voted against the motion which I am about to read, yet they stood in the House of Commons yesterday and today, yapping that they required an emergency debate about an issue which they created that will cost Canadians a great deal of money. The following motion was moved by the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell):
That before this house adjourns for a summer recess, the House calls on the government to declare that it will not proceed with the construction of the prebuild portion of the Northern Gas Pipeline until complete financial guarantees for the whole pipeline have been obtained and an agreement has been reached between the Government of Canada and the Government of the United States that the Canadian gas exported through the southern portion of the proposed pipeline will be replaced by Alaska gas at an equivalent price.
They both voted against it. The situation is very interesting. I should like to go back a little further to remind both these parties how the issue came to be. On April 4, 1978, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, Mr. Tommy Douglas, commented upon the minister of energy in 1971, Mr. Joe Greene, who said at that time that there were hundreds of

May 5, 1982
years of oil, that we could export it for years and years, and that there would be plenty for Canada. Six months after he made that statement standing in the House, Canada was in a deficit. Canadians have been led by some very wishy-washy statesmen who have not even taken the time to compile scientific material upon which to base their statements. Joe Greene simply telephoned the oil and gas companies and asked, "How much gas and oil is there?" When he found out that there was enough oil for hundreds of years, he said, "Sell it off. We will have a good time, everyone can have new cars". A terrible fraud was perpetrated on the people of Canada.
I think Mr. Douglas put in a nutshell where these two old line parties are leading the country when he said:
It makes one ask whether this government is like the Bourbons who learned nothing and forget nothing. Have we forgotten that it is only five years ago that some of us were pleading in the House to phase out exports of oil?
Today we are doing it with gas. He continued:
Today we are a net importer of oil and we are told by the National Energy Board that in the 1990's we will be spending $4 billion or $5 billion per year to pay for imports of oil.
We now know that it will be much more than that. Also he said:
Are we going to make the same mistake with reference to gas? We are exporting 60 per cent of our gas production. We are going to increase it now by almost 40 per cent.
When our children stand in the House, they will be puzzled about the members of Parliament who sat here in the 1970s and 1980s. They will think there really was madness then. Perhaps the hon. member for Athabasca is correct. The only problem is that when his frontbenchers are on the government side, they find themselves involved in exactly the same kind of madness. Mr. Douglas went on to say:
The government say: "Just a moment, we are going to work out a swap arrangement". I think a swap arrangement could be worked out if it were on an energy equivalent, so that for every 100 units of BTU energy we sold we would get back a similar amount, if and when we wanted it.
That was never followed. He also said:
Do we realize what we are doing? We are walking blindfolded into a continental energy policy. The Americans have always wanted a continental energy policy, particularly when they ran short of energy. We are like the couple of brothers who went into town: one saved his money and did well, and the other one had a high old time until he was broke and then said, "Let's pool our resources".
This is what they are saying to us now. This is precisely what the Liberals and Tories are saying that we should be doing. They throw it all away; they sell it off as cheaply as they can to the United States. They sell it to the United States more cheaply than we are required to pay to heat our homes and run our vehicles. They sell it all off and say that the economy is having a great time. But we are getting into a deeper and deeper pit on the energy side. We can manage for quite a few years, but we do not have inexhaustible supplies. Mr. Douglas continued:
If we enter into a swap arrangement by which we sell 370 billion cubic feet of gas per year at $2.16 at the border, and 10 or 15 years down the road we buy it back at $3.50 or $4 per thousand cubic feet, we will have sold Canadians down the river. This House had better be aware of the manner in which the pieces are falling into place.
Now they are talking about starting the pipeline at the south end and building it so that it will take Alberta gas down to the United States, and the companies involved will make enough money out of that to finance in part the rest of the pipeline. The primary purpose in the immediate future is not to take Prudhoe Bay gas to the United States. The primary purpose is to take Alberta gas to the United States, and then hope some day, when the line is completed and Prudhoe Bay gas is coming down, if we need it, we can buy it back at a price. I suggest with great conviction that price will not be the same price we got for the gas we sold.
Mr. Douglas was prophetic when he spoke in the House six years ago. The present situation is such that the Tories are trying to convince the Canadian public that the collapse of the northern end of the pipeline is somehow related to the Liberals. Their voting record and speeches are very clear. Anyone who analysed the situation six years ago knew that we would be in the position we are in today and that the northern end of the pipeline would never be built. It is a preposterous proposition for them to put forward continually.
The hon. member for Yukon is trying to make a great deal out of the issue. In 1978 he said the following:
-let me make it abundantly clear that this party does not in any way intend to delay unduly the passage of this vitally important legislation through the House. Members of my party cannot advance amendments that will cause irreparable harm to the viability of this project, nor can any amendments be advanced that will go beyond the provisions of the international agreement that has been negotiated. Amendments are possible, and we will attempt to assist the government in a constructive and positive manner-
It is preposterous for them to be taking the position they are taking now on this very important issue. Of course it is not unusual. If our amendments for guaranteed financing had been put in place, we would not have to debate this side of the issue. That part of the line would have been constructed right now. It would have been in the interests of our neighbours to the south, so that they could move their gas from Alaska, down through the Yukon, and the southern portions of British Columbia and Alberta, and into the United States. We would have been left with the legacy from these two parties of a prebuild line exporting only Canadian gas.
I should like to make a couple of more quick points. One is a quotation from a Calgary newspaper under the headline entitled, "Proving small is beautiful". As I said earlier this afternoon, every Liberal member has indicated a desire to launch into megaprojects to stimulate the Canadian economy through the trickle-down theory. Even the Calgary newspapers tended to stay with the megaprojects until this week. Now they are starting to move away from them. The article which appeared in The Calgary Sun reads as follows:
There are rumblings already to the effect that some conventional energy schemes, largely neglected while we held our breath over the megaprojects, may be returned to favour.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired. He may continue with the unanimous consent of the House. Is there unanimous consent?

Agreed.
May 5, 1982

Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. members present for allowing me to continue. They said the following about the underground gas storage scheme:
-putting gas underground without making it work hard at some specific task is a very inefficient procedure.
If the same couple of trillion cubic feet of surplus gas went into good old Turner Valley, for example, according to even the most conservative estimates, we could avail ourselves of an additional 100 million barrels of the finest quality crude ever found in Canada.
And of course there is the plus of the gas that would come out again. That's $4 billion worth of oil-
It goes on to say:
Oil sand experiments-nearly two-dozen larger than bench-sized projects-are still proceeding despite the Alsands fiasco.
I have two final comments. One is simply to repeat the position taken by the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) who says that, "Greed, greed, greed, killed Alsands". The position taken by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) is that the private sector killed Alsands. A very interesting quote for me to end on is, "It all depends on whose ox is being gored. On Bay Street they are saying it is a recession when your neighbour is out of work and a depression when you are unemployed."

Madam Speaker, I wonder if you might wish to explain to the public in the galleries what is happening in the House today, particularly to the people who have come to see question period. Perhaps you could explain that we are in an emergency debate under Standing Order 26 on the subjects of the collapse of the oil sands project and the Alaska pipeline.
I would hope, Madam Speaker, that you would say that we have been here since eight o'clock last night with your permission. We would hope that perhaps we could stay here long enough so that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources may come back from Texas.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: All I can say is that the sitting which began yesterday at eight o'clock has not yet terminated.

Madam Speaker, I wish to address the problems of the economic disaster which has been caused by this government. It is a very sad time for many Canadians. The government has wasted the sacrifice that has been made by many pioneers and has destroyed hope for the free enterprise system. It has killed the initiative and spirit of Canadians. It is a sin how the "gang of five" has destroyed the incentive of Canadians through the failure of the Alsands project, the Cold Lake project, the tar sands and the Alaska highway pipeline. One of the causes of the collapse of Alsands is the inefficient budget which was produced and manipulated by this government. However, the government is not totally to blame since the bureaucrats played a large role in the formation of the budget. Our bureaucracy is now completely out of control. The government must take the blame for this, and it can now be said that this government is no longer capable of governing.
What this country needs is a new budget, a new Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and, in fact, a new government which can restore confidence and provide a new direction for
Canadians. The Liberals have created this bureaucratic monster which is completely out of control. It has destroyed the hope and incentive of Canadians.
Instead of the government addressing itself to the economic problems of this country, it has been preoccupied with the Constitution. As well, the government has been taxing us to death while bankrupting Canada.
Members in the government have referred to the 18-cent increase in gasoline which brought about the defeat of the Conservative government. The fact is that the Liberal government has raised gas prices three times that amount, an act which was accomplished with the co-operation of the New Democratic Party. They are also responsible for the situation in which we find ourselves today. This is a heavier cross they will have to carry which will be reflected in the next election.
The Liberal government set out to buy oil companies at a time when Canada could least afford them. It is clear that the money which had been invested is now in the United States. It is no wonder that our economy has been crippled. The government is out of touch with reality. While the government was negotiating agreements with Alberta on the Alsands project, it was negotiating with Mexico at the same time and thereby shortchanging Alberta on its heavy oil. It is not surprising that this Constitution, which was intended to unite our country, has divided it more than it has ever been. However, no one is against the Constitution because it is part of our country's growth.
In spite of what has occurred, the Alberta government has once again introduced an incentive in an attempt to get the Alsands project started again. The federal government is not addressing that situation at all. It is still playing with matters which are not relevant to the economy of Canada at the present time.
It is interesting to hear Liberal backbenchers ask us not to blame the government because it is the bureaucrats who are causing our current problems. This morning, I spoke to the Minister of Finance and he indicated that he was looking forward to receiving assistance, with respect to the economy and interest rates, from the United States. It is quite clear that at this time the government no longer governs. It has absolutely no control over the economy. It is the bureaucrats who are running the country. However, they had no alternative because the responsiblity was delegated to them.
As I mentioned, this government is looking to the United States for some direction or some sign of relief in the United States economy. The government has certainly not followed the lead of the United States with respect to the metric system. Metrication is costing billions of dollars. The government is not implementing a proper system for bilingualism. No one is against the French language, but the fact is that it is being pushed down the throats of some Canadians in areas where it is not necessary. This is also true for some civil servants who must be bilingual in order to hold a job. The fact is that it is not necessary in some positions. The unemployment situation is one of the worst we have experienced since the Great

May 5, 1982
Depression. In fact, it is a depression, and it is a serious one at that. People are losing their jobs and homes, businesses are going bankrupt, and 70 per cent of companies are in receivership this year as compared to this time last year, 34 per cent of which have declared bankruptcy. This is a very serious situation. Canadians have an abundance of natural resources and human resources, yet we are not capable under the system, because of the way it is being bungled by the government, of owning or building a home in this land of plenty. One certainly cannot blame the United States, other foreign countries, business or anyone else. One must put the blame where it belongs. It is the Liberal government which has seriously mismanaged this government.
O)
May I say that the time has come for Canadians to realize the situation we are in. Some people say that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) is inexperienced, but I am sure that everyone is now convinced that we would not be experiencing the present sad economic situation if there were a Conservative government in power under the leadership of its present leader.
I appreciate the opportunity of speaking here on an issue which has crippled the economy and taken away jobs, opportunities and the hope of Canadians. It was not needed or wanted; it was forced by a government which did not have the foresight and the courage to do what was best for the country and did rather what was best for the party.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Dingwall (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, appreciate the opportunity of participating in this debate. At the outset, I must say that I am somewhat alarmed at the positions and, indeed, some of the rhetoric being thrown around, particularly by the New Democratic Party. In one instance, that particular party took its place in the House of Commons and said to the people of Canada that the government should back off the Alsands project. When the private sector makes a decision, and it no longer wishes to continue with that project, the New Democratic Party of Canada tells the people that it is in support of the project. It also says that we need it because we need the jobs. It is hypocrisy at its best. However, what does one expect from that party?
Throughout this session of Parliament, we have seen that party flounder on one issue, on another issue and then on many issues. But of course, the official opposition, the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada, also talks out of both sides of its mouth. All through this debate, and we started last evening at eight o'clock, we have heard a lot of rhetoric from the official opposition, but we have not heard any suggestions as to how we could improve on the situation.
