Yes, we have. A former minister just gave us some suggestions, the hon. member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn).
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Not only are the hon. members of the opposition intellectually bankrupt, but they have no leadership, either. They lack the intestinal fortitude to put their policies, particularly their energy policies-
We put it forward.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: -to a vote before their own party. That is how lackadaisical, how inappropriate they would be to govern this country. It has been argued by some individuals that the mere fact that they have attacked the Government of Canada on its position on the Alsands project means, in essence, that they are attacking the Conservative government of the province of Alberta.
They don't care.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: It has been suggested by some that there is a leadership issue in the forefront of all of this-
Don't you believe it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: -and that somehow that great white knight of the oil and gas industry, Mr. Lougheed, has ambitions to go on to federal politics.
What about Brian Baloney?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Now we have a clearcut issue. The Official Opposition wishes to dissociate itself with the government of Alberta and its position, particularly as it relates to Alsands. That is typical of the Conservative Party of Canada. When the going gets tough, it buries its head in the sand.
Alsands.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: I assure hon. members that Mr. Lougheed, the Premier of Alberta, is watching this debate very closely because he has worked with the Government of Canada to come up with very generous proposals-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
-in order to help the Alsands project succeed. But, of course, the official opposition, in its daily mutterings, whether from the hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) or from an hon. member from Newfoundland, whichever one you wish to take, must have it both ways. If the Conservative Party does not have it both ways, it feels very uncomfortable. It is extremely uncomfortable in this position because it knows that the offer made by the Government of Canada and the province of Alberta was a fair and just one, and the decision taken by the Alsands consortium was a decision based on economic circumstances which are not only in evidence here in Canada, but across the world as well.
The opposition refers to the Alsands project going down the tubes. What about the $30 billion nuclear energy program in Mexico which has been delayed? A $14 billion liquefied natural gas export program in Nigeria has been delayed. The gasification project in Texas, estimated at $4 billion, has been
May 5, 1982

deferred. This situation is occuring not only in Canada but also in other jurisdictions throughout the world which are experiencing the same sort of worldwide recession and which have made business decisions based on those factors, thereby delaying projects. 1 suggest that it is not good enough for the official opposition, the Conservative Party of Canada, to abandon its provincial wing under the leadership of Mr. Lougheed and then say that Canada can be immune from certain factors which are affecting all countries of the world.
You cannot tell us because you have no provincial weight.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Of course, another project which was cancelled was in Venezuela. The hon. member knows very well that that country, too, based its decision on economic factors. But notwithstanding the fact that the Alsands project has been delayed or shelved for an indefinite period of time, there are still a number of energy projects which are under active construction, such as Dome's Beaufort Sea project, amounting to $500 million, the Esso Beaufort Sea drilling system, amounting to $130 million, the Gulf Beaufort Sea drilling system, amounting to another $700 million and the Norman Wells oilfield development program, amounting to $600 million. Therefore, despite what the official opposition and the New Democratic Party may say about the gloom and doom in this country, construction is taking place. There is movement in the energy field.
Tell us about the 12 per cent inflation and the 9 per cent unemployment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
The official opposition obtains a great thrust from feeding off the misery of other people. But that is why its members are in opposition and that is why we are in government. We are responsible and we will make decisions. We will give Canada a direction in which it should go whereas they have failed to do that and failed to make any suggestions on that. Many other projects are now taking place. The $700 million, Quintette coal development in British Columbia is taking place, as well as Ridley Island coal and grain terminals in British Columbia, another $400 million, the Algoma Seamless Tube Mill in Ontario, $300 million, the metal mining and refining modernization and expansion program in British Columbia, another $700 million.
The Canadian people ought not to be fooled or duped by the official opposition when they talk about the gloom and doom in this country. There are projects going ahead. No one on either side of this House would say that we are not living in difficult economic times. That is the reason and the rationale why the Alsands consortium made the decision they did in terms of high interest rates and the economy.
We have heard a lot of mutterings from the official opposition about an incentive to invest in oil exploration in Canada. I do not want to rhyme off a number of factors that come from the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, but I will
give the hon. member some quotes from sources to which they have referred on previous occasions.
Solomon Brothers, October 1, 1981, first-year netbacks on new oil reference price oil will be up to 80 per cent higher in Canada than in the United States. Pemberton Securities, November, 1981, conceivably the dramatically higher netbacks for new oil could ultimately lead to a resurgency in industry activity approaching that experienced in the mid-1970s.
Greenshields in February 1982 had a number of factors they wished to share with the Canadian people. These are as follows: exploration for new conventional oil will forge ahead because the price for new oil has almost doubled since December 1, 1981. The relative netback to new oil discoveries is two and a half times higher than in 1979, adjusted for interest rates. With higher netbacks, some small or poor quality reserves that were previously passed by will merit development. New oil discoveries can be put on production within two to 12 months. Finally, new oil plays are available, favouring both companies with land leverage but allowing even those without to participate.
There is something positive happening in the energy sector. It is not as positive as all members would like. We would certainly like to have the Alsands project proceed but the private sector, which supposedly has a philosophy which is akin to that of the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada, says they want the free market to operate. However, when the free market comes up and makes a decision like the Alsands consortium has made, they blame the government of Alberta, the Tory government of Alberta, the provincial wing of their party. I suggest there is a major split in the Conservative Party of Canada. It is Alberta versus the federal Tories.
You had your provincial wings clipped.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
A lot of the mutterings last evening centred around the fact that our goal of oil self-sufficiency will not be met as a result of the failure of the Alsands project. I wish to indicate to members opposite that in terms of the projections we have, we feel there is going to be a shortfall in 1990 of about 285,000 barrels a day.
That shortfall can be met by the possibility of further development on the east coast, the possibility of the Beaufort Sea as well as other oil sands projects. The shortfall which the opposition members have alluded to in their speeches in this debate will be addressed. I am very confident, although 1 sense from some opposition members a real negative attitude about east coast development, particularly as it relates to oil and gas. On one hand that party wants to have development of the oil and gas industry, but you have to question very seriously some of their mutterings and statements to see if in fact they want to see the east coast of Canada, particularly Atlantic Canada, prosper in this important sector.
I am hopeful that with the Hibernia find, with the offshore development in the province of Nova Scotia, particularly as a result of the agreement which the Government of Canada and the province of Nova Scotia have reached after many months

May 5, 1982
of negotiation, a great deal of activity will take place off the coast of that province.
There is one individual whom some members of the official opposition like to quote from time to time. That individual said, "It may be that only time will tell that the activity factors we saw in the summer of 1980 were perhaps somewhat unrealistic as a result of the natural gas marketing situation, so perhaps the really important variable in terms of meeting the recovery dates I have mentioned in this answer will depend upon the prospect for improved natural gas market sales in the United States." The individual who made that statement is the Premier of the province of Alberta, Mr. Lougheed.
When hon. members refer back a couple of years, particularly to the summer of 1980, I place that before them very politely. That was said not by me or by any member of my party, but by the Premier of the province of Alberta, a member of the Conservative Party of Canada.
The utterings, doom and gloom and personal attacks being levied by members of the official opposition does absolutely nothing to improve the situation. I had hoped when this debate began that we would hear clear, concise recommendations and proposals from the official opposition. We have heard absolutely nothing. They are still crying over spilled milk in February 1980 when the people of Canada said no to "Joe Who". They will say no to that party in the next general election and the one after that.
They have no policies. If they do, they hide them from the Canadian people. They hide them very well because they came together as a party to discuss policy and then made some very serious resolutions for that policy conference. One of the resolutions that they have is that they are not going to have any resolutions. They are not going to take any votes on any policies that their party supposedly wishes to have enacted into law for the people of Canada, none whatsoever.
That is the party which is trying to portray to the Canadian people that somehow they have a right or an obligation to govern this country. If they cannot put their own policies before a vote by their own party and have a vote on the leadership of their party, how can they expect the Canadian people to have confidence in anything they say as it relates to energy policy? The official opposition and the New Democratic Party have pretty well had their own way in terms of criticizing. I had hoped, when the 22 members of the New Democratic Party spoke, that we would have had some valid suggestions on how to improve the situation, but we did not have one.
What about Mr. Broadbent's economic strategy?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am glad the hon. member has raised the Broadbent economic strategy.
The member for Oshawa.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: With all due respect to the hon. member, the usual practice in this House is to refer to members by constituencies or by their functions.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am always very willing to take your advice and I will refer to the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent). It is good that that hon. member from Vancouver-Kingsway (Mr. Waddell) has made reference to his particular economic policies. I do not wish to take up too much time of the House of Commons.
You have already done that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Let me refer to one of their policies which affect my own constituency, Mr. Speaker; that is, in relation to the nuclear industry. It was that party, the New Democratic Party, it was their philosophy, their economic strategy, to create jobs. They said, it is on the record, that the two heavy water plants, in Port Hawkesbury and in Glace Bay, would be closed-thereby throwing out 1,000 jobs. But they stand in their place, they tell members of this House, they tell the gallery, they tell the people of Canada, "We, the NDP, are in favour of creating jobs."
We are not in favour of nuclear bombs for the Argentine.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: They cannot have it both ways. The NDP are clearly on the record as saying, "We want the two heavy water plants closed." I hope that the hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway has got the guts to go to Port Hawkesbury, to go to Glace Bay, to stand in the union hall-
I have been there.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: -with his friends in the CLC and tell them, "We want to close down the heavy water plant." I challenge the member for Vancouver-Kingsway to do that.
You are going to close that very plant next year, I bet you.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: The Conservative Party muttered numerous things in this debate which are totally false. They know that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) devoted a large amount of his time in the previous month and in the previous year trying to effectuate a settlement in regard to the Alsands project. He has worked endlessly, Mr. Speaker, and he has worked closely with the government of Alberta to try to achieve this particular goal, and I think his efforts should be recognized by all members of this House, regardless of their political faith.

speakeroldname: Hon. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the parliamentary secretary who has just taken his seat said some very interesting things during his 20 minutes. I was rather intrigued by something he said a few moments ago. He said that we seemed to be crying over spilt milk, implying that we have not quite gotten over the election of February, 1980. He threw out a number of challenges. I would like to throw out one challenge to the hon. gentleman-who is still in the House.
May 5, 1982

I would like to ask him how he intends to go back to his constituency in Cape Breton and justify the position that he took during the election of 1980, consistent with the position that was taken by his leader, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), when he campaigned against increases in gas and oil products.
What has happened since that time? Notwithstanding the promise of the Prime Minister in 1980, when he said on February 12:
The Liberal price hike will be less than half of what the Tories plan to inflict on you; we will negotiate an increase of less than 14 cents.
We know that the price of a gallon of gas has gone up by 75 cents since this government took office, and most of that is tax. We also know that the price of home heating oil has increased by 50 cents a gallon.
1 would like to know how the hon. gentleman intends to go back to the depressed economy of Cape Breton and justify that situation, a situation which he campaigned against in the election of 1980, notwithstanding the fact that he knows full well that the Crosbie budget provided a shelter for home heating oil, a shelter against increases in the world price. The people who are hurting most as a result of the increases in home heating oil are the people who live in places like Cape Breton, in areas of the country where the economy is not in recession, where the economy is in depression, where the people are really feeling it.
Notwithstanding the pronouncements of the hon. member to the contrary, we know that that situation will get worse as a result of the breakdown in the national energy plan, as a result of the failure of the so-called megaprojects, as a result of the failure of the Alsands project. Not only will that exacerbate an already serious unemployment problem, which is currently hovering around 9 per cent, depending on where you are, which in the hon. gentleman's constituency is about 20 per cent, and which in my own province is over 15 per cent. We know that will contribute to the unemployment situation and will mean further increases in the price of home heating oil and in the price of gasoline. That, Mr. Speaker, is the fact.
1 listened last night to the speech of the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola). I listened very carefully because that was the government's official response to this emergency debate. Naturally, we had hoped that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources could find the time, with the JetStar at his disposal, to get here from Texas. I do not think it was impossible for him to fly from Texas to be here in time for the debate, given the time frame. The permission for the debate was granted at 3 p.m., the debate was started at 8 p.m. The minister could have got here at some point during the evening, but he did not. He chose not to get here. Instead we had to hear the Minister of State for Mines trying to make a strong argument on a weak case. And, of course, she failed.
It is not without interest to the people of Canada that this debate has taken place. I am sure the people of Canada well know that we have been sitting here continuously without a break since eight o'clock last evening. That is over 18 hours of continuous sitting. The Chair accepted the motion of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and agreed that
there was in fact an emergency situation in accordance with the provisions of Standing Order 26 as a result of the breakdown of the megaprojects. Her Honour, the Speaker, realizing that that emergency situation existed, granted the emergency debate. One of the reasons we have carried it through to this point in time is that we had every reason to believe, and we still have hope, that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources will find his way back to Canada from Texas and will stand in this House, and not only tell this House but tell the people of Canada just exactly what the position is in this country, vis-a-vis the energy situation, vis-a-vis the economy, as a result of the breakdown of the megaprojects, as a result of the breakdown of the Alaska gas pipeline, with respect to unemployment and with respect to its impact on increased energy prices. We hope he will find time to come here and give us the official position of the government.
Let us get back to the Minister of State for Mines. One of the things that kept cropping up in her speech, and it has emerged in subsequent speeches of members of the Liberal Party, refers to "the potential of the Hibernia field". You see how the situation has changed? Up to last week the position of the Government of Canada was, "We can wait it out. We can wait out the Newfoundland project because we have the megaprojects, we have the Alsands project, that is going to give us energy self-sufficiency and we can just take our time on Hibernia because of gas; the oil is there. It is just like having gold in Fort Knox." Now, of course, with the breakdown of the megaprojects and with the collapse of the Alsands project all of a sudden Hibernia emerges as the real alternative. We now are being told that with Hibernia and with the potential of the Beaufort Sea-which does not have proven reserves as does Hibernia; the proven reserves of Hibernia are about one billion and could be as high as 1.8 billion barrels of oil-we can still achieve energy self-sufficiency by 1990.
What is the position? As of this point in time the position is that the two governments are not even talking to each other. There has been a total collapse in the negotiations between Newfoundland and Canada on jurisdiction over offshore oil and gas, and nothing has happened. That in itself contributes substantially to the delay in getting on with the development of that very important reserve.
In addition to that-and this is a factor-the loss of the Ocean Ranger and 84 lives in February tells us one thing. Apart altogether from the tragedy of it, it tells us very clearly that we still do not have the technology to cope with that hostile environment out there and to extract reserves from the ocean floor. It is not without interest that the spot where the Ocean Ranger, the world's largest floating oil rig which was supposed to be unsinkable, went down was just about 30 miles from where the Titanic, which was also supposed to be unsinkable, met the same fate with an iceberg. We were not coping with icebergs in the Ocean Ranger disaster; we were coping with mountainous seas, high winds and blizzard conditions,

May 5, 1982
and we still do not have the technology-that is what emerged loud and clear from the Ocean Ranger disaster-to cope with that environment. However, even forgetting that factor for a moment, the loss of the Ocean Ranger means that the development of this important reserve will be set back by at least two years.
That must be added to what we hear from the industry. The industry tells us-this does not come from the Newfoundland government or the Government of Canada; it comes from the oil and gas industry-that if an agreement were to be reached today, it would take anywhere from eight to ten years to get the first barrel of oil from the Hibernia field. So let us take eight years and add two years to that because of the failure of our technology to cope with that environment; we are looking at 1992. That is supposing we could get an agreement today. So we can see we cannot all of a sudden look to Hibernia as the promise to make up for the loss of the failure of the Alsands project.
Let us examine the position of the Government of Canada and why negotiations are not taking place today. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) said, on February 24, that he was prepared to be flexible in his talks with Newfoundland and that he was prepared to compromise. He said Newfoundland must be prepared to do the same thing. We looked upon that as an opportunity to make peace and to sit down and negotiate. Negotiations did resume early this year. I believe they were making some progress, until an interesting thing happened in the midst of those negotiations.
Let us remember that there was an agreement on both sides to set aside the question of ownership and to negotiate joint management and joint revenue sharing. In the midst of those negotiations the province of Newfoundland was double-crossed by the Government of Canada. There was a case at that time before the Federal Court of Canada which had been brought by the Seafarers' International Union regarding jurisdiction over rigs. Included in the terms of reference of that case was not only the question of jurisdiction over rigs but also the whole question of which government has jurisdiction over the offshore.
The Government of Newfoundland felt that this was a betrayal of the undertaking which had been made precedent to the reopening of the negotiations, and made the reasonable request to the Government of Canada that it instruct counsel to withdraw that question from the court. The Government of Canada refused to do so. As a result, on February 12, the government of Newfoundland announced that it was referring the question of ownership of the mineral resources of Newfoundland's continental shelf to the appeals division of the Supreme Court of Newfoundland, an action which was made necessary by the federal government's decision to introduce this question into the SIU labour relations case before the Federal Court of Appeal and its subsequent refusal, as I have said, to join with Newfoundland in asking that court to delay hearing the case while negotiations were in progress.
During the course of those negotiations Newfoundland, in response to the reasonable request of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources for compromise on both sides, put on the
table a compromise proposal which formed the basis of the new negotiations. As a result of what happened in the SIU case, as I have said, negotiations collapsed. The Newfoundland government then decided to appeal to the people of Newfoundland and called a general election. However, in the process of doing so the government of Newfoundland decided to go one step further and be even more reasonable in its compromise proposal, in other words, to set before the people of Newfoundland in a general election an even more reasonable proposal than the government of Newfoundland had set before the Government of Canada during the course of the negotiations last winter.
Those compromise proposals were released on the day the election was called, and it would be worth putting them on the record. Very simply, what we are looking for is a true partnership. We are not looking for a partnership in which one government has the dominant say and one government controls the majority of the management board. That is not a partnership but a co-partnership. The government of Newfoundland proposed a true partnership in which each partner would have equal representation on the board and there would be a neutral chairman agreed to by both partners. That is a partnership. Anything else is a majority-minority position, and the people of Newfoundland were not prepared-and are not to this day-to accept the minority position on a management board respecting that important resource which holds so much promise for our people. We can wait. We can wait because the onus now, as a result of the failure of the megaprojects, is on the Government of Canada.
The proposals put forward were very simple. Both governments would set aside ownership claims and become co-owners of the resource. What could be more reasonable than that? Both governments would be equal. Both governments would receive their share of revenue directly from a joint agency. Arrangements could be changed only with the consent of both governments. That is a reasonable proposition. The proposal went on to talk about how prices would be established and what the province would receive. For example, the province would initially receive the traditional share which has been received by the western provinces for onshore oil and gas. The province's traditional share would continue until a trigger point based on fiscal and economic objectives had been arrived at, and the share would then change in favour of the Government of Canada.
What was the response of the people of Newfoundland in that general election? The response of the people of Newfoundland was that the Liberal Party of Newfoundland was practically wiped out. The great Liberal Party of Newfoundland, the founding party of Confederation in Newfoundland's union with Canada, was practically wiped out at the hands of Premier Peckford and the government of Newfoundland on the basis solely of this reasonable proposal.
The people of Newfoundland want to be reasonable. They want to share. They want to be good Canadians. They want to share in this partnership. They want to contribute their share
May 5, 1982

to Confederation. We are tired of being a "have-not" province. For once we have an opportunity to rise above that "havenot" situation. For once we can see ahead to the time when we will not have to come cap in hand to Uncle Ottawa as a colony and look for more where we can share a resource that is ours.
The response of the people of Newfoundland was 62 per cent in favour of that position, and only eight Liberal seats out of 82 survived.
What was the response of the Government of Canada? Almost before the ink was dry on the writ, the very next day on April 7, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, who is now somewhere in the oil fields of Texas, had something to say. According to an article in the Ottawa Citizen of April 7, the minister accused Premier Peckford of resorting to "outright lies" in the campaign, and said that the election results meant nothing as far as the federal government was concerned. He said "Our principles remain the same. We have no new proposals to put forward."
That was his provocative and insulting response not only to the government of Newfoundland but to the people of Newfoundland-"We have no new proposals to put forward-our principles remain the same."
That situation has now changed, Mr. Speaker. Within a few days of the announcement of the failure of the so-called megaprojects, the breakdown of the Alsands project, the minister told the House that he had been on the phone to the minister of energy for Newfoundland and that he hoped they could get together again.
How things change, Mr. Speaker. I can tell the minister that hard times are no stranger to Newfoundland. We not only live in a hostile environment but we live with hard times. Through the four or five hundred years of our history we have learned to exercise patience. That patience is still there today. We can wait, Mr. Speaker. Our position is reasonable. It has the support of the people of Newfoundland. We can wait. My question to the minister through you, Mr. Speaker, is how long can the people of Canada wait?
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate I want to say that I have not had an opportunity to examine Hansard as thoroughly as I would wish and note all the input into the debate since yesterday afternoon by hon. members opposite. On the basis of the examination I have made and the reports that I have received from others-
It has not been printed yet.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
speechtext:
-it strikes me as being a most unusual emergency debate on the question of the collapse of the Alsands
project and the concern of the official opposition about megaprojects in general.
It is a surprising debate because, as one who is concerned about energy and the economy, I would have expected that a request for an emergency debate when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) was known to be out of the country on an important engagement meant that the opposition had concrete, positive, alternate proposals about what the government should do.
Hear, hear!
Oh, oh!
Look what we have flushed out. The eyes of Texas are on Ottawa.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: You said he was in Texas.
How was J. R. Ewing?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when hon. members opposite settle down I will try to continue. I am very pleased that the minister has arrived in the House.
As I was saying, hon. members opposite decided that the situation is such an emergency that all the business of the House must be put aside and for two days or so we must talk about the problems that arise from the collapse of the Alsands project.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am either getting to them already or I am about to get to them, because that is when they make those noises. If they would just listen politely they might learn something.
Not from you.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
speechtext:
I expected them to come forward with a positive plan. I expected that if they sincerely wanted an emergency debate so urgently, that if they could not wait until the minister was in the House and could answer questions, they would have offered five or six alternatives. If people want to know what their actual purposes were and what they had been doing, they should read Hansard and find out how hon. members opposite have talked about the economy, about an election, and many other things that have no relation to the subject matter of their emergency resolution whatsoever.
I want to compliment you, Mr. Speaker, on your tolerance in regard to the breadth of comments that you have allowed them to make which are far from the subject.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: With all respect to the minister, the Chair has observed that on both sides there has been a certain tolerance.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
speechtext:
Thank you for that assurance, Mr. Speaker, and I will try to follow the principle that has been established about the breadth of debate in my remarks.

May 5, 1982
The opposition asked for the emergency debate, however, and if they talk about a wide range of matters then it is quite obvious that it will bring forth a response on a wide range of matters. The fact that they have brought no new ideas, made no concrete suggestions or alternatives, indicates that there is more politics than economic concern in their action.
1 believe that the temporary collapse, we hope, of the Alsands project is regarded as unfortunate by everyone. But I think the vast majority of Canadians would be more unhappy if the government of Alberta and the Government of Canada had decided together to go ahead in changed world circumstances where this would result in higher energy costs to the Canadian people and would provide us with the security of supply that we badly need but at a cost higher than alternatives that exist elsewhere. Hon. members opposite are trying to convince Canadian people that this is the responsibility of the government. Perhaps they have to try to convince people that despite the fact that the price has softened internationally, and that the costs for the Alsands project were very high, we should have gone ahead regardless of the fact that the private partners who put up their own money withdrew because they considered it to be too expensive.
What hon. members opposite are saying is that the government should have gone ahead nevertheless, and should have imposed a project upon the Canadian public that would result in an even higher energy cost than is the case at present.
That is nonsense.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
speechtext: I should like the hon. member to explain why that is nonsense.
1 will.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
speechtext:
I will listen very carefully because that question deserves to be answered. The hard cold facts are that hon. members opposite have not answered that question in this debate. Instead they have rambled on about the problems of the economy as though we lived on an island floating in the sky somewhere and are not affected by the American markets, the European situation, and international conditions in general. But that is not an unusual ploy for the opposition. Indeed, I recognize it is perhaps a legitimate ploy, but it is not the sort of constructive approach which results in a party gaining the confidence of the public. I therefore think it is ill-advised.
It is my view, Mr. Speaker, and I am confident it is the view of the Canadian public, that if the Alsands project was going to result in a higher cost of energy than available alternatives, the Canadian public would not want that project to go forward. They will be very much influenced in their judgment on the wisdom of the government's decision by the fact that the private companies decided not to go ahead under these circumstances.
The new-found capitalistic principles of Gerry Regan.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
speechtext:
I think the people will also be influenced, as I am, by the fact that the government of Alberta, which is not noted to be of the same political stripe as this government or to take the same views in relation to the economy, also felt it had gone as far as it should go in trying to make this project go forward. So I want to applaud the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources who had the courage to take the right step. I applaud Premier Lougheed also. Between them, they decided they should not go ahead with a project which had become uneconomical and uncompetitive in today's world market conditions. In many ways the easy task would have been for the minister and the premier to have gone ahead regardless of cost, and that is why I applaud the fact they had the courage to recognize that the long-term interests of the Canadian public in relation to pricing have to be their first responsibility.
Let me, Mr. Speaker, say a few words about the National Energy Program which these people say is in a shambles.
It is.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
speechtext:
Sure, we have problems in western economies at the present time. We have a softness in markets which affects a province like mine, Nova Scotia, where we sell the vast portion of our fish into the American market. We sell the products of our large pulp and paper mills, most of the tires from Michelin, and many of our other industries into the American market. The result is that when the United States catches a cold, Nova Scotia sneezes. The same thing applies to British Columbia, indeed to a large part of the Canadian economy. If the Americans do not build homes, then we do not sell our gypsum from Windsor, Nova Scotia, my home town, or the forest products from British Columbia. So do not try to tell us that the economy is not dependent upon world markets.
What have we done in the NEP?
Nothing.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
speechtext:
Before it even existed we had established PetroCan, something which hon. members opposite wanted to do away with. Had they been in office a little longer, they might have done that great violence to Canada's future. In the meantime they bury their heads in the sand when the subject of PetroCan comes up because it was PetroCan's participation which kept the drilling going off the east coast when the private companies were not prepared to put up more money without having a major share paid for by the federal government. I applaud the minister for that because that brought about the successful gas discovery off Nova Scotia which will provide for the economic future of that province, and do much to help Canada's economy. It was PetroCan's involvement in Newfoundland which provided such a tremendous role in the success of Hibernia and adjacent areas. The NEP, with its investment incentives which might otherwise not have been possible, have of course resulted in the Beaufort moving forward.
I guess we all felt there had to be a selection, Mr. Speaker, as to which projects went ahead more rapidly. Can you think
May 5, 1982

of any better basis for making that selection than on the basis of which projects can bring Canadians the lower-cost energy? That again justifies the action taken on this particular project.
I am rather surprised to see hon. members questioning the judgment of Premier Lougheed. Usually they are such servants, under the leadership of the Leader of the Opposition, of provincial Conservative governments that they hesitate a long while to disagree one iota with the position of a provincial Conservative government when they should be recognizing their national interests.
What else has been happening, Mr. Speaker? We have had the settlement with Nova Scotia. As the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) just said, Newfoundland has not settled, but I would suggest to you that the development of Hibernia has been set back a substantial period of time over the last three years because of the lack of a reasonable settlement on the part of Premier Peckford. I suggest we would be well under way in the development of that great resource if Frank Moores were still the premier of the province.
I also want to point out that we have achieved something else under the leadership of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources over the past year. The programs of conservation and home insulation have resulted in a situation equivalent to having had the Alsands plans go ahead. These programs, introduced by the minister and widely used by Canadians, have resulted in a 7 per cent decrease in the consumption of energy.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
speechtext:
I think this House should be moving a vote of thanks to the minister. There probably has not been anything in the history of the country as successful and widely used by Canadians as the insulation program which will provide us with savings, not just now, but permanently.
Another thing which comforts me in the belief 1 am correct in applauding the minister is the fact that this changed world economy, the change in world oil prices, and the rate of inflation, have also resulted in most other major international projects of this type being cancelled or delayed. They have been stopped for the same reason. Why is it, for example, that the French have shelved the idea of bringing in heavy crude from Venezuela and putting in a $1 billion up-grading plant? Because it is too expensive in the circumstances. Why is it that Exxon has cancelled their huge shale oil project in Colorado, a $5 billion investment? Why is it that the coal gasification project in Wyoming has been scrapped? Or the $30 billion nuclear energy program in Mexico delayed? I could list several others if I had the time.
The reason is that there are changed circumstances in the world with respect to pricing, and those companies, like the companies and governments involved in Alsands, had enough common sense to recognize that you go ahead when it is in the interests of providing a competitive product. When the price gets out of line, then you have to go back to the drawing board.
The progress which has been made through NEP incentives in the Beaufort Sea, the Revelstoke hydro undertaking, the Bruce operating station, the gas pipeline through Quebec into the Atlantic provinces, and others, indicates that this is
probably the most active department at any point in the history of Canada. It is bringing about the development of alternatives. You have more and more new sources of energy coming on stream. Hon. members opposite are hard pressed indeed when they try to tie a tough but wise decision to a debate on Alsands. The emergency debate indeed should instead have been an endorsement of the action taken by the hon. member.
What action?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
speechtext:
I want to say to the hon. member for St. John's East that I was gravely troubled by his words in relation to the question of an equitable agreement between Newfoundland and the Government of Canada about a resource which legally belongs to one or the other. It is not a question for politicians to argue about. If they can make a settlement, that is wonderful, but otherwise the court decides. But I was bothered by the fact that he said, "We can sit back and wait and sit back and wait." I do not think that is a good Canadian attitude. I think it important to Canada that those resource developments which can help the people of Newfoundland now and can help Canada now in relation to energy should go ahead. That is the sort of attitude I would like to see on his part. I ask him to reconsider the whole question.
I believe I have nearly exhausted my time. Let me say to you in relation to this particular project that, as hon. members opposite say "I have exhausted them", I have exhausted their arguments. I have answered them effectively. I think they will find that the Canadian people will not buy this sort of use of time for which the Canadian people are paying their salaries. I think Canadians would like to see some constructive work. Save your electioneering until election time and come here to represent the people who elected you, and do constructive work.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I wish I could say it is a pleasure to participate in this emergency debate. Unfortunately it is not, because of the loss of the Alsands project. This loss is probably the biggest blow to Canada and its economy in all our history.
At the outset I would like to welcome the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) who has just returned from visiting Texas and all the oil rigs and Canadian investment that he chased from Canada. I am sure that Texas was very happy to get rid of him in a hurry because I believe the Americans would not want to end up in the same economic and energy situation which the minister has created here in Canada.
As far as the statement made by the Minister of State (Mr. Regan) are concerned, I will not comment on them except for one statement. The Minister of State questioned my party's position on a positive plan. I do not know where the minister

May 5, 1982
has been for the last couple of years that he does not even know what the position of this party is on energy matters.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Amateur Sport
speechtext: I do not know your position on your party's leadership either.

The minister knows very well that this party when it was in government, and since then, has established incentives for Canadian companies, incentives for Canadian ownership. During the short time we were in office we had entered into an agreement with Alsands which would have put that project into production by 1986. As the minister knows, and as all Canadians know, we would keep the excise tax increase on the price of gasoline at the gas pump to 18 cents per gallon.
Oh, oh!

But the price has increased by a dollar. The Liberals promised to keep the excise tax at 14 cents a gallon. But look at what has happened to that promise. The Conservative government said it would not increase the cost of home heating fuel. But the Liberals have increased home heating fuel by over 50 cents a gallon. The Progressive Conservative government established an energy tax rebate for low and middle-income families. We were in the process of recycling increased revenues into economic development packages which would have assisted mass transit programs and steel production, etc. The list goes on, all leading toward energy selfsufficiency in 1990. Now with the actions of this government opposite, that energy self-sufficiency dream and potential of Canadians have gone down the drain. Members opposite are the ones to blame.
And if the cancellation of the Alsands project was not enough following the cancellation of the Cold Lake project the minister of energy and the government kept telling us and kept telling Canadians that other things were going downhill as well.
I can refer to all the economic standards, whether it is inflation, unemployment-

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The hon. member who has the floor now is either intentionally or unintentionally misleading the House. When he made the remark about the minister being in Texas, the fact of the matter is-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is making a point of argument. The minister will have an opportunity to be recognized. The hon. member for Halton (Mr. Jelinek) has the floor. Order, please.
Mr. Speaker, it will be very nice when some of those Liberals become Canadians before politicians.
Hear, hear!
That is Joe's mentality.

Mr. Speaker, hon. members on the other side get upset when they hear the truth. They know that the Progressive Conservative government had an energy policy which would have led to energy self-sufficiency.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: A point of order must be a genuine point of order and not an argument.

I have a point of order, Mr. Speaker, if you would be prepared to listen to it. I would like to know whether or not you will allow me the opportunity of at least two minutes to make my point before you rule on it.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Halton has the floor.
Mr. Speaker-
Respect the Speaker. Hold others in contempt if you wish, but respect the Speaker.
It is very obvious members on the other side get frustrated when they hear views. I would not blame them at all when they have a Prime Minister-
You are skating on thin ice.
Sit down.
Mr. Speaker, as I was saying-
Order.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I request hon. members to keep order in the House. The hon. member for Halton has the floor.

As I was saying, Mr. Speaker, it is very obvious that Liberal members get very frustrated when they hear the truth from this side of the House. It must be very damaging to their egos to know they have gone downhill, for the last 14 years, as a matter of fact, and now have blown the potential for Canadians of energy self-sufficiency.
You have a lot of nerve. You are skating around.
Skating again.
Hon. members over there talk about-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I again request hon. members of the House to observe the appropriate decorum. The hon. member for Halton has the floor.

Mr. Speaker, they keep talking about my figure-skating background. They have done better skating today in this House of Commons than I ever did. I can tell you that I am proud of my achievements as a figure skater.
May 5, 1982
Hear, hear!
I won a gold medal for Canada, with my sister, and I am proud of that achievement. 1 wonder what that hon. member has contributed to Canada.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This has been a long debate. The hon. member has been given the courtesy of the House to have the floor. I invite him to speak to the subject.

Mr. Speaker, now that I have reminded the Minister of State of the policies and programs of our government, I am sure he is satisfied enough because he has left the Chamber, hopefully to study some of those programs to try to encourage his cabinet to copy some of them for the benefit of Canada and Canadians.
I have talked about the Alsands project, but if that was not the final straw, let us go back a year or so. During the last year and a half there have been many problems which Canadians were faced with in various industries. There were problems in the textile industry, the automotive industry, the agriculture industry, along with problems in the small business area. The list goes on. Over the course of last year whenever we questioned those specific problems in this House of Commons, the government would say, "Wait until the budget comes down in November." Finally the budget was brought down, and even the Liberals must agree that it was the most disastrous budget in the history of this nation with the policies and programs that were in it. Not only have we had 40 changes already by the Minister of Finance, but most of the budget has not yet been passed. Yet the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) is too cowardly to introduce a new budget.
I do not have to get into the specifics of the budget, because we in this House, and all Canadians, realize what the consequences of that budget have been to the economy of this nation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I hesitate to interrupt the hon. member, but I think I heard an expression that has been deemed unparliamentary. He referred to an hon. member as "cowardly". I invite the hon. member for Halton to withdraw the remark and rephrase it.
Withdraw.
I will withdraw that and replace it with "stubborn", Mr. Speaker.
You are a pretty good skater.

In lieu of assisting some of these industries, particularly the small business sector, we were told that a budget would be brought down-and we all know what the consequences of that budget were.
Then the answers to our questions and to the problems in the country were, "Don't worry, because the National Energy Program is going to save the economy of this nation".
But what happened to the National Energy Program? Very quickly, I shall give a few statistics, Mr. Speaker. For example, drilling activity in Canada, down 25 per cent in 1981 over 1980-and I want to point out that that is in contrast to an increase of 25 per cent in the same period in the United States, to counter the contention of the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister that it is an international problem.
Well completions in Canada in 1981 were 7,183, compared to 9,480 in 1980-a drop of 25 per cent; exploratory drilling in Canada declined by 19 per cent; development drilling in Canada was down 28 per cent. And since the introduction of the National Energy Program, Mr. Speaker, on October 28,
1980,	226 drilling rigs have left Canada. The number of active rigs in Canada declined by 33 per cent between 1980 and
1981.
So much for the National Energy Program. So, what do the Liberals do then? They come back and they say, "We have all of the megaprojects that are going to save everybody and everything, because the spin-off is so terrific from these megaprojects right across the country." The Alsands project alone was a $14 billion project. And it is true. The spin-offs from that project would have been tremendous. One hundred thousand jobs would have been created between that project and the Cold Lake project. The spin-offs would have affected Ontario by 40 per cent of the total cost of those projects, be it in steel production or in automotive plants, manufacturing, or the parts sector. Even the small business sector in secondary manufacturing would have profited tremendously.
I agree that the spin-offs from this project would have assisted the economic situation tremendously right across the country. But now, Mr. Speaker, now that is down the drain. And the Minister of State has the audacity to come before this House and question why we are debating this in an emergency session, when the Speaker herself agreed it was an emergency situation to be debated by this Parliament because it is a tragedy for the economic welfare of this nation.
This is not just one small industry-and I have some compassion for those small industries, as many of my colleagues know; this is a major project affecting all of those industries from coast to coast and affecting the employment opportunities for Canadians, of which there are over one million and a quarter unemployed today. That is the tragedy of the situation, and that is why this debate, Mr. Speaker, is continuing. It is because of the government's policies.
One has to question why it is that some of the policies and programs that have come from that side have been established. No one has really answered why. But I have an inkling that perhaps the philosophy of their Prime Minister, which is well known to many, has a lot to do with it, Mr. Speaker. The socialist tendencies of the Prime Minister are on record. I know that members opposite do not like me to refer to them-
Oh, go ahead.

Go ahead.

May 5, 1982

-but I will refer to them again. One of the Liberal members says, "Go ahead".
We can start back in 1940 when the Prime Minister was booted out of the Canadian Officer Training Corps during the war for lack of discipline-

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: I thought you were talking about socialism.
I challenge the Prime Minister to denounce-
Spit it out.
-to denounce these accusations.
Spit it out.
You can tell him what I am saying.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: You are blushing, Joe. Your leader is blushing.

In 1941 the Prime Minister was associated with the anti-war and red supported Bloc Populaire in undermining the war effort. Then, Mr. Speaker, in 1945 he enrolled at Harvard, which at that time was a spawning ground for leftist intellectuals.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: Where are you getting your information?

I just read your old reports.
In 1950, Mr. Speaker, he was in Shanghai, when the communists took over, and became a rabid admirer of Mao Tse Tung and his red regime. And the list goes on.

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
speechtext: You are blushing, Joe.

In 1952, today's Prime Minister of Canada led a delegation of communists to the Moscow Economic Conference. In 1953 he was barred entry into the United States as an inadmissible person, a persona non grata. And I will go on. In 1955 he launched Le Rassemblement, a leftist united front rally in Quebec. But the CCF, which was later to become the NDP, refused to join because it was too leftist. In 1960 he led a communist delegation to Peking for the red victory celebration. And on and on. This list goes on, including a quote from The Practice and Theory of Federalism, which he wrote in 1961-and I will quote what today's Prime Minister of Canada said then:
Federalism must be welcomed as a valuable tool which permits dynamic parties to plant socialist governments in certain provinces, from which the seeds of radicalism can slowly spread.
That is today's Prime Minister-and thank goodness-

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: How much are you paid to spread hate in this country?
Spread hate. That is your party. You are spreading hate in Canada. That is the policy of your party-to spread hate.
Thank goodness for the provinces that this dream of socialist governments from coast to coast has failed.
Spreading hate; you are spreading hate.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You are paid too much to spread hate in this country.
Hate, hate, hate.
Listen to them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please.
Hate, hate, hate.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Halton has the floor.
Mr. Speaker, the Liberals are saying "Hate, hate, hate". It seems that the Liberals-
That is all that you know,
It seems that the Liberal government hates the Canadian people-
Oh, oh!
You are a red neck, Jelinek.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I appeal to hon. members in the House to observe decorum. The hon. member for Halton has the floor.

They are very excited over there. They are talking about hate. One would question whether they liked the Canadian public when they created an economic situation where in this great country-a country which has more natural resources per capita than any other nation in the world, that possesses technological know-how unmatched by any, a country whose human resources are better than those of any other country in the western world-we have one million and a quarter unemployed; where we have an inflation rate of nearly 13 per cent; where we have high interest rate policies supported by this Liberal government-
And by the Tories.

And they talk about hate! Why don't those Liberals, especially the backbenchers, go to their ridings and listen to what their people are saying, because I can tell you that the people out on the street are starting to hate this government for its ineffective monitoring of the economic situation that it has created.
Right on.
That is what hate is all about.
You are spreading hate in this country.
You should be ashamed.

The minister himself should go to his people and hear what they are saying on the street. They are not
May 5, 1982

happy-and this was before the Alsands project fell apart and created what is potentially the greatest economic disaster from coast to coast in this country.
If they can refute any of these statements I have made regarding this Prime Minister, I welcome them to stand up in this House and say that they are not so. I challenge them to do that. I do not see anyone standing up.
Total silence.
What is not so.
Mr. Speaker, in closing-
Ask the question.
In closing-
Ask the question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member for Halton has the floor.
He asked for a reply, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Halton has the floor.
He asked us to reply, Mr. Speaker. He has offered us the floor.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member for Restigouche has made a number of interruptions that are out of order. I invite him to keep his seat. The hon. member for Halton has the floor.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It will be hard for him to keep his seat in the next election.
Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. In closing, because I know time is running out-
Hear, hear!

I am sure the Liberals are happy that I am closing, because I could go on and tell them a few other things that they wouldn't like. Sometimes we must stop pussy-footing around and call a spade a spade so that they know where they are sitting-and many of them know and feel embarrassed about the situation.
Go and wash your mouth out.

In closing, Mr. Speaker, I just want to say that the potential that this country has to offer Canadians is matched by no other country in the world. It is here. And we admit that there is an international problem economically speaking-inflation-wise and otherwise. But the facts speak for themselves. This government is dealing with those international problems worse than any of the other industrialized nations. That has been established as well. One need only look, for example, at the inflation rate in the United States-which in
the first quarter was only IVi per cent, compared to a 15 per cent inflation rate in the first quarter in Canada.
One need only look at some of the western European countries, or even the Far East or Japan, to see that, yes, those countries are being hit with problems, with economic problems, but they are dealing with them better than we are, and yet they do not have the natural resources and potential-the great potential-that this country has to offer Canadians. And therefore there is only one solution, Mr. Speaker, that this government resign and allow the people of Canada to make a decision. And if it does not, I would, in closing, make one suggestion, that being that, because of the seriousness of this debate, the Governor General should dissolve this House and call an election on behalf of all Canadians.
Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I do welcome this debate. 1 am very happy to see that a number of members have participated. In a way, however, it is a strange emergency debate. 1 was in the House on Monday, the decision by the Alsands group having been announced on the previous Friday, and I noticed at that time that neither the energy critic for the Progressive Conservative Party nor the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) was in the House.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Where were you yesterday?

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: I don't know where they were, but it took the Conservatives four days before they discovered there was an emergency which they wanted to debate.
Shame!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: On our side, Mr. Speaker, we were in this House and we were ready to debate. We have been ready to debate all along. We have been debating today, and we will continue to debate as long as the opposition wants to debate.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: I want to begin by saying that the National Energy Program, notwithstanding the attacks of the Conservatives, is alive and well and getting the job done. It has done so for 18 months now, and it will continue to do so, Mr. Speaker.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
The government, through the National Energy Program, is meeting the energy challenge in three ways: providing security of supply-security with regard to oil in particular; providing the opportunity for Canadians to participate; and providing fairness in pricing.
The progress we have made in the short 18 months since the NEP was announced is not only enviable, it is remarkable indeed. Eighteen months ago we said that we would move Canada toward energy self-sufficiency-and we have already done so, Mr. Speaker. According to Oilweek magazine, the

May 5, 1982
voice of the industry, our self-sufficiency in oil has increased from 79.5 per cent in 1981 to 80.9 per cent in 1982, in spite of very difficult conditions all around the world.
Under the National Energy Program, our potential domestic supplies have increased. According to the Canadian Petroleum Association figures, our oil and natural gas reserves both increased in 1981.
Three oil discoveries have been made since the National Energy Program came into being, and delineation drilling at Hibernia has established proven reserves of more than one billion barrels of oil. That is progress, and that is what the opposition is criticizing. That is what they would want to undo.
Canada's enormous thirst for oil-and I think it is equalled only by the Tories thirst for power-has decreased, and this is something that cannot be said for the Tories, who are still following the mirage out there in their political desert. Consumption of oil in Canada has been lowered from 282,910 cubic metres in 1980 to a predicted 268,000 cubic metres per day this year. Canadians have made great strides in reducing their dependence on oil through conservation and by switching to more abundant and less costly energy sources.
Nobody can afford to do anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Over 170,000 Canadians have taken advantage of the National Energy Program grants for converting from oil, and over one million Canadians have received federal grants for increased insulation. Over 1,200,000 Canadians have been helped by the Government of Canada to reduce oil consumption in this country-and that is much more important than whether one or two oil companies got everything that they wanted. It is important because it has meant a 17 per cent reduction in the use of heating oil over last year and a 7 per cent drop in total use by Canadians of crude oil over the past year.
As my colleague stated earlier, more oil has been saved by those measures than the whole production of Alsands would have been-and at a fraction of the cost, Mr. Speaker; at a fraction of the cost.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Apply that theory to job creation.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
In short, we are getting closer, with each passing day, to energy security, and the National Energy Program is delivering on that score.
Edmund Burke once observed that if we command our wealth we shall be rich and free, and if our wealth commands us, we are poor indeed.
Eighteen months ago we said we would give Canadians a say in their energy future-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: They are all saying "No".

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: I am pleased to report that the Canadian share of oil and gas production revenues has increased by about six percentage points, from 28 to 34 per cent, under the National Energy Program.
It has gone down in absolute numbers.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we are quickly attaining our goal of 50 per cent Canadian ownership. We challenged Canadians to play a new role in meeting their energy needs- and Canadians, contrary to the contention of the Conservative opposition, are responding, Mr. Speaker.
Our third goal in formulating the National Energy Program was fairness-fairness in the pricing and taxation of oil and gas; fairness for each and every Canadian from one end of this country to the other; and fairness in revenue sharing among governments and the industry.
In a period of 18 months we have successfully achieved agreements with the producing provinces-with Alberta, with Saskatchewan, with British Columbia, and recently with Nova Scotia. Again, remarkable progress-progress the Tories were obviously incapable of achieving.
They are determined to live up to a statement made many years ago by the Earl of Derby to the effect that the opposition's duty is a very simple one-to oppose everything and propose nothing.
The increased federal share of revenues have made possible the very programs which will ensure energy security for our nation-exploration incentives, off-oil conversion, home insulation grants, and many more. Why was Alsands suspended? The consortium gave the following reasons: the unsettled state of international oil markets and the possibility of lower than anticipated prices; the falling world demand for oil; and escalating project costs and concern about inflation.
There are two very significant points to bear in mind. The consortium did not deny that the Canada-Alberta offer was very generous, nor did it describe the National Energy Program as a cause for concern. True to form, federal Tories have shamelessly abandoned their Alberta counterparts. They are desperate men seeking desperate solutions, as usual.
The government worked closely with Alberta to develop this very generous proposal. I find it most regrettable that federal Tories blindly refuse to recognize the constructive and cooperative efforts of the two governments during the past few months. It is a classic dog-in-the-manger stance, one at which the Tories have become past masters. Indeed this is another typical classic Tory trait. It is not only pelicans, as nature teaches, that turn on their kind; the Tories are just pelicans in that regard.
I should like to draw the attention of hon. members of the Conservative opposition to the statements made by the Premier of Alberta at his press conference on April 30, 1982. Those statements are on the record and they clearly indicate that we have done everything which could be expected from the govemnments in this regard, and that the governments could not responsibly go any further than they did. I invite hon.
May 5, 1982

members opposite to look at the record and to take the lead of the Premier of Alberta in what is a responsible attitude in terms of finalizing situations, and what is a responsible view of the world taken by a man who does not put his head in the sand and refuse to see reality.
I suppose there is nothing more appalling than the contradiction of the Conservative Party and the hypocrisy of the New Democratic Party. They have taken their traditional stance of coming down soundly on both sides of the fence on this issue as they do on every other issue. They have repeatedly called for the shelving of Alsands. It follows that they should now be rejoicing at the news of the suspension of the project. Unex-plainably, or perhaps quite understandably, they are now moaning and groaning over its demise. I will not spend too much time commenting upon the NDP.
I should like to return to the facts of the situation. The Tories, with their overblown rhetoric, claim that we have starved the oil industry. Let us get the facts straight. Canada is a major energy explorer, something which benefits our balance of payments. In 1981, exports of natural gas, electricity, uranium and coal exceeded the value of oil imports by $3 billion. As well, declared dividends of the industry increased by $400 million or fully 33 per cent, as compared with an increase of 12 per cent in other sectors of the Canadian economy. This is the record. It does not reflect the behaviour of an industry which is extremely short of cash.
Let me compare our situation with that prevailing in the United States. According to International Petroleum Finance estimates, Gulf Canada, Shell Canada and Texaco Canada substantially outperformed their foreign parents in 1980 and again in 1981. This morning the Oil Daily, the national magazine in the United States of the energy industry, reported the first quarter results of the main oil and gas companies in the United States. I think it will enlighten the opposition to indicate the earnings of the following companies for the first quarter: Occidental, minus 76 per cent; Marathon, minus 71 per cent; Standard of California, minus 65 per cent; Mobil, minus 49 per cent; Texaco, minus 44 per cent. There is no national energy program in the United States. This is the situation faced by these companies in the United States. I could refer to dozens of other companies with similar results. This is the situation which the oil industry all over the world is facing at the present time.
As I indicated, we have seen better results for subsidiaries of American companies in Canada, such as Gulf, Shell and Texaco, than in the United States. This does not take into account the very substantial incentives announced by the government of Alberta in the last few weeks, such as royalty reductions which will amount to $5.5 billion over the next five years.
It is clear that it is the opposition, not the government, which has been withholding up to $1 billion in petroleum incentive payments to the industry this year by its bell-ringing exercise and its delaying tactics. If there was an iota of sincerity in its actions, it should approve forthwith the bill which is
before the House to ensure that Canadian oil and gas companies receive those benefits without any further delay. They say that the cow which moos the most gives the least milk. I would say that Tories are the best examples of such animals.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext:
What results do we see today? First we see exploratory drilling for oil in Alberta where the majority of Canada's oil is currently produced. It was higher in 1981 than it was in 1980. Oilweek magazine predicted an increase in drilling this year in all western provinces as well as in frontier and offshore regions. By way of comparison, in that bastion of free entreprise, the United States, rig activity plummeted in 1982. Compared with the last quarter of 1981, the number of active rigs in the United States is down 20 per cent. In Canada geophysical activity, the precursor of drilling activity, is also on the increase. It is up 62 per cent over the last quarter of 1981. These are facts which the Tories continue to refuse to see, despite the fact that everyone else sees them and reports them.
There is one final undeniable fact which the opposition- and the Tories in particular-refuse to recognize. The National Energy Program is succeeding. It is getting the job done. It is working to ensure a better and brighter energy future for all Canadians. The Tories cannot stop it, not by holding the Chamber to ransom, not by any number of theatrics such as this debate, not by empty and unfounded criticism. We will not let them stop progress; the people of Canada will not let them stop progress. They are bombarding Canadians with words. Canadians require deeds. They can react, but they are unable to act. They can criticize, but they cannot propose. They can attempt to tear down, but they cannot build.
Years from now, long after most of us have gone from this Chamber, the senseless and vituperative criticism which has flowed from the benches opposite will be only so many lines in Hansard.
It is said that we often discover what will work by finding out what will not work. That is something the Conservative opposition cannot seem to grasp. It is the essence of the opposition's mentality to react like Pavlov's dogs to daily events. It is the challenge of those who govern to rise above those events and to fix their sights on the future.
I would invite the official opposition to take a leaf from the Premier of Alberta and the minister of energy of Alberta who have worked very closely with us on this program and who have come to the conclusion that it would have been irresponsible for the federal government and the Alberta government to venture any further than we did. If some hon. members argue, as they have, that we should have had an agreement before, I refer them again to the statement of Premier Lough-eed to the effect that if we had approved the project a year or 18 months ago, the agreement provided that the companies could still walk away from the project.

May 5, 1982
This is what Premier Lougheed had to say:
I wonder what would have happened to Alberta businessmen if Alsands had been cancelled because of the international situation, after seeming to go ahead.
We have seen this as recently as last weekend. At the same time that the Alsands project was cancelled, we saw Exxon in the United States literally walking away from a project in which $1 billion of investments had already been committed. They walked away from it.
We have seen the Alaska pipeline being postponed for two years. We have seen a number of other projects in the United States and abroad being either delayed or shelved or cancelled because of the uncertainty about world oil prices, inflation, and the cost of inflation generally.
I invite the Tories to do the impossible, to come out of their fantasy world, face the reality, and realize that what is important is that we can achieve self-sufficiency in this country without being dependent on the realization of a program like Alsands.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, this weekend I have to return to my constituency office in the east end of Vancouver.
