When I meet people who come there to complain about being unemployed, or high inflation, or all the different problems which they now face, I can quote the immortal words of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) by saying that it is the challenge of the government to raise itself above these events.
We have just seen the collapse of a $13.5 billion energy project. Although the government is attempting to mislead us, we have, in reality seen the collapse of the financing of a $40 billion to $60 billion energy project which is the Alaska pipeline. But what does the minister say? He says that it is the challenge of the government to rise above these events. Furthermore, we have just seen the collapse of the whole economic strategy of the Canadian government which is built on megaprojects. Once again the minister says that it is the challenge of the Canadian government to raise itself above these events.
Someone once told me that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources might be a socialist. He is not a socialist. He is a Stalinist. He says that the NEP is alive and well and performing its job. That is a fatuous statement and completely inaccurate.
If the minister took the time to read the National Energy Program he would find that it says the Alsands project was at the heart of the National Energy Program and one of the main pillars of the program to provide energy self-sufficiency. Now that it is gone, the minister must rely on Hibernia, as he said. All Canadians know that there are technical and environmental problems in Hibernia. An example is the Ocean Ranger which tragically sank.
If the minister listened to the remarks of the member from St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) he would realize that there is an implacable dispute between the government of Newfoundland and the Government of Canada. The minister is now relying on Hibernia, but when will it come on? The minister
also referred to the Beaufort Sea. We have not had one barrel of oil from the Beaufort Sea, and there is some doubt as well about the formations there. There is no way at this time to get oil from the Beaufort Sea. There is no pipeline there nor any actively producing wells.
Where are the great facts that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources is so proud of putting before the House? The fact is that the NEP is collapsing, and I predict that the minister will collapse with it.
I want to quote from the November, 1981, budget papers. It states that the leading opportunities lie in the development of Canada's rich bounty of natural resources. It also states that major projects, according to a task force, amounted to $400 billion of potential projects, predominantly in the energy and resource sectors. Well, they have gone. What is happening is the collapse of the government's energy policy.
The minister makes a mockery of us having an emergency debate on behalf of the people of Canada here today. The minister referred to Monday, when I asked the House for an emergency debate and the Leader of the Opposition was good enough to listen, and also ask on Tuesday for that debate. I congratulate him for that.
The government says that there is not an emergency, yet if the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources will listen, they will find that the people of Canada feel that they have a government which does nothing but dither.
We see an edgy business community, a scared labour force in Canada, and now there is a government which is at a standoff with business, with labour, with the provinces and with both opposition parties. It is at a stand-off with all the people in the country whom we need to unite in order to make the country work.
All we hear from the Prime Minister is that co-operative federalism is dead. All this has the earmark of the policy of the Prime Minister himself. I say, as a western Canadian member of Parliament and as a New Democrat, that it is time for the Prime Minister to go for the sake of the country.
I will make some suggestions for a program to the Prime Minister. The Conference Board of Canada, in its quarterly provincial forecast which was released last night, shows that there is a decline in economic activity which began in mid-1981 and which is forecast to continue well into this year and represents the most severe setback experienced by the nation's economy in decades.
We know that we are in a recession, maybe even worse. The question is, can we do anything about it? The minister quoted the Earl of Derby saying that it is the opposition's duty to oppose and that is all. I disagree with that. I propose to make some concrete suggestions to the Prime Minister, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and their government. It seems to me that it is time for the nation to shift its direction decisively. Instead of waiting until November, we should have a new budget now. Instead of focusing on megaprojects which
May 5, 1982

are megadisasters, we need to focus on our manufacturing ability.
This is a country which has everything. However, what we do is export it all. I live in British Columbia and I see how we ship out our raw resources and how there is no manufacturing taking place. Our Canadian market, with 24 million consumers, is the key to our economic recovery. We do not have to blame, as the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan) did, everyone else in the world. We can deal with our own market here.
Last year Canada experienced a devastating record S21 billion deficit in trading and manufacturing goods. This has cost the country 200,000 jobs in production. For every one job you get in megaprojects, you get 40 jobs in manufacturing. That is the direction in which we should head.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources should get his facts straight. Alsands is no longer economically viable. The minister said that, the chairman of Shell said that, and we said that. Yet he accuses us of being hypocritical when we say the same thing. What we have said all along is that if we must have Alsands, and in the future we will perhaps need Alsands, but not now, we should not give a 20 per cent rate of return to Shell and Gulf, big multinational oil companies. We should look to Petro-Canada, our company, and we should look to the government of Alberta and its company, to develop Alsands jointly. That makes sense. We agree with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources that there is a glut on the world market. There are high interest rates, partly because of the making of his own government. So, Alsands is not to go ahead. We accept that, but let us have some alternatives. We can go to enhanced oil recovery, to heavy oil recovery and to coal gasification. We could put some of that $13.5 billion into conservation, and we could literally insulate everyone's house in this country, which would be equivalent to about five Alsands plants. So, there are alternatives.
The minister mentioned the National Energy Program. We support the thrust of the program to Canadianize. We support that kind of thrust. However, the Government of Canada, the Prime Minister, and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources have taken a program with a good thrust and they have mucked it up. This program has become unworkable. It has become bureaucratic and it is just not effective. There are alternatives. You do not Canadianize by giving one third of $6.5 billion to Dome Petroleum and one's friends up in the Beaufort Sea. What you do is to expand Petro-Canada by taking over one of the multinationals like Imperial. If you want 50 per cent Canadian ownership by 1990, that is what you should do. You do not have to get into a series of unworkable grants.
And it would cost less.

It would cost less. What do you do about energy taxes? The National Energy Program is supposed to help Canadian industry, but I have heard from my friends to the right and people in Alberta that the small Canadian oil
companies which the program is supposed to help are not being helped. I wish the Prime Minister would listen to this. They are hurting, they are not getting help. So, what we would do if we had any sense in this country would be to remove the PGRT, the IORT and the excise tax, but, in return, ensure that the provinces assign some of their provincial royalties to the federal government. They must share them. Then we will have one person to pay, one system of royalties. We would not have all the paperwork and bureaucracy and we would be able to help the small Canadian companies. Then we could go in and, instead of exporting our gas to the United States, we could gas bank it. We would pay the small gas companies and we would pro-ration it so they would have a chance like the big guys. The little companies would have a chance in Alberta.
I know these are all western ideas which do not ostensibly concern the Prime Minister. But these are concrete suggestions of things we could do to break this log jam. I challenge the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources to look on that.
I want to speak about the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources himself for a moment. He is in deep trouble, not so much concerning Alsands, although he is in trouble there, but, rather, concerning the Alaska pipeline, because the minister put his neck on the line concerning the pre-build of the pipeline. The story has not yet finished.
Just to recap, in 1977 the New Democratic Party, although criticized for our role in the pipeline matter by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), favoured the Alaska highway natural gas pipeline. However, we wanted job guarantees for Canadians, we wanted environmental protection, and protection of native land claims. Our caucus voted against the Northern Pipeline Act of 1978 because it did not include these guarantees, because it was flawed and because Tommy Douglas, our energy critic at the time, anticipated the problems that would arise on this pipeline if we accepted that act as it was.
In the 1980s, this government brought in the pre-build of the Alaska Highway gas pipeline. In the fall of 1979, when the present Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources was in opposition, he said:
In our view, exports of natural gas to the United States should be authorized only on the basis of, first of all, an ironclad commitment regarding the building of the whole Alaska gas pipeline. Everything has to be signed, sealed and delivered, particularly the financing guarantees, before we start exporting one cubic foot of gas out of this country to the United States.
What happened? The Conservative Party agreed to export the gas. The minister gave the speech that I quoted. Then the minister took office and completely reversed himself. He then agreed to export the gas without the ironclad guarantees being signed, sealed and delivered. That is the credibility of the man who last spoke, the credibility of the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. Those were his words and actions. What happened in 1982? There was the pre-build of the Alaska pipeline. We have built that length to take Alberta gas to California. In September, we will have finished the western length of the pre-build to take Canadian Alberta gas to the American mid-west, and the whole line will not be built. The project is classic.

May 5, 1982
I was in New York and called Washington last week and I obtained the American reaction. One Congressman said, "I would not put a nickel on any federal assistance to that pipeline. It will never go." The general feeling is that the total cost of $40 billion to $60 billion could never be privately financed. The government was misleading the Canadian people. It never could be privately financed. As if that were not bad enough, the government is continuing to mislead us. Mitchell Sharp, the pipeline commissioner, has threatened the American government. The minister has threatened the American government.
It is really scared.

The American government is really scared of that, because we have nothing left with which to bargain. We have pre-built the line and we are left with a line which is now taking Canadian gas to American markets. We have only one quarter of the number of jobs we would normally have, and we have no guarantee that the whole line will be built. As a matter of fact, Mr. Sharp, or a Canadian official on his behalf, went to the President of the United States within the last two weeks and asked for a reaffirmation of the guarantee, but did not get it. So, the government is misleading this House to state that it is still to come. This is a real shame. 1 remind the party to my right that it voted with the government. I believe the vote was 153 to 28 on that infamous day in July, 1980, when we warned the government and pleaded that if it went ahead it would have to stand alone on the pre-build and that it would sell out Canadian gas like it sold out the oil industry.
I think Canadians know, or should know, why we have problems with the Alsands today and why we need this oil, why we are prepared to do almost anything or to give any amount of money to get oil in Canada. The reason was that in the early 1970s we exported one half of our daily production to the United States. Can you imagine? We exported our oil to the United States. Now, because of the pre-build of the Alaska pipeline, we will export our gas. One is an idiot to make a mistake like that one time, but to repeat the same mistake one must be a fool.
You have to be a Liberal.

I weep for Canada.
Let me conclude by quoting the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) when he spoke during the pipeline debate of 1956. He stated:
What shall it profit Canada if we gain a pipeline, and lose a nation's soul?
What shall it profit the people of Canada, if we gain a thousand pipelines, and lose Parliament?
In this recent pipeline debate, what shall it profit Canada if we lose a pipeline and we lose our reputation and our soul? The minister is continuing to mislead us concerning the pipeline. He has stuck his neck out. He gambled with Canada's energy future. He failed, and he should resign.
As a westerner I want to say to the Prime Minister, because his party has called us the doom and gloom experts, that we love this country. This country has all the resources known to man. It has everything, the energy and the oil. There is another Saudi Arabia out there in heavy oil. We have everything. All we need is the will to do it. Once we have that, we need the confidence to say we can do it ourselves through Petro-Canada, directing it with the people behind it. Once we do that, we will have energy security and self-sufficiency in Canada. It is there; we can do it.
The hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) said in his speech that Canadians are ready for a new economic strategy. We do not want to be hewers of wood and drawers of water any more, the megaprojects' fools. We want a new strategy for the west where I come from, and for the east where the hon. member for Oshawa comes from, to stimulate our manufacturing industry. We know that is where the real jobs are in Canada. Canadians in both the west and the east understand that and will support it. They are ready for tough government action to do that.

Our options include natural gas, the use of which is being expanded throughout Canada. We have programs to encourage gas production in Alberta, to support natural gas development off the Nova Scotia coast. Oil-burning electrical generating plants in Atlantic Canada are being converted to coal. There is exploration for oil and natural gas in the Atlantic offshore and in the Beaufort Sea. Natural gas distribution systems in eastern Canada are being extended and we have a wide range of energy renewable projects.
If we use our ingenuity and if we plan carefully ahead, we as Canadians can achieve energy self-sufficiency in the 1980s. The suspension of the Alsands project is disappointing but the whole history of energy projects in Canada is one of project delays.
During the 1970s many projects were delayed, not only because of pressure by environmentalists and other public interest groups, but also because of the conflicting interests of the companies concerned and the conflicting interest of the different levels of government and different regional governments. Project delays can be expensive and may lead to missed opportunities. They may also result in better and more carefully planned projects.
These are difficult times. That is all the more reason to concentrate on finding appropriate solutions rather on the kind of unconstructive complaining we have heard in the last day.
The decision of private oil firms not to proceed with the Alsands project at this time is one of a number of similar decisions that have been made internationally. French El Aquitaine has postponed its plan to buy heavy crude from Venezuela and build an upgrading plant in France at a cost of over$l billion.
In the United States the Exxon Troupe liquid gasification project in Texas, estimated at $4 billion, has been deferred, and the Exxon colony shale oil project in Colorado which is estimated at $5 billion. In Mexico a $30 billion nuclear energy program has been delayed. These are examples of the current situation with world oil surpluses and soft prices and difficult financing problems. The positive side of all this is that some of the reasons that demand for oil has been reduced is because conservation has increased.
It has been estimated that even Saudi Arabia's oil supply capability is going to peak at something between nine and 15 years so that the western world will not be able to rely on oil from that traditional source indefinitely. We must be pleased that all nations of the world, including Canada, are reducing consumption.
However, in Canada among our many other possibilities we have a natural gas supply much larger than we had hoped for at this stage, and great promise of further increases. People in the industry consider that we now have so much natural gas supply that we can begin to see natural gas rather as we see coal, that is, as a non-renewable resource available in such quantity that it can be used without compromising our future.
Apart from the fact that we are so fortunate in having large reserves of gas and coal, we are also fortunate in having a welleducated, innovative scientific community. In the alternative energy field, the Government of Canada is involved in two major projects with the Quebec government, for instance. One is a $35 million large scale vertical axis wind tunnel, the so-called eggbeater which is being developed to fit into the Hydro-Quebec grid. The other is a $36 million project to construct an experimental nuclear fusion device in conjunction with two Montreal universities.
The delay in proceeding with the Alsands is disappointing, but it is not a disaster unless we make it so. Probably no other country on earth has the raw material that we have, together with a well-developed infrastructure and a highly educated hard-working and innovative population. We have the advantages and we must seize the opportunity to develop them.

Mr. Speaker, I regret I did not have the opportunity to speak while the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) was still in the Chamber, having just arrived by Challenger jet from Texas. Presumably he was asking the Texans to bring some of their money back to Canada or, more accurately, asking Canadians in Texas to come back to Canada.
The Minister's speech underlines the major problem with energy policy in Canada, and that is the minister himself. He simply cannot be trusted to keep his word, to honour government contracts, or to tell the truth.
Oh!

He said that the National Energy Program has resulted in an increase of crude oil reserves in Canada, and he offered oil rigs as proof.
On Thursday last, William Hopper, the Chairman of Petro-Canada, said before the Energy Committee in this building that those reserve additions were the result of the discoveries of Hibernia in 1979, a year before the National Energy Program came along. But that did not prevent the minister from standing up and claiming that under the National Energy Program reserves have increased. Under the National Energy Program, reserves have continued to decrease and decrease dramatically. He should consult his window on the industry, if he wants to know what is going on.
The minister quoted from some magazine he picked up in the airport in Texas, that we are doing so much better in Canada in terms of oil and gas exploration than they are in the United States. I would like to quote a few remarks from a research document prepared by the firm of F.H. Deacon Hodgson, Incorporated, investment counsellors. They made a comparison. They said, on data provided by the Petroleum Information Corporation of Denver, that here is how we have done:
Drilling activity in Canada down 25 per cent in 1981 over 1980, in contrast to an increase of 25 per cent for the same period in the United States. Well completions in Canada in 1981 were 7,183 compared to 9,481 in 1980, a 25 per cent drop. Exploratory drilling in Canada declined 19 per cent ... Development

May 5, 1982
drilling in Canada was down 28 per cent ... Since the introduction of the National Energy Program on October 28, 1980, 226 drilling rigs have left Canada. The number of active rigs in Canada has declined 33 per cent in 1981 over 1980. The number of seismic crews, a leading indicator of future exploration activity, also declined 25 percent in 1981 compared to 1980.
That is the comparison, Mr. Speaker, and that minister stands in the House and says, "Look how wonderful my National Energy Program is working because we are doing so much better than the United States." That, Mr. Speaker, is a minister whose words cannot be trusted.
In 1981 Canadian citizens and Canadian companies financed drilling of more wells outside Canada than inside Canada.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: That is a shame.

More wells were drilled in the rest of the world, mainly in the United States, than were drilled by Canadians in Canada in 1981. That was not the situation in 1980. What intervened? The National Energy Program, to Canadianize the industry.
What is Canadianization worth? Here is an article from a magazine, the "McAllen-Monitor", Texas:
Ed McGhee says the warning cry of "The Canadians are coming, the Canadians are coming!" is going up throughout the U.S. oil patches ... Canadian money and a lot drilled by Canadian rigs. "Coming they are-rigs, trucks, men, know-how, and money," McGhee said.
They are Canadians driven to Texas by that Minister of Energy who supposedly is doing it in order to Canadianize the oil and gas industry. That is what has been happening for this last year, and the minister has the audacity to stand up in this House and claim the opposite, when all this data and information are there and available. If he had stopped at Calgary on his way to Texas he could have found out first hand.
He says that he is really proud of how Canadianization is working. He had some figures about increased Canadian ownership. I wonder what would happen to some of those figures if he took out some of those companies who responded to his blandishments last year, and went ahead with the takeover-like Dome, like Sulpetro, like Turbo, like Drummond.
What is really the height of hypocrisy is that this is the same minister who, on January 25, was in Paris speaking to the Canada-France Chamber of Commerce saying that he would welcome French money for investment in energy projects in Canada. That was just on his way from Kuwait where he made the same plea to the Kuwaitis. What is wrong with a minister who prides himself on driving Canadians to Texas and then to make up for the loss goes to Kuwait and Paris, saying, "Please come, please come and invest in Canadian energy projects; we want you to come."
The minister then stood up and said that PIP-the Petroleum Incentive Program-which is supposed to give grants to Canadian-owned companies, is being held up by the Progressive Conservative party. Mr. Speaker, I wrote to him on December 21, 1981, several months ago, indicating that the PIPs program was the only part of this energy package that had some time urgency and that, if he would separate it from
the package, I would recommend to my caucus that we give it expeditious treatment. He wrote back and said, no. Now he stands up in the House and says that we are responsible for delaying this program.
Parliamentary rules prevent me from describing his statement accurately. The interesting thing about that program, one of the reasons we wanted to see it studied in committee, is that we wanted to have outside experts report on it. Well, we did have some outside experts report on it. The Canadian Bar Association has examined that legislation. In the opinion of the lawyer who presented the views of the Canadian Bar Association, that legislation is unconstitutional. It violates the Canadian Charter of Rights. So the entire foundation, what is left of that colossal mess called the National Energy Program, may well be in violation of the Canadian Charter of Rights. Isn't that interesting? What chaos is going to be left after that little exercise, Mr. Speaker?
I have at least 12 or 14 inches of file holders of letters from Canadian-owned companies talking about how the National Energy Program has destroyed them. I could not bring them all, but here is one. Badger's Drilling, which is 100 per cent Canadian owned, say that since the budget of October 28, 1980, the Canadian independent companies they have worked for have indicated they will complete their winter program and will spend anywhere from 40 to 80 per cent of their budget in the United States.
The Canadian companies have all moved their production to the United States. Mr. Speaker, up until last week the Minister of Energy was not worried about the effect this might have on self-sufficiency. He did not care, because we had an ace in the hole, we had tar sands, and the National Energy Program was going to spur contracts. It says so right here, on page 94: "The National Energy Program will spur oil sands development." Then it talks about the Alsands project and says that the positive impact of the program on oil sands development can be illustrated by its effect on the commercial viability of the Alsands project. It lists eight other projects which were going ahead because of this marvellous policy, every one of which is dead, dying or postponed indefinitely. As a result of this minister's energy policies, according to Statistics Canada, $18 billion of long-term capital departed Canada last year.
To finance that, plus our regular current account deficit, because of the disastrous shape of our economy we have to rely, basically, on short-term funds to the tune of $31 billion. That means this year we have to find an additional $5 billion or $6 billion for the interest on the money we had to borrow last year as a result of the disastrous consequences of the National Energy Program.
If Alsands had gone ahead, if Cold Lake had gone ahead, if Judy Creek had gone ahead, and if the heavy-oil upgrader had gone ahead, we could have counteracted that. Now I frankly do not know what we will do. If we believe Morton Shulman, the way to make money out of this is to short the Canadian dollar. Morton Shulman sees nothing but catastrophe in trying
May 5, 1982

to cope with this, and if we want to make money, we should short the Canadian dollar because Morton Shulman and every other investor in Canada has completely lost confidence in this government, and for good cause. This government cannot be trusted to keep its word.
Why did the Alsands project fail? In January of 1980 men and equipment were on site. They were constructing the work site. They were ready and anxious to go.
When it was re-elected the very first thing this government did, on April 3, 1980, was to invoke the force majeure clause in the Syncrude agreement, rescinding international prices for Syncrude. The very first thing the government did was break a contract. That caused Mr. Mensel, then the Alsands project chairman, to hold a press conference and to say to the government, "If you are going to do that to Syncrude, we in Alsands are not too interested in going ahead without something much stronger than you gave to Syncrude". Ultimately it took a year and a half to straighten that out. Did the government learn its lesson from trying to break a contract, and from what it did to the confidence of Alsands? Not at all.
By way of a letter-contract dated November 20, 1978 Great Canadian Oil Sands Limited wrote to the then minister of energy, mines and resources, Mr. Gillespie, outlining details of the contract, and the following is the relevant paragraph:
We understand that you will commence the process under the Petroleum Administration Act, as amended, to secure for GCOS the benefit of such international crude oil prices, commencing on the later of January 11, 1979, or the date on which the approval of the government of the province of Alberta is given in accordance with the law of Alberta.
Then the letter said if the minister agrees with this contract, he should sign the bottom of the letter. The signature of the Hon. Alastair Gillespie, the then Liberal minister of energy, mines and resources, is on this letter-contract. The signature is dated November 27, 1978.
Then the present minister brought forward the National Energy Program on October 28, 1980, and at page 29 the program document says:
Therefore, the production from the existing plant-
This is referring to the GCOS plant.
-will henceforth receive the conventional oil price.
A written contract with the Government of Canada is not worth the paper it is written on. That is the clear message. Never mind an oil statement, and never mind an election promise about keeping gasoline prices down. The government violated that promise. The government cannot be trusted to keep written contracts, and that is the problem.
Who in his right mind would make a risky investment in Canada with this government and the trained donkeys supporting it, when the record shows they will not honour written contracts? That is the dilemma. How can we restore credibility when people know their contracts will be torn up and when they know the government will invoke force majeure for phony reasons and introduce retroactive legislation like Bill C-48 to confiscate 25 per cent of the privately-owned assets of companies? When the government has that record, how can it restore confidence in order to bring some of that $18 billion of
Canadian money which left Canada last year back to Canada for investment in Canada to provide Canadian jobs for Canadian citizens who want to work and prosper and survive? How can the government get over that confidence factor? It must be obvious to everyone except the man who is now our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The government could get that confidence by demanding the resignations of those who tore up those contracts. If the Prime minister had the slightest concern for Canada as opposed to concern for the pride of his friends Marc and Allan, he would ask for their resignations right now. Nothing could do more in the short term to restore the confidence of Canadians in Canada. We are not even talking about foreign investors; we are talking only about the confidence of Canadians in their own country.
What a tragedy it is that Canadian citizens who live here, who send their children to Canadian schools, who have an attachment to this country and who feel pride in the marvellous geography of Canada lack such confidence in their government that they would rather drill in the United States, in Australia, in Indonesia, in the Philippines, in Vietnam or in China rather than in Canada. What a tragedy.
Unfortunately, these projects are dead. The window was wide open two years ago. People were so anxious to start on these projects that they had taken the risk of putting men and equipment on site to start construction, but they are dead. They are gone. We can weep for their loss. We can try to comfort those who are unemployed as a result of those projects not going ahead, but what we have to do is look at what we can do to replace those projects and to get this country working again. But it is almost hopeless to propose anything unless we deal with personalities. It is almost hopeless to talk about new policies, to talk about tax changes, or to talk about new budgets or new energy policies if they are going to come from the same people.
For the sake of Canada we have to start with a change in those two ministers, and I plead with the Prime Minister for once in his life to put Canada ahead of the Liberal Party and to put Canada ahead of the pride of his friends. I plead with the Prime Minister to put concern for the million and a half unemployed Canadians first and to get the resignations of those ministers, and then we can get on with the job of a new budget and new energy policies and putting this country back to work so that we can have the future of which we are capable.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, it seems that this afternoon we are having an emergency debate because the opposition has just realized that the Alsands project cannot be implemented right away. As the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) said, it took the opposition several days to realize that the project would not be

May 5, 1982
implemented, although the announcement was made last week. The fact remains that today we are having what seems to be an emergency debate and an important one, at the request of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark).
It is rather funny, Mr. Speaker, because after two years as a member of this House, I am beginning to understand what makes the official opposition tick. I cannot say the same for the New Democratic Party because you never know what they are thinking. There are perhaps 30 members representing that party, and probably as many attitudes, ideas, points of view or positions. I do not intend to dwell on their position, in this debate, since they have not really expressed their views very clearly, and the hon. members who did speak to this issue differed in the versions they gave.
As far as the official opposition is concerned, there is no mistaking what they think. For one thing, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Progressive Conservative Party has no idea what it is doing. And it had no idea what it was doing in the past either. Let me explain. Today, we have in the House a Leader of the Opposition with an opposition party that is astonished that the Alsands project is not going to be carried out. Going back a few months and a few years, who was in favor of a world price or at least 85 per cent of the world price, for oil and oil products? The Progressive Conservative Party. Who was telling Canadians oil prices would be raised to make Canadians learn to conserve oil? The Progressive Conservative Party. They took exactly the same position as the OPEC countries: we are going to raise oil prices so you will start conserving oil and our reserves will last longer, so we will be able to live on this resource for a long time. Thanks to their advice and their policies which were partially implemented, and thanks to the advice of the western oil producers, the premiers of the producing provinces and the leaders of the Arab countries, oil prices went up, and now that Canadians and Americans have learned to conserve oil, the Progressive Conservative Party finds to its surprise that because of this and because oil is more expensive as a result of their policies, we now have an oil glut, and prices did not go up as much as they expected. Consequently, it will no longer be necessary to extract expensive oil from the tar sands and in the near future new discoveries will give Canadians the oil they need. What a surprise! Mr. Speaker, it was their philosophy, their policies and their decision. Otherwise, I would like to know why Mr. Lougheed and his Conservative colleagues wanted higher prices for oil if it was not to make Canadians conserve it? Why? This is what the Arabs tried to teach us, but even more important, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people now understand something more essential.
In the seventies we always thought in Canada that while we imported oil from Arab countries, we also had some of our own and there would never be a shortage. A westerner, a former football player named Peter Lougheed, made us understand something, and with the help of his friends in this place, including the right hon. member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark),
he made it clear that Alberta oil did not belong entirely to the Canadian people. At a given time, he told us: "I shall cut back 60,000 barrels a day." A few weeks later, it was 120,000 barrels a day. I remember having discussed this with some of the opposition members and having told them: "This is a dangerous game that you are playing, because if the Canadian people realize that the resources of their own country do not necessarily belong to them and are not necessarily easily available, they will look to other resources from their own regions, such as wood, peat, coal or gas." However, some of the people with whom I discussed this in private told me: "Pierre, you are wrong; all we want is for our own people to have the money produced by their oil so that our regions may develop after experiencing problems for 50 years." The Canadian government has always understood this, and I understand it myself. Why do you think there is a Heritage Fund in Alberta? Because billions of dollars were put in this fund and no one objected. However, the point that I want to emphasize, Mr. Speaker, is that the Canadian people have understood that the oil in Alberta belongs to all Canadians as long as Mr. Lougheed or the Conservative Party in Alberta agree.
Mr. Lougheed showed them that when he wants that oil, it belongs to Alberta only. It does not belong to Canada. He can even prevent it from belonging to Alberta if he decides that the oil will remain in the ground. In that case, even the people from Edmonton will not have it. It is therefore surprising today to hear the party that developed such policies, and especially its leader, the right hon. member for Yellowhead, whom I accuse of being behind the Western Canada Concept. Mr. Speaker, this same man came to my constituency of Lac-Saint-Jean in 1980 to sign a petition sponsored at the height of the referendum campaign by the separatist party, the Parti Quebecois. The Leader of the Official Opposition came to my constituency to sign this petition and support Rene Levesque and his accomplices.
Let us look at the Western Canada Concept. What are the ideas supported and developed by this party in western Canada? First, there is the metric system. The western Canada Concept is opposed to the metric system. Mr. Speaker, for several months, I have seen members opposite rise in this House and criticize the metric system. When I was knee-high to a grasshopper and the greatest scientists were still young, everything was metric in chemistry. You should try, Mr. Speaker, to do chemistry with quarts and gallons. Everthing is done in millilitres and in litres. Chemistry has been based on the metric system for years. This did not happen because Gimaiel from Lac-Saint-Jean wanted it. This is how things are; it is an international phenomenon.
The Conservative Party of Ontario, the party of Mr. Bill Davis, has been teaching nothing but the metric system in schools for ten years. The sons and daughters of the people
May 5, 1982

who elected the Progressive Conservative members from Ontario to this place learn only the metric system at school because the Ontario premier and the Conservative provincial government so decided ten years ago. While the sons of these members are learning the metric system from Bill Davis, Joe Clark stands here and tells me that he is against that system. What is this? It is simply because people in western Canada like to say that the metric system comes from the French. In other words, the objection is somewhat racist. That is the problem. Yet, chemistry is international.
I shall mention another issue that is raised by the Western Canada Concept before dealing with the matter which concerns us directly. Bilingualism. Mr. Speaker, I have asked the library to prepare a list of the statements made by members of any party during the past two years against the legislation on bilingualism or against French. There are so many that I have been waiting for three weeks and they are still working at it. I will not say what party most of those statements come from. But I have heard people say: "You went too fast! The government went too fast when it put up bilingual signs in western national parks, etc. However, it must be kept in mind, Mr. Speaker, and my colleagues from the west have told me so, that most young English-speaking westerners today are attending French primary schools to become bilingual. Are we going to spend our lives trying to develop unilingual citizens with a single culture? We are lucky enough in Canada and in North America to enjoy two languages. This is another theme developed by the Conservative members. And when the Progressive Conservative leader comes to my constituency and signs a petition on behalf of the separatists, he does not say: "Let us speak English only". He says: "Let us speak French only." It is practically the same thing, but the other side of the coin. He is again, therefore, behind the Western Canada Concept that made it possible for an Alberta member to get elected to the legislature. Go tell that to Mr. Lougheed and his Alberta colleagues and let us talk about the energy agreement signed by Peter Lougheed and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources on behalf of the Canadian government.
That is a theme which has been used and abused by members of the official opposition. Why? Because they have no respect for anything. Nothing is sacred to them. But what is most incredible is that they dare come to us after all this time and say: "If the Alsands project has collapsed, it is because of the National Energy Policy". I can hardly believe it, Mr. Speaker. The party that has been fighting tooth and nail to make people understand that the Canadian price for oil should be 75 per cent and not 85 per cent of the world price is the Liberal Party of Canada. We have never been able to sell that principle. Even those who have fought against it are quite surprised now to realize that Canadians are buying less gas because gas is more expensive and therefore we need less.
Yet, there are some aberrations, and I often appeal to the good sense of my Conservative colleagues and urge them to please help their country. Mr. Speaker, please ask them to help our country. The party opposite has had great leaders. They were certainly not opportunists, they knew what a country meant, they would not sign petitions presented to them by separatists of the first order and they had something to give. I need not mention names, because the members opposite know them better than I do. But what is happening now in connection with their party, Mr. Speaker, is that even Tory members do not know who their leader really is. Even they do not know. Ask them. Maybe Mulroney can answer that question, maybe the hon. member for Yellowhead (Mr. Clark) can, I do not know. But one thing is sure: It is easy to understand how a party unable to fight with ideas would resort to all kinds of childish games to try to disrupt the business of the House. We have had point of orders, questions of privilege, the ringing of bells and now, an emergency debate. At least this procedure is legal. It is not on the borderline of legality or more or less out of order. It is according to the rules. But the fact remains that the political party which, more than any other, urged Canadians to reduce their oil consumption is now telling us, that an emergency debate is necessary because they have done that and we will need less oil in the future. It is most surprising. But that puts one in mind of their leader, who prances right and left, like a young calf cavorting around, tail up in the air, until you know what comes out. The politics we have been dished out of late by the Progressive Conservative Party in this country resembles that somehow.
Mr. Speaker, we must recognize that other men will come forward. I am sure of that. Premiers like those of Ontario, perhaps Alberta, will come forth, who knows, perhaps a fellow from Sept-iles, or a friend of my colleague the hon. member for Manicouagan, one of his very good friends, in fact, who may be interested in taking over the position now held by the hon. member for Yellowhead. They are free to do so, but as far as the well-being of Canada and our population are concerned, we need a serious opposition, one that comes here with the intention of being constructive.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources said a while ago that sarcasm and criticism are usually the order of the day, that there is no end to them, but that constructive proposals in the field of energy and others coming from the Progressive Conservative Party are something we will never see. Oh, no.
Once again, for I have done it several times already, instead of presenting such stupid, such backward, such self-serving motions, that are based on the latest news I appeal to the good common sense of my colleagues of the opposition. Every time something new comes up on television, we are sure to get a motion the next day. They come after the news because the policies of the parties of the opposition are conceived by the news media. After the reporter has spoken, then comes the

May 5, 1982
opposition with politics. This is how it always goes. I would urge the official opposition to be serious. Canadians need something more than parrots repeating what the media said the day before. They need statesmen to help them with worthwhile policies and structures for this country. In that context, I would refer to a sentence often heard from the Alberta premier: "We have no wish to sell all our oil today, as the Arab countries also say; we want to keep some for tomorrow so our children may also derive benefits. It is not enough to accumulate billions, to put them in the Heritage Fund and loan them at less than the going rate, because that money depreciates. Our children must have revenues down the road. Therefore, we will conserve oil."
I would urge opposition members to applaud at the decision taken by the Alsands companies not to proceed for the time being. This is exactly what they have decided. To postpone matters in order that our children may get the benefits. There is one thing we should not forget, Mr. Speaker. As I said, although it always pays to resort to regionalism and to a measure of racism, to oppose everything new by fighting the metric system, this leaves marks on people. When premier Lougheed decided to stop oil sales to Canadians, Canadians got a message they will never forget. That message is that what belongs to Peter Lougheed or the Alberta Conservatives does not necessarily belong to all Canadians. When a politician is not bright enough to realize that once he puts that message across, people will understand it for life, which means that such a politician is an opportunist and got where he is by accident, and probably will disappear by accident.
As far as 1 am concerned, as a member for the constituents of Lac-Saint-Jean, I have no objection whatsoever to the Alsands project proceeding later on, because I know we will still need energy. What is important to me is that people in my constituency have oil, energy. For now, they have them at a reasonable cost. This country has more reserves than ever. We have a Canadianization policy that has a tremendous impact. The simple reference to Petro-Canada having bought Petrofina is a matter of national pride in my constituency. We see Petro-Canada advertisements everywhere. We see everywhere the excellent service provided by Petro-Canada. We are proud that this country gave itself a structure not only to drill holes and to pump oil, but a structure based on the premise that every Canadian should have access to energy, both in the east and in the west.
Mr. Speaker, you are giving me an extra minute and I will use it to say how much I appreciate the way this energy policy was built on respect for everyone, on respect for the people of today and the people of tomorrow.
In the future, I would ask my colleagues of the opposition, when they want to blackmail Canadians, to use other means that cannot be turned some day against themselves or the people. Do not serve your leader's interests, but those of your constituents!
[DOT] (WOO)

Mr. Speaker, it is always interesting to hear the hon. member for Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Gimai'el). He has covered everything from soup to nuts. I am surprised that he has not given us the definition of a Liberal of today.
You got that the last time and you are still thinking about it.

There are still many Liberals in this country who are surprised at that definition. I do not think I can quote it as I cannot find the speech in Hansard. I remember that he ended by saying something to the effect "If Liberals have to move, to be socialists or communists, that is the way we will move." They will do anything to stay in power. The people of Canada are catching on and it will not be long until hon. members opposite are communists the way they are carrying on.
I do not think that anyone in Canada will ever forget Friday, April 30. It could easily become remembered as the 1982 counterpart to the "Black Friday" of 1929, when the economy collapsed in a state of confusion. This time, however, the blame can be laid squarely on the doorstep of the Liberal destroyers.
The destructive policies followed by this Liberal government have almost ruined the energy industry, the most vital sector of our economy. The National Energy Program will be seen as a blueprint for disaster that finally culminated in "Black Friday" 1982-the day that our energy sector was devastated-the day that 13 years of Liberal economic mismanagement culminated in the collapse of the Alsands megaproject.
We would be foolish to think that only Alsands died on April 30. We would be optimistic to think that this failure was even limited to the energy sector. The ramifications of last Friday will send a shock wave through the entire Canadian economy. It will directly, or indirectly, affect every family in Canada from coast to coast. What we have witnessed is a milestone on the path leading us from prosperity to poverty.
The death of Alsands hits us squarely below the belt. Investor confidence in Canada has now reached a new low. As a matter of fact Alsands failed partially because investors felt that they could no longer trust a government that invited them in as partners. The first effect of "Black Friday" could be seen as the value of the Canadian dollar dropped to mirror international opinion of this failure. But that was just one result.
In the weeks and months to come Canadians will be faced with the true extent of this total failure by the Liberal destroyers. They will see it in terms of lay-offs, in terms of bankruptcies, and in terms of ruined lives, lost pride and lost hope. But most of all Canadians will feel it as the ultimate blow-the final destruction-of their confidence in the Liberal government and its bankrupt economic policies.
For years now the Liberals have been hiding behind energy megaprojects. When questioned about their industrial strategy,
May 5, 1982

they would always say, "Well, we have the energy megaprojects. They will bring in much needed jobs and investment as well as more revenue for the government. They will provide us with energy security in the future."
The final curtain has dropped. On April 30 Canadians saw the naked truth. There is no industrial strategy. There is no pian to bring us out of our economic difficulties. The government has no plans, no ideas, no strategy, and apparently no real desire to address the problem. We are adrift, in a sea of economic mismanagement.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has fiddled and he has burned Canada. He fiddled in 1972, and a former finance minister, John Turner, played second fiddle, at a time when they should have been pressing ahead on the projects that would have left us energy self-sufficient today with projects like Alsands and Cold Lake. The Prime Minister also fiddled as he ineptly toyed with wage and price controls in 1975 and failed to address the underlying problems that caused inflation. He continued to fiddle, next with the Constitution, when all around him Canadians were crying out for an economic policy. This had to be the greatest fiddling job in the history of Canada.
Last week we were treated to another farce. The entire Liberal cabinet emerged from a weekend meeting at Meach Lake to announce to a concerned Canadian public that they were determined to continue on their ruinous economic course. They fully supported the November MacEachen budget, the most vilified economic document in two decades. Surely it was not that they believed in what the MacEachen budget was doing. It could not be. Already it has been roundly condemned by three cabinet ministers and many Liberal backbenchers. It was not a statement of favour, it was a statement of failure. They admitted that they had no ideas, no plans, no direction. And in doing so they left the Canadian people in a vacuum to fend for themselves as best they can.
I think W. A. Wilson put it very well in an article in last week's Calgary Herald under the title "Federal Brainstorming Meets With Failure." One sentence at the end sums it up where he said that the Chretien-Regan statement after Meach Lake really meant "Sorry, we do not know what to do next."
They are bankrupt. Then came "Black Friday", the final blow. It was the final statement by industry and business as to what they think of the government's economic plans, and they said very clearly what they think of the National Energy Program.
I think that the oil industry's point of view was best expressed by Mr. John Stoik of Gulf Canada. He said:
Over the years, the government has so strained its credibility with retroactive rule changes that those of us in the industry now must ask ourselves, "How can we undertake to make huge investments in long-term megaprojects when we have good reason to fear that the government will come along again and pull the rug on us?"
This lack of faith, however, is not confined only to the oil industry. In the April, 1982, edition of Executive Magazine Mr. Kenneth MacDonald wrote:
At a political meeting last January the sitting member, a Liberal, remarked, almost as an aside, on the abuse he gets from constituents. At times vitriolic, it was to him commonplace, part of the job. A few days later. Finance Minister MacEachen was given personal protection by the Parliamentary security service after two threats had been made upon his life. Prime Minister Trudeau himself had been the target of a man who was arrested after being found with the ingredients of a bomb.
He went on to say:
It would be easy to dismiss these incidents as extreme expressions of discontent with an unpopular government. Citizens who feel aggrieved by government actions have nowhere to turn but to their MPs. If their livelihoods were threatened by MacEachen's budgetary measures, some might be driven to threaten him in return. The Prime Minister's penchant for confrontation is hardly a calming infuence upon the unstable.
I have yet to be subjected to abuse, much less abuse of a vitriolic nature, by my constituents. But then again I have yet to support a government as incompetent and unfeeling as this one. It should not be part of an MP's job. It should not be part of our job to be subjected to threats and abuse. This is not a normal attitude, it is an act of extremely frustrated people. It is an indication of the lack of faith, the lack of hope, felt by the people of Canada.
It is a growing lack of hope that ultimately will result from the loss of the megaprojects. That is probably the most damaging aspect of their cancellation. Canadians have now discovered that the finance minister's policies are disastrous. He has constantly contended that when American interest rates come down, then Canadian rates will follow. Well, Mr. Speaker, American rates are coming down. The American inflation rate has dropped. For one month this year the U.S. actually experienced deflation. Why have we in Canada not experienced similar results from high interest rate policies? The answer is that the Americans have a plan.
The Americans support their monetary policy of tight money with a fiscal policy of government restraint. They are cutting back spending. They are deregulating. They are getting government off the backs of the people. President Reagan has reduced taxes and helped industry. In contrast, in Canada, we have high interest rates and huge increases in government spending.
Suddenly and with alarm, Canadians are realizing that we may not be pulled out of this recession by the Americans. There is every chance that we will soon find ourselves living at a standard markedly lower than that of our American counterparts. We are being forced to accept inflation. They are even now overcoming it. And it is rapidly becoming apparent that even the bankrupt Liberal strategy of waiting to ride the American coattail to recovery is not going to work. As this reality sinks in, it will become increasingly difficult to convince investors that they should invest in Canada. We need dramatic changes in policy, if this country is to recover. This government needs to make some tough decisions and to exhibit some leadership.
But ministers are not going to do this. Instead, their actions remind me of the sacking of Rome. The last few weeks have
80114 20

May 5, 1982
brought us unending tales of Liberal patronage and corruption. Example: we find out that Privy Council Clerk, Michael Pitfield, had his weekly first class airfare to Boston paid for by the people of Canada. The purpose of these trips was to ensure that Mr. Pitfield could moonlight at Harvard University. Example: last week, we learned that Mr. Arthur Erickson, a personal friend of the Prime Minister's, had been chosen as the architect for the new Canadian embassy in Washington. He was chosen by the cabinet-and this in spite of the fact that he did not make the short list, sent to the cabinet by a distinguished panel chosen by the government to sort through the applicants. Said the Prime Minister, "I pick my friends".
Shame!
A personal toady of the Prime Minister's.
Right. Example: Jack Horner-
Tory, Tory.
Who is he?

The Minister of Transport admitted that Mr. Horner will probably be rewarded with a seat on the board of Canadian National-and this for committing political suicide for the Liberals in the days before May, 1979.
Mr. Horner obliged the Prime Minister again in 1980 with a repeat performance of his remarkable kamikaze act. Rather than join Senator Stollery in the other place, the government has opted to offer the politically deceased Mr. Horner a position at CN.
1 wish I could stop there, Mr. Speaker, but I cannot. Another example: last week we found out that while the government has been urging restraint on Canadian workers, the Prime Minister's personal minions in the Prime Minister's Office, the Privy Council Office, and the Federal-Provincial Relations Office, were getting raises in excess of 20 per cent, considerably above the guidelines set down by the Minister of Finance of something under 14 per cent. A fine example for Canadian workers!
And, Mr. Speaker, we found out last week how the Prime Minister himself demonstrates personal restraint at home. We found out that the Prime Minister apparently does not pay for any of his food, or his liquor, or any of the expenses incurred at 24 Sussex Drive.
An incredible cheapskate. He does not even pay for a babysitter.

That is right. The Canadian taxpayer picks up the tab. As a result, inflation has no meaning to the Prime Minister. He is inflation and interest rate-insulated. It is just a pity we could not soak him in urea formaldehyde.
Mr. Speaker, all of these things, these scandals, add to the sense of distrust by the taxpayer. They have the feeling they are being cheated rather than governed. Businessmen have lost confidence in the government. There is a growing feeling that this nation is turning into a banana republic, governed by a
dictatorial junta rather than a modern industrial state governed by a responsible and sensitive parliament.
This Liberal wrecking crew has destroyed Canadian faith in honest government. Without this faith and trust, we cannot hope to lead the nation out of its current recession. The Liberal government has not provided leadership; it has squandered our heritage.
There is a joke circulating in the Canadian business community, and it is that if one wants to own a small business in Canada, you simply buy a large one and wait six months. This may be a joke, but it has a lot of truth in it. It is a strong indicator of the attitude among investors at this point. If nothing else, the demise of Alsands will foster a continuation of this attitude.
And Alsands is not an isolated example of Liberal failure. It is the culmination of 13 years of ad hoc policy. It is the ultimate proof that a nation cannot prosper through crisis management.
In 1968 Canada was third in the world in terms of per capita gross national product. Today we are thirteenth. Other countries are gaining, and we are definitely losing. Expensive and wasteful government is robbing the Canadian people of their standard of living. It has killed their initiative by taxing away incentive.
I would like to draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, how the cancellation of Alsands will affect the people of my constituency and how the National Energy Program and the failure to build the pipelines will affect the people across the country.
Our life's blood in my part of Canada is the forest industry, and it has been staggering through a period in which the collapse of the housing market has cut deeply into the lumber market. The Alsands project, as well as other megaprojects, would undoubtedly have stimulated some demand for lumber and plywood for construction purposes. As spin-off industries grew, the people who worked in these areas also would need new housing and wood products. Instead, the forest industry is on its knees in British Columbia. Unemployment has reached crisis proportions. In one community in my riding, the community of 100 Mile House, unemployment for the first three months of 1982 is up 121.9 per cent over what it was a year earlier. In my home town of Williams Lake unemployment is up 91 per cent over a year ago; and in Quesnel there are 78.1 per cent more people unemployed this year than in the first three months of 1981.
Over all in my riding, unemployment is now running at about 25 to 30 per cent. These three communities, like so many others in my riding, depend on lumber sales to keep them going. The megaprojects would have, indirectly, provided needed jobs. But instead families of the unemployed are losing their homes; dreams are being shattered. Men and women are experiencing first hand the frustration and humiliation of unemployment.
These people are losing their hope for the future. As the November budget was a stinging left jab for Canada, the death
May 5, 1982

of Alsands will go down as the punch that will bring this country to its knees.
You probably do not know this, but in my riding last year there was a company from Calgary searching for oil. They spent over $27 million test drilling for oil. They found some encouraging results, and are now assessing data. But they are not going to spend any more money in my riding, or probably anywhere else in Canada, until the economic climate improves. Why should they? So, there is a whole bunch more jobs that have gone down the drain in my riding.
And yet, Mr. Speaker, none of this had to be. The Liberal wrecking crew could have avoided it. This government's lack of policy and direction has put us where we are. It was government greed that killed Alsands. It is government greed that has robbed the people of Quesnel, of Williams Lake, of 100 Mile House, and all Canadians, of their jobs and their futures.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, in the last 14 years of Liberal mismanagement, we have seen a complete lack of commitment to the future. Several weeks ago in this House I gave a speech that compared this country's pitiful economic record with the superior performance of Japan. I urged the government to study Japanese economic strategy, their formula for success, and especially the importance they place upon research and development.
If our government had displayed a similar commitment, we would not now be debating the loss of projects that represented our only hope. If only our government could have learned from the Japanese example. Other countries certainly have.
I wonder if this government is aware of what is going on in France at the present time. That country cannot depend on energy megaprojects. Instead, it has placed paramount importance on science and technology. They are pumping billions of dollars into research, all the way from the cost of educating young scientists right up the ladder to the conversion of research into productive innovation. They are passing legislation right now, a law, to fix the government research budget to an increase of 17.8 per cent a year in real terms over the next three years. The only thing rising that fast in the Canadian context is the deficit.
Furthermore, this law redefines the role of the ministry of research and development, giving it four main tasks: First, to pursue research in every domain; second, to ensure discoveries are brought to application wherever possible; third, to spread knowledge; fourth, to educate and train people for research. The government of France recognizes how to tackle problems; it does not just sit on its hands and hope things will improve. It is a pity that the Liberals have not taken advantage of the last decade to build a country, brick by brick, rather than to destroy it, budget by budget.
We have a long way to go. Last Friday was another setback for Canadians. When the government is thrown out in the next election, we will have that much further to go to bring about
the economic recovery of Canada. The sooner the election, the faster we can get on with the work of rebuilding. The time has come for Conservative construction, rather than Liberal destruction.

speechtext: The only time they come alive or wake up is when an hon. member stands in the House and points out reality. It is a sad state of affairs.
Yell louder.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
I am required to yell because it takes a great deal to get through the thick skulls of hon. members opposite. I also remind my friends opposite that none of them have recognized publicly in the debate-and I know what many of them have recognized privately over the last week since the collapse of the Alsands project-that the Government of Canada and the government of Alberta played a role in assisting the development of the Alsands project. Those governments assisted private enterprise and private capital in developing that megaproject. There has been no mention today of the government of Alberta.
I do not want to commence my remarks by examining the situation from day one, or returning to the debates or negotiations on the National Energy Program and the agreement which was subsequently signed by the Government of Canada and the government of Alberta. I know what was the role of the government of Alberta, but I remind hon. members opposite who at least share party affiliation, if nothing else, with the government of Alberta, that two governments were involved. One of those two governments as I recall-and this is my private view-held up for ransom Alsands in the name of dotting every "i" and crossing every "t" which it wanted to cross and dot. That party held up the project for ransom, but there was no mention of it today.
I regret I am becoming somewhat emotional and that in order to be heard I must yell slightly. Instead we have heard references to military juntas by hon. members opposite to describe the Government of Canada. We have not witnessed a rational or reasoned approach. We have not heard any constructive comments or suggestions. We have seen a group of grown men behaving like children today. We have seen the built-in prejudice of a group of fellows supposedly participating in an emergency debate on energy. Frankly I found that rather disappointing.
Let me talk about the National Energy Program. Hon. members opposite will have noted that the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) indicated that self-sufficiency in the country increased to 80.9 per cent in the last two years and that domestic supplies of oil and gas increased in 1981. Also they will have noted that there have been several major finds of oil and gas in Canada in the last few years, not the least of which is the Hibernia field off the coast of Newfoundland. They will have noted that consumption of oil in Canada has decreased from 291,000 cubic metres to 261,000 cubic metres and that 170,000 Canadians have taken advantage of programs to switch off oil. Also they will have heard that over one million Canadians took advantage of programs to provide additional insulation. All these matters have resulted in reduced consumption and, in the final analysis, a lessened need to import expensive crude oil and to pay the difference, the oil compensation charge.
Those are the facts. I am disappointed, as I am sure every member of the House is disappointed, that Alsands is not going ahead. The rationale of hon. members opposite is that because the Alsands project is not going ahead, somehow the entire National Energy Program should be scrapped. Primarily because of a decision taken by those who control private capital in the country, the project is not going ahead and we should put an end to Petro-Canada. It is like saying that if one stubs one's toe, one should shoot one's foot. The government will not be bamboozled by such inane logic.
Let us look at hon. members opposite who have had no constructive comments or suggestions to make. Let us look at their record. They started out in 1978 by saying that the idea in the country was to get rid of all socialist politicians who thought up Petro-Canada. While they were contemplating moving the Canadian embassy to Jerusalem, they were contemplating selling off Petro-Canada at the same time. That is their policy. Let the future of Canada's energy needs be placed totally and irretrievably in the hands of the boards of directors of the multinational oil companies out of this country. That is their rhetoric.
I would like to believe differently but at times you really sound like a trained parrot, of those who would see the National Energy Program and Canadian-owned and controlled national oil company as a threat to your profit margins. Shame on you.
That is why you backed down. That is why you backed down from your so-called commitment to sell off Petro-Canada, because Canadians spoke with a voice and it was loud and clear, and it was angry and fed up with your rhetoric. We are fed up again today with that rhetoric.
I remember when the hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Crosbie) rose to talk about the budget two years ago. He referred back to his own budget which he introduced seven or eight months previously. I remember when he condemned the National Energy Program in his speech. He suggested that in some manner we could persuade-can you imagine that he believes Canadians are so naive-Canadians that their best interests and the best interests of Canadian oil and gas and energy reserves of this country could be decided upon and directed by the boards of directors of companies outside of this country. That was his argument.
What I find frightening is that the people of Canada in every Gallup poll have unequivocably expressed their support for that concept. Still today, two years later, we hear the same rhetoric.
You are still buying oil from Mexico. You let Canadians go unemployed.

Mr. Speaker, I will certainly permit a question from the hon. member if he will kindly have the patience to sit quietly for a moment. He can yell if he likes. I enjoy the applause. I will be glad to answer a question if there is time at the end.
The Hibernia find, with over a billion barrels of oil in proven reserves off Newfoundland, unquestionably now becomes more important than ever. Its development in a relatively quick period of time is now more important than ever. First and foremost, I say this as a proud Canadian but also as a proud Newfoundlander for my province, that jobs are badly needed in the industrial development and jobs are badly needed in the spin-off industry. I can assure you that the economy needs a shot in the arm.
That development is needed now. I say this as a Newfoundlander, but that development is badly needed by the people of Canada more than ever. I simply want to take this opportunity during this debate to say two things. There have been two elections in Newfoundland in the last couple of years. During the election in 1980, offshore was an issue and five Liberals out of seven were elected in that election. Offshore was an issue in that election. We had a recent provincial election and there is no denying that Premier Peckford was given a very strong mandate. A great number of Conservative members were elected.
Members opposite should listen and learn. Perhaps it could be described as a paradox, given that that issue was raised during these two most recent elections in Newfoundland. I suggest that it makes it very clear to all concerned that the people of Newfoundland view Hibernia as a very important resource for that province and as a key for its future development. That fact must be recognized by everyone in the House.
I also feel that if you look back to 1980, no one can deny that the people of Newfoundland also clearly recognize that that resource is important to the country as a whole.
I would simply say that we have had the elections and the battles. Now is not the time to continue the game of winners and losers. For the sake of Newfoundland and for the good of this country, it is time for both sides to sit down and negotiate an agreement. It is needed now. I would caution all those concerned to remember that political parties, whatever their stripe, are more than any one man. Political philosophies are more than any one man.
You would never know it.

I would caution Premier Peckford not to view what I am sure is a very gratifying election result as a blind trust to pursue this issue in a purely political fashion. on any particular matter would see any other approach than that.

Now more than ever, the potential lies off the shore of Newfoundland in Hibernia. Hibernia comes to the fore in this House of Commons and in this country. I plead that Premier Peckford and the Minister of Energy sit down to negotiate with good will.
