speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Now that the lights have gone out on both sides, I will recognize the hon. member for Regina East.
A debate over a bottle of scotch. Urgent debate, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity of entering into the debate and being able to make a contribution to a very important topic. This debate, of course, was touched off with the postponement of the Alaska highway pipeline and the collapse of the Alsands project. As hon. members who have spoken formerly have indicated, the opportunity that this debate presents is being used to discuss a whole range of topics. Indeed, the question in the debate does not only concern energy, but also the sense of direction and purpose before the country.
In the debate thus far, a great many partisan feelings have been expressed and, in some ways, rightly so. I think this reflects the sense of frustration and anger Canadians from coast to coast have felt at the total lack of purpose and sense of direction of this government over the last number of years.
First, let me deal with the Alaska highway pipeline. This party is the only party which voted against the proposed resolution which would have allowed the pre-build to be built. At that time, we stated that unless we got ironclad guarantees from the United States, the more expensive portion of the pipeline would not be built. Events have proven us and continue to prove us right. Unfortunately, what we are now witnessing is the sale of cheaper Canadian gas, cheaper because it is more accessible. This resource is being sold off even though in the long run we will have to purchase the more expensive gas from the more northern regions.
Canada has played an historic role in the selling off of our resources. It is stated that we need to sell off this gas in order to improve our balance of payments position. Again, that has been our historic role. We have sold off the resources in order to create a balance in our balance of payments. So, it is as though we dig a hole and then we must dig a deeper hole in order to fill up the former hole. Each time we get further and further into trouble as we sell off the assets of Canada. We have sold off major portions of our oil during the sixties and the early seventies. We are paying now for that mistake. We are selling off our cheaper gas, something for which we will pay in the future. The cancellation by the United States, or the postponement as it is optimistically called by some, of the Alaska highway pipeline will have a negative economic impact in my riding. A fair number of the steelworkers who work at the Ipsco plant reside in my riding of Regina East. The bread and butter of Ipsco is not the manufacturing of the multidiameter pipe, though it was expecting orders from the Alaska gas pipeline. As well, the National Energy Program has resulted in a lessening of drilling and exploration in western Canada and, as such, has reduced the demand for the casings and tubings needed for drilling wells which are the bread and
butter of Ipsco. I am afraid to report that Ipsco might very well be laying off people later this year as a result of the misguided policies of the government opposite.
The other area of concern in this debate is the Alsands. The cancellation of this megaproject could very well indeed bring some blessings in disguise. There are some serious problems with the proposal concerning the megaproject proposal, as it stood. Megaprojects bring about or can bring about megaproblems. This megaproject is one of tremendous economic and political risk, an investment of some $14 billion in a new, untried technology. If it does not work, it could be a spectacular failure which the country can ill afford. Indeed, we could be building a white elephant of tremendous magnitude. There are some feasible alternatives. For example, we could build smaller tar sands projects which, instead of producing 140,000 barrels a day, could produce some 14,000 or 15,000 barrels per day. The attractiveness of going to the smaller units is that they can be brought on stream much faster. The risk is spread from a production point of view. There would be a longer production run in terms of the parts manufacturing plants for the smaller tar sands projects. Therefore, the economic benefits could be spread over a wider area. In the end result, we could produce the same amount of oil, by building ten smaller tar sands projects instead of one huge megaproject.
The cancellation of the Alsands project could also mean some good news for Saskatchewan. It could mean that some of the money which was to be spent-
How could it be good news in Saskatchewan?

-in the Alsands project could be used for some of the heavy-oil upgraders. Hopefully, the government will now find that it is imperative to move faster to complete the plans for a heavy-oil upgrader in Saskatchewan. In fact, it makes more sense to invest more in heavy-oil upgraders than it would be to invest in the tar sands as the Alsands would have done. The technology for tar sands is a totally unproven and untried technology. While much of the technology for heavy oil would still be new and experimental, it would be closer to the known technology of the light-oil refining. We would run less of a risk. It would not be of the same magnitude as the Alsands. The economic benefits would be more widespread. I hope that the cancellation of this project will allow the capital to be used for some of the other energy programs, including a heavy-oil upgrading plant, hopefully near Regina and Moose Jaw.
Had we gone ahead with Alsands, and this is something the government never quite admitted publicly, Canada could have been committed to energy prices of $5 to $10 more per barrel than the world price. Everything considered, we can perhaps be thankful that project did not go ahead. It is important to emphasize, however, the point that we must achieve selfsufficiency in energy. We must begin to use our imagination a bit. Instead of pinning all our hopes on a few megaprojects, we
May 5, 1982

should begin to realize that alternatives exist. I have talked of the possibility of smaller tar sands projects and heavy-oil upgraders. I also wish to talk about the area of conservation.
Government members have proudly stated that the conservation program they introduced, and in all fairness when in power the Conservatives increased the allotment for the CHIP program, has had good success. I understand that over the past year Canada reduced its consumption of oil by 7 per cent, approximately the same amount Alsands would have been producing.
That saving occurred at less public expense than what Alsands would have cost. As well, conservation is inflation-proof. Had we gone ahead with Alsands, we would have been stuck with high oil costs in the years ahead. That in turn would have helped to fuel inflation. It would have created inflation.
While the conservation route is cheaper and creates more jobs, it is also inflation-proof. It reduces the cost of energy to average Canadians. Surely intelligence would indicate that is the direction this country should go. It is cheaper, produces more jobs and saves money for consumers. It reduces their cost of living instead of increasing their energy costs as Alsands surely would have resulted in.
One wonders as well at the economic and energy projections that government economists have been toying around with. In 1973 the then energy minister, Joe Greene, made the statement that we had enough oil for the next 400 years. In the fall of that year, he admitted that we were running out of oil. We then saw the price increase. Government economists and oil experts applauded the increase and projected price increases in a straight line over the next several decades.
That never made sense to me. It seemed to me that a curve had to occur. As the price of oil increased, people tried to conserve, and find other, cheaper energy forms. Increased oil costs dramatically fuel the fires of inflation, making goods and services more expensive. This has resulted in lost productivity and lost production, and therefore less use of oil and now we have a situation where there is an oil glut.
It seems as though this curve could have been predicted. Had it been predicted, we would not have ever thought of putting all our eggs into one basket such as Alsands. We have to realize there is a limit to how high energy prices can go.
I sat here late into last night and a good part of today anxious to hear what my Conservative friends to the right have as an alternative to the lack of government direction. Ever since having been elected, I have not heard an honest solution to the problem we face, from them. 1 anticipated that the philosophy of the Conservatives would be conservation and that this would be reflected in their proposals.
The whole notion of conserving is not where the Conservative Party is today. They talk even more than members opposite about the big megaprojects. They want more of them and they want them bigger. They want more public funds to go in that direction. They are even more dumb than those opposite.
What are they offering in this debate? They are suggesting more public funds should be given to the oil companies. Where
is the line? How much do we go for? When do we finally say enough is enough, it does not work, it does not make sense, it does not connect and does not add up. The philosophy of unbridled free enterprise, let the oil companies take care of it all and we will have energy self-sufficiency, is one of the major reasons why the Conservative Party was turfed out of office and not re-elected.
In the aftermath, they blamed us for chucking them out of office. We did not do that. The Canadian people did that and they did it for one major reason. They suspected the Conservative Party and their friends in the oil industry would sell them down the river. Their attempt to dismantle Petro-Canada made the Canadian people lose all faith which they may have had in the Conservative government. I find that unfortunate in many ways. A change of government was badly needed. We needed some fresh air. This is what the Canadian people felt, yet they said no when the government of that day was going to dismantle public participation in the oil sector.
The people of Canada do not trust the oil companies to look after the public interest. They recognize that the oil industry, like any private corporation, is there for its own good. Of course it is. The people of Canada began to realize that oil and energy is too important to leave it to private interests and that there was a need for a public involvement and presence in this area. I suggest that energy be considered like other utilities such as water, sewage, roads, telephones and be under public control. It should no longer be an area for private exploitation.
I am disappointed that I did not hear in any of the Conservative members' speeches the notion of conserving. I suggest if we are going to solve the economic and energy problems that this country and the whole world face, we have to begin to realize that we are at the end of an era, the end of a road. The era of unlimited consumption and production and huge megaprojects is over. We do not have the capital to feed the monster for ever and ever. We do not have the resources to go on for ever and ever, just splurging away. The days of unlimited consumption, surely, we must all begin to recognize, are over. We have to begin to conserve our human and capital and natural resources. We must learn how to make the best use of what we have. If we as a society and a civilization are to survive, if we are going to have enough energy for tomorrow, if we are going to have enough employment for all, if we are to have enough wealth in order to maintain a decent standard of income for all, we must begin to plan how to use our resources, our capital.
We must begin to plan not only for today, but for tomorrow. Had we been doing that in the 1960s and the 1970s as my predecessors-like Mr. Tommy Douglas, who was the energy critic for my party for many years had suggested back then, we would not have half the problem that we have today. Had we begun to conserve our resources and our energy and our oil back in the 1960s and 1970s, we would not be in the spot we are in today.

May 5, 1982
How long can we continue going forward and forward in this ever-consuming type of lifestyle? It is coming to an end, and all of us on all sides of the House surely must begin to recognize this and begin to look at some of the new realities that are facing us. Surely, projects like the Alsands are not the best way in which we can conserve and use our capital resources. Selling cheap gas in the United States now surely is not the best way in which we can conserve and husband our natural resources for the future.
We are creating problems again for tomorrow that inevitably we will have to face.
The style that the Liberal government has followed in the decades in which they have been in power, spending everything today and not worrying about tomorrow, saying we will face tomorrow when it comes, has come to an end; the chickens have come home to roost.
We are now beginning to face the results of those policies, of selling off our resources for today and forgetting about tomorrow. Well, tomorrow has finally arrived.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I have to inform the hon. gentleman that his allotted time has expired.
Mr. Speaker, may I-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: If there is unanimous consent, the honourable member may continue.
Agreed.
Mr. Speaker-
It is time to lay an egg. That is the speech.

I will not comment on the remarks of the members to the right. Their comments have indicated the difference in mentality and outlook between them and the government party is not all that much different. Their only suggestion is that they can sell off resources faster than the other ones can.
Mr. Speaker, unanimous consent was granted on this side of the House on the basis that the member's speech would be positive in nature.
Oh, oh!
It was positive.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Unanimous consent is not by negotiation. It is unanimous consent.
Mr. Speaker, in conclusion, I would like to say-
Say it, say it.
Or sit down.

The debate, is not only about energy, but as well our economy and employment. Again I would suggest that a wholly new attitude is needed, one that begins to realize that our resources are scarce, that capital is scarce, that human
resources are precious, that we must begin to conserve and to husband what we have, to plan for tomorrow and to stop blowing it today.

Mr. Speaker, it is just about 22 hours ago that the Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) rose to commence this debate. He raised the question for consideration of the House; where is 1990 with regard to self-sufficiency in petroleum energy, which the policies of the government led by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition would have given this country?
After 22 hours, Mr. Speaker, I think we can answer the question, where is 1990? It is down the drain, that is where 1990 is, down the drain with 71,000 direct jobs that would have been involved in the Alsands project. It is down the drain with 255,000 indirect jobs that would have been spread all across this country.
With these jobs would have gone money, Mr. Speaker, specifically $9 billion into the Alberta economy, constructing the Alsands plant, $10 billion into other parts of Canada, and in a total over the 30-year lifespan of the project the estimated benefits that would have been spinning around in the economy of Canada, a total of $415 billion. All that money is down the drain with 1990, and all of this at a time when industry all over Canada is facing unprecedented problems, most of them caused by the policies of the government opposite.
My colleague from Cariboo-Chilcotin alluded to the problems in the forest industry in British Columbia. The forest industry is not selling because people are not building houses, people are not expanding factories, the export sales are not there either, and in the first quarter of 1982 the giant MacMillan Bloedel Limited registered a loss of $10 million. I think that is the second time in history that that company has registered a quarterly loss.
In the mineral industry in British Columbia, 63 per cent is the reported rate of unemployment at this time.
In the face of all of these figures for job numbers and so on, last night we had the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola) telling the House that 1.2 million Canadians supported the National Energy Program. She gave some examples. Mr. Speaker, 1.2 million Canadians, that is 5 per cent of the population. I wonder why the Minister of State for Mines did not tell the House what the other 23 million Canadians thought of the National Energy Program. I imagine we could tell then what some of them think. The government is, I hope, hearing what some of them think on that.
The Minister of State for Mines could have told us about the ten million taxpayers whose total personal federal income tax, in the last year for which figures are available, 1978, went to cover the oil import conservation program. All Canadians? What about all the rest of the Canadians who are now paying 77 cents a gallon more at the gasoline pumps than they were
May 5, 1982

paying two years ago? That is what the Minister of State for Mines did not tell us, Mr. Speaker.
I want to refer to an article in this week's Maclean's magazine, where Suzanne Zwarum was writing about the demise of the megaprojects. She quoted the president of Alsands, Mr. Ed Czaja, explaining why the consortium was closing down. He said that the time for the project to move ahead had been lost. He cited increasing costs, rising interest rates, continuing inflation, reduced cash flows of oil companies and the downturn in world oil prices. Those are five very good and valid reasons for any project to be shut down, but I think we have to look at those five reasons and find out why each of them exists. I would not suggest Canada could do much about increased costs or even about the downturn in world oil prices, but those are only two reasons, and I suggest this project would not have failed if those two reasons had been the only ones. However, the other three reasons, rising interest rates, continuing inflation and reduced cash flows of oil companies, are directly the result of policies of the present government.
I will go through them one by one. When he was finance critic for the Liberal Party in 1979, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) campaigned and said he would resign if high interest rates continued under a Liberal government and he was in the cabinet.
Don't trust a Grit.

My colleague says, "Don't trust a Grit". That is true. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce did not resign, and the policies of the present government are directly responsible for the interest rates we are experiencing in Canada today. That was a No. 1 reason why the project was shut down.
Another reason cited by the consortium was continuing inflation. We have seen time and time again that continuing inflation is directly related to government spending, lack of revenues and the resulting deficits and the government's having to go into the money markets to borrow funds to make up for its continuing deficits.
The third major reason cited by the consortium is the reduced cash flows of oil companies. This again is a full-fledged result of the interventionist policies of the government opposite, and the massive subsidies which have been paid to bring foreign oil in to Canadian refiners to be consumed by Canadians, as if consumers were not taxpayers. The National Energy Program resulted in long overseas contracts at high world prices and, as we have heard many times, the result is that 300,000 barrels a day are being shut in in Canadian oil wells. It is no wonder oil companies are experiencing reduced cash flows.
The article to which I referred earlier went on to explain that three remaining sponsors had been considering and deciding the fate of the project. Of those three, Shell Canada and Gulf Canada had decided to pull out, the other private
sector partners already having decided to pull out of that project.
I think it is curious that all hon. members to my left seem to have disappeared. I suppose it is dinnertime in NDP-land right now.
They are always at the trough.

At the trough. The New Democratic Party made a big thing complaining that the Government of Canada and the government of Alberta had offered too much by way of incentives to coax the project's entrepreneurs. That demands an answer. If such a good deal was being offered to those companies, why did they not take up the offer? The deal obviously was not good enough, or the companies would have jumped at it and taken it up. I do not know what the NDP would like to do now. I suggest members of the NDP should go to their offices and hammer out little medals which would say to each of the oil companies which pulled out of the Alsands deal, "Thank you for not taking up the government's offer because you saved us a lot of money". However, that will not help us get oil, and we will be in serious trouble in relation to oil production.
I have spoken to many people about the failure of this project and many other economic problems we have right now. What bothers them, and me, is why a government would carry out policies which obviously have such disastrous results as those we have seen with respect to this project.
I can only think of one reason why any government would want to go ahead with policies which it knew would have disastrous results, and that reason is one I almost hesitate to state because it is so outlandish. However, I cannot think of another one. Perhaps the lone Liberal over there can rise when his turn comes and tell the House why the government carries on with these policies when they have such obvious disastrous results. The only reason I can think of is that the present government wants to create a situation in Canada from which the government will have to save the Canadian people. Ministers have created such a situation with their unnecessary and stupid policies. When these projects fail the government can say it gave the private sector a chance, the private sector truned it down and now we need that energy so the government will step in "in a Canadianization effort" and take over those projects.
The Liberal Party has always talked haughtily about Canadianization in the energy field and in whatever other field it can Canadianize. I do not know where the Liberal Party was in 1947 when only foreigners were willing to come in and explore for oil in Canada, but that is another debate and another story.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: We were in office.

I ask the lone Liberal sitting opposite what was wrong with the Canadianization that existed in Vancouver where the Merit Oil Company chain sold 50 million gallons of gasoline to Canadians every year. It was totally Canadian owned. What happened? Petro-Canada, the government agency, went in and bought it from private entrepreneurs who

May 5, 1982
were all Canadian. Petro-Canada bought many service stations with sales of $50 million.
State control is all they want.
My colleague says "state control". What other reason could there be for Canadianization of Canadian companies? That is ridiculous.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: They weren't forced to sell.

In the 1980 election campaign the Liberal party opposite told Canadians they would be able to pay less at the pumps under a Liberal government for their gasoline than they would under a Conservative government. 1 have driven all around Ottawa and Vancouver and in the areas surrounding those cities. I have seen many Petro-Canada stations, and they all sell gasoline for exactly the same price as Esso, Shell and all the other companies which are so bad for Canada.
More.
More.

My colleagues have seen Petro-Canada stations selling for more. The hon. member for Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) spoke about the naivete of Canadians. The Canadians in his area must be awfully naive because they sent him here to peddle the garbage he was peddling here half an hour ago. Perhaps "naivete" is not the correct expression to use for the residents of Newfoundland. They probably made a mistake in sending the hon. member here. However, in two years we will give them another chance. Perhaps it will be sooner, but they will have another chance to correct that mistake.
What about Canadianization and Canadian ownership? Canadians are now searching for oil in other countries, but the energy the Liberals are talking about is in Canada. It is under Canadian lands. What more secure form of ownership is there than to have the asset, whatever it be, lying under Canadian soil? The power to tax is with the government. The power to tax is supreme. Hon. members opposite talk about the riches lying under our own ground. The government totally controls the production and export of all petroleum products found in Canada. I do not know how much more Canadianization you can get. The power to tax is supreme. The government has created taxation policies which have driven the producers of these riches from Canada. It has forced them to go to the United States and elsewhere with their talent, their money and their equipment. My colleagues have referred to the number of drilling rigs leaving the country.
That is the way things appear to me at the moment. I wonder how they appear to people on the international scene.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: They admire us.

I think they are laughing. They would certainly be laughing if they could see the sole representative of the Liberal government who sits across the aisle.
In ten years there have been four Liberal finance ministers. The first was Mr. John Turner who was in the House when I first came. He quit because he could not stand being near the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who is still around. Then there was Donald Macdonald. He could not stick around so he went to Toronto. Then came the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) and he served for a time as minister of finance. Now we have the present Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen).
The taxing policies are in the hands of the Minister of Finance. Even when the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) has something to say, the Minister of Finance says it for him. Those four ministers have so fouled up the national energy policy over the last decade that nobody knows how we are going to survive and achieve the selfsufficiency we have been seeking. This has resulted in longterm contracts which means Canadians are now paying more than world prices for oil because of the subsidy. We are not able to go to the spot market and buy the cheap oil that is available there. Instead, we have to pay billions of dollars to foreign producers.
I have been trying to assess what people might think about our international reputation and whether they are laughing at the efforts of this feeble government. I should like to refer to an article which appeared in The Wall Street Journal of Monday, May 3, 1982. The article reads in part as follows:
Canada was counting on Alsands and the Alaska Highway Natural Gas Pipeline now delayed for two years and looking increasingly doubtful, to stimulate economic growth in this decade. The cancellation of Alsands throws "into question the Government's medium-term economic strategy which focused on megaprojects such as Alsands."
Then the article goes on in the next paragraph:
The Alsands failure will reduce business investment spending in Canada by $360 million this year and sets the stage for a steady loss of real output, employment and foreign investor confidence.
That is the opinion of William Empey, vice president and director of economics with Data Resources of Canada, and economic forecasting concern.
Mr. Empey says that the total investment spending loss will rise to $2.7 billion in 1985. Another aspect of the cancellation of these projects that has not been mentioned in this debate is the cost of close-up. The article deals with that question it says that after five years of planning, at a cost of $125 million, there will be additional winding-up cost of $30 million. That is a total of $155 million which is going down the drain. That project with its 137,000 barrels per day production represented 10 per cent of our current oil production.
As others have said, things would not be so bad if just the Alsands project were involved but we have also lost the Cold Lake project, the Judy Creek project and the Syncrude Expansion.
We are in a terrible mess, Mr. Speaker, and this government ought to dig out the policies that we presented in 1979. They
May 5, 1982

could find solutions there to help them out of their present predicament.
Elear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, this is a very interesting debate. I suppose all debates bottom out sooner or later but it seems more than a coincidence that the debates that I have observed usually reach their lowest level when the hon. member for Humber-Port-au-Port-St. Barbe (Mr. Tobin) speaks. From that point, it must be upward all the way. That particular member complained bitterly about the lack of strength in the Conservative Party. I notice that at the present time there is one faithful member of the Liberal Party in the House. 1 also notice that the hon. member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), who attended so faithfully last night that he claimed he was a permanent fixture, is not here. He did step behind the curtain occasionally which meant that at times, there was no Liberal in the House. But the hon. member for Beauharnois-Salaberry (Mr. Laniel) was here and he attends faithfully.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: I am from Don Valley East.

That is correct, and you are a graduate of Victoria High School. That is all that makes the member acceptable on this side of the House.
There was a very peculiar start to this debate yesterday. The fact that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) was away seemed to throw the Liberal Party into a spin as nobody else seemed to know anything about the subject of the motion.
Then there was the rather peculiar speech given by the Minister of State for Mines (Mrs. Erola), that amiable chatterbox from Sudbury. She seemed to think that the high point of the National Energy Program was the CHIP program. This is like the president of Cunard boasting about the Titanic because it would stop faster in mid-Atlantic than any other ship. She seems to believe that the CHIP program is something that the Liberals should boast about.
For those who are not aware, that is the Canadian Home Insulation Program through which the government subsidizes a type of insulation called urea formaldehyde that has since had to be removed from houses at fantastic cost. The government refuses to pay for this.
The minister may think that this is the best part of the National Energy Program but 1 hope that there are other parts that are better than the CHIP program. I do not have time to correct her ignorance at this stage.
Last night the Minister of Supply and Services, (Mr. Blais) supplied his usual comic touch. As often happens when the Liberals have a poor case-and that is frequently-then a personal attack is made on the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). 1 have been here long enough to see that happen to the Right Hon. John Diefenbaker, the Hon. Bob Stanfield and to the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition. It is too bad that this happens as it does not help the debate.
It is also interesting to watch the NDP scrambled desperately to get away from the Liberals in this debate, particularly those members from Saskatchewan and Newfoundland who have just been through provincial elections. I listened with what was almost glee to the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) give a rather frantic speech today implying that, for heaven's sake, he did not want ever to be thought to support the Liberals!
Many of the motions that the New Democratic Party proposes are not acceptable to the Liberals and consequently they deliberately load them so that no one who believes in free enterprise could possibly support them. Then they are proud because they vote on the opposite side to the Liberals.
There is a longer history to voting than they would like to acknowledge. Those who participated in the Saskatchewan election ran into this at almost every door. They are so upset about the terrible incompetence of this Liberal government that they say to each other: "How did we ever get such a government in this civilized country? How did we pick this bunch of incompetents to run the country? What were our NDP members from Saskatchewan doing?" Well, they remember very well what the NDP did. In the 1972 election there were some 20 or so NDP here, enough to have the balance of power in a minority Liberal government. The House met on January 4, 1973, and during the succeeding 18 months there were 19 votes of confidence. On each and every one the NDP supported the Liberal Party.
What happened in 1974? The Liberals found they were high enough in the polls that they no longer wished to avoid an election, they brought in a budget which even the NDP could not support, went to the people and of course came back with a majority government. The NDP had been used for the dupes they are and consequently we inherited a Liberal majority government.
Is that dupes or dopes?

I suppose the words are interchangeable. The "Simple Simons" of politics is the best way to describe them. They come around when they are needed by the Liberals, and the rest of the time the Liberals give them the back of the hand, which is what they get these days.
In 1979 we came back to Ottawa with a minority Conservative government. How the story had changed. We did not get 19 votes of confidence, having won the election; we did not get one vote of confidence out of them. We won the first vote of confidence by only two votes, and the NDP voted against us. It was on a supply motion, I believe. Interestingly enough, it was on an amendment by the right hon. gentleman who is now the Prime Minister. I like to look back at these things because 1 find them rather ironic, perhaps even amusing. Most of the NDP I have spoken to about this have no idea what it was they were voting for, but it was against the Conservatives and for the Liberals. The motion was:
That this House has no confidence in the government-

May 5, 1982
Why do you suppose they had no confidence in the government? First, because:
-it will cause severe economic hardship for the Canadian people this winter: first, through its neglect of the grave possibility of shortages in heating fuel; second, through its failure to support existing intergovernmental agreements on oil pricing and supply;
Imagine that coming from the leader of the then opposition. It goes on:
-third, through its inability to conclude agreements preventing immoderate price increases in the future;
Can you imagine that coming from that group? It goes on:
-and, fourth, through its acceptance of record high interest rates.
I find that one particularly ironic and sad. They wanted to vote the government out because they were worried about its failure through its acceptance of record high interest rates. That was the motion that the NDP supported the Liberals on, to get rid of the Conservative government. They did not know what record high interest rates were until they got the Liberals back in.
When you knock on doors in Saskatchewan, Mr. Speaker, the message you get is that they are very, very upset with the NDP for having allowed the Liberals to have and win an election. They are mad at the NDP Members of Parliament, and their provincial brethren went down like tenpins during the recent election, this despite the fact that the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville, (Mr. Nystrom), during the constitution debate split the NDP to avoid being lumped in with the Liberals. We are going to see a lot more of this phoney hyperbole from the NDP as they try to dissociate themselves from the Liberal Party even more, because anyone who is a friend of the Liberals these days is not going to get too many votes in the next federal election.
The NDP want Canadianization of everything. That was a word which was not heard until about two or three years ago, and I expect the flack who thought it up will be richly rewarded by the Liberal government; if not now, at some other time. The hon. member is leaving us without a Liberal in the House.
Not one Liberal in the House.

Thank you for your return, sir. We are glad to have you back. I think the Liberals started this debate hoping it would go away because they really had nothing to contribute. When they saw it was not going to go away last night, then they decided they must participate. During some of today's speeches, frankly, I think they would have been better off to stick with the first decision.
I would like to speak for a moment about what the Liberals and NDP have in common. The common ground is Canadianization, which is a Liberal word for nationalization, which in turn is an NDP word for socialization of the means of production.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: We are free enterprisers.
The only free enterprise they may have is in their caucus as they battle for the spoils to which they think they are entitled.
Three minutes a week.

I would like to point out something which happens when government gets into business, including Crown corporations. There is a rather nice example in Question 3893 which was put on the Order Paper by my colleague, and it was answered on April 1. It has to do with a subject which is close to both my colleague and myself, having to do with the Argus aircraft which were scrapped. This is a small example of how you should never conduct business, yet I daresay no one is going to suffer for this because nobody will ever be considered to be the culprit.
Some five years ago the Department of National Defence hired IMP of Halifax to determine how long the fleet of 24 aircraft could remain in service. The study, done at government expense, showed that five years was about how long they could stay in the air and still be sold as flyable aircraft. They then decided they would sell the planes and put out a tender to have the fleet disposed of. They made some effort to sell the aircraft and were unsuccessful. At nearly the same time they put out a tender to mothball the fleet, so it would be ready for some other purpose, I suppose.
The amount spent on mothballing the fleet was $349,298.87 so it would be preserved for future sale as flyable aircraft, I have to presume. In any event, I have not heard of people mothballing junk. At that time, just to add to the ridiculous situation they were in, an aircraft museum in Calgary wanted to buy one of the aircraft and it offered $60,000. They turned the museum down because they were afraid it was going to sell it to some other country as a war plane. The next thing we hear is that they sold the whole lot for $70,000. Not only did they sell them at less than $3,000 each, but they turned down the guy who was going to pay them $60,000 for one aircraft.
Liberal business practice.

Then the junk company came in and cut the aircraft up-after $349,000 worth of mothballing. This should not happen. Somebody in an ordinary business place would no doubt move on and look for some other business place at a lower level. Nobody, I suspect, will ever find out who really took the decision, not only to sell them as junk, but also to mothball them at the same time and go through both options.
That is what happens when you get nationalization and Canadianization. We get decisions like that.
I notice that the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) is very fond of blaming the United States and President Reagan for the failure of the Alaska gas pipeline project. I can never quite understand how the minister can
May 5, 1982

stand up in the House and pretend that he had a firm commitment from the Government of the United States that the gas trunk line would be built to Alaska. This is of course when he wanted the pre-build portion.
Let us have a look at the great words which the minister used. I hope they will haunt him to his grave. He was in opposition at the time. We can find his words, as reported in Hansard at page 2101 on December 6, 1979. I will just read a paragraph because it contains the minister's most famous comment. 1 suppose when they write down popular Canadian quotations forty years or one thousand years from now they should include Marc Lalonde and this following quotation:
So far as the statement of the minister is concerned, we note the vagueness of the statement about the building and completion of the pipeline which is essential. It leaves open the door to delays in the pipeline construction by extending the authorization of exports over a period of seven years and the possibility of reviewing the authorization after exports have started, therefore authorizing exports before the commitment for the building of the line has been made.
There is no word in this statement regarding swaps, and nothing about the eastern Canadian situation, the building of the Quebec and maritime pipeline-
Where have you heard about that lately? We used to hear quite a bit about it but not too much any more.
It is a paper pipeline.

It is too small at one end, I am told. The minister's statement continues:
-and the possibility of exports to the northeastern states. In our view, exports of natural gas to the United States should be authorized only on the basis of, first of all, an ironclad commitment regarding the building of the whole Alaska gas pipeline. Everything has to be signed, sealed and delivered, particularly the financing plan and the financing guarantees, before we start exporting one cubic foot of gas out of this country to the United States.
I am sure my metric friends will be pleased that we were dealing with gas in cubic feet at that time. That appeared to be a pretty firm position, I would say, from an ironclad minister. All that went by the boards last Friday. There is no commitment. He is now blaming President Reagan.
President Reagan was here in this Chamber on March 11, 1981. In his remarks he said:
I am happy to say that in the recent past we have made progress on matters of great mutual importance. Our governments have already discussed one of the largest joint private projects ever undertaken by two nations-the pipeline to bring Alaskan gas to the continental United States. We strongly favour prompt completion of this project based on private financing.
Hear, hear!

speechtext:
We have agreed to an historic liberalization of our trade in the Tokyo Round of the multilateral trade negotiations.
That was all the president had to say. They took it very clearly that it would depend on private investment. They took it to mean some kind of government commitment. What kind of dummies have we running this country that not only would they make a mess of the deal but they would also try to blame the other guy for doing it?
1 would like to talk about the effect on the provinces of some of these failures to carry out business in the normal fashion and to get any project operating. I took this up with the minister at the time he brought in the excise tax on natural
gas. I pointed out in a question to the minister that the National Energy Program, which was announced as part of the federal budget, is really a grab for money by the federal government and takes money away from provincial revenues. This rather upset the minister because he did not like to have that pointed out. What he said was kind of foolish. He said, as the hon. member knows, that there are many more consumers of natural gas in Ontario than there are in British Columbia. Those consumers pay the same federal tax the people in British Columbia are paying.
I was talking-and he knew I was-about the sale that British Columbia makes to Washington State of natural gas. They could no longer compete with energy in Washington State because of the amount of the excise tax which the federal government had imposed.
Let us have a look at the National Energy Program of 1980. I believe it was brought in as a budget at the time. Let us see what it promised for western Canada. On page 77 of the document we find:
The National Energy Program is beneficial to the West.
Can people from the west, including those from Alberta, believe this statement that the National Energy Program is beneficial to the west? The paragraph continues:
It provides an oil pricing schedule that yields substantial and growing revenues to provincial governments and the industry from existing production, and establishes certain and attractive prices for the risky and costly sources that will form the basis for a sustained prosperity. The oil sands and heavy oils will make a major and enduring contribution to the economy of the west, while enhancing national energy security.
It is hard to believe anybody could possibly have said this is a year and a half ago. On page 78 of the National Energy Program document we find the following:
With initiatives in the program such as financial support for the Vancouver Island gas pipeline, the province can move rapidly to reduce its oil dependence, using its own energy sources.
I do not want people from the maritimes to think they are the only people waiting for a pipeline. We were promised one too, and we are just about as far along as maritimers are in terms of having one, which is nowhere.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order, please. 1 regret to interrupt the hon. member, but I must advise him that his time has expired. Nevertheless, he may continue with the unanimous consent of the House. Is there unanimous consent?
Agreed.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleagues and the sole survivor on the Liberal Party benches.
He is the fellow who put out the big charts concerning Parliament.

Mr. Speaker, I will conclude by making just a few more remarks. I want to quote from the papers on the budget of November 12, 1981. On page 55 of the booklet entitled "The Budget in More Detail", we find:

May 5, 1982
The pricing and taxation structure will provide significant stimulus for new tar sands projects.
I hope someone around here lives long enough to see some sign of the significant stimuli that are promised for new tar sands projects. One hardly knows what to make of it or what to recommend to the Canadian people. I am forced to agree with many of the remarks that have been made today. The problem is that two or three of the people at the top have the affairs of this country in an iron grip. 1 realize we live in a democratic country, but it suffers under some severe strains with the voting system we have at the present time. I believe in representation by population. 1 also agree with the second Prime Minister of Canada, Alexander Mackenzie, who said, "The worst possible thing that could happen in Canada would be if we started voting along racial lines and racial lines only in Canada". 1 am sure he was thinking that people could be elected to this House for the wrong reasons.
I might close by bringing something to the attention of hon. members. It does not have to do with racial backgrounds but with the intellectual. In 1935 Mr. Harold A. Innis said:
Intellectuals in large numbers will sink the raft of any party, and if allowed to write a program will kill it.
I am afraid that is what has happened here. We have a lack of practical men on the other side. We have some pseudo-intellectuals. They all think they are intellectuals. But as pseudointellectuals they are unable to be practical enough to bring forward a program from which anyone can expect reasonable results.
Mr. Speaker-
Tell the truth, now.

1 am told by the member opposite to tell the truth. As he well knows we always do that. I will do my best to accommodate him. We are pleased he is here to hear the debate tonight.
Before I begin, I want to mention the fact that we have been debating the Alsands matter for 23 hours now, and many of the House of Commons staff have been here since yesterday morning at eight o'clock or nine o'clock. They have put in two very long days. I am thinking particularly of the Hansard staff, who have gone without sleep for over 24 hours. I know all members really appreciate their hard work.
Hear, hear!

Whenever I think of people listening, I am reminded that my uncle, not very long ago, had some open heart surgery and ended up spending quite a bit of time at home. He spent much of his time listening to the debates in the House of Commons. When we think of that and we know there is someone out there listening, we tend to become very conscious of where we are speaking and of what we are saying. Unfortunately, very often we tend to sit in these hallowed halls and get caught up in little buzzwords and words that have significance to us here but not to the people across the country. To those people they do not have much significance.
I am thinking in particular of one of the expressions that possibly is key to this debate tonight, that is, this whole idea of economic development. That expression has become a favourite buzzword of the government. In fact, the budget of 1981 said that national economic renewal is the overriding priority of the Government of Canada and that the policies and programs of the national government represent major instruments for managing and exploiting development opportunities.
In that statement the federal ministry claimed to be devoted to economic development. The question that remains then, is: where is this economic development?
Was it really nothing more than just a buzzword in the Liberal caucus, another buzzword around Parliament Hill?
We begin to wonder when we see how busy the government has been robbing us through energy taxes rather than taking any form of real action. The government has been too busy writing about economic development to make economic development a reality. We have been suffering from a little bit of what I think could be called "analysis paralysis". We have been getting a lot of pretty paper, pretty wrapping and pretty packages. But what the government is really wrapping up is a disastrous energy policy and a disastrous budget. The real economic development we should be experiencing, which would have come through the development of major projects such as Alsands, the Alaska pipeline and Cold Lake, is further away today than ever before. Those projects are today further away from completion, or even beginning, than they ever have been before. Today, they are effectively dead.
But they have not just died. They have actually been killed. They have been killed by mismanagement by this government; they have been killed by the National Energy Program; they have been killed by the 1981 budget; they have been killed by the greed that has been demonstrated by the massive tax grabs this government has made on our energy revenues by closing what it calls loopholes, which are the very same policies that it put in place a few years ago. Those projects are dead today, and with them are a lot of dreams and a lot of hopes.
A news story-and I just refer to a short article in a paper in Fort McMurray which, as we all know, is the heart of this province-said this: "Those who will be hurt are property developers and small local construction contractors.
We tend to talk in terms of big numbers, but we forget, in fact, that what we are really talking about is jobs. One job, two jobs-we can multiply that several times, of course; but, in fact, it is individual people and individual businesses to whom we really should be addressing ourselves.
Where are we now without Alsands? Where does that leave us? First of all-and I think probably the most important thing-Canada is today further away from self-sufficiency than it has ever been in the past. Second, Canada will not enjoy the economic benefits that would have been the spin-offs from this project. Those benefits, those spin-offs, will no longer be enjoyed by Canadians. The National Energy Program has said that Canada has a diversified energy resource base to
May 5, 1982

support a relatively quick and clean shift away from world oil prices.
This government promised to make Canada energy selfsufficient by 1990. It promised to free us from the bonds of OPEC. But, Mr. Speaker, one of the cornerstones of those promises, of that freedom, was Alsands, because Alsands was going to provide for us somewhere around 157,000 barrels of oil per day. It would have slashed imported oil into this country by around 20 per cent. Now, because of the loss of this project, we will have to import into this country about 300,000 barrels a day in 1990. We cannot expect much slack to be picked up by our conventional sources of oil, our oil other than tar sands oil, simply because that source of energy has also been discouraged by the federal government's policies. And so we are left in the position of not being able to reduce those imports. In fact, we are left today with a much clearer indication that that is going to continue well into the 1990s.
Each barrel of imported oil brought into this country means higher taxes for individual Canadians-taxes that already are too high for so many Canadians. We know that, and we know that we have had 15 increases in petroleum prices since this government has been returned to power with the help of the NDP. We know that federal taxes are responsible for roughly 75 per cent of the energy cost increases in 1981. We have places in the United States today where gasoline is cheaper than it is in Canada, and yet in the United States they moved to world price. We are nowhere near world price today, and yet our prices are already higher than theirs. What is the difference?
